stories.Headline: Your phone knows you're at the doctor, and data brokers do, too — then profit from it
stories.Summary:
Chris McQueen finished leukemia treatment a year and a half ago, yet ads for fake cures have never stopped appearing on his mobile phone. The ads, including juice cleanses to cure cancer and clinics in Mexico promising full recovery with little chemotherapy, showed up during routine oncologist visits and monthly bloodwork. McQueen and others have taken to social media to complain about data brokers, which track their whereabouts through smartphone location data. The brokers connect that location data with other information gathered about each person and then draw inferences about their health struggles. Those inferences are sold to companies hawking unproven treatments, according to a KFF Health News report by Michael Scaturro published on November 13, 2026.

Location data emitted from a phone in a hospital, an abortion clinic, or an Alcoholics Anonymous meeting in a church basement is not covered by the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, known as HIPAA. California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, vetoed a bill on Sept. 27 that would have blocked the sale and sharing of location and other sensitive personal data. A recent Stanford University study found that only 9% of data brokers are following an existing California privacy law that lets consumers delete their data, correct it, and learn what records are being sold. In January, Consumer Reports released model legislation giving state lawmakers a framework to ban or limit the sale of geolocation data, which uses GPS to identify a person's movements in real time. Connecticut, Delaware, Maryland, New Jersey, Oregon, and Virginia have already banned the sale of precise geolocation data, and at least 20 states let residents demand that data brokers delete their personal data.

In May, the Federal Trade Commission placed limits on Idaho-based data broker Kochava, which the agency began investigating in 2022. The settlement prohibits Kochava and a subsidiary from selling, sharing or disclosing sensitive location data without consumer consent, following allegations that the companies sold location data from hundreds of millions of mobile devices. That data could be used to trace people's movements when they visited hospitals, churches, abortion clinics, and other sensitive locations. Kochava did not respond to requests for comment on the case. In August, the Federal Trade Commission also warned retailers about using private consumer data to increase prices, and Newsom said the vetoed California bill went "a step too far."

Jim Potter, executive director of 4As Health, a subsidiary of the American Association of Advertising Agencies, said a national privacy law should protect consumers from harmful or unexpected uses of data without preventing businesses from providing requested services. Advertising trade groups say targeted advertising saves consumers time, lowers the cost of searching for products, and lets websites and apps offer services without paywalls or subscriptions. Eric Ellsworth, director of health policy and innovation at the Center for the Study of Services, said data brokers typically hoover up data from the open web and buy it from anybody. Privacy advocates welcomed the government actions but noted that settlements are not laws or regulations, so their terms do not bind other companies. Julien Cavanagh, a neurologist in Atlanta, now asks patients with unexplained neurological symptoms whether they take supplements bought online, warning that sham treatments can be toxic, cause deficiencies, or counteract prescribed medications.

More than 92% of patients in a 2022 American Medical Association survey said their health data should not be available for purchase. The San Diego-based Privacy Rights Clearinghouse and the Electronic Frontier Foundation identified 750 data brokers operating in the U.S. as of last year, though many have not registered with state governments. A Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis report from 2024 found that profit margins at Alphabet, Meta, and Microsoft were at least twice the services sector average. A 2019 study found that data brokers held data tied to more than 90% of Facebook accounts in the United States, and a 2020 Electronic Frontier Foundation report said Google shared sensitive user data with potentially hundreds of advertising companies. Microsoft has supported a national privacy law similar to the European Union's, and spokesperson Paige Fisher said people should not have to give up their privacy simply because they use modern technology.

Privacy and legal experts do not expect actions against a few companies to stop an industry built on collecting Americans' private data, so they are calling on more states or Congress to ban advertisers from tracking phone locations. Meanwhile, Trujillo recommends that people limit which apps track their location and disable ad tracking on their phones. California offers a centralized portal for opt-out requests at privacy.ca.gov/drop, while consumers elsewhere typically must file requests with individual data brokers. Policymakers are still debating new privacy laws, and no federal law yet addresses the problem. Google and Meta did not respond to requests for comment, so their plans remain unknown, and the articles do not say whether any state will pass a ban next.

stories.Headline: As AI stakes its claim in higher education, colleges and universities across Chicago aim to embrace it
stories.Summary:
DePaul University in Chicago recently released a document called "Guiding Principles on Artificial Intelligence," which calls for academic integrity, intellectual honesty, transparency and human-centered use of the technology. The principles were published last month, according to a Chicago Tribune report on how Chicago-area colleges are responding to artificial intelligence. About a dozen students routinely work at the university's Responsible AI Systems and Experiences lab, known as the RAISE Lab, on its Loop campus. They spend hours there exploring how artificial intelligence affects daily life and how much it should influence the human experience. The story, reported by Kate Perez, describes a wider push by Chicago-area schools to embrace the technology.

The principles came out of DePaul's 26-member Provost's Advisory Committee on Artificial Intelligence, which worked for more than a year to develop them. That committee meets monthly to discuss policy, practices and how artificial intelligence is used in the classroom. Elsewhere in Chicago, the University of Chicago will launch a new master's degree in applied artificial intelligence in fall 2027. Northwestern University launched an undergraduate major in artificial intelligence this fall, along with a webpage of tools and resources for students, faculty and staff. At Wilbur Wright College, City Colleges of Chicago introduced its first artificial intelligence degree this fall, an Associate of Applied Science in Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Development.

John Shanahan, a professor of English, chairs DePaul's advisory committee and brought together faculty who held very different views of the technology. He said the committee gives faculty from acting to computer science a shared space to talk, to hear what is happening in their units and to vet ideas for the future. Jay Cunningham, the RAISE Lab creator and an assistant professor of computing, said the principles go beyond academic integrity. His goal is for students to see artificial intelligence as a tool that attempts to model human behavior, interactions and decision-making. Cunningham, who launched the lab in 2025, said it is the job of humans to wield such tools in ways that serve them best.

At City Colleges of Chicago, Provost and Chief Academic Officer Mark Potter told the Tribune that the new degree applies across all disciplines, from history and law to transportation and distribution. He said the system cannot shy away from the technology or bury its head in the sand, and that students need artificial intelligence competencies, including responsible and ethical use. Ayoka Noelle Mota Samuels, the system's associate vice chancellor of technology sector strategy, said City Colleges should be a trusted and affordable place for people of all backgrounds to learn about artificial intelligence. She warned that without educators in leadership on the subject, some people risk being left out. City Colleges serves more than 73,000 students a year through its network of public community colleges, so its approach reaches a large student body.

Shanahan said DePaul has increasingly recognized over the last two years that artificial intelligence does not have to be feared. He described a mix of enthusiasm, excitement, skepticism and fear, and said the advancements have benefited the university, though he acknowledged that we are at the beginning of this. DePaul had published an earlier statement on artificial intelligence in 2023, which Shanahan said now feels like it came 100 years ago given how fast things are changing. Before launching its degree, City Colleges created a district-wide artificial intelligence steering committee that helped articulate its position on preparing students for an AI-enabled workforce and society. Other Chicago campuses have formed committees, launched classes and majors, and pushed for artificial intelligence literacy among students and faculty, and the University of Chicago's law school prohibits note-taking on electronic devices in some classes.

Over the past half-decade, Cunningham has watched more fields demand that workers understand artificial intelligence, creating a need for students to learn the technology as it progresses. DePaul remains faced with how to manage, embrace and integrate artificial intelligence use while weighing the opinions of faculty, administrators and students. Shanahan said the university is having conversations and being proactive about meeting the challenges of integration. He said there will be times when the technology is useful and times when it is better to think your own thoughts and write your own sentences. The articles do not say what changes the advisory committee will recommend next, or how the many schools' approaches will compare over time.

stories.Headline: Google’s new AI ‘ultimatum’ sparks concern over tech giant’s power in California schools
stories.Summary:
Google announced this week that from January it plans to block K-12 students from using its search engine unless school districts opt into the company's AI-generated version of search. The announcement was made on Monday during a virtual briefing, with a blog post following on Tuesday. The decision affects California students who have long used Google search, Chromebooks and Gmail as part of their daily education. The articles describe the relationship between Google and schools as one lasting decades, which turned into a furor this week. The reports were published by EdSource partners in early to mid-November 2026, shortly after the company made its plans known.

Under the plan, Google will block both its integrated AI tool and Google search for K-12 students unless a district decides to turn either feature on. There is no option offered for a search engine without AI integration, according to the reporting. Google said in its blog post that it will update the school search function by making its Guided Learning AI product the default. That product will offer step-by-step guidance through problems, so that students do not get quick answers to schoolwork, the company said. In a separate post on X on Tuesday, Google clarified that schools can turn off its other AI products, Gemini and Gemini Notebook.

Chris Phillips, Google's vice president and general manager of education, spoke during the virtual briefing on Monday. He said that if a school is uncomfortable with the AI and simply wants it off, then it has the choice not to have Search on at all. Google also said in its Tuesday blog post that it will update its search function for schools by making Guided Learning the default. The company further said that it has engaged with educators in recent months and will continue to engage deeply with them. It added that it aims to give schools more choice, more controls and improved Search for learning.

Lila Byock, founder of the parent advocacy group Schools Beyond Screens, called the decision an act of bullying. She said educational value, not shareholder value, must determine the technology used by students. Byock said Google forced its AI products into classrooms and parents fought back, and that the company is now refusing to take no for an answer. Rory Mir, director of community tech engagement at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, said districts should reclaim their authority from corporate interests, though de-Googling may be easier for individuals or smaller organizations than for districts. He added that the trick comes with real monetary costs as well as labor costs and disruption.

Los Angeles Unified, the state's largest district, has already placed restrictions on generative AI, and districts across California are debating limits on AI and technology use in classrooms. Google's decision could complicate those efforts, particularly because schools rely on the company's digital workspace for daily lessons and its search engine for research and assignments. About three-quarters of American teens and tweens use or interact with the AI summaries in search results, according to a recent report by Common Sense Media. In a series of 180 tests, Common Sense researchers found that Google's AI Mode completed students' homework for them every time. The AI feature also invented fake questions and cited unreliable sources such as Reddit and Facebook.

Many school districts will have to decide whether to opt into Google's AI-integrated search or find a new search alternative in the middle of the school year. Common Sense Media researchers have not reviewed Google's Guided Learning mode, according to the reporting. Rory Mir of the Electronic Frontier Foundation said Google's new policy should provoke a big discussion about Google's role as a monopolist, with undue power over schools' decisions. Some parents of Long Beach Unified students who are part of a new tech policy group will have an opportunity to provide input into the district's options, a district spokesperson said. The group also includes teachers, students, administrators and industry experts, and it is not yet clear how districts will respond once the January change arrives.

stories.Headline: Who would be next CEO at Nvidia? Top engineer and CFO favored as candidates
stories.Summary:
Nvidia's board announced on Nov. 12 that Jensen Huang had resigned as president, chief executive and board member, according to Bloomberg and other outlets cited by Seoul Economic Daily. The resignation was formally voluntary, but it came while the board was discussing his possible dismissal and searching for a successor. Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 with two engineers and had served as CEO ever since, so his exit is the first change of chief executive in the company's 33-year history. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress was named interim CEO and keeps her roles as executive vice president and CFO. Semafor had reported on Nov. 11 that the board was preparing to oust Huang as soon as Wednesday, after media reports detailed a second extramarital affair.

Kress will oversee Nvidia's management until a permanent successor is appointed, and Huang gave up his board seat along with the CEO post. Under the bylaws he could have kept his board seat after leaving the CEO role, because the board can remove a CEO without a shareholder vote but removing a director requires a separate process. Nvidia also appointed Harvey C. Jones as its first board chairman, a technology executive and venture investor of more than 30 years who previously led the chip design software company Synopsys. The company said nothing about the circumstances of the resignation or any agreement with the board. Nvidia will still release third-quarter results for fiscal 2027 and hold a briefing on Nov. 17, regardless of the management change.

The board is responsible for the leadership change, and it thanked Huang for his contributions to the company and to the advancement of the technology industry. Semafor reported that the board briefed the White House on its planned meeting, according to a senior administration official. Some directors favored naming Kress interim CEO if Huang was ousted, and the directors were scheduled to meet Wednesday evening. The board has begun a formal CEO search covering internal and external candidates, working with an outside search firm. It also launched an independent investigation, led by outside legal expert June Kim, a Korean-American former federal prosecutor, into whether a foreign intelligence operation targeted Huang.

Others reacted quickly, and Nvidia's stock fell more than 8% in after-hours trading, hitting a 52-week low. Bernstein analyst Stacy Rasgon said the company's enormous earnings and growth outlook remain intact and that operations are unlikely to suffer serious disruption during the search. He nonetheless cut his rating to "market perform" and lowered his price target to $200, saying it is unclear how the AI investments, financing and backstop agreements will be sustained. Democratic senators Chris Coons and Elizabeth Warren wrote to Trump's cabinet members, asking Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller to preserve documents on Nvidia's chip exports to China and on Huang. Some lawmakers have demanded that Huang testify and warned they would issue a subpoena if he refuses.

The crisis began when Huang acknowledged on Nov. 8 a relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed International. U.S. intelligence authorities have reportedly suspected that Alice Huang, a Chinese national, may be linked to Chinese intelligence agencies. The New York Times reported on Nov. 11 that Huang also had an affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, who reported directly to him. Megaspeed is a major Southeast Asian customer under investigation over allegations that it illegally diverted advanced AI chips subject to U.S. export controls to China, which Nvidia and Megaspeed deny. Huang led Nvidia from a graphics chip maker into core AI infrastructure, with market value that at one point topped $5 trillion, and he invested in OpenAI and Anthropic and supported CoreWeave and Nebius.

The board has begun its CEO search, and U.S. media and prediction markets have floated Johny Srouji, Apple's chief hardware officer, Rene Haas, the Arm CEO and Nvidia alumnus, and former Google CEO Eric Schmidt. Srouji was among the executives considered for Intel CEO in 2019, according to a person familiar with the matter cited by Semafor. Kress joined Nvidia in September 2013 and has overseen its finances for 13 years, after about 25 years in finance roles at companies including Microsoft and Cisco. Her finance-focused career leaves long-term technology leadership succession as an unresolved challenge. The selection of a permanent CEO, the findings of the independent investigation and whether the large-scale AI investment plans continue remain open.

stories.Headline: Protest against AI in schools, search block planned outside Google's Chicago office Wednesday
stories.Summary:
Parents, students and teachers plan to protest outside Google's Chicago office on Wednesday at 4 p.m., in the 300 block of Morgan St. in the West Loop. They object to the company's restriction of Google search in schools and its embedded generative AI. Google recently announced that students will not be able to reach its search engine at schools that ban AI use. Alphabet, the company that owns Google, said it will turn off all artificial intelligence in its education apps for K-12 students unless administrators expressly enable it. Google's announcement of November 3 came as the protest group, which includes teachers, parents and students, prepared its rally.

Under the change, Search and the standalone AI tools will be off by default for K-12 student accounts unless school administrators turn them on, and the changes are scheduled to take effect in early 2027. Google later clarified that schools could enable Search without enabling the standalone Gemini chatbot. Schools that want to block AI-generated answers within Search would still have to turn off Search itself. For schools that enable Search, Google has proposed two options, and the first is conventional search with AI Overviews plus the option to ask questions in an AI chat. The second option is search with Guided Learning, a Gemini feature that Google says prompts students to work through a physics problem or a book report step by step before giving an answer.

Alphabet says AI is so ingrained in Google search that it cannot offer an AI-free version, and Chris Phillips, Google's vice president for education, said Search and AI are deeply integrated. Google claims its own research found measurable improvements in student learning with Guided Learning. Brit Mennuti, Google Classroom's product lead, told The New York Times that the version being piloted in schools has extra restrictions and would let teachers review students' chatbot transcripts. Google began piloting Guided Learning in Search at selected US schools in November and has made it available globally through Google Classroom. On the lawsuit over a schoolgirl's use of Gemini, Google said it was reviewing the allegations and had worked with medical professionals and researchers on safeguards for young users.

Chicago Public Schools announced Monday that it will block generative AI tools, including Gemini, ChatGPT and Claude, on student accounts for student privacy and safety, and to comply with FERPA, COPPA and SOPPA. The protest group says CPS pulled its Gemini chatbot rollout in August after pushback from families, yet Gemini AI features remain baked into every CPS student's Google account. It also says data is still flowing from CPS-approved apps to AI companies without notice to or consent from parents. The rally is organized by Illinois Families for Public Schools, Schools Beyond Screens, Distraction Free Schools, the Illinois Federation of Teachers, the Chicago Teachers Union and the Chicago chapter of Veterans for Peace. Lina Khan, former chair of the Federal Trade Commission, accused Google of using its search monopoly to coerce schools into adopting AI, and on November 9, Senator Ed Markey called on Google to reverse its decision.

CPS is one of hundreds of school districts nationwide that rely on Google hardware and software for students, and Google's low-cost Chromebooks have been the most widely issued student devices in the US since a 2010 pilot. By 2016 they made up 58% of mobile computing devices shipped to US schools, according to Reuters. In August, Google enabled AI features by default in Google Classroom for schools that already allowed students the Gemini chatbot, which drew objections from school leaders and parents. A lawsuit filed in California earlier this year alleges that AI Mode search on a seventh grader's Chromebook pushed her into a mental health crisis that included planned suicide attempts. In September, New York City announced a one-year moratorium on student-facing generative AI covering nearly 600,000 public school students through eighth grade, and in January 2024, Denmark's data protection authority ordered 53 municipalities to change how they shared pupils' data with Google.

The protest is set for Wednesday afternoon, and Google's changes are scheduled to take effect in early 2027. Whether Google's policy for schools raises antitrust concerns, given its dominance of the search market, remains an open question. A US federal judge dismissed an antitrust claim by publisher Penske Media in September, finding it had not established that Search and AI Overviews are separate products. Senator Markey has asked Google to explain whether it could separate generative AI features from Search, and the articles report no answer. Ben Williamson of the University of Edinburgh called for stronger procurement and evaluation processes, including clear ways for schools to exit contracts and move their data between platforms.

stories.Headline: ModelOp Named a Market Shaper in the 2026 Gartner® Emerging Market Quadrant for AI FinOps Tools - Startup Vendors
stories.Summary:
ModelOp announced on November 12, 2026, from Park City, Utah, that it has been positioned as a Market Shaper in the Gartner Emerging Market Quadrant for AI FinOps Tools - Startup Vendors. Gartner published the report on October 28, 2026, and ModelOp describes itself as the Enterprise AI Command Center for Fortune 500 and Global 2000 organizations. Revenium, the AI Economic Control System based in Herndon, Virginia, announced the same Market Shaper designation on November 12, 2026. Coralogix, the data and AI platform for observability, announced from Boston on the same date that it was also recognized as a Market Shaper in the October 2026 quadrant. ModelOp says it is one of four vendors in the Market Shapers quadrant, among 18 vendors recognized in the report.

The quadrant examines vendors in fast-changing technology markets and assesses their Potential for Market Disruption and Potential to Execute. Gartner defines AI FinOps tools as solutions that measure, attribute, forecast, control and optimize AI costs. The report describes Market Shapers as vendors with strong cost optimization insights and automation who are pursuing end-to-end proactive AI cost management. Gartner says they are moving from weekly reporting toward realtime control, building controls into AI systems that limit costs, choose the right model for each task and enforce policies before money is spent. Gartner also says the emerging market is shifting beyond cost reporting toward AI economics management, and that organizations must connect token consumption, compute and other costs to measurable business outcomes.

ModelOp chief executive Dave Trier said enterprise AI faces a financial accountability crisis, because companies deploy more models and autonomous agents than ever without knowing whether the investments pay off. He argued that counting tokens and tracking invoices does not tell a chief executive or chief financial officer how spending affects specific business use cases. According to Trier, ModelOp therefore ties AI costs to the use case, the business owner and the expected outcome, and AI FinOps should be part of how enterprises govern AI rather than a dashboard added later. He added that the next phase of enterprise AI will be defined by measurable returns, not the number of agents deployed. Revenium chief executive and co-founder John Rowell said most companies learn what their AI agents cost only when the invoice arrives, and that Revenium prices every agent decision as it happens and can halt a runaway workflow.

Rowell said he believes the designation reflects how quickly enterprise buyers are moving from cost reports to cost control. ModelOp's capabilities include use case-level cost attribution, a usage and FinOps dashboard, portfolio analysis, discovery of ungoverned shadow AI assets, and business value monitoring against intended outcomes. ModelOp supports financial oversight through integrations with Microsoft Agent 365, Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Amazon Quick, OpenAI and tools based on the Model Context Protocol. Revenium's recent releases include skill cost and adoption analytics for AI coding assistants, guardrails that check spend limits and model access rules the moment a call is placed, and AI Insights, which ranks wasted spend by potential monthly savings.

Coralogix says enterprises are focusing on the cost of complete workflows rather than individual model requests, and it notes that autonomous agents, multi-model environments and rising token consumption are creating new financial challenges. ModelOp says this is its third Gartner recognition since June 2026. In June it was named a Visionary in the Gartner Magic Quadrant for AI Governance Platforms, and it received the highest score for the AI Agent Governance use case in the accompanying Critical Capabilities report. ModelOp has been building its enterprise AI delivery and governance foundation since 2018.

Revenium's leaders previously scaled and exited RightScale, acquired by Flexera, MuleSoft, acquired by Salesforce, and OpSource, acquired by NTT, and the company is backed by Two Bear Capital and WestWave Capital. Coralogix says traditional cost management, which reviews spending after it occurs, is becoming harder to sustain as AI workloads grow in scale and complexity. The articles describe no further steps for the three vendors beyond the announcements themselves. ModelOp invites readers to visit its website and blog for more on its AI FinOps capabilities, and Revenium continues to expand its platform for engineering and finance teams.

Gartner states that it does not endorse any vendor in its publications and that its publications are opinion rather than statements of fact. It also does not advise technology users to select only vendors with the highest ratings or other designations. The Coralogix article is cut off before its quoted executive statement, so what its leadership said about the recognition is not given here. The articles also do not name the other vendors in the quadrant or say how the 18 recognized vendors are distributed across it.

stories.Headline: Google Unveils Gemini Decision 1: Its First-Ever Decision-Making AI Model That Tops 7 Out of 9 Benchmarks With Up to 92.2% Accuracy
stories.Summary:
Google has released Gemini Decision 1, which it describes as its first dedicated decision-making model, together with the Gemini Decisions API that is powered by it. The release was announced on 2026-11-12 in coverage from 36Kr, and Google's own blog post is dated 2026-11-11. Unlike a conventional generative language model, it does not write answers token by token, and instead scores a set of candidate answers supplied in advance in a single forward pass. Google says the model took first place in 7 of 9 benchmark tests, reaching a top accuracy of 92.2%. The API is available in Google AI Studio, and Google's own teams have already started to use the technology.

Developers supply the input, the questions to be judged and the candidate options, and the model returns a judgment, a probability and a confidence level between 0 and 1. It handles three kinds of decisions: yes or no judgments, multiple choice with 2 to 255 options, and ordered rubric scoring that returns a weighted score and the probability of each level. Up to 1000 independent questions can be sent in one request, in text, image, audio, video or PDF form, with a multimodal context of up to 256K tokens. The three task types can be mixed in a single request, such as asking whether a pantry countertop photo shows a spill, what cleaning is needed and how severe the scene is. Pricing is $0.10 per million input tokens with no charge for output tokens, and end-to-end latency is about 150 to 250 milliseconds.

Google is the party responsible, and Chief Executive Sundar Pichai announced the launch in a post on X. He said the API is now live in Google AI Studio and that the model is built for decision tasks within a closed set of options rather than for generating text. He highlighted the three decision types, the low price, which he put at about one-fifth of the cost of Flash-Lite, and its leading results on several benchmarks with the lowest calibration error. Google's technical material adds that the median latency of the model calculation phase stays between 50 and 100 milliseconds in contexts of up to 16K tokens. Google also says latency stays basically stable when a request grows from 1 question to 100.

Google compared the model against three rivals: OpenAI's GPT-6 Luna, TypeSafe Jev 1.14, which is dedicated to classification and decision-making, and its own Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite. On JevBench, Gemini Decision 1 scored 92.2%, ahead of 90.9% for GPT-6 Luna, 90.0% for TypeSafe Jev 1.14 and 86.6% for Flash-Lite. On the New Yorker Caption test it scored 79.7% against 68.4% for GPT-6 Luna, and on PubMedQA it scored 79.8% against 74.4%. TypeSafe Jev 1.14 led two tests: Mind2Web Multimodal, at 86.8% to Gemini's 86.2%, and When2Call, at 82.0% to Gemini's 79.9%. Developers who build agents are the most affected, since tool selection is a key scenario for the model, and the article says competitors also still perform better on total invocation cost in some cases.

Before this, developers who wanted an AI to judge whether an email was spam, or to pick which agent should receive a task, usually called a generative model and extracted the result from its text. Gemini Decision 1 removes the step of decoding word by word. Google says the API costs nearly 5 times less than calling Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite through the Interactions API on the common benchmark set it used. On other benchmarks, Gemini Decision 1 scored 58.7% Macro-F1 on Amazon ESCI product search relevance, 86.0% on Global-MMLU-Lite against 79.6% for GPT-6 Luna, and 71.8% on MMAU and 69.1% on Video-MME, both above Flash-Lite. Its Top-1 expected calibration error is 0.0250, against 0.0721 for GPT-6 Luna, 0.0494 for TypeSafe Jev 1.14 and 0.2104 for Flash-Lite.

Google has described several uses inside its own products. Gemini Notebook uses the Decisions API as a real-time router that picks a model tier and reasoning intensity based on how complex each request is, which Google says can cut latency on daily queries by up to 40%. In Google Stitch, the experimental Rapid Canvas feature uses it to generate interactive product flow wireframes in seconds and to respond to changes made by voice or click. In the CC product from Google Labs, it picks emoji reactions from more than 200 options, and inside Google Search it forms a safety detection layer for MCP tools that looks for adversarial behavior and content. The articles do not say when the model will reach more developers, what pricing will apply after launch, or how it performs outside Google's own comparison.

stories.Headline: Fireworks AI Breach Widens to Expose Customer Billing Data and Incomplete Model Weights
stories.Summary:
AI infrastructure company Fireworks AI said hackers stole customer data during two separate breaches in October, according to a notice it updated on Monday, November 9, 2026. Fireworks hired Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 to investigate the first incident, which it discovered on October 6. A well-known, financially motivated cybercriminal group carried out that attack and took account and billing information, plus secrets that grant access to human users or apps. The second breach came through a third-party cloud provider hosting Fireworks research and development machines, which was attacked on October 23. Fireworks contained the second incident on the same day it occurred, according to SecurityWeek.

On October 24, the unauthorized party used the provider to reach Fireworks development machines and ran an unauthorized workload that affected additional customer data. The exposed data included internal Fireworks data, resource metadata, billing information, invoices, payment history, and datasets and other AI-related data. TechGig reported that some customers also had incomplete model weights exposed. Customer payment card numbers were not accessed, because Fireworks does not store them. Fireworks said it revoked and replaced compromised internal credentials and service accounts, restricted unauthorized network pathways, isolated affected systems, and tightened access to data storage and analytics systems.

Fireworks, a San Mateo company founded in 2022 that has more than 10,000 customers, is the party responsible for notifying those affected. It said the first incident touched only a limited number of customer accounts, and that all of them were notified. The company said the impacted customers from the second incident were also notified, and that it is working with Palo Alto Networks on hardening its security and revoking compromised credentials. Fireworks described its breaches as part of a larger string of attacks recently spotlighted by incident responders at Google. It said it detected the activity on October 24 and began remediation immediately.

Digital workspace company Notion said it was notified of the incident on November 2, disconnected its systems from Fireworks, and deleted all data in the Fireworks system. On November 6, Fireworks told Notion that malicious actors may have accessed potential customer data, and Notion began another internal investigation. Notion found that the hackers accessed Notion AI chat transcripts used for its Insights feature, and that fewer than 1% of Notion workspaces were affected. Most transcripts could not be tied to a customer or workspace, though Notion did not say how many customers were affected. Notion told customers to treat the data as exposed and to rotate any credentials, such as passwords or API keys, that they pasted into Notion AI during the incident.

Notion had used Fireworks for classification jobs behind Insights, which helps customers understand their own AI usage, and as a general inference provider serving open-weight models. Fireworks is a cloud platform for running and fine-tuning open source AI models. SecurityWeek reported that the second incident was linked to a recent rise in LLMJacking activity, in which hackers hijack an enterprise's access to large language models. Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant published a blog about the tactic last week and said they have responded to multiple LLMJacking incidents in 2026. Those incidents hit organizations in North America, South America and Asia Pacific, across the financial services, retail, technology and transportation sectors.

Mandiant researchers said LLMJacking can generate large spikes in fraudulent cloud charges within hours, unlike the gradual resource consumption of cryptojacking. Individual incidents showed fraudulent charges above $100,000 in a single day, and cumulative charges at some organizations reached $1 million before access was revoked. Google's group identified a diverse set of financially motivated threat clusters operating out of multiple regions, and some are maturing by handing off initial access to groups that resell it. Multiple investigations showed the groups were mainly trying to steal tokens or credentials that give footholds into target infrastructure. Google said that as enterprises adopt higher-tier models and agentic workflows, cybercriminals will likely refine automated reconnaissance targeting exposed API tokens and vulnerabilities in model routing middleware.

Fireworks is still working with Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 to investigate the full scope and impact of the breaches. Notion has disabled its Insights feature while it investigates, and it no longer serves open-weight models through Fireworks. Notion contacted the affected customers with instructions on how to securely retrieve and review the data in their workspaces. SecurityWeek has emailed Notion for additional information and said it will update its article if the company responds. The articles do not say how many Fireworks customers were affected, or when Insights might return.

stories.Headline: Getty tests limits of law in pivotal AI hearing at UK Court of Appeal
stories.Summary:
Getty Images is appealing to the Court of Appeal in its dispute with Stability AI, the developer of the Stable Diffusion image generator. The appeal is being heard over two days, Wednesday and Thursday, in the week of 11 November 2026. The High Court gave its first instance judgment in November 2025 and largely favoured Stability AI. Getty succeeded on only a small part of its trade mark claim, and its copyright claim failed. Getty's barrister told the court that Stability "doesn't think it should have to pay" for Getty's content.

The central question is whether an AI model can be an "infringing copy" under section 27(3) of the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988, even if the model never contained copies of the works. Stable Diffusion was trained outside the UK, so Getty dropped its primary copyright claims during the trial and kept only a secondary infringement case. That case argued that the model was an infringing copy imported into, and distributed in, the UK. The High Court accepted that an intangible AI model can be an "article", but held that an infringing copy must actually be a copy. Because the model weights had never stored Getty's images, the High Court ruled that the model could not be an infringing copy.

Getty says that "making" a model includes training it, which involves copying images, and that the finished model need not itself contain copies. In its view, if making the article in the UK would have infringed copyright, the article is an infringing copy whether or not it holds copies. Getty's barrister said Stability wants to separate what was done with the copyright works from the act of training, but can only do so by mischaracterising the facts. Stability AI argues that whether something is a copy depends on what is actually produced, not on how it was developed. It says Getty's approach would produce odd results, such as making it unlawful to import the model but lawful to copy it once it is in the UK.

The British Recorded Music Industry Limited, known as BPI, represents the UK recorded music industry and has permission to intervene in support of Getty. It warns that the High Court's approach could let developers train models offshore and bring them back into the UK, with significant consequences for the music and wider creative industries. BPI also notes that Getty accepted at trial that the versions of Stable Diffusion did not contain copies, and cites two recent German cases in which the Munich Court found that models had memorised works they were trained on. On that basis BPI says the Getty judgment has "no wider significance" on whether models contain copies, because the question depends on the facts of each model. Stability AI also argues that extending the law to models trained overseas is a matter for Parliament, not the courts, and it has cross-appealed two findings that went against it.

The High Court case was heard in June 2025, and Getty dropped one of its primary copyright infringement claims just two weeks into the trial. The claims that remained before Mrs Justice Joanna Smith were secondary infringement, trademark infringement and passing off. The court found that Getty succeeded in part on trademark infringement, but only for older models and on isolated examples. Getty had alleged that Stability copied and processed millions of copyrighted images to train Stable Diffusion in the US. Stability's directors include the filmmaker James Cameron, and Stability argues that the images were downloaded and stored in data centres outside the UK, so UK copyright law does not apply.

Stability AI is asking the Court of Appeal to overturn two findings that went against it at first instance: that an intangible model can be an "article", and that Stability itself imported or distributed the model in the UK. Getty disputes both points. If Getty succeeds, developers could face UK copyright claims over models trained abroad on unlicensed works, even where the imported model stores no copies. If Stability succeeds, where a model is trained and whether it stores copies will remain key to any claims. The judgment has not yet been handed down, and the Government continues to consider its approach to copyright and AI following its March 2026 report.

stories.Headline: Drug Ads Can Influence AI Treatment Recommendations, Study Finds
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai reported on November 11 that a clearly labeled pharmaceutical advertisement can shift which treatment an artificial intelligence model recommends. Their study appeared in the November 11 online issue of The Lancet Digital Health, under the title Pharmaceutical advertising and drug recommendations by consumer-facing artificial intelligence: A controlled study. The team tested 12 AI models from major technology companies, including Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic. Each model received a physician-written clinical case, and an advertisement for a drug was placed immediately before the case. When that advertisement was present, the models became more likely to select the advertised drug.

The study covered 33 clinical scenarios, and the researchers analyzed 258,559 AI responses. The advertised drug was selected in 47.6 percent of responses when an ad was present, compared with 35 percent without one. In four cases, models moved from selecting the advertised drug zero percent of the time to selecting it 100 percent of the time once the ad appeared. The patient information and the treatment choices stayed the same in every case, so only the presence of the advertisement varied. The researchers assessed both the treatment selected and whether it was consistent with clinical guidance, and they used real drug advertisements.

Mahmud Omar, MD, the first author, is a lecturer in the Windreich Department of Artificial Intelligence and Human Health at the Icahn School of Medicine. He leads research on the safety, reliability, and real-world effects of generative AI in clinical care, and he said he found it surprising how reasonable the answers often appeared. He explained that a model could still recommend an appropriate treatment while its preference among several reasonable options changed after it saw the ad. Because the final answer could still look medically sound, he said the influence could be easy to miss in typical research evaluations and in other personal use cases facing patients and physicians. Girish N. Nadkarni, MD, MPH, the senior author, said an answer can be clinically reasonable and still raise a question about why the AI arrived at it.

Nadkarni holds several roles: Chair of the Windreich Department of Artificial Intelligence and Human Health, Director of the Hasso Plattner Institute for Digital Health, and Irene and Dr. Arthur M. Fishberg Professor of Medicine at the Icahn School of Medicine. He is also Chief AI Officer of the Mount Sinai Health System. He said that as AI becomes part of how people get health information, it must be possible to tell clinical guidance from commercial influence. He added that people should be told transparently when advertising is part of the interaction. The article names no other outside commenters, though the investigators stress that the findings do not mean advertising will necessarily cause AI models to recommend unsafe or inappropriate treatments.

The study notes that people are increasingly turning to artificial intelligence for health information, which raised the question of what happens when commercial advertising appears beside a clinical question. In a subset of free-text responses, the models explicitly mentioned the ad in only 29.9 percent of responses. They repeated information or claims from the advertisement more often than they acknowledged it. In the study, advertisements did not clearly increase recommendations for unsupported supplements or clearly suboptimal drugs. The researchers did not examine whether changes in AI recommendations ultimately affected prescriptions, patient decisions, costs, or health outcomes.

The researchers say the findings point to several practical steps for AI developers and health systems. These include testing AI systems with and without promotional content to see whether recommendations change, and clearly disclosing when advertising is presented to an AI system. They also include keeping promotional material separate from clinical advice. The findings may also matter to regulators as they consider how existing rules on pharmaceutical advertising apply when promotional content is built into AI-generated health information. The research team plans to extend the work through its ongoing evaluation of AI and human-AI interaction in real-world clinical cases, and the articles leave open whether any such regulation will follow.

stories.Headline: Chinese AI firms rush to secure Nvidia chip capacity as spy scandal stirs fear of US curbs
stories.Summary:
Chinese artificial intelligence companies are trying to rent Nvidia-powered computing capacity at data centres outside China, according to three people familiar with the matter who spoke to Reuters. They worry a scandal involving Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang could push Washington to tighten limits on their remote use of advanced processors. A major Chinese cloud provider has discussed internally whether to lock in overseas Nvidia chip capacity, while some firms have contacted data centre operators about reserving it. Smaller AI labs are considering similar steps, including approaching major providers of rented computing power in South-east Asia, two of the sources said. Huang said on Sunday, Nov 8, that he had been unfaithful to his wife, and the story was published on Nov 12, 2026.

The companies fear the controversy could add political momentum to the Remote Access Security Act, known as Rasa, a US bill giving the Commerce Department authority over remote, cloud-based access to restricted technology. The House of Representatives passed the bill in January by a vote of 369 to 22, and it now awaits action in the Senate. Washington already restricts exports to China of Nvidia's most advanced AI chips, yet Chinese firms can reach such processors by renting computing power at overseas data centres. Restricting overseas cloud access would make it harder for Chinese developers to obtain high-end computing power without importing the chips directly. The prospect of tougher enforcement has also fuelled demand in China's grey market, where traders and intermediaries have begun stockpiling restricted Nvidia AI chips, two of the sources said.

The people who described these moves declined to be identified, and would not name the cloud provider, because of the sensitivity of the matter. Nvidia, Megaspeed and the US Commerce Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Tencent and Alibaba also did not immediately respond, and Reuters said it could not independently verify the allegation that the woman involved was a Chinese intelligence asset. China has denied that allegation, and Megaspeed has denied illegally diverting chips to China. Seoul Economic Daily, citing Reuters, The Information and other foreign media, reported that Alice Hwang, whom it describes as an alleged Chinese agent, built a multilayered business structure linking China, Singapore and Malaysia.

The New York Times reported that the woman involved was Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singapore-based cloud-computing company Megaspeed, and that US authorities had concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset. Alice Huang had business dealings and investment ties with several leading Chinese technology companies, including Tencent and Alibaba, according to two people familiar with the matter. Singapore business filings show that Alibaba subsidiary Apex Enterprise Solutions provided financing to Speedmatrix, a Malaysian company linked to Megaspeed, according to records Reuters reviewed. Singapore authorities summoned her over suspicions of false import declarations but closed the investigation for lack of evidence. Taiwanese authorities also monitored her visits at Washington's request, and she later left for Shanghai, although Megaspeed's business continues.

Washington has struggled to stop Chinese access to advanced chips, and the articles point to several earlier cases. A Chinese university with deep ties to the People's Liberation Army bought Nvidia's powerful H200 AI chips in October despite being on a US export blacklist, procurement records show. US prosecutors in March charged Super Micro Computer co-founder Yih-Shyan "Wally" Liaw and two others with conspiring to divert servers containing Nvidia chips to China through a South-east Asia-based company. Prosecutors said that company bought about US$2.5 billion of servers from Super Micro between 2024 and 2025, and that a substantial portion went to China, while the defendants have not been convicted. Megaspeed has faced scrutiny over suspicions that it helped Chinese customers gain access to restricted chips, and Seoul Economic Daily reported that its Malaysian arm Speedmatrix pledged servers and intellectual property to Alibaba affiliate Apex as collateral.

Seoul Economic Daily reported that Alice Hwang's chip dealings were estimated at about 240,000 units, including H100, H200 and A100 processors, either smuggled into China or supplied as leased data centre capacity. The paper said the Malaysian figures linked to her have reportedly pressed ahead with data centre construction in Malaysia. The articles do not say when the Senate will act on Rasa, or whether the Commerce Department will take any step against remote access. They also leave open whether Chinese firms will succeed in securing overseas capacity, and whether a wider US crackdown on smuggling of chips and AI servers will follow. Headlines linked to the story say Nvidia is preparing to oust Huang, though the articles give no detail on that.

stories.Headline: AI Is Killing Autonomously. Time for New Rules.
stories.Summary:
Next week, leaders will gather at the United Nations in Geneva to decide whether to negotiate a treaty on autonomous weapons, according to León Castellanos-Jankiewicz, writing on November 13, 2026. He says machines of this kind have already killed soldiers in eastern Ukraine, and three civilians in Zaporizhzhia last July. The first such incident came two years ago, when a swarm of ten drones struck a field near Bakhmut and killed at least two combatants. In the July case, a Russian drone guided by experimental AI killed three Ukrainians after failing to clear a building and exploding near sheltering civilians. Separately, UVA Darden professors Mike Lenox and Alex Cowan have proposed that AI firms using unlicensed training material release their model weights to the public once a year.

The Geneva meeting is where officials will decide whether to start negotiating a binding treaty, and the report drafted by governmental experts is the latest text on the table. That report covers human control before and during deployment, but once a drone is jammed, only inputs made before launch remain relevant for liability. The Russian drone was programmed by human operators to destroy propane fuel tanks at a gas station, and forensic analysis showed it flew with no link to an operator. It steered itself with a commercially available Nvidia chip, and the writer notes that the operators selected a target category, not a victim. Under the Darden proposal, any firm training models on unlicensed material, or building on a model that did, would release those weights annually, while keeping a lead of six to 18 months, about a year on average.

Castellanos-Jankiewicz is a senior researcher in International Law at the University of Amsterdam Faculty of Law and a non-resident fellow at the UN Institute for Disarmament Research. He argues that the experts' report is a good start but fails to close the enforcement gap for weapons operating in unobserved environments. He says it assigns no responsibility to the tech companies building these systems, which fiercely protect their commercial secrets from public scrutiny. He calls for enforceable obligations on states that field unpredictable killing machines, and for liability on the companies that build them. On the other side, Lenox and Cowan say their annual release rule would advance safety, competition and fairness, and that the time to adopt it is before AI companies go public.

Ukrainian drone maker Alexander Kokhanovskyy said the Bakhmut targets were identified by AI, adding that they simply launch it and know everything in the selected area will be dead. The International Committee of the Red Cross has called for unpredictable autonomous systems to be prohibited outright. Some argue that drone commanders already carry liability under existing laws, but the writer says this is hard to sustain when drones fly in dark mode behind enemy lines with no pilot input. In electronically jammed missions, he says, it becomes impossible to verify what the drones saw or targeted, even after strikes happen. Civilians such as the three killed in Zaporizhzhia are among those affected, while the Darden authors point to a public that is worried, with 55% to 77% in five national polls saying AI is moving too fast or should slow down.

Castellanos-Jankiewicz says international humanitarian law assumes each attack flows from a discrete decision, whereas drone swarms are decentralized by definition. He adds that machine learning systems can show emergent behavior, so their choices cannot be fully predicted or explained ahead of time as the law requires. A 2019 US Army report identified neural, ocular and auditory enhancement as technically feasible by mid-century, which he says further blurs the line between operators and their platforms. The Darden authors note that on October 26 Anthropic filed to go public, with reports putting its valuation between $1.5 and $2 trillion. Three days later, Alphabet lost nearly 13% of its value in a single day, about $500 billion, on worries about whether its AI spending will pay off.

The articles do not say whether the Geneva leaders will vote to open treaty negotiations, only that they meet next week to decide. Castellanos-Jankiewicz warns that if diplomats fail to negotiate a new treaty, ever more lives will hang by a line of code. The Darden authors say their proposal could be tried first, and that if it proves insufficient the public could ask for more regulation. They add that under Nasdaq's new fast-entry rules, a newly public company of significant size can join the Nasdaq 100 after 15 trading days. The articles leave open how states and companies would respond, and whether any treaty or release rule would reach weapons that operate while jammed.

stories.Headline: The Human Flaw in the AI Trade: Analyzing Jensen Huang’s Nvidia Downfall
stories.Summary:
The Financial Times has published a report on the final days of Jensen Huang at Nvidia, dated 13 November 2026. Its headline says his downfall exposes the company's internal politics. A source quoted in the report says Huang ran Nvidia as a "feudal system" in which his daughter and son-in-law held powerful positions. The article itself sits behind a subscription wall, and the text available here contains only the headline, a short summary line and subscription offers. It does not set out what led to Huang's departure, when it took place, or in what form it happened.

No figures, dates or contract terms connected to the story appear in the material provided. Nor does it say what Huang's exit changes for the company, its leadership structure or its customers. The only account of responsibility and motive comes from the unnamed source cited by the Financial Times, who describes the management style as feudal. The material gives no response from Huang, from Nvidia, from the board or from the two relatives the source refers to. It also does not name them or describe the roles they held.

Without that detail, it is not possible to say who made the decision or how it was explained. There is no background in the available text on Nvidia's recent performance, its place in the artificial intelligence market, or any investor reaction. It also says nothing about who might lead the company next or what steps the board may take. Until the full report or an official statement is available, the picture remains incomplete. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Robin Li: Why Build a New Factory in the AI Era? Insights into Baidu’s AI-Driven Manufacturing Strategy
stories.Summary:
Baidu founder Robin Li urged companies to reorganize around artificial intelligence on November 12, 2026, speaking at the 2026 Baidu World Conference in Beijing. He called for an "AI-native" organizational structure to replace the conventional hierarchies that most companies still use today. Li argued that the productivity gains from AI depend on changes in how businesses actually operate, and he described AI as an organizational revolution beyond a technological one. He held the discussion with Lenovo Group Chairman Yang Yuanqing, and both men said corporate exploration of AI remains at an early stage. The remarks came as Baidu, listed on both Nasdaq and Hong Kong, turned to AI agents to expand its user base.

Li presented "Smart Organization" as the new factory of the AI era, arguing that companies have only replaced the motor without redesigning the factory. He set out three principles of organizational evolution for the first time, which are to break job boundaries, to precipitate tacit knowledge, and to design closed process loops. Inside Baidu, daily active agents rose from an average of 5,000 to 37,000 in a year, an increase of more than six times. Tasks completed by agents grew from 84,000 per week to more than 1 million per week, and Baidu built 4,300 Workspaces with more than 20,000 organizational Skills. Baidu also unveiled Ernie 5.5 Flash Preview, which has 280 billion parameters, 14 billion of them active per token, and a context window of 1 million tokens.

Li said Baidu hit some pitfalls in its own AI transformation, from letting business departments train models on their own to chasing hot agent applications. The company gradually found that even highly enthusiastic AI use by employees did not necessarily improve organizational efficiency. In his view, traditional organizations are centered on jobs, while those of the AI era will center on tasks and break down job boundaries. He summarized his method as "Measurable + Looping = Continuous Evolution," so that each completed round of tasks passes lessons to the next. He also said the large model industry advances along two paths, pushing up the upper limit of intelligence and releasing industrial value, and that Baidu will keep building next-generation base models while optimizing models for applications.

A McKinsey survey of 1,719 respondents from 97 countries found that 80% reported personal productivity gains from AI, but only 37% said AI contributed positively to their organization's EBIT, about the same share as in 2025. A World Economic Forum report found that global AI investment exceeded 2,500 billion US dollars in 2025, yet only 25% of enterprises said AI brought disruptive change. That report blamed organizations for grafting AI onto existing processes instead of rebuilding operations around intelligence. An industry insider told 36Kr that pilot figures such as tools deployed and hours saved are easy to show, but where the saved hours go is hard to calculate. Employees also move tasks between tools, leaving enterprises with scattered AI permissions, audits that are hard to trace, and business value that is hard to quantify.

The articles trace the problem back to 1987, when Nobel-winning economist Solow wrote that the computer age shows up everywhere except in productivity statistics, a remark later called the Solow Paradox. Boston Consulting Group described a European energy service provider that ran dozens of AI pilots but saw limited impact because customer problems crossed several departments. The company then formed three cross-functional teams, each owning a key process from start to finish, and decided which tasks went to agents. Afterward its customer satisfaction reached the level of manual service, its reliance on external service providers fell by more than 90%, and the cash released funded further transformation. At Baidu World 2025 Li proposed internalizing AI capabilities, and at the Create developer conference in May 2026 he proposed DAA, urging attention to agent output and results over Token consumption.

Baidu plans to build on its four-layer architecture of Chip, Cloud, Model and Agent, and Li is now turning attention to the organizational layer. Questions he raised include what tasks an agent can take on, what data it can call, who accepts its results, and who takes over after a failure. The articles describe Baidu's agent push as centered on its Dazi application, which ranked second among office AI apps with 9.8 million monthly users in September, behind Tencent's WorkBuddy at 32.4 million. Alibaba's Qwen Office had 7.9 million monthly users, according to QuestMobile, and Baidu said Dazi was the fastest-growing general-purpose agent in its category last quarter. Baidu shares fell 2.3% to HK$76.8 on the day, and the articles do not say whether the Smart Organization approach will turn individual efficiency gains into company profit.

stories.Headline: Huang's exit, Anthropic's entrance
stories.Summary:
Hugging Face CEO Clément Delangue said on Thursday that the departure of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was a "really sad day." In a post on X, he pledged that Hugging Face would "keep fighting for open-source AI, harder than ever." The comments were published by TechGig on November 13, 2026. The article does not explain the circumstances of Huang's exit, and the headline's mention of Anthropic is not covered in the text provided.

Nvidia announced in September 2025 that it planned to acquire Hugging Face for $12.9 billion. That makes it Nvidia's second-largest acquisition, behind the roughly $20 billion deal for the assets of chipmaker Groq in December 2025. The Hugging Face purchase is still scheduled to close in the first half of 2027. The article says the deal would give Nvidia control over a major distribution channel for AI models.

Delangue is the person speaking for Hugging Face here, and his statement is the only direct reaction the article reports. Nvidia, for its part, has pledged that Hugging Face would keep its open support. The US Department of Justice began inquiries in October into how the deal could affect competition in the AI market, according to Reuters. The article does not report any response from Nvidia or the Justice Department to Huang's departure.

The article frames Huang as a well-known supporter of open-source AI and open-weight models, which is why his exit raises questions about how Nvidia will approach open source going forward. In July 2026 he published an AI policy letter signed by 25 companies, including Microsoft and Meta, urging the US government not to over-restrict open-weight models. This year Nvidia also expanded its Nemotron family of open-weight models with a 120-billion-parameter model and two new lightweight Bolt models. What happens next depends on the antitrust scrutiny and the planned closing of the deal in the first half of 2027. The article gives no further detail on who will lead Nvidia or how its open-source strategy may change.

stories.Headline: Norway, Britain agree to deepen AI cooperation
stories.Summary:
Norway and Britain signed a letter of intent in Oslo on Thursday, 12 November 2026, to deepen their cooperation on artificial intelligence. Norwegian Minister of Digitalisation and Public Governance Torgeir Micaelsen and British Minister for Artificial Intelligence Kanishka Narayan announced the cooperation in a joint statement. They met on the sidelines of the Atlantic Future Forum, a British defence, security and technology conference. The forum was held aboard the British aircraft carrier HMS Prince of Wales, which was making a port call in Oslo. The ministers agreed to develop the cooperation further as part of the strategic partnership between the two countries.

Under the statement, AI Norway, a national hub within the Norwegian Digitalisation Agency, would seek closer cooperation with Britain's AI Security Institute. That work covers the testing and evaluation of AI models and the assessment of risks posed by advanced systems. The countries will also explore computing capacity and digital infrastructure, including secure commercial hosting of national compute assets and public workloads, and the deployment of semiconductors and novel AI hardware from either country. Britain's Taskforce RAID and Norway's Defence Centre for Data and AI are to look at jointly developing, testing and adopting AI-enabled defence capabilities. Further areas include cybersecurity through the NCSC and NSM, research and innovation ecosystems, and the convergence of AI with quantum technologies, biotechnology and robotics.

The statement of intent is nonbinding, and the Norwegian government said the two sides aim to follow it with a memorandum of understanding that will specify future cooperation. Responsibility for coordinating the work sits with the Norwegian Ministry of Digitalisation and Public Governance, alongside a British government department. The British government's statement names that department as the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade, while the Norwegian announcement calls it the Department for Business and Trade. Both ministers agreed to remain in regular contact to build the cooperation, working with the relevant ministries and authorities in both countries. Micaelsen said artificial intelligence offers significant opportunities for value creation, research and better public services, but that the security challenges of the technology must also be addressed.

Micaelsen added that international cooperation is essential and that this is a high priority for the Norwegian government. He described Britain as one of Norway's closest allies and a trusted partner. Narayan said Norway is one of Britain's closest and most trusted allies, and that there is much the two countries can achieve together. He pointed to combining British expertise in AI with Norway's strengths in energy and computing, calling it practical cooperation. He said it would help build greater technological independence, strengthen collective security and support good jobs in both countries.

The articles name the government agencies, research institutions and industry stakeholders of both countries as those the cooperation will bring closer together. The aim is to work more closely on the safe and responsible use of AI, on combating AI-enabled cyber threats, and on effective international oversight of advanced AI systems. The ministers also want to promote innovation, economic growth and better public services. The two countries plan to coordinate more closely on international standards, and to strengthen dialogue so that international AI governance becomes more complementary and interoperable. They will also explore cooperation across multilateral forums and on capacity-building, and will exchange views on how AI policies support research and innovation, drawing on Britain's Industrial Strategy and Norway's industrial policy priorities.

The initiative builds on the strategic partnership announced by the two countries in December 2024. The Joint Declaration on the Norwegian-UK Strategic Partnership was agreed on 16 December 2024 by Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and British Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer. The ministers described the relationship as one between neighbours, partners and allies, underpinned by shared democratic values and a commitment to open, secure and resilient societies. They presented AI as a new area of bilateral cooperation building on the partnership's existing objectives on security, resilience, sustainable growth and innovation. They noted that the two countries have complementary strengths in AI, research and innovation, secure digital infrastructure and clean energy, and said the statement complements existing cooperation under the partnership and the UK-Norway Green Industrial Partnership.

The next step set out in the articles is a memorandum of understanding that will specify the cooperation across the various areas the ministers listed. The articles give no date for that memorandum and do not say when talks on it will begin. They also give no budget, funding commitment or timetable for any of the areas the countries will explore. The areas are described only as ones to explore, and the letter of intent is nonbinding. The statement lists the Lunna House Agreement among the existing cooperation it complements, but the available text breaks off before describing it.

stories.Headline: Warby Parker bets on Google AI glasses for growth, but privacy fears still loom
stories.Summary:
Warby Parker is entering the smart glasses market in partnership with Google and Samsung, betting that demand for AI wearables will balloon in the coming years. The New York-based fashion brand, known for affordable eyewear, also wants to head off privacy concerns that have weighed on existing producers of such glasses. Most smart glasses embed small cameras that let wearers record their surroundings without taking out a phone. Warby Parker held a demonstration event for its Intelligent Eyewear in New York City on November 9, 2026. Shoppers can start placing pre-orders from Warby Parker on Thursday, which the articles date to November 12.

The glasses connect to Google's Gemini AI assistant for everything from directions to language translation, much as Meta's glasses connect to an assistant. Alphabet's Google will not use visuals captured with the glasses to train its AI. The glasses will bar facial recognition of bystanders. A small white notification light on the front turns on automatically when a user starts recording video. Google says it will also guard the recording indicator light against tampering, redact people's faces from video before it is sent to Gemini, and ban targeted advertising on the glasses.

Warby Parker Co-CEO Neil Blumenthal told Reuters the big difference from existing versions on the market is the privacy framework embedded in the glasses from the outset. He said that as long as the tools provide utility to customers, the company will be successful. Juston Payne, who leads extended reality products at Google, acknowledged that public skepticism could be a risk to growth. He said trust was understandably lost in this area, and that Google intends to change the conversation and raise the bar. A Meta spokesperson said Meta's AI glasses also include a camera notification light on the front, and that input from safety experts helped inform their privacy features.

Calli Schroeder, who leads the AI and human rights program at the Electronic Privacy Information Center, an advocacy group, said she was happy that footage is not automatically fed into AI systems for training. She said that still leaves open the worry of a stranger having footage of her child on a phone, which she called concerning however it is phrased. It remains to be seen whether Google's measures will ease concern about widespread surveillance if the glasses become ubiquitous. One of Britain's biggest pub chains has restricted the use of the frames. Norway's government is planning a temporary ban on the use of AI glasses in certain locations, and Australia is considering barring camera-equipped smart glasses in government workplaces.

The Warby Parker glasses are broadly similar to Meta smart glasses from Ray-Ban and Oakley maker EssilorLuxottica, which have faced regulatory scrutiny from Norway to Australia. Ray-Ban's Meta glasses still dominate, representing 81.3% of AI glasses shipments in the first half of this year, according to research group Omdia. Global AI glasses shipments more than doubled in the first half of 2026 from a year earlier, though growth has slowed since the second half of last year. Optimism about the plan has helped Warby Parker shares rally by nearly 40% this year, against a 10% gain in the S&P 500. Analysts at TD Cowen wrote last week that smart glasses are poised to be an increasingly important driver of the company's growth outlook, even as the core optical backdrop remains soft.

Pre-orders open this Thursday, and Warby Parker expects the new wearable technology to add several percentage points to fourth-quarter revenue growth, executives said on an earnings call earlier this month. Luxury group Kering is poised to release glasses of its own in partnership with Google, as other brands seek a foothold against Ray-Ban's Meta glasses. The articles leave open whether Google's privacy measures will ease concern about surveillance if the glasses become widespread. They do not say whether Norway's planned temporary ban or Australia's government workplace restrictions will take effect. The articles also do not give a shipping date, a price or the full list of locations affected by the restrictions.

stories.Headline: California teachers urge 3-year pause on AI use in K-8 schools
stories.Summary:
The California Federation of Teachers on Wednesday asked Gov. Gavin Newsom to order a three-year pause on artificial intelligence in K-8 public school classrooms. The union said schools are bringing in AI tools without adequate protections for students and educators. Its request followed Newsom's September executive order directing state agencies to develop AI safety regulations. That order includes a potential "kill switch" for certain AI programs during emergencies.

The union, which represents 120,000 educators and faculty, wants Newsom to issue an executive order pausing AI use in classrooms before his term ends in January. It also asked that schools be given time during the pause to address the emerging concerns. The union sent a letter to the outgoing governor warning that unregulated AI could harm students' development and limit teachers' control over instruction. It said educators are not prepared to supervise AI use, while students may struggle to tell which tools are safe or harmful. The letter also cited an MIT study linking AI use with lower brain activity on tests than among students who had not used it.

CFT President Jeff Freitas said in a statement that students' brain development should not be monetized for billionaire profit. He described the matter as a public health and safety emergency and said leaders need to treat it as one and act now. The statement framed the pause as a response to how quickly AI is spreading into schools. The union argued that the pace of adoption has outrun the safeguards meant to protect children and teachers.

Newsom has largely embraced the growth of AI in California throughout his governorship. Advocacy groups have urged him to impose stronger accountability and protections as the technology expands. The union's letter adds a school-specific demand to those calls. The articles do not say how Newsom or his office responded, or whether any action on the pause is planned.
