stories.Headline: Growing AI Use Raises Cybersecurity and Privacy Risks
stories.Summary:
Kaspersky has published a survey showing that growing use of artificial intelligence for personal advice, health questions and everyday planning is raising worries about privacy and cybersecurity. The survey covered respondents across the Middle East, Türkiye and Africa region, known as META, and was reported by Pakistan Observer and The Patriot on 12 November 2026. Nearly 79 percent of respondents said they use AI services, including chatbots and tools for making images and videos. Experts warned that sharing sensitive information with these platforms could expose users to data leaks, misuse by third parties and cyberattacks. The IAPP also published an analysis on 12 November 2026 on how Italy is handling AI, privacy and cybersecurity.

Searching for and summarising information was the most common use of AI, cited by 74 percent of those surveyed. Writing texts followed at 50 percent, generating images from written prompts at 42 percent, and editing personal photos at 41 percent. Another 32 percent turned to AI to create videos, while 37 percent used it for health-related questions and 41 percent sought advice on personal matters. Planning weekends, holidays or events drew 29 percent, and creating meal menus and diet plans drew 23 percent. Almost one in 10 respondents had already met incorrect AI-generated information, and 24 percent believed AI could give inaccurate answers.

Seifallah Jedidi, Kaspersky's Head of Consumer Channel for the Middle East, Türkiye and Africa, is the named spokesperson. He urged consumers to understand the limits of AI services and the risks linked to them. He said even widely used platforms can have vulnerabilities that lead to data leaks. According to him, information shared with these platforms may be processed under the relevant service and its policies, or may be reached by third parties. He urged users to verify AI-generated content, avoid sharing confidential information and stay alert to fraudulent AI services designed to spread malware.

Kaspersky experts advised users to avoid giving sensitive, confidential or private information to AI services in order to reduce cybersecurity risks. They warned that phishing web pages, malicious software and fake websites often imitate genuine platforms or deceive users with fake tools. The company also recommended checking each platform's data-handling policies. It advised consulting reliable sources before relying on AI for medical, financial, legal or educational advice. Users of AI services are the people affected, particularly those who share health details or personal matters with chatbots.

The IAPP analysis, written by Ludovica Mosci, Manager of Privacy Compliance EMEA at The Walt Disney Company, describes Italy as one of Europe's most interventionist jurisdictions on privacy, AI and cybersecurity. Two legislative decrees recently completed Italy's transposition of the EU AI Act into national law. Legislative Decree No. 160, adopted on 9 September, introduced corporate and individual criminal liability provisions. Legislative Decree No. 179, adopted on 8 October and in force from 23 October, clarifies the roles and responsibilities of Italy's national AI supervisory authorities. In July, the data protection authority, the Garante, concluded its investigation into Character Technologies, the U.S.-based provider of the Character.AI companion app, which also touched on minors' online protection.

The articles do not say what follows from the Kaspersky survey, and they give no sign of any regulatory response to its findings. They describe Italy's cybersecurity position as one of no new regulatory developments, with 2026 marking the move from legislative implementation to operational compliance and active supervision under the NIS2 Directive and the Digital Operational Resilience Act. They say the Garante has continued its scrutiny of AI providers, including a decision on an AI-powered plug-in for sentiment analysis of employees. The IAPP excerpt does not set out the outcome of the Character.AI investigation or of the employee plug-in decision. Kaspersky also points to its Kaspersky Premium security solution, which it says protects users in everyday digital activities through AI-based technologies.

stories.Headline: S&P 500, Nasdaq fall as Nvidia CEO's exit rattles AI stocks
stories.Summary:
U.S. stocks ended slightly lower on Thursday after Nvidia announced that Jensen Huang had resigned as president, chief executive and board member, effective immediately. The company named its chief financial officer, Colette Kress, as interim CEO. The news shook confidence in the artificial intelligence trade, and Nvidia shares plunged as much as 14 percent at the open before recovering part of the loss. By the close, the stock was down 4.34 percent at 166.19 dollars.

The three major indexes all finished in the red. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 189.4 points, or 0.36 percent, to 52,297.09. The S&P 500 lost 26.98 points, or 0.35 percent, to 7,592.4, while the Nasdaq Composite dropped 100.1 points, or 0.39 percent, to 25,366.09. Nvidia is due to report quarterly results next Tuesday.

Not every chip stock followed Nvidia lower, as investors looked for companies that might benefit from the leadership turmoil at the AI industry's biggest supplier. Advanced Micro Devices rose 5.86 percent and Broadcom gained 5.54 percent. Jed Ellerbroek, a portfolio manager at Argent Capital Management, said the AI revolution is much bigger than any one company. He argued that if Nvidia's chips were no longer the best, buyers would switch to rivals such as AMD or Google, and that demand for the chips is not falling.

Other market moves added to the pressure. Traders kept pricing in a Federal Reserve rate hike in December, with markets putting the chance of a quarter-point move at about 91 percent. The yield on the 10-year Treasury note rose to 5.1 percent, after closing at 4.98 percent late Tuesday, before the Veterans Day bond market holiday. Oil prices jumped after a social media post from President Trump dampened hopes of a deal with Iran any time soon, with West Texas Intermediate settling at 88.74 dollars a barrel, up 2.55 percent, and Brent crude at 95.82 dollars, up 3.3 percent. AI cloud company Nebius fell 16.84 percent after its quarterly report, even though its revenue rose sharply from a year earlier.

stories.Headline: Portland parents protesting use of AI in schools
stories.Summary:
On Wednesday, concerned parents and advocates with a group called OR Unplugged protested outside Google's downtown Portland office. Their message was that technology in the classroom should be reined in and, for some of them, that artificial intelligence should be removed from schools entirely. The protest was reported by KOIN 6 News reporter Joey Vacca, in a story posted on November 11, 2026, and updated that evening. The protesters gathered in front of the Google office, and KOIN published a photograph of parents standing outside the building. Theirs was one of several protests planned outside Google offices across the country on that same Wednesday.

The protest centered on a claim about how Google treats schools that do not want to use its AI. The group's outreach coordinator, Kathy Masarie, said the company threatened to cut schools off from searching on its platform if they do not agree to use its artificial intelligence. The articles do not give a number of attendees, a time of day, or a count of the other protests planned elsewhere. Masarie said AI is outsourcing students' learning, which is the core of the group's objection. The only slogan the articles report is the group's motto, skills before screens, which Masarie called the best motto.

Google responded through a spokesperson, who said the company hears the concerns of parents and teachers about students using AI to shortcut their learning. The spokesperson said Google shares the goal of helping students learn. To improve Search for the classroom, the company said it is starting to pilot Guided Learning capabilities in Search this month. The statement said those capabilities would walk students step by step through a range of complex problems, rather than just giving quick answers. The spokesperson added that Google is building these experiences in partnership with educators and is listening closely to make sure its products support students and teachers.

Masarie said she was not convinced by Google's response, and she described a pattern she has seen from technology companies. She said tech companies have told the group many times that they are putting in protections and barriers, and she repeated the word many four times for emphasis. She said a whole group is now checking these so-called protections and finding that they do not work. As she put it, a parent who turns a product on believes the child is safe, and a school that turns it on believes the same, but they are not. Parent Nataliya Pirumova said she is not entirely opposed to technology in class, so long as it is used properly, and that it makes sense to include AI literacy courses.

Pirumova said such courses would let students understand how the technology works, and she argued that it makes sense to teach students to use it. She said AI is not going away, and that schools need to figure out how to teach students to engage with it in an intelligent way rather than in a free-for-all. The articles give no background on OR Unplugged beyond the fact that it has an outreach coordinator and took part in a protest that was one of several across the country. They do not say when the group was founded, how many members it has, or how it came to know about the alleged threat to schools. They also do not say which schools or districts Masarie had in mind when she described the threat of being cut off from searching on Google's platform.

Google's statement also describes changes that are still to come, beginning with a new approach to controls for schools next year. The company said it is updating that approach to address feedback it has heard from educators. Under the change, the Gemini app, Gemini Notebook and Search will be off by default until schools decide which services to enable. The articles do not say whether the protest will be repeated, or whether OR Unplugged plans further action in Portland. They also leave open whether Google denies the claim that it threatened to cut off school search access, since the company's statement does not address that claim directly.

stories.Headline: Surging AI chip revenue and Microsoft deal boost Cerebras Systems stock by 17%
stories.Summary:
Cerebras Systems, the artificial intelligence chipmaker, released third-quarter results on Thursday, November 12, 2026, and the figures comfortably beat expectations. On the same day the company announced a new customer deal with Microsoft, and its stock rose almost 18 percent in late trading. Core adjusted revenue for the quarter came to $230.9 million, up 70 percent from a year earlier and ahead of the $214.7 million that Wall Street had targeted. The company reported a loss before certain costs such as stock compensation of 67 cents per share, against Wall Street guidance of a 14-cent loss. The article cautions that the two numbers are not directly comparable, because of accounting idiosyncrasies at Cerebras.

Cerebras includes some pass-through revenue that is subtracted from the total, which explains part of the gap between its adjusted figures and its reported ones. It also issues warrants to its major customers, and these are amortized as noncash reductions in revenue under standard accounting rules and are left out of the adjusted number. Its adjusted operating margin was negative 14 percent, a clear improvement on the negative 24 percent it had guided to three months earlier. The backlog for hardware and cloud services rose from $25 billion in August to $26 billion at the end of the quarter. For the fourth quarter, the company expects a core gross margin of 47 to 49 percent and revenue between $310 million and $330 million, compared with analyst estimates of 42.1 percent on sales of $271 million.

Chief Executive Andrew Feldman told analysts on a conference call that Cerebras holds an advantage because its competitors are struggling to keep pace with customer demand and are dealing with growing order backlogs. He said long lead times and higher costs for Nvidia's graphics processing units create an opening for Cerebras, particularly in selling hardware. Feldman said a significant portion of the backlog comes from the company's deal with OpenAI Group PBC, which implies that other customers do not have to wait so long for their orders. He said the agreement with Microsoft was signed a month earlier and that the company believes revenue from it begins to show up in the first quarter of fiscal 2027. Feldman also said the company is evaluating financing options to meet customer demand and to work down its order backlog, and that it believes revenue will triple by the end of fiscal 2027.

Investors were clearly impressed with the growth over the quarter, and perhaps even more with the progress toward profitability, though Cerebras has not yet shown a profit. The article notes that the small rise in the backlog does little to settle concerns that the deals are on the small side. Wall Street's long-term forecast for fiscal 2027 revenue is $2.92 billion, slightly above the roughly $2.85 billion that tripling would produce. Capital has become much harder to secure in recent months amid growing nervousness about the huge sums being spent on AI infrastructure buildouts. Microsoft, the newest customer, is affected by the new agreement, though the company did not provide many particulars about it.

Cerebras has recently signed deals with Amazon Web Services and Oracle, and it added Microsoft as a new customer on the day of the report. Nvidia remains its biggest rival and still dominates the AI chip industry, accounting for over 90 percent of all chip sales, according to some analysts. Nvidia is in turmoil following the resignation of its co-founder and chief executive Jensen Huang. It is believed he was likely forced out after being outed for an affair with an executive of a Singapore-based data center infrastructure firm, who is believed to have been acting as a spy for Chinese intelligence and a conduit for illegal GPU shipments into China. Reports that emerged a day earlier said Huang had a second affair with a Nvidia executive, and reportedly a third.

Nvidia is trying to maintain stability by naming longtime Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim chief executive. The article says it may take a while for Cerebras and other chipmakers to take advantage of the disruption at Nvidia, though the short-term prospects for Cerebras still look good. Revenue from the Microsoft agreement is expected to begin showing up in the first quarter of fiscal 2027, according to Feldman. The fourth-quarter guidance and the goal of tripling revenue by the end of fiscal 2027 are the next figures against which the company will be measured. The articles do not say what form the financing will take, nor do they give details of the Microsoft agreement.

stories.Headline: OpenAI launches local API inference for GPT-6 Luna in India
stories.Summary:
OpenAI has launched local processing and inference for its API in India, so eligible organisations can run supported AI workloads without sending any requests outside the country. The announcement was reported by Inc42 on 12 November 2026 and by TechGig on 13 November 2026. The service is limited to the GPT-6 Luna model at launch, and it expands the data residency options OpenAI already offered in India. With the update, both the handling of an API request and the model computation take place on servers located in India. Supported customer content is also kept within the country, which gives businesses greater control over where their data is processed.

The new offering supports GPT-6 Luna input and output through two interfaces, the Responses API and the Chat Completions API. To use it, developers must create a new API project, select India as the region for both storage and processing, and use the India regional endpoint. Local processing applies only to direct API usage, so it does not extend to other ways of reaching the model. Businesses can use it for text-based tasks, including document summaries, drafting replies, and analysing information for employees. With the launch, India joins Australia and Japan as the markets where OpenAI has introduced regional API inference capability.

Nitin Bawankule, who heads enterprise in India at OpenAI, said the need for in-country processing had stopped some Indian businesses from using AI for important work. Local inference is intended to remove that barrier, and he said it could help more organisations move from experimenting with AI to deploying it in everyday operations. He also said it gives businesses greater control over where their data is processed. OpenAI is responsible for building and offering the service, and it has presented the launch as part of its broader push in India. The company has set out specific steps for customers to follow in order to use the new offering.

Reports from Inc42 and TechGig say the feature is aimed at sectors such as financial services, where data handling rules dictate how AI applications are deployed at scale. Inc42 notes that banks, financial institutions and government agencies cannot compromise on how data is stored and processed before a model is deployed. For these clients, data residency and infrastructure requirements can limit the use of international frontier AI models in production environments. Indian businesses that need in-country processing are the main group affected by the change. Inc42 also says the entry of OpenAI and Anthropic into this segment could narrow the advantage that locally hosted inference gave Indian AI startups such as Sarvam AI.

Until now, OpenAI's residency options in India only covered the storage of customer data, which left the processing of requests outside the country. Inc42 says OpenAI is not the first international AI company to address India's data localisation requirements. In August, Anthropic announced plans to bring in-country inference for its Claude models to India through Amazon Bedrock, the managed service from AWS for building generative AI applications. Anthropic has since made similar data residency capabilities available for certain models on AWS Bedrock. The launch also follows the OpenAI for India initiative announced earlier this year, which covers AI infrastructure, enterprise adoption, skills, and local partnerships, including a partnership with Tata Group to build domestic AI data centre capacity.

Inc42 reports that OpenAI has a strong position in the Indian market, where more than 10 Cr people use ChatGPT every week, and that the company is looking to earn revenue from it. Data inference is described as another piece of that India revenue, alongside new business tools such as Businesses in ChatGPT. That beta lets companies claim and manage their profiles through a Business Hub, where eligible businesses in markets including India can claim profiles subject to verification requirements. Business Agents, which let customers ask product questions inside ChatGPT, are initially available only to eligible ecommerce and online service businesses in the US. The articles do not say when local inference will extend beyond GPT-6 Luna, and they give no timeline for supporting other models or other ways of accessing them.

stories.Headline: AI privacy starts with your data
stories.Summary:
The European Union has fined Match Group, the owner of the dating app Tinder, €11 million for failing to give users proper access to their personal data. The fine was reported by AFP on 13 November 2026, and the penalty was imposed by Ireland's Data Protection Commission. The regulator found that Tinder's "Download My Data" tool left out certain categories of personal information, which broke EU data protection rules. In other cases the tool offered only summaries of the data without clearly telling users that this was all they were receiving. The investigation behind the decision was launched in 2020, so the case has taken roughly six years to reach this outcome.

The decision does more than impose a financial penalty, because it also orders Match Group to change how it handles personal data. Ireland's Data Protection Commission requires the company to bring its data processing practices into compliance with the General Data Protection Regulation, known as the GDPR. The deadline set for that compliance is three months, which gives Match Group a short window to correct the problems the regulator identified. The €11 million figure applies to the failures found in the "Download My Data" tool, and the order covers how the company processes personal information more broadly. The articles name Ireland as the country whose regulator led the case, and they identify Tinder as the service whose users were affected.

Responsibility for the violations lies with Match Group, which owns Tinder and operates the "Download My Data" tool at the centre of the case. Match Group rejected the findings of the Irish regulator and said it does not accept that it broke the rules as described. The company announced that it plans to appeal the decision, so the penalty and the order may be challenged rather than simply accepted. It also insisted that Tinder maintains strong privacy protections for its users, offering that as its answer to the regulator's conclusions. Ireland's Data Protection Commission stands behind its findings and is the body that issued both the fine and the order to comply.

The people most directly affected are Tinder's users, who were meant to be able to see their personal data through the "Download My Data" tool but did not always receive all of it. Some of the information they were entitled to was missing from what they could download, and some was provided only as a summary without a clear explanation. Match Group's own response is the main reaction the articles report, since the company disputes the regulator's account and says user privacy is well protected. The AFP report, relayed by BGNES, presents the €11 million fine as an action taken by the European Union as a whole, even though Ireland's regulator carried it out. A separate opinion piece published the same day by TechRadar discusses data privacy in a different setting and does not mention Tinder or Match Group.

The background the articles give begins with the investigation, which was launched in 2020 and examined how Tinder let users reach their own data. Under EU data protection rules, people are entitled to access their personal information, and the regulator judged that the Tinder tool fell short of that standard. The TechRadar opinion piece, written by Adam Mayer, who is Technical Product Marketing Director at Qlik, describes how privacy challenges grow as artificial intelligence gains access to more company data. It reports that 95% of enterprises have delayed or cancelled AI projects because of infrastructure and data governance challenges, a figure it ties to the difficulty of managing privacy. The same piece says personally identifiable information such as names, addresses or financial details should be clearly labelled, and that sensitive information should stay in live systems wherever possible.

The next step in the Tinder case is the appeal that Match Group has said it will bring against the findings of Ireland's Data Protection Commission. The three-month deadline for bringing its data processing practices into line with the GDPR is already running under the regulator's order. The articles do not say where or when the appeal will be filed, nor whether the order and the fine remain in force while it is pending. They also do not say whether the missing categories of personal data will be restored to users or how any changes to the tool would work. Nothing in the articles explains how Match Group will answer the specific omissions the regulator found, or when the dispute might finally be resolved.

stories.Headline: BIM Trichy and UT Arlington Redefine International Education: US Master's Degree in AI for Business Comes to India
stories.Summary:
Bharathidasan Institute of Management, a business school based in Tiruchirappalli, has signed a Memorandum of Understanding with The University of Texas at Arlington. The agreement covers a joint Master of Science in Artificial Intelligence for Business, known by the abbreviation MSAIB. The signing was reported by The Hindu BusinessLine on November 13, 2026, and a photograph shows officials from both institutions at the ceremony. The programme is aimed at working professionals and will integrate AI machine learning, data engineering and generative AI into business strategy. It will be hosted at IIT Madras Research Park rather than at either partner's own campus.

The programme will begin with an initial trial cohort of 25 students, and faculty from the University of Texas at Arlington will facilitate it. It carries an indicative tuition fee of US$27,000, set as an alternative to the substantially higher overall cost of two years of full-time residential study in the United States. The hybrid learning model uses eight-week courses, with seven weeks of online instruction followed by one week of in-person learning. Students will be taught by the American university's faculty throughout the programme. They will also take part in a one-week immersion in the United States, which includes company visits, interactions with business executives and exposure to industry applications of artificial intelligence.

Ravi Appasamy, Chairman of the Board of Governors at BIM Tiruchirappalli, described the partnership as a deliberate step in building a globally recognised institution. He said the Board is firmly committed to positioning BIM as globally connected, academically distinguished and industry-relevant. He added that BIM is entering a new phase of its transformational journey, and that the institute is not simply building for the next decade. In his words, it is laying the foundations for the next generation of management education. Asit K. Barma, Director of BIM Tiruchirappalli, was also at the signing, as was Fernando Jaramillo, Associate Dean of Academic Affairs at the Texas university.

Radha K. Mahapatra, Chair and Professor of Information Systems and Operations Management at the University of Texas at Arlington, spoke about how students will be admitted. He said enrolments will be conducted through the university's own specialised framework. Although the programme is designed for working professionals, he said the university is also open to selecting capable students who have just completed their undergraduate studies. Separately, Anurag Behar, CEO of the Azim Premji Foundation, wrote in Mint on November 11, 2026 that India's higher education is in worse shape than its school education. He argued that artificial intelligence could be the death blow to the country's higher education institutions if the existing mess is perpetuated.

The partnership comes at a time when international student mobility has been disrupted by visa policies, rising education and living costs, and geopolitical developments. The Institute of International Education's Open Doors 2025 report said new international student enrolments in the US fell by 7 per cent. Australia saw international student commencements drop by 12 per cent compared with the corresponding period. The UK reported a 16 per cent year-over-year decline in sponsored study visa grants to Indian nationals. Meanwhile, several global universities have set up in India, including the University of Liverpool in Bengaluru, the University of Bristol in Mumbai and the University of Western Australia in Mumbai and Chennai.

Behar's article offers its own account of the problems facing Indian higher education. He argues that many college classrooms sit empty because neither students nor teachers show up, and that research is conflated with teaching. He says public funding has been squeezed while enrolment ambitions have grown, and that his estimate is only 10 to 15 per cent of institutions are serious about their work. He pictures a loop in which a machine prepares the lesson, another writes the student's answer and a third marks it, so that no human mind learns anything. He calls for AI to be mostly banished from education and for a good higher education system to be built on new foundations.

The articles say the programme will start with a trial cohort of 25 students, but they give no start date for classes or for the first intake. They do not say how many students might be admitted after the trial cohort, or how the programme will be assessed. The articles do not say whether the Master's degree will be awarded by the University of Texas at Arlington, by BIM or jointly by both. They also leave open when applications will open and what admission criteria the university's own framework will use. The sources do not explain how the indicative tuition fee of US$27,000 might change, or whether any part of the cost will be covered by the partners.

stories.Headline: Meta, TikTok join Google to push back on Indonesia’s planned AI copyright law revisions
stories.Summary:
Meta and TikTok joined Google on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, in pushing back against proposed revisions to Indonesia's copyright law at a parliamentary hearing in Jakarta. The revisions would require digital platforms to pay publishers for displaying news content, and would also set rules for artificial intelligence. Reuters reported the story from Jakarta in a dispatch dated November 11, reporting by Stanley Widianto and editing by Emelia Sithole-Matarise. The three companies each sent a representative to speak before lawmakers about the proposed changes to the law. Reuters first reported the planned revisions exclusively in July, citing a draft of the bill.

If the bill is passed, Indonesia could become the first country in Southeast Asia to incorporate AI into its copyright law. The proposed revisions would require digital platforms to pay publishers when they display news content, a requirement that is central to the objections raised at the hearing. The bill would also set rules for AI, a field in which governments around the world are grappling with the technology's impact on copyright rules. One open question globally is the use of work created by humans to train AI models. TikTok's objection concerned disclosure requirements, which it argued should not apply where AI is used only in an assistive capacity rather than to fully create content.

Agung Pamungkas, Google's Indonesia government affairs and public policy manager, told the hearing that requiring tech platforms to pay compensation for showing links to news content from publishers would limit Indonesians' access to news. Berni Moestafa, Meta's public policy head in Indonesia, said that requiring platforms to pay compensation meant publishers could lose readership traffic, along with potential advertising and subscription revenue. Berni added that directing readers to an article is different from reproducing or republishing the article itself. Noudhy Valdryno, TikTok's head of public policy in Indonesia, spoke separately and told lawmakers that disclosure requirements should not apply to assistive uses of AI. Noudhy also urged lawmakers to preserve safe-harbour protections, saying platforms cannot reliably determine copyright ownership or licences.

The people and groups affected include digital platforms, which would face the payment and disclosure obligations, and the publishers who would receive payment for news content shown by platforms. Indonesians who read news through these platforms are also affected, since Google argued that the payment requirement would limit their access to news. Meta argued that publishers themselves could lose readership traffic as well as potential advertising and subscription revenue if the payment rule were adopted. The articles do not report any statement from publishers, from lawmakers, or from the Indonesian government in response to the platforms' testimony. The Reuters report records only the three companies' positions at the hearing, with no reply from those who drafted the bill.

The background the articles give is limited to the bill's origin and its place in a wider global debate. Reuters exclusively reported the planned revisions in July, citing a draft of the bill, which is how the proposal first became public. Governments globally are working out how AI affects copyright rules, including the use of human-created work to train AI models. Indonesia's draft would put it among the first countries to write AI directly into its copyright law, and the first in Southeast Asia. The same week, a separate report from Japan's Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications examined how Google, LINE Yahoo, Meta and TikTok handle personal information through conversational AI and advertising, though that report concerns privacy rather than copyright.

The articles do not say when Indonesia's parliament will vote on the bill, so the timetable for any decision remains open. They also do not say whether lawmakers will change the draft in response to the objections from Google, Meta and TikTok. It is not stated whether the payment requirement for news content or the AI disclosure rules will survive in their current form. What compensation publishers would receive, and how it would be calculated, is not set out in the reporting. The Japanese report on privacy risks was not finalised until after deliberations held from October 19 to 21, 2026, and the available text does not say what steps Japan will take next.

stories.Headline: Global AI stocks sink as Nvidia crisis deepens sector selloff - CNA
stories.Summary:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday, Nov 12, 2026, following a deepening scandal around his affairs, and global AI-linked stocks tumbled as a result. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will take over as interim CEO while the company looks for a permanent successor. Nvidia's shares fell 8.2 per cent to a more than 16-month low in early trading that day. Its market value was on track to close below US$4 trillion for the first time since July 2025. The chip giant has lost more than US$550 billion in market value since its board announced an investigation on Sunday.

The investigation concerns Huang's relationship with a businesswoman called Alice Huang, who is alleged to be a Chinese spy. Chipmakers led the selloff, with the Philadelphia chips index sliding 1.3 per cent, while Marvell Technology slumped 3.8 per cent and Oracle shed 2.6 per cent. Micron Technology fell 2.5 per cent, Sandisk eased 6 per cent and Western Digital 3.7 per cent. Lumentum, Coherent and Dell eased between 3 per cent and 5.1 per cent, while Caterpillar and Vistra slipped about 0.5 per cent each. Japan and South Korea closed nearly 0.7 per cent lower, and tech stocks in Europe were down about 1 per cent.

Nvidia's board announced the investigation on Sunday, and the company said Kress would serve as interim CEO as it searches for a successor. The articles give no comment from Huang himself on his resignation. On Tuesday, Nvidia had already hired lawyers for an internal investigation tied to its CEO. Yahoo Finance's page also carried a banner reporting that Huang had been accused of a second affair. Nvidia's leadership now rests with Kress while the search continues.

Analysts and investors voiced concern about what the turmoil means for the wider sector. Joe Saluzzi of Themis Trading noted that Nvidia has been called the "Bank of AI" and asked whether a step back could cut off funding to smaller companies that need it. Steve Sosnick of Interactive Brokers said the interlocking deals raise the question of whether they created more stability or more fragility, and that the coming weeks will show. Tim Ghriskey of Ingalls & Snyder said he sees selling in Nvidia and other AI firms as buying opportunities and does not see Nvidia falling apart. Neocloud firms CoreWeave fell 9.1 per cent and Nebius dropped 16.2 per cent after saying its 2026 revenue would come in at the low end of its forecast, while IREN and Applied Digital also traded lower.

Nvidia finances infrastructure built around its chips, a strategy that has drawn scrutiny over circular funding. CoreWeave, which Nvidia backs, had surged more than 27 per cent in the previous session when its earnings ignited a relief rally in AI stocks. Earlier this month the Nasdaq entered a technical correction after the Democrats swept the midterm elections, including in states opposed to data centres, stoking fears that tighter regulation could slow the AI build-out. On Tuesday, selling was also driven by a hot US inflation report that raised expectations the Federal Reserve will raise rates again next month. Over the past month the Nasdaq Composite has dropped by 1 per cent or more eight times and risen by that much six times.

Short sellers of Nvidia have made US$9.6 billion in on-paper profits so far this week, according to the data firm ORTEX. Nvidia trades at about 12 times its 12-month forward earnings estimates, its lowest since November 2012, according to data compiled by LSEG. AMD and Broadcom rose 3.7 per cent and 5.6 per cent on expectations that the turmoil could create opportunity for rivals, and Alphabet, Amazon.com and Microsoft rose between 0.8 per cent and 2.7 per cent. Analysts have said the scandal could spur tighter US scrutiny of AI cloud providers in Southeast Asia. The articles do not say who will become permanent CEO, how long the investigation will last, or whether the allegations against Alice Huang will be substantiated.

stories.Headline: Claude Whiteboards, Claude Sheets, and Claude Data
stories.Summary:
Anthropic launched Claude Whiteboards and Claude Sheets in beta on November 11, 2026, according to an announcement posted on claude.com that morning. The same announcement said Claude Dashboards, which had launched in beta in October, became generally available under the new name Claude Data. All three tools are available on every paid plan, and they work on web, desktop, and mobile. Anthropic said the aim is to keep documents, boards, sheets, and dashboards inside Claude so teams can keep editing them together. When users are ready, they can bring the outputs directly into partner tools and continue working there.

Claude Whiteboards is a shared board where a team brainstorms with Claude, and it can turn a spoken plan into a timeline with owners and dates. In a retro meeting, everyone can add notes, and Claude can group them by theme and draft action items for each person. Users can drag a box around any part of the board and ask Claude questions about it, and finished boards can become a doc or deck. Claude Sheets builds spreadsheets with tabs, formulas, formatting, and drop-downs, often from a prompt like a campaign tracker or a hiring budget, and it outlines each edit so changes can be tracked. Claude Data adds certified queries, live sharing, data stories, design systems, caching with per-dashboard refresh cadences, and tracked changes that let users roll back to a specific version.

Anthropic wrote the announcement in its own voice, and it said sheets have only simple spreadsheet functionality for now, with more being added. Anyone needing the full power of Excel can export a file to .xlsx or CSV, or use Claude for Excel. The company said it renamed Dashboards because the way companies use their data is broader than dashboards, and the product now covers how they work more broadly. Its stated reason for the launch was that working with Claude often meant moving output into another tool, where Claude lacked live access to follow progress and changes. Anthropic also said certified queries and live sharing are in beta, and that Claude Data needs a data connector, such as a warehouse or CRM.

On November 13, ZDNET published a hands-on review by senior contributing editor David Gewirtz, who tested Claude Sheets on surveys, shopping, and app feedback. He said Claude updated five spreadsheet tabs and two whiteboards in about 10 minutes, while he made coffee, after he asked it to rerun his customer-feedback analysis with an earlier start date. He found four major advantages over using Claude with Google Sheets, including that one dataset can feed a sheet, whiteboards, and a slide without any importing or exporting. He liked pointing Claude at a specific statistic and typing "Explain this," and he said Claude can review its own work from within the app. His Waterpik research became a three-tab sheet whose top pick was the MOCEL model he had already bought, and his app-feedback analysis suggested users want one page opened for free and do not realize the feature already exists.

Among Claude Data's partners, Anthropic named Amplitude, Mixpanel, Omni, PostHog, and Sigma. Partner tools named for continuing work from Whiteboards include Lucid, Miro, and Vani by Zoho, and those named for Sheets include Airtable, Asana, monday.com, and Smartsheet. Gewirtz said Whiteboards is somewhat competitive with FigJam from Figma, Mural, and Lucidspark. Data teams are affected because they can certify the queries everyone should use, and charts built on those metrics carry a certified badge so dashboards do not end up with conflicting data. Viewers of a live-shared dashboard see the results of approved queries and cannot run others with the sharer's access, even if they lack access to the connectors that keep the data current.

Claude Dashboards launched in beta in October, enabling teams to ask quick questions of company data in tools like Amazon Redshift, BigQuery, and ClickHouse. Before this release, Anthropic said, every dashboard would reload on every load, which caching now avoids. Anthropic also said starting November 11 that interactive connectors can open as full apps beside a conversation or in full screen, in tools like Adobe, Atlassian, Box, and Notion. A November 10 article said partners can now embed their apps directly in Claude, so users and Claude work in the same tool on the same screen. Gewirtz's August survey of two expert-to-journalist matching services began as a Claude conversation and a Google Sheet, and he first ran his uninstall data through ChatGPT in 2023.

The date for administrators to watch is November 19, 2026, when Claude Data turns on by default on Enterprise plans. On Team plans all three tools are on by default, while on Enterprise plans Whiteboards and Sheets are off by default. Administrators can change these settings anytime under Organization settings > Artifacts. Anthropic did not say when Whiteboards, Sheets, certified queries, or live sharing will leave beta, or how much more spreadsheet functionality is coming. Gewirtz's review was cut off partway through his rerun test, and the articles do not describe the rest of his results or his final verdict.

stories.Headline: Google Brings Gemini Live to Apple CarPlay
stories.Summary:
Google announced on Wednesday, November 11, a global rollout that brings its Gemini Live assistant directly to Apple CarPlay, extending its conversational AI to Apple's in-car platform. The rollout lets drivers hold natural, back-and-forth conversations with the assistant through their vehicle's display, giving iPhone users another hands-free way to use Google's services. A separate announcement came on November 12 from HeartCore Enterprises, a Nasdaq-listed IPO consulting company based in Tokyo. HeartCore said its wholly owned subsidiary, HeartCore Financial, had entered a non-exclusive business development and sales agency agreement in Japan with ONE AI Co., Ltd. ONE AI is a Korean developer of CPU-native, on-device physical AI, and the deal will introduce its Axis.ONE platform to Japanese manufacturers.

Drivers can start a new Gemini conversation or resume a recent one by tapping the Gemini icon on the CarPlay screen. They can interrupt the assistant to add information, change subjects or pause when they need to concentrate on driving. Through connected Google Workspace applications such as Gmail and Google Calendar, drivers can ask Gemini to summarize unread emails, review long message threads, check upcoming appointments and prepare for meetings. The feature is available globally to Gemini users on iOS in every language supported by Gemini Live, and users must update the Gemini app, enable microphone permissions and have used Gemini Live on their phones at least once. Under the HeartCore agreement, the term is three years, with automatic one-year renewals unless either party gives notice of non-renewal, and HeartCore earns a tiered commission of 15% of net revenue in the first year, 10% in the second and 8% in the third.

Google said the CarPlay integration is designed to let drivers accomplish more during their commutes while minimizing distractions. HeartCore's chief executive, Sumitaka Kanno, said he believes ONE AI's technology could transform how manufacturers put AI to work, noting that industrial robots have been precise for decades but mostly cannot see, adapt or learn. He added that Axis.ONE is designed to change that for robots already installed, without forcing manufacturers to replace systems they spent years and significant capital building. ONE AI's chief executive, In Chan Baek, said industrial robots should not have to be replaced to become intelligent. He said his team spent more than two decades optimizing AI on Intel silicon, and called HeartCore's local presence and Nasdaq-listed experience an ideal fit for entering the Japanese market.

Gemini's arrival follows the expansion of other AI assistants onto CarPlay, including OpenAI's ChatGPT, Anthropic's Claude, Microsoft's Copilot, Perplexity and xAI's Grok. The additions give drivers more ways to reach conversational AI through their vehicles rather than relying only on traditional voice assistants. For manufacturers, the pitch is to keep existing equipment investments, reduce reliance on dedicated GPU infrastructure and keep sensitive production data inside the factory. ONE AI estimates total cost reductions of up to 90% compared with conventional GPU-based deployments, and says per-site learning cycles fell from about 100 days to 10 days and, in some cases, from 30 days to one hour. HeartCore noted that these technology descriptions and performance figures come from ONE AI, have not been independently verified, and are not guarantees of results in any particular customer deployment.

The Google move expands its competition in the growing market for conversational AI assistants across mobile and connected devices. Gemini already supports Android Auto and vehicles with Google built-in, while its earlier CarPlay integration was limited to Google Maps. Google said in September that its Gemini 3.8 Live and Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking models were designed to power more capable voice agents, with gains in real-time reasoning and complex task completion. The company said the Gemini app passed 1 billion monthly active users in August, its fastest-growing product to reach that milestone. On the industrial side, the International Federation of Robotics reports more than 4.6 million industrial robots operating in factories worldwide, and ONE AI was founded in January 2026, is led by former Intel APAC AI leadership, and is headquartered in Seoul.

Under its agreement, HeartCore will introduce Axis.ONE to Japanese manufacturers, system integrators and industrial operators while coordinating proof-of-concept deployments and pilot programs. It will also present demonstrations and technical information to prospective customers and partners and lead the negotiation of commercial agreements, while ONE AI provides technical support and demonstration resources for each deployment. Both parties intend to explore future expansion opportunities with manufacturers and industrial partners in the United States. HeartCore's release lists risks that could change outcomes, including whether the technology performs as expected with robots and control systems from different manufacturers, whether HeartCore Financial can generate customer introductions and commission revenue, and whether ONE AI, an early-stage company, can scale its operations. The articles do not say when any Axis.ONE customer will sign or deploy, and they give no timeline for further Gemini features on CarPlay.

stories.Headline: Trust Stamp launches biometric approval tool for AI-agent transactions
stories.Summary:
Trust Stamp, listed as IDAI on Nasdaq and AIID on the Irish Stock Exchange, has launched a product called Knowing Consent, announced on 10 November 2026. The product confirms that a bank customer knowingly approves each transaction that an AI agent initiates on their behalf. It relies on proprietary processes covered by issued patents, together with a new process the company says is being patented and is ready for immediate use. Trust Stamp, described as a global provider of AI-powered trust, identity and security solutions, is based in Atlanta, Georgia. The company says the tool separates an AI agent initiating a request from the human account owner who consents to that request.

Under the system, either the AI agent or the financial institution can start the authorization flow, and customers register biometrically on first use to create a personal identity token. For later requests, customers can be prompted through SMS, email, push notification or the relevant software application to take a secure selfie. Proof-of-life and anti-spoofing checks, with optional device verification and other authentication protocols, confirm that the account owner is present when approval is requested. In an integrated deployment, the authorization screen shows the specific action and its details before the customer finishes live verification, which ties the approval to that request. Trust Stamp filed U.S. provisional patent application number 64/195,409 for the process on 11 November, adding to its existing patents.

Trust Stamp CEO Gareth Genner said more than one hundred financial institutions are already integrated with the company's Orchestration Layer. He said the biometric authorization adds a live, customer-centered approval step to agent-initiated activity, and that it can be implemented within days, either through the Orchestration Layer or a single API call. Genner told shareholders the process is triggered within an institution's own access and transaction policies, with no significant changes to its authentication flow. Biometric Update reported that the system distinguishes an agent's access to a customer's account from the account holder's authorization of a specific transaction. It also reported that the biometric step applies even when the agent already has permission to access the account.

The announcement points to concern in the banking sector about agents using customer credentials. NIST's Bill Fisher and Ryan Galluzzo wrote in a NIST Cybersecurity Insights article that credential sharing is a bad idea in all contexts, warning that it can create accountability gaps. Reuters reported that major U.S. banks are blocking some third-party agents from customer accounts. JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon described unrestricted outside agents as too risky for clients and for the bank. Biometric Update added that the banks' restrictions reflect worries about credential sharing and unauthorized transactions, and that iProov has introduced an implementation of the Human Approval and Presence Specification, which uses biometric liveness checks to support human approval of specific AI-agent actions.

Trust Stamp has used biometrics to authenticate financial transactions before, and Knowing Consent applies similar checks to agent-initiated ones. The company earlier introduced Trusted Authentication for high-value and high-risk transactions, using biometric verification. Last year, Neural Payments integrated Trust Stamp's technology for identity enrollment and later selfie-based payment authentication. The company's recent activity also includes a selection as a direct participant in the Important Project of Common European Interest on Advanced Semiconductor Technologies, and a partnership with Seiko Solutions on a facial recognition service for Japan. Biometric Update's coverage of the launch was written by Abhishek Jadhav, while the Proactive report on it was written by editor Angela Harmantas.

Trust Stamp says Knowing Consent is available for integration now, and the articles give no customer names or deployment dates. The provisional patent application is filed, but the articles do not say when or whether a full patent will be granted. The articles report no financial terms, pricing or revenue expectations for the product. They also do not say whether any of the banks restricting third-party agents have tested or adopted the system. How the product will perform in live use is left open, since the claims about speed and low friction come from the company.

stories.Headline: Applied Digital Sinks 8% as Nebius Outlook and NVIDIA CEO Exit Hit AI Data Center Stocks; Cipher Digital Falls 4%, TeraWulf Slides 3%
stories.Summary:
Applied Digital stock fell about 8 percent in Thursday morning trading on November 12, 2026, as two separate shocks hit the AI infrastructure trade at once. The shares were at $16.45, which erased the company's 7 percent gain from November 11, when the stock had closed at $17.91. Nebius, an AI cloud provider, reported its third quarter 2026 results on November 12 and issued a weak outlook that rattled the sector. At NVIDIA, the chipmaker at the center of AI data center spending, Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive, and news of the exit broke before the open. David Moadel of 24/7 Wall St. wrote that Applied Digital's heavy borrowing makes it especially sensitive to doubts about how AI customers will pay for capacity.

Nebius said it expects capital expenditures of $40 billion to $45 billion in 2027, a spending load that raises questions about how quickly AI cloud providers can keep leasing the capacity Applied Digital builds. Huang's resignation sent stock futures lower, and technology was the weakest major sector, while the small-cap Russell 2000 index was down 1 percent. Cipher Digital traded at $6.80, down 4 percent, and TeraWulf traded at $12.90, down 3 percent, the smallest decline among the four names. Core Scientific was at $13.88, down 5 percent, a steeper slide than Cipher Digital's but milder than Applied Digital's. Applied Digital's quarterly interest cost, including capitalized interest, was $113.1 million in the quarter ended August 31, well above its $65.8 million of base rent.

The article attributes the key figures to named people and firms rather than to a single company statement. Morgan Stanley analyst Stephen Byrd kept an Equal Weight rating on Applied Digital on November 9 and cut his price target to $25 from $41. Byrd raised the discount rates and debt costs he assumes across the AI data center group, which helps explain why the debt-heavy company is more exposed than its peers. Applied Digital chief executive Wes Cummins stated on November 2 that the company still needs funding for roughly 800 MW over the next 12 months. Management also describes demand as extremely robust, and the company points to $36 billion of contracted revenue.

Several other companies were affected by the same pressures, and the article describes how each is exposed. Cipher Digital also had its price target cut by Morgan Stanley on November 9, and like Applied Digital it is converting former Bitcoin mining power and land into AI and high-performance computing data centers, so it faces similar financing and tenant questions. TeraWulf took in $62.99 million of revenue from high-performance computing leasing in the third quarter as more Lake Mariner capacity came online. CoreWeave, an AI cloud provider, is among Applied Digital's tenants, and bears point to Applied Digital's reliance on it alongside its $6.4 billion of debt. The article also notes that Texas's governor-elect promised a data center moratorium last week, following the November 3 midterm elections.

The article draws a contrast between Applied Digital and its peers in how each one builds and funds its campuses. Applied Digital owns the land, designs the buildings and operates its AI factory campuses, then leases them to investment-grade hyperscalers under long take-or-pay contracts. Its biggest campuses are in North Dakota, where cheap power and a cool climate support large builds, and it is expanding into Louisiana and Alabama. The first Polaris Forge 1 building was designed for liquid-cooled NVIDIA systems, which is why the leadership change at NVIDIA adds uncertainty. Cipher Digital funds each campus with ring-fenced project bonds and still runs a legacy mining site in Odessa, Texas, while TeraWulf backs its Anthropic lease with investment-grade credit support and Core Scientific plans to exit mining by year-end and operate as a pure colocation provider.

The next test for Applied Digital is whether it can finance its remaining expansion at rates its leases can cover. Its fiscal second quarter 2027 report is expected in January 2027 and could bring the next funding update. The Louisiana campus could back up to $4.6 billion of local revenue bonds, though no rate has been set. The article leaves open how much of the roughly 800 MW will be funded within the next 12 months, and it does not say whether Huang has a successor at NVIDIA. It also says each business model still depends on tenants that can keep paying for computing capacity as costs rise, and it suggests a cautious approach until Applied Digital's funding plan is clearer.

stories.Headline: HK ranks 11th in digital and AI competitiveness
stories.Summary:
Hong Kong placed 11th in the world and fourth in Asia in the World Digital and AI Ranking 2026, which the Switzerland-based International Institute for Management Development (IMD) published on Wednesday, November 11. The ranking covered 70 economies. It assesses how well an economy can develop, adopt, deploy and govern digital technologies and artificial intelligence in a way that produces lasting economic and social value. Hong Kong's result was announced alongside the rest of the list, which showed several other Asian economies placing in or near the top ten.

The benchmark is built on five factors, and Hong Kong did best in workforce development, where it came second in the world. It ranked fifth for efficiency and 10th for technology and infrastructure. At the sub-factor level, the city came first globally in technological framework, practices, and education and training. It also placed among the world's top ten in talent, societal attitudes and regulatory framework.

The Hong Kong Special Administrative Region government responded through a spokesperson, who said the result recognised the city as one of the world's most competitive economies in digital and AI development. The spokesperson said the government is fully committed to turning Hong Kong into an international innovation and technology centre, in line with the First Five-Year Plan for Economic and Social Development of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region. Plans include strengthening the institutional framework for innovation and technology development and speeding up alignment with key national technology strategies. The government also intends to build a new model based on three major innovation and technology parks and five key research and development institutions.

The spokesperson added that the city will create a full industrial ecosystem that covers research and development, commercialisation, pilot production and mass production. It will also push new industrialisation and use AI to empower different parts of the economy. For comparison, South Korea's science ministry said its country climbed eight places to rank tenth, just ahead of Hong Kong. The United States took first place after rising three spots, Singapore was second among Asia-Pacific economies, China was seventh and Japan was 19th, while last year's leader Canada fell to fifth.

stories.Headline: New York's AI Safety Law Hits OpenAI, Anthropic Today
stories.Summary:
New York's RAISE Act, short for Responsible AI Safety and Enforcement, took effect on November 10, 2026, making the state the first to enforce comprehensive safety rules on major AI developers. The law requires OpenAI and Anthropic to register with state regulators, publicly disclose their safety practices, and report critical incidents involving their systems. Companies that fail to comply face financial penalties, though the exact structure of those fines remains under regulatory review. Governor Kathy Hochul signed the bill into law earlier this year, according to The Tech Buzz. Separately, a large Microsoft outage disrupted Outlook, Teams, Copilot and other workplace tools, and it also hit Microsoft 365 connectors used by OpenAI and Anthropic.

Registration requirements apply immediately, and companies must file detailed disclosures about their model architectures, training data sources, safety testing protocols, and incident response procedures. The law also mandates ongoing reporting, so if a registered system causes or contributes to a critical incident, developers have 72 hours to notify state authorities with a preliminary assessment. A critical incident is defined broadly as any malfunction, misuse, or unexpected behavior that results in significant harm to individuals, critical infrastructure, or public safety. The act focuses on advanced AI systems, meaning models with broad capabilities across multiple domains that could pose systemic risks, a definition that clearly covers large language models and their fine-tuned versions and API offerings. The law stops short of banning specific capabilities but creates a paper trail that regulators can follow if something goes wrong.

New York's Department of Financial Services will oversee compliance, but it has not disclosed how many investigators it has assigned to AI oversight or what its audit schedule looks like. Governor Hochul is the official who signed the act, and the department holds the enforcement role. Neither OpenAI nor Anthropic has issued a public statement about the enforcement deadline, though both have previously expressed support for thoughtful regulation in congressional testimony. On the Microsoft outage, OpenAI's status page opened an incident titled "Elevated errors affecting the Microsoft 365 connector," saying new connections might fail and tools might not work as expected. Anthropic logged an incident with the same title, which began at 17:52 UTC, and by 18:34 UTC it said it had identified an issue with an upstream provider.

Behind the scenes, lobbyists are working to shape implementation details and push for federal preemption that would override state laws, the article reports. The federal government remains absent from AI safety regulation, which let New York move first but also creates a patchwork compliance problem for companies operating nationally. OpenAI and Anthropic now face the prospect of navigating 50 different state frameworks if the trend accelerates. In the outage, Anthropic said mail, calendar and search tools were failing for most requests, and that Claude for Outlook was also affected, with some users unable to open the add-in. The status page also showed claude.ai and Claude Cowork as degraded, while the Claude API, Claude Code and Claude Console were listed as operational.

Anthropic is days away from its IPO, having priced it at $70 to $78 per share ahead of a November 19 public debut. The company now faces the added task of explaining its regulatory compliance posture to prospective investors during roadshow presentations. It has also been on a product blitz, launching Claude Meetings and shipping new Mythos and Fable models before going public. OpenAI, meanwhile, has turned ChatGPT into a business discovery engine, letting companies create profiles and listings inside the chatbot as it pivots toward commerce. The article says that expansion gives regulators more to scrutinize, since the law targets systems capable of general-purpose reasoning, and it notes that California's legislature debated similar measures this year but declined to pass comprehensive AI regulation.

Colorado and Massachusetts have working groups studying the issue, and the article predicts that if New York's enforcement goes smoothly, a wave of copycat legislation will follow across blue states by mid-2027. If it instead turns into a compliance burden that stifles innovation, the article says the backlash could freeze AI regulation nationwide for years. The enforcement test is still ahead, since the fine structure is under review and the department's staffing and audit plans are undisclosed. On the outage, Anthropic said at 22:23 UTC that a Microsoft 365 service incident caused the failures and that the tools were still failing for most requests. Microsoft said it applied an upstream authentication and routing configuration patch and is seeing positive results, but it gave no timeline for full restoration.

stories.Headline: The Next AI Chip Shortage May Be the Machines That Make HBM
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics said on November 12, 2026, that it had moved up the planned opening of its new high-bandwidth memory packaging plant in South Korea by one year. The new opening date is June 2028, according to Digitimes, and the company said the change was made to meet rising demand for AI server memory. The announcement came on the same day that ground was broken at the company's Onyang semiconductor campus in Asan. At the groundbreaking, President Lee Jae-myung spoke of a new advanced packaging fab there, followed in sequence by advanced equipment.

The articles give figures for the Onyang campus, which sits in Asan, South Korea. The new advanced packaging fab is put at about 6 trillion won, and the follow-on advanced equipment at about 40 trillion won. Together the fab and equipment come to 46 trillion won, which Aju Business Daily put at about $34.4 billion. At the day's base rate of 1,336.7 won per dollar, the equipment alone is about $29.9 billion, by FourWeekMBA's arithmetic. That equipment is about 6.7 times the fab figure.

President Lee Jae-myung spoke at the groundbreaking of the Chungcheong mega-project, where three investment projects began construction. They are an advanced semiconductor packaging fab and an advanced display line in Asan, plus a plant for high-performance AI server substrates in Sejong. He said companies and the government pledged the investment plan in July, and that the promise was becoming reality just four months later. He said the campus will become a key hub for advanced HBM packaging. Samsung chairman Lee Jae-yong, who attended, said the site, which centred on simple assembly and testing of general chips, will become a hub for advanced HBM for AI chips, as Financial News reported.

The articles carry few outside voices on the groundbreaking itself, though SMIC is cited by Digitimes on the wider memory market. Digitimes lists a report that AI memory may balance after mid-2028 while compute and supporting chips stay short, according to SMIC. The speech also named other Chungcheong projects whose groundbreakings are on schedule, including a memory and advanced packaging fab in Cheongju, an AI data centre in Dangjin and a biopharmaceutical plant in Osong. For HBM buyers, Samsung said on its earnings call that its 2027 HBM supply was already sold out. Samsung's market value rose about $11 billion at the Seoul open on November 12, as FourWeekMBA reported.

The articles give background on Samsung's spending, which FourWeekMBA took from the company's third-quarter release of October 29. Samsung said its capital expenditure reached 29 trillion won in the third quarter, up 19.8 trillion won from a year earlier. It expects about 84.4 trillion won for the full year, including 76.8 trillion won in its Device Solutions chip division. By FourWeekMBA's arithmetic, the 40 trillion won of Onyang equipment equals about 47% of the full-year figure, about 52% of the division's budget and about 1.4 times the third quarter's spending. Samsung also said it significantly scaled up sales of HBM4 in the third quarter, and that it expects AI infrastructure capital expenditure to reach a historic level in 2027.

Samsung has given the new opening date of June 2028 for the packaging plant, but the articles leave much open. President Lee gave no schedule or split by year for the 40 trillion won of equipment, saying only that it follows the fab in sequence. How much of that spending falls inside the 84.4 trillion won 2026 guidance is not stated, according to FourWeekMBA. Samsung's Korean newsroom had not published a release on the groundbreaking when FourWeekMBA checked, and it could not load the presidential office's own transcript. FourWeekMBA also said it did not contact Samsung for its piece, so the figures rest on the president's words as quoted by Korean outlets.

stories.Headline: CoreWeave Boosts AI Trade. Bloom Energy, Other Power Stocks Are Big Winners.
stories.Summary:
Shares of Bloom Energy rose 12.97% on November 11, closing at $209.47, a gain of $24.05, as renewed confidence in spending on artificial-intelligence infrastructure lifted suppliers of on-site electricity. MarketWatch tied the rally to upbeat results and financing comments from CoreWeave, which eased worries about how data-center construction will be funded. The article describes this as a sector-wide reassessment of demand rather than a new Bloom earnings announcement. Larger percentage gains reported during the day were intraday readings, and the closing price is a regular-session figure, not a live quote.

Bloom's most recent results, published October 22 for the quarter ended September 30, showed revenue of $1,235.8 million, up 138.1% from a year earlier. GAAP operating income reached $225.4 million, and operating margin rose to 18.2% from 1.5%. Diluted GAAP earnings were $0.78 a share, with non-GAAP diluted earnings of $0.94. The company raised its 2026 revenue outlook to between $4.4 billion and $4.6 billion, which implies 122% growth at the midpoint, and set non-GAAP earnings guidance at $3.10 to $3.40 a share. On November 5, NTT DATA announced an agreement to deploy 900 megawatts of Bloom equipment across data-center projects worldwide, with initial shipments starting in 2027.

The cash picture is less comfortable. Third-quarter operating cash flow was negative $27.1 million, and purchases of property, plant and equipment totaled $153.5 million, which works out to roughly $180.6 million of negative free cash flow, an analytical figure rather than a reported line. At September 30, Bloom held $2.487 billion in cash and equivalents against $2.473 billion in recourse debt, alongside non-recourse debt, financing obligations and operating leases. Common shares outstanding rose to 295.5 million from 280.0 million at the end of December.

Analysts are split on whether the valuation leaves room for error. J.P. Morgan's Mark Strouse kept an Overweight rating on October 23 but cut his target to $292 from $314, citing lower peer multiples despite strong execution. Roth Capital's Chip Moore stayed Neutral and lowered his target to $230 from $260, pointing to valuation and limited visibility, while Jefferies' Julien Dumoulin-Smith kept a Hold with a $242 target and asked for a formal backlog update. Evercore ISI's Nicholas Amicucci reiterated Outperform and a $350 target on October 26, calling the cash-flow-related selloff excessive.

The closing price is about 62 to 68 times management's 2026 adjusted earnings range, and trailing price-to-sales stands at 16.17, up from 10.15 at the end of 2025. stories.Headline: Cloud engineering teams must protect AI agent data in use
stories.Summary:
Cloud engineering teams at financial companies running AI agents on Kubernetes face a security problem that encryption alone cannot solve, according to a SiliconANGLE report published on November 11, 2026. The report says container orchestration has become the default foundation for AI workloads, and that the data those agents use is now the main target. Krishna Mayuram, senior principal engineer and vice president of cloud engineering at Mastercard Inc., made the case for protecting data while it is being processed. He spoke with theCUBE Research's John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media's livestreaming studio. A second article, published a day earlier on November 10, 2026, by the Tribal College Journal, covers how tribal colleges and universities are protecting their data as artificial intelligence spreads through their operations.

The SiliconANGLE report says protecting data in use, and not just while it is stored or moving, has become central to running agents at scale. Mayuram described confidential computing as launching applications in highly secure virtualized or confidential environments, including confidential containers, so that data in use is protected. Mastercard runs its platforms on Red Hat Inc.'s OpenShift, a Kubernetes platform that Red Hat is extending to support AI agents. Red Hat has also brought confidential containers to OpenShift on bare metal. On the college side, the Tribal College Journal says institutions are establishing a comprehensive institutional posture and sovereign infrastructure, with policies and clearly defined processes serving as guardrails to prevent the exposure of sensitive information.

Mayuram said agents act much like microservices, so they need the same elastic infrastructure that applications get from Kubernetes, including horizontal and vertical scaling. He said Mastercard has protected data at rest and data in motion, and the open question now is what happens to data in use. Mastercard recently added trust services for agentic commerce, and internally the same idea applies, with guardrails at every step from development to deployment. In his words, whether the software is agents or regular applications, the guardrails and the enterprise security remain the same. The journal article was written by Chad J. Davis and appears in Volume 38, No. 2, the Winter 2026 issue, under the theme of building local economies.

The tribal college article quotes several officials on how institutions are managing the work. Eric Johnson, the American Indian Higher Education Consortium's health initiatives communication coordinator, said participants in its training are learning not only to use AI tools but to do so responsibly, with an understanding of data sovereignty, privacy, ethics and community trust. Sarah Barott, an English instructor at Red Lake Nation College, said shared governance across multiple committees, including the AI committee, produced frameworks guided by the seven grandfather values. Tristan Stevens, director of information technology at Lac Courte Oreills Ojibwe University, credited strategy and skills training with building a human firewall across campus. Jeremy Bennet, interim chief information officer at Leech Lake Tribal College, said every solution goes through a risk assessment, with contracts, privacy statements, security practices and data ownership provisions reviewed against institutional standards.

Mayuram said the stakes rise with scale, especially for a company operating under the laws of many countries. He described the business and the industry as very distributed, with different laws of the land, which is why everything needs to be encompassed with guardrails. The SiliconANGLE report says payment networks feel the pressure more than most, because every transaction carries customer data and regulatory exposure. Bennet added that data governance and Indigenous data sovereignty are not just technology issues but institutional ones, and that leadership must prioritize the work, educate stakeholders and provide resources. Dr. Colton Wood, general studies coordinator at the College of the Muscogee Nation, said its Onvkuce Voice Database is a multimedia language database meant to revitalize Mvskoke as a living, spoken language.

The articles give some background on how tribal colleges arrived at their current approach. The American Indian Higher Education Consortium has partnered with the National Institutes of Health through its AIM-AHEAD initiative, the Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Consortium to Advance Health Equity and Researcher Diversity. Johnson said many programs begin with publicly available and practice datasets, so participants build skills before working with sensitive data from their tribes and communities. The National Science Foundation Tribal Colleges and Universities Program's Cyberinfrastructure Planning and Cyberinfrastructure Health, Assistance, and Improvements initiative supported Lac Courte Oreilles Ojibwe University and other colleges in improving cybersecurity for STEM education and research. With that funding, Lac Courte Oreilles Ojibwe University completed an IT strategic playbook with stakeholders, which guided later proposals and upgrades to its server, wireless network and firewall.

The tribal college article describes several next steps now under way. Colleges are taking first steps toward on-premises AI capabilities, using localized hardware and shared resources, in an environment where code and data processing are private so that tribal information, Native languages and student data do not train public models. Some are strengthening their tribal institutional review board protocols for AI-enabled research and offering optional syllabi statements that let faculty set appropriate AI use in their courses. They are also classifying institutional data, applying identity and access management and encryption, monitoring how data is accessed and shared, and drafting incident response plans. The SiliconANGLE report leaves open how confidential containers will perform as agent workloads scale, and the excerpt of the journal article ends before it finishes describing how colleges will build trusted relationships to share expertise and infrastructure.
