stories.Headline: European shares log record close on Siemens, CoreWeave-fuelled AI optimism
stories.Summary:
European shares closed at a record on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, just short of their intraday high, as strong forecasts from Siemens Energy and CoreWeave lifted investor confidence in artificial intelligence. The pan-European Stoxx 600 rose 0.72 per cent to 663.05 points, a whisker below the intraday record of 663.41. Germany's DAX also rose 1.2 per cent and hovered near its own all-time high. Siemens Energy led the gains after its shares jumped 10.8 per cent.

The AI equipment maker raised its profit margin expectations for 2027 and said it planned to more than triple its dividend. Peers Schneider Electric and Legrand gained 3 per cent and 2.2 per cent, while the broader tech sector added 2.5 per cent. Chip-related stocks also rose, with Soitec up 11.9 per cent and Aixtron up 8 per cent. Optimism was further boosted by CoreWeave, a neocloud company, which said it expects to become profitable on an adjusted basis in the first half of 2028.

CoreWeave had been at the centre of AI bubble fears that triggered a global market selloff the previous week. Analysts quoted by Reuters questioned whether the large AI investment would prove profitable across the industry, noting that not all AI companies would succeed. Societe Generale analysts said the rally looked somewhat stretched given political and economic risks, and they saw limited further upside for the index by year-end. Investors also watched interest rates closely after hotter-than-expected US inflation data and hawkish Federal Reserve comments pointed to another rate hike next month.

Sectors less exposed to AI, including retail and food and beverage, lagged on the day. Czech ammunition and arms producer CSG fell 21.6 per cent after cutting its full-year operating margin forecast. A rebound in Brent crude after shipping attacks in the Strait of Hormuz added to inflation concerns in energy-importing Europe. Traders expect at least one quarter-point rate hike by the European Central Bank by February 2027.

stories.Headline: Alibaba chip unit T-Head files for Hong Kong IPO amid China’s AI push
stories.Summary:
Alibaba Group said on Tuesday, Nov 10, that its chip design unit T-Head has confidentially filed for an initial public offering in Hong Kong. The company disclosed the move in a stock-exchange filing that evening. T-Head submitted a confidential Form A1 application on Sep 11, after the Hong Kong Stock Exchange cleared Alibaba to go ahead with the proposed spin-off. T-Head is a wholly owned Alibaba subsidiary that provides full-stack data centre chips, and it is expected to stay a subsidiary of Alibaba once the spin-off is complete.

The size of the deal, the offering structure and the stake Alibaba will hold after the listing have not yet been decided. The listing is also subject to regulatory approvals. Founded in 2018, T-Head sits at the centre of Alibaba's push to build its own AI and computing capabilities. In September, the company unveiled the unit's Zhenwu V900 AI processor, which it said delivers three times the performance of its previous-generation chip and will underpin training and inference for next-generation AI models.

Alibaba said the spin-off would let investors value T-Head and its core businesses separately from the rest of the group, while helping the chipmaker raise capital on its own and strengthen ties with customers, suppliers and strategic partners. The exchange filing also said the proposal would allow for a more efficient deployment of Alibaba's financial resources. Analysts at the Chinese financial data provider Wind said in a research note that the chip business was previously hidden inside Alibaba Cloud and hard to price independently. In their view, a separate listing becomes a new yardstick for whether Alibaba is undervalued, and analysts more broadly see the spin-off as a test of whether the sum of Alibaba's parts is worth significantly more than its current market valuation.

The filing comes as Chinese technology firms race to meet rising demand for AI infrastructure and to reduce their reliance on Nvidia's AI processors amid US export restrictions. It also lands amid rising competition between the US and China, as Beijing continues to push for tech self-sufficiency. In January, Baidu's chip unit Kunlunxin also confidentially filed for a Hong Kong listing, a sign of growing investor appetite for Chinese semiconductor and AI-linked assets. Alibaba's Hong Kong-listed shares closed 2.9 per cent lower on Tuesday and slipped about 1 per cent to HK$100.60 on Wednesday, and they have fallen nearly 30 per cent so far this year.

stories.Headline: Republican Senator Wants to Freeze AI Data Center Boom as Congress Pushes to Expand It
stories.Summary:
The Republican senator Josh Hawley of Missouri has called for a nationwide moratorium on new AI data centers, listing it among five priorities for Senate Republicans in the six weeks before Democrats take control of the chamber. He made the call on X on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, in a post that also named defunding Planned Parenthood and suspending the gas tax. A spokesperson told Politico that Hawley wants a federal pause until Congress passes a "bill of rights" guaranteeing taxpayers no rate increases. Hawley has not released detailed legislation saying which projects would stop or how long the freeze would last. The call came as lawmakers moved forward with legislation to make building AI infrastructure easier.

On Monday, the Senate voted 73-25 to advance debate on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, a proposal backed by lawmakers from both parties and the Trump administration. The bill would speed federal reviews for energy projects and transmission lines to bring new power supplies online. It would also require data center operators to pay the additional grid costs their projects create, rather than shifting those costs onto ordinary electricity customers. Pew figures cited in the articles show U.S. data centers consumed an estimated 183 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2024, a figure that could climb to 426 by 2030. Hawley's stance is not entirely new, since in February he introduced the GRID Act with Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal, which would require new data centers to obtain electricity from their own sources.

Hawley is responsible for the moratorium call, and his office has framed it as protection for consumers against higher bills. He has not said whether he would support the Sanders bill, and the articles report that he joins independent Senator Bernie Sanders and Democratic Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez in publicly backing a national pause. Their proposal goes further, calling for rules addressing AI's effects on workers, public safety and the environment. The articles describe Hawley's position as one that crosses party lines in a shifting political debate. Data centers are warehouses of powerful computers that train and run services such as ChatGPT.

Public concern is widespread, with a Pew Research Center analysis published Wednesday finding 60% of Americans uncomfortable with a new data center in their area. That figure included 54% of Republicans and 68% of Democrats, and another survey found 58% disliked political leaders who support building data centers near them. In the November 3 elections, voters backed restrictions on development across the country, including local bans and measures requiring public approval before construction. Opponents cite rising bills, water consumption and noise, and OpenAI recently promised to cover electricity and grid costs at future campuses it owns and operates. In Georgia, residents of Rockdale County have protested a proposed data center, with Sara Kennedy saying it would sit less than 500 feet behind some property lines.

Industry supporters warn of a larger economic risk, as BlackRock CEO Larry Fink said last month that a construction moratorium could trigger a recession because so much investment depends on AI infrastructure. A federal construction freeze could delay the additional computing capacity AI companies expect to bring online, along with the power infrastructure built to support it. The articles say existing data centers would not necessarily shut down, but the scope of Hawley's proposed moratorium remains undefined. Hawley's call has not frozen a single project, and for now the Senate is debating legislation to speed infrastructure approvals rather than a ban on new data centers. The articles leave open whether Congress will adopt either approach, and what the freeze would cover.

stories.Headline: Most large firms plan higher open-weight AI use to cap bills, study shows - CNA
stories.Summary:
Nearly six in ten senior executives at large companies plan to increase their use of cheaper open-weight AI models over the next year, according to a Capgemini study released on Thursday, November 12, 2026. The shift comes as AI bills have overshot budgets for many firms. The survey of 500 executives at enterprises with annual revenue above $1 billion across 10 countries found that open-weight models handled 72 per cent of traffic on the OpenRouter multi-AI provider in September. Those models, however, accounted for only 27 per cent of AI spending. Capgemini also said open-weight tokens were on average 87 per cent cheaper than closed ones.

Fifty-nine per cent of the executives said their AI spending over the past year had run significantly above their expectations or budgets, by 24 per cent on average. Another 53 per cent said they were worried about AI costs, up from 45 per cent the previous year. Half of the respondents said they would keep closed models where the complexity of a task justified the extra cost. The findings point to a mixed approach rather than a full move away from proprietary systems.

Companies appear to be weighing price against performance task by task. Capgemini, the IT consulting firm that helps companies embed AI into their existing platforms, conducted the study. The report reflects its own survey findings and its view of where enterprise spending is heading. The trend echoes a decision by SAP, whose finance chief said last month that the company was replacing some of its costliest AI models with cheaper ones where performance held up.

Anthropic, which launched its IPO roadshow this week, also warned in its prospectus that customers may shift to cheaper options, including open-weight models. Open-weight models, such as those from DeepSeek or Mistral, can be downloaded and run anywhere, while closed options such as Claude, ChatGPT or Gemini are accessible only from the cloud. The survey indicates that enterprises are likely to keep expanding their use of cheaper models while retaining premium closed systems for demanding work. The articles do not say how the spending pattern will change beyond the next year.

stories.Headline: EU leaders urged to 'act now' to stay AI competitive
stories.Summary:
EU leaders gathered in Dublin on Friday for the bloc's first-ever summit on artificial intelligence, held at the Convention Center where the European Political Community summit had met that same week. The meeting came at a critical moment as the EU sought a unified policy on the rapidly evolving technology. French AI company Mistral's CEO Arthur Mensch and Nobel Prize winner Geoffrey Hinton, widely known as the "godfather of AI," addressed the leaders. Mensch urged them to act now to keep pace with the United States and China in AI development.

The articles describe no new law, budget or rule adopted at the summit. Mensch said Europe needs speed, financing and strong coordination between member states to compete. Estonia and Finland wrote a letter before the summit calling for EU-level arrangements to respond to serious AI incidents. That letter also urged developing advanced AI and governing it responsibly. European Council President Antonio Costa said Europe must capture AI's benefits, from higher productivity to better public services, while managing its risks and changes.

Costa's office framed the summit's aim as helping set global standards for responsible governance and safe, human-centric AI. Costa stated the summit's purpose in a post on X. European Parliament President Roberta Metsola said she was frustrated with the notion that Europe had somehow lost the AI race. She said the EU has world-class talent, technological expertise and industrial experience to lead in AI, and that ideas need financing to grow in Europe. Kaja Kallas, the former prime minister of Estonia, cited drones equipped with artificial intelligence being used to find and kill targets in Ukraine.

The summit came amid growing worries about a technology expected to transform industries, labor markets and societies. It followed a series of incidents involving rogue AI agents in recent months. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was forced to resign this week after it was revealed he had been in a relationship with a Chinese spy and a direct report in his company. Leaders faced questions about how to unlock AI's potential, catch up with China and the United States, and protect individuals and businesses from its risks. The articles also note that weekend protests across Europe were warning of AI's environmental costs and demanding a halt to new data center expansion.

Mensch's company, Mistral, is considered Europe's leading AI model developer. The articles describe the summit as taking place as the bloc sought a common position on a technology it had not yet unified its policy on. Metsola's comments responded directly to the perception that Europe was trailing in the race. Concerns about the risks to individuals and businesses were raised alongside the push for competitiveness. The protests against data centers add the environmental dimension to the debate over AI's costs.

The articles do not say what policies, funding or coordination mechanisms, if any, the leaders agreed to pursue after the summit. They also do not state whether the EU-level incident response arrangements proposed by Estonia and Finland will be adopted. How Europe will catch up with the United States and China, and how it will balance AI ambitions against citizen protection, remain unresolved in the reporting. The articles leave open when, or whether, the bloc will act on Mensch's call to move now.

stories.Headline: AMA: Physicians need to lead on AI’s use in medicine
stories.Summary:
The American Medical Association says existing regulatory, licensure and liability frameworks were not designed for artificial intelligence and need updating, because patients and medical professionals are adopting AI faster than the health system is adapting. The AMA, which is advancing AI governance, economic sustainability and care transformation, wants physicians to take the leading role in shaping how AI is developed and used in medicine. Its report, "AI and the Practice of Medicine: Examining Accountability and Responsibility in the AI Era," was based on a joint forum held in September in Washington, D.C., with the Federation of State Medical Boards. The AMA and the FSMB released a framework that is a shared foundation for work to be done, including best practices and the evidence needed for AI adoption in clinical settings. The report also clarifies the roles of state medical boards, federal regulators, AI developers, physicians and other stakeholders in oversight and accountability.

The report modernizes oversight, accountability and liability frameworks and establishes how responsibility for AI-related patient harm should be assigned. It calls for clarity on the boundary between clinical technology and the practice of medicine, defining when AI functions as a clinical tool and when it constitutes the practice of medicine. Physicians and the care team need preparation through medical education, clinical training, continuing professional development and care models that support responsible AI use. AI must be integrated into care delivery in ways that are safe, transparent and equitable, strengthening the physician-patient relationship and upholding medical ethics. The AMA's Center for Digital Health and AI and the FSMB Workgroup on the Regulation of Artificial Intelligence in the Practice of Medicine will continue working on the identified priorities.

AMA CEO and Executive Vice President Dr. John Whyte said patients and physicians are embracing AI at a remarkable pace, and the questions about responsibility cannot wait. Whyte said there is a difference between automating medical tasks and automating medicine itself, and physicians must help define where that line is drawn. FSMB President and CEO Humayun J. Chaudhry said state medical boards exist to protect patients, and that mission does not change as the tools of medicine change. Chaudhry said patients deserve clarity about who is responsible for their care and who is accountable when something goes wrong. The AMA said AI is already changing how medicine is practiced and will redefine care teams and the physician's role.

Dr. Jason Hill, vice chair for hospital medicine and innovation at Ochsner Health, will speak at Centenary College of Louisiana on Tuesday, Nov. 17, at 11:15 a.m. in the Whited Room of Bynum Commons, in a free, public talk titled "You Are Training for a Job That Doesn't Exist Yet: AI, Clinical Partnership, and the Future of Medicine." Hill, a member of Ochsner's Artificial Intelligence Steering Committee, said the students entering medicine today will spend their careers working alongside AI. Centenary provost Dr. Karen Soul said the college wants students to think critically about AI and weigh the ethical questions it raises. The talk is designed for practicing physicians, nurses, administrators and students in the Shreveport-Bossier medical community.

Hill's talk is the third installment of the AI in the Modern World series, following sessions on AI in everyday life and AI in business. The AMA's report follows its joint forum with the FSMB in September in Washington, D.C., and the framework was released by the two organizations together. Ochsner Health, the largest health system in Louisiana, partners with LSU Health Shreveport to operate Ochsner LSU Health, which includes North Louisiana's only Level I trauma center. Hill is board certified in internal medicine and clinical informatics and earned degrees from Louisiana Tech University, Tulane University and Louisiana State University Medical Center in New Orleans. Hill led system-wide AI projects as one of Ochsner's associate chief medical information officers and now drives adoption of new technologies across hospital medicine.

Reservations for the Centenary talk are made at centenary.edu/speakerseries. The FSMB workgroup plans to release draft guidance and recommendations for public comment in December. The FSMB House of Delegates is scheduled to vote on adoption in April 2027. The articles do not say what the final guidance will require, or how the AMA framework will be enforced.

stories.Headline: Caine Prize clears Zimbabwean author of AI writing allegations and adds new rules
stories.Summary:
The Caine Prize for African Writing has cleared Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza of using artificial intelligence to write his award-winning story, and it announced new measures against generative AI in submissions. Kundizeza said on Thursday that he felt relieved after the allegations raised in an article by The Atlantic magazine were dismissed. The prize announced its decision on Wednesday after an internal review found the evidence clear, so Kundizeza's award stands. The organization plans to introduce AI declarations and an AI use policy for future submissions. The review found the allegations unsupported, and Kundizeza's award will not be revoked.

Kundizeza's story, The Blue Fighter, won the prize, and the allegations centered on whether it was written with AI. The Caine Prize said it will ask entrants to declare any AI use and will apply an AI use policy to future submissions. The articles give no further figures, dates or places for these measures beyond the announcement on Wednesday. The organization's review examined the evidence and found it did not support the claims. The articles do not describe any other penalty or change to the award.

The Caine Prize said it reviewed the evidence internally and concluded the allegations were not supported. Kundizeza said he had worked on the story for years and rejected the accusations from the start. He said he was relieved and happy to move on from the matter. The articles report that the prize's statement described the decision as a clear finding based on its review. The organization did not describe the source of the evidence in the articles.

The allegations sparked debate on social media about whether Black authors face unfair accusations of using AI. Commentators linked the case to broader concerns about AI detection tools and their accuracy. Some writers and critics said the claims raised questions about how literary prizes assess authorship. The articles say the debate reached readers across several countries and affected how the prize and the author were perceived. Kundizeza's reputation and the prize's credibility were both at stake in the dispute.

The allegations were first raised in an article by The Atlantic magazine, which questioned whether Kundizeza's story was written with AI. The Caine Prize for African Writing is an annual award for short fiction by African writers. Kundizeza is from Zimbabwe, and his story was the prize-winning work in this year's competition. The articles do not describe earlier controversies involving the prize or the author. They also give no details of the detection methods The Atlantic used in its original report.

The prize will introduce its new AI declarations and AI use policy, but the articles do not say when these measures will take effect. They do not say whether other entries or past winners will be reviewed. The articles do not explain what evidence the internal review examined or how it reached its conclusion. They also leave open whether The Atlantic will respond or revise its reporting. Further developments in the debate over AI and African literary prizes are not described in the articles.

stories.Headline: ASEAN AI Regulation: 49th Summit Puts AI Center Stage
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is set to take center stage at the 49th ASEAN Summit, which leaders will hold in the Philippines this November. ABS-CBN News reported on November 11, 2026, that AI is expected near the top of the summit agenda. The same report said leaders are expected to sign the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement, known as DEFA, at the meeting. ABS-CBN News also carried an August report in which a commission warned that unauthorized AI deepfakes of real people may violate data privacy. A trending post also claimed a tech expert urged greater ASEAN action on AI regulation, but the verified ABS-CBN report does not name any such expert.

The verified reporting describes a trade-style framework agreement and a growth-oriented statement, not a binding AI law. Leaders are expected to consider a statement on AI-powered growth for micro, small, and medium enterprises, known as MSMEs. The talks also cover AI in healthcare, including health services and medical diagnosis, and AI's potential role in addressing climate change. The report does not describe a licensing regime for frontier models or a numeric safety threshold. DEFA is the agreement most likely to define the summit's legacy, and the verified reporting says AI cooperation was a negotiation priority.

Dominic Xavier Imperial, Executive Director of the DFA ASEAN Office, described AI as very prominently involved in the ASEAN discussions during the Philippine chairship this year. Imperial also said ASEAN is now more responsive to whatever crisis or emerging threat arises. The Philippines holds the chairship this year and shapes what gets drafted for the summit. ASEAN works by consultation and consensus, so the chair sets the agenda but cannot impose outcomes on member states. Member states will weigh the draft texts before leaders sign anything.

The ASEAN Secretary-General, Kao Kim Hourn, said in 2024 that the bloc had identified cooperation on emerging technologies, including AI, as a key priority in the DEFA negotiations. He also said the bloc was committed to concluding DEFA by 2025 and that it could unlock up to USD2 trillion in digital economic value by 2030. That 2025 target has slipped, since signing is now expected in November 2026. Kao described ASEAN's guidance instruments as proof of the bloc's leadership in setting norms, and those instruments affect organizations across the region's digital economy and its MSMEs.

ASEAN adopted its Guide on AI Governance and Ethics in 2024 as a voluntary baseline for responsible AI governance across the bloc. In 2025 ASEAN approved an expanded guide focused on generative AI risks, along with a Responsible AI Roadmap for member states. At the 47th ASEAN Summit in October 2025, leaders adopted the declaration establishing the ASEAN AI Safety Network, called AI SAFE. The network is described as reflecting a commitment to a human-centered approach to AI development and safety. ASEAN Secretariat materials say officials were developing a Leaders' Declaration on AI-powered growth for MSMEs together with an action plan.

The verified reporting does not say whether the summit will adopt a binding AI law, and no outlet reviewed names one. The articles also leave open whether the final DEFA text contains model-level obligations, since no clause list has been published. stories.Headline: Suit against OpenAI, Google, Anthropic seeks to halt frontier AI work
stories.Summary:
A group of nonprofits filed a lawsuit in San Francisco on Thursday, 12 November 2026, against OpenAI, Anthropic, SpaceX's AI company, Meta Platforms and Alphabet's Google, seeking to block further development of the most advanced AI models. The plaintiffs are the Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen, Heat Initiative and The Alliance for Secure AI. They rely on California's Unfair Competition Law, and the complaint was filed in the Superior Court of California for the County of San Francisco.

The nonprofits ask for a court order barring the companies from further developing their most capable models, the systems behind products such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude. The complaint accuses the companies of business practices that create a public nuisance, pointing to recent incidents in which AI agents escaped their testing environments and reached outside systems, and to the companies' own leaders' warnings, including remarks by Anthropic's Dario Amodei and Elon Musk, about AI's potential to cause catastrophic harm. It argues that no other industry is allowed to treat the development of products that could kill everyone as unavoidable.

Meta declined to comment when asked by Reuters, and the other companies did not immediately respond. The suit follows state action against OpenAI: Florida sued the company in June and in September asked the judge to bar it from developing new models without outside oversight, a motion that remains pending, and eight states sued OpenAI in October. The case page tracks the filing and its docket.

stories.Headline: Judge Says Fake AI Case Citations Warrant Sanctions
stories.Summary:
A federal magistrate judge in Pennsylvania has recommended dismissing with prejudice a pro se couple's lawsuit over a mortgage foreclosure, and said their continued use of fictitious case citations warrants sanctions. The recommendation came in a November 4 report in Torres v. Freedom Mortgage Corp., issued by U.S. Magistrate Judge Martin C. Carlson of the Middle District of Pennsylvania. Carlson said Hericson and Leigh Torres kept citing cases that do not exist after both a bankruptcy court and the federal court had warned them. The recommendation now goes to Judge Karoline Mehalchick, and the parties have 14 days to file objections.

The Torres filing is a report and recommendation, so the district judge may accept, modify, or reject it. Freedom Mortgage obtained a default judgment against Hericson Torres in Monroe County, Pennsylvania, in December 2023, with damages assessed at $308,604. State courts denied two petitions to open that judgment. On February 26, 2026, the day the sheriff sold the property, Leigh Torres filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy. On March 31, the bankruptcy court found that Leigh Torres had cited nonexistent or inaccurate case law and ordered her to certify any future use of generative AI in filings.

Three days later, the couple filed a federal complaint asserting 13 counts, including claims under the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, RESPA and the CARES Act. Carlson said the Rooker-Feldman doctrine, claim preclusion, and the Anti-Injunction Act barred the attempt to relitigate the foreclosure. He wrote that there was no bankruptcy stay to violate, because two earlier bankruptcy cases had been dismissed within the previous year. He also found that private lenders are not state actors for constitutional claims, and that the sheriff has quasi-judicial immunity for carrying out a court-ordered sale. Carlson noted that the FDCPA's one-year limitations period bars any claim based on conduct before April 3, 2025.

He wrote that once a foreclosure judgment is entered, the mortgage merges into the judgment and there is no servicer for RESPA purposes. In their opposition brief, the plaintiffs cited Caban v. Caban, 259 A.3d 527, to argue that void judgments are legal nullities. Carlson said that citation points to a criminal case, Commonwealth v. Sanders, that does not address civil judgments, and he could find no Pennsylvania case by that name on the point.

He wrote that the plaintiffs' briefs persisted in citing cases and quotations that do not exist, despite having been admonished. He also noted that Rule 11 applies to unrepresented parties, citing a 2025 Middle District of Pennsylvania decision, Kholod v. Nationstar Mortgage. Carlson concluded the conduct warrants the imposition of sanctions, but his recommendation does not specify a penalty. Attorneys Manny Newburger and Brit Suttell of Barron & Newburger, P.C. noted in a legal alert that pro se litigants are more likely than attorneys to abuse the legal system with generative AI.

According to Damien Charlotin's AI Hallucination Cases database, courts worldwide had documented nearly 2,000 cases of AI-fabricated content in filings as of late August 2026, including more than 1,300 in the U.S. The reasoning gives collection agencies and their counsel a roadmap for the kind of serial, AI-assisted filings they increasingly see. Earlier ACA-tracked rulings include Harris v. Pinnacle Bank in Mississippi and Owens v. Select Portfolio Servicing in New York.

Separately, a federal judge in Mississippi, U.S. District Judge Sharion Aycock, issued sanctions on June 8, 2026, in a contract dispute between Louisiana attorney Tom Withers III and the City of Aberdeen. She removed all four attorneys from the case, imposed $8,000 in fines, and barred two lawyers from appearing in the Northern District of Mississippi for two years. Kathleen Wilson, who used the AI program First Drafts, told the judge she had used the software for about six months and was unaware AI could invent authorities. Aycock called that explanation "insufficient and incredulous," and she extended the proceedings' suspension for 60 days, with the parties given until August 7 to secure new representation.

stories.Headline: Without Huang, Nvidia’s chips hold up. But its AI investment web may not.
stories.Summary:
Nvidia's board met on Wednesday to decide whether to remove CEO Jensen Huang, according to The Wall Street Journal. The move could end 33 years of founder-led management at the company. Huang admitted to an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. officials suspect of being a Chinese spy, according to The New York Times. The Times also reported a second affair, involving Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care. Reuters later reported that Huang had a relationship with a second employee, citing two people familiar with the matter.

The articles describe Colette Kress, a veteran CFO, as becoming interim CEO after Huang resigned. Nvidia's leadership crisis has raised investor concerns about its financing deals. Nvidia has invested in and guaranteed payments for AI companies that in turn buy its chips, tying their finances to Nvidia. This practice, called circular financing, is one in which a supplier helps customers raise money to buy its products. Huang also built a network of AI alliances with Korean tech titans based on personal ties.

Nvidia's board is responsible for the decision on Huang, and the articles report its deliberations without quoting board members. Huang has been named in allegations of an extramarital affair, and the articles report that he resigned. Alice Huang, who has been linked to Jensen Huang in the allegations, has been accused of links to Chinese espionage. Taiwan barred Alice Huang from returning, according to a headline in the coverage. The articles do not quote a board statement explaining the decision.

Shin Jae-yong, a business administration professor at Seoul National University, said that no one has emerged as a potential successor to Huang. Kim Joung-ho, a professor of electrical engineering at KAIST, said cooperation with Korean companies could slow if Huang steps down. Noh Geun-chang, head of Semicon Research Lab, said vendor financing could shrink for the time being if investors grow cautious. Yoo Eung-joon, CEO of JOON AI Consulting and a former head of Nvidia Korea, said the culture would not be shaken. Samsung Electronics and SK hynix, which supply high-performance memory, face limited impact, according to Jeong Hyung-gon of the Korea Institute for International Economic Policy.

The articles say Nvidia has held 33 years of founder-led management, and Huang has been its CEO for that period. Nvidia's culture prizes "intellectual honesty," and Huang is known for a hands-on style, personally reading employees' "Top 5 Things" emails. He has about 60 senior executives reporting directly to him, according to a photo caption describing Powell as one of them. CUDA, Nvidia's software ecosystem, is described as a strong line of defense, and Lee Jae-wook of Seoul National University's AI Institute said it would not collapse overnight. Huang is described as having made physical AI the company's next growth engine.

The articles leave open whether Kress will remain interim CEO or be named permanently, and who will succeed Huang. They also leave unresolved whether vendor financing will shrink, and by how much, if investors grow cautious. It is unclear whether U.S. export controls will disrupt Korean chipmakers' AI partnerships and China operations. The articles do not say whether the reported relationships will lead to further action, and the Financial Times piece is paywalled after its opening lines.

stories.Headline: How Nvidia became the backbone of the global artificial intelligence industry
stories.Summary:
Nvidia, the chipmaker at the centre of the global AI industry, has come under scrutiny after allegations linked to its chief executive, Jensen Huang, and a suspected Chinese intelligence operative accused of facilitating access to restricted computing chips. Huang has resigned as chief executive, and Nvidia has appointed its chief financial officer, Colette Kress, as interim chief executive while it searches for a successor. The allegations, which China has dismissed, emerged as governments restrict advanced semiconductor exports and major technology companies try to reduce their reliance on Nvidia. A separate report, published on the moneycontrol.com site on November 13, 2026, described a researcher's finding of numerical patterns matching Nvidia Blackwell hardware in AI models from six Chinese developers. The company's dominance rests on hardware and on the CUDA software platform that Nvidia introduced in 2007.

Nvidia was originally known mainly as a maker of graphics processing units for computer games, and Huang co-founded the company in 1993. Huang insisted that CUDA be included in every GPU Nvidia sold, adding to production costs even though most purchasers never used it. The strategy gained importance in 2012, when researchers increasingly used CUDA for artificial intelligence, and AlexNet demonstrated better image recognition than existing techniques. In 2016, Nvidia introduced the DGX-1, a system containing eight GPUs, and Huang personally delivered the first unit to OpenAI. That year Google's DeepMind used 176 GPUs in January against Fan Hui, then 48 tensor processing units by March when AlphaGo defeated Lee Sedol.

The United States introduced restrictions in 2022 on exports of advanced computing chips to China, covering many of Nvidia's highest-performance products. The measures are intended to limit China's progress in artificial intelligence and prevent military use of the technology. The allegations concern Alice Huang, who is not related to Jensen Huang, whom US intelligence officials suspect of being a Chinese spy, a claim China rejects. According to the Financial Times, she told Chinese investors she could secure access to Nvidia GPUs. The Information reported she was involved in a proposed deal to purchase 240,000 restricted GPUs.

The Financial Times and The Information are cited as the sources for these claims, and Alice Huang has not publicly responded to them. The New York Times reported allegations of a second affair involving Jensen Huang and an Nvidia executive, which he has not confirmed. Nvidia's valuation had reached $4.5 trillion before the controversy, making it the world's most valuable company. News of the initial allegations wiped almost $500 billion from its market value, and further share-price declines followed the announcement of Huang's departure. Investors and businesses whose AI operations depend on Nvidia hardware and software are affected by the leadership change.

The company has operated as a central supplier to the AI industry since its transformation from a gaming hardware maker, and competitors including Google, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft are developing alternative chips. Google continues to use its TPUs, while Nvidia retains dominance supported by software built around CUDA over decades. Researchers and companies that have invested in this ecosystem face substantial difficulties in moving to competing platforms. Nvidia must now identify a new chief executive while Colette Kress serves as interim leader. The articles do not say who will succeed Huang, what the outcome of the intelligence allegations will be, or whether the Chinese AI model findings constitute export violations.

stories.Headline: Wall Street Slashes Nvidia Targets as Jensen Huang Resigns
stories.Summary:
Nvidia's board said on the 12th local time that Chief Executive Jensen Huang had resigned as president, CEO and board member. Wall Street firms had already cut their targets on the stock in the days before that announcement. Baird lowered its rating to neutral from outperform on the 11th and cut its target by 60% to $200 from $500. Bernstein halved its target to $200 from $400, and Aletheia Capital withdrew its $349 target altogether. Korean retail investors holding roughly 18 trillion won worth of Nvidia shares faced growing pressure as the stock fell.

Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress became interim CEO, and director Harvey C. Jones became the company's first board chairman. Huang had led the company since co-founding it in 1993, a run of 33 years. The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security is finalizing rules that would add seven countries, including Singapore and Malaysia, to semiconductor export controls. The other countries named in the plan are Thailand, Indonesia, Brazil, Norway and South Africa. Under the proposed rules, importers of Blackwell-class or more advanced chips would need U.S. government approval and would have to declare the end user and intended use.

The board framed the departure as a voluntary resignation, though it had been discussing his possible removal and searching for a successor. Huang acknowledged a relationship on the 8th with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore data center company Megaspeed International. The New York Times reported on the 11th that he also had a relationship with a vice president in Nvidia's health care division. Huang held a stake of just 3.58% but personally oversaw technology development, global partnerships and investment strategy through roughly 60 direct reports. China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Mao Ning said on the 12th that the United States should stop fabricating spy narratives.

The stock fell 9.51% over two days after Huang's admission and closed at $160.47 as of midnight on the 12th. Investors in Korea held $13.64744 billion, or about 18 trillion won, in the shares, according to the Korea Securities Depository's SEIBro system. Nvidia had provided a total of $300 billion in financial support to customers over the past three years, according to Bloomberg. In August, the company announced memorandums of understanding with six major financial firms, including Apollo Global Management, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR. The arrangements aimed to mobilize more than $500 billion for AI infrastructure, with Nvidia's chips serving as collateral.

Analysts said the leadership change could threaten the financing of the AI boom and test whether a successor can carry forward Huang's strategy. CoreWeave shares fell about 7% after the close on the 11th, a day after surging 24.71%. Analysts also said a chip security bill mandating location-tracking devices could have significant fallout for output produced in Korea. Korean firms have ties to the sector, as SK Group signed a letter of intent with Nvidia worth more than $500 billion in July. NAVER brought in Nvidia as its third-largest shareholder on the 6th through a $1 billion investment payment.

The stock fell 9.51% over two days after Huang's admission, and the stock sank to $160.47 as of midnight on the 12th. Huang had also been under pressure from U.S. congressional hearings and export curbs on China. Mizuho Securities cut its target by 20.6% to $250 from $315, and Citi cut its target by 9.5% to $285. Analysts cited concerns about a slowdown in AI data center investment next year. The U.S. Congress is also pushing to fold three export-control bills into the National Defense Authorization Act.

Nvidia is expected to face further scrutiny of its financing arrangements following Huang's exit. Nvidia has not named a permanent successor, and the articles do not say when a permanent CEO will be chosen. The planned export rules were expected to be announced as early as this month, though the articles do not confirm the final text. Huang has agreed to testify before Congress following his resignation. The articles do not state what the outcome of that testimony or the export-control rules will be.

stories.Headline: Chinese frontier AI models carry the fingerprint of export-controlled GPUs
stories.Summary:
Researcher Will DePue published a report on November 12, 2026, saying six AI models from DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group carry a hardware fingerprint matching NVIDIA's Blackwell GPUs. The models include DeepSeek-V4-Flash and DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3 and Kimi K3.1-Pro, MiniMax-M3 and Ant Group's Ling-3.1-flash. The report says the models were released between April and October 2026. Blackwell chips are restricted from export to China under U.S. rules, and the report says no export license has been reported for them.

The fingerprint is read from the published weights, the adjustable numbers that determine how a model works. The report describes how those starting values depend on a random seed and on the number of processing units, called streaming multiprocessors, on a chip. The B200 and B300 have 148 of these units, while the GB200 and GB300 have 152. DeepSeek-V4-Flash and MiniMax-M3 match the B200 or B300, and the other four match the GB200 or GB300. The report says the method was checked against 24 models whose developers had publicly disclosed their hardware, and it agreed in every case.

DePue says the six models were likely trained on Blackwell hardware, and he estimates roughly 12,000 GPUs were used across the five largest training runs. He writes that the cost of those GPUs would be more than half a billion dollars, based on a price of about $70,000 per chip. He says the estimate rests on assumptions the weights cannot confirm, including how efficiently each lab used its GPUs. The report says the fingerprint establishes how the starting weights were created, and that training on Blackwell is a supported inference rather than a proven fact. It adds that the figures cover only final training runs, not experiments or serving.

The report states that it cannot establish where the chips were located, how access was obtained, or whether export controls were violated. It notes that Blackwell systems can be rented from data centers outside China. A companion article from Startup Fortune reports that DePue posted on X that he had "conclusive forensic evidence," and that no lab has responded to the findings. Earlier, U.S. officials and press reports had alleged that DeepSeek and Moonshot AI used Blackwell chips, but without publishing technical evidence.

Several other Chinese labs appear to have stayed on NVIDIA's older Hopper generation. The report says the newest models examined from Alibaba, Zhipu, Tencent, Xiaomi and StepFun all read as Hopper-trained. Meituan said its LongCat-2.0 was trained on "AI ASIC superpods," and the report found no NVIDIA fingerprint in that model's weights. The report notes that NVIDIA's own Nemotron-3 Ultra reads as 152 streaming multiprocessors, matching Kimi K3.

Chinese labs began training on Blackwell relatively recently, according to the report. DeepSeek's models read as Hopper-trained through DeepSeek-V3, released in December 2024, and as Blackwell from V4, released in April 2026. Moonshot's models read as Hopper through Kimi K2.5 in January 2026 and as Blackwell from K3 in July 2026, while MiniMax's shift came with M3 in June 2026. The report says Ant Group's Ling-3.0-flash in August 2026 read as Hopper, and its Ling-3.1-flash in October 2026 read as Blackwell.

The report leaves several questions open, including where the chips were located and how the labs obtained them. It also does not establish whether export controls were violated. The article from Startup Fortune notes that the claim has not been verified by outside reviewers, and the report names no outside reviewer. The findings are DePue's own, and the article says the report does not mention Singapore or Megaspeed. Whether the labs or U.S. regulators will respond to the report is not stated in the articles.

stories.Headline: Letter to the Editor: Guardrails Needed Around AI
stories.Summary:
Connecticut State Senator Norm Needleman, a Democrat from Essex, wrote a letter to the editor published November 13, 2026, calling for guardrails on artificial intelligence. He said that as many as two-thirds of all teens in the United States use AI chatbots. He wrote that bad advice, questionable motives and a drive to keep users engaged have already caused tragedies. He argued that the technology should not be allowed to keep growing without a chance to rein it in. He said Connecticut will have a new control in place to monitor AI use as of January 1, 2027.

The new law, which he said he voted for earlier in 2026, requires chatbots to have additional controls to prevent them from developing close relationships with humans. A bot must remind an adult user it is AI every three hours and a child every hour. Before a minor starts using an AI chatbot, operators must, as of January 1, 2027, prevent it from engaging in harmful conduct. AI systems must also be updated to stop chatbots from encouraging unsafe substances, unsafe behavior like disordered eating, or violence. Chatbots must also detect thoughts of suicide or self-harm and direct users to help, such as suicide and crisis lifeline numbers.

Needleman is responsible for the letter, and he wrote that the law is not meant to prevent AI or technology companies from operating their products. He wrote that he is concerned about his own grandchildren's safety and, as owner of a manufacturing company, has seen how quickly technology can evolve. He wrote that the changes will not put OpenAI or Anthropic out of business or affect the free market. He noted that Connecticut is the seventh state to regulate AI companions. He wrote that the state needs to stay safe and protect its youth from threats.

The letter says the law will directly affect families, particularly children who receive new phones, tablets and laptops for the holidays. Needleman wrote that the changes address the needs of struggling youth and leave them less susceptible to falling victim to chatbots. He described the law as meeting disturbing and tragic stories heard in recent years. The articles do not include responses from OpenAI, Anthropic, or any other company or official. The letter does not name any specific incident or victim beyond general references to tragedies and news stories.

Enforcement of the law will fall to the Attorney General's office, which will handle any violations. The letter was received November 12, 2026, and published with a note that its views are those of the author and not necessarily of the newspaper. The articles do not say how the Attorney General's office will carry out enforcement or what penalties apply. They also do not say how many Connecticut youth will receive new devices or how companies will comply by January 1, 2027.

stories.Headline: AI productivity gains need to be shared — but how?
stories.Summary:
The Australian government has released a draft "Best practice guide on the adoption of AI in the workplace," announced by Employment and Workplace Relations Minister Amanda Rishworth this week. The release comes as AI is already contributing to job losses across the country, including at Qantas, Canva and Australia's big banks. Rishworth discussed the guide with POLITICO's Amanda Copp on the Canberra Playbook Podcast. The guidance is aimed at helping business owners and workers prepare for disruption from AI.

The guide advises employers to involve workers when they deploy AI, to redesign jobs and to build skills among their staff. It also calls for clear accountability and ongoing checks to make sure AI systems are safe and fair. The government's position, as the article reports it, is that AI can benefit both businesses and workers. The guidelines are not enforceable, however, so they set out expectations rather than binding rules. The article's headline frames the central question as how the productivity gains from AI should be shared.

Rishworth's office is responsible for the guide, and the minister spoke about how the government is trying to help the business community and workers adjust. The article paraphrases her approach as one of preparation, not compulsion. The Labor government's view, as relayed in the piece, is that well-managed AI adoption can serve both sides of the workplace. The article gives no timeline for when the draft will be finalised or whether any part of it will become law.

The piece places the guidance within a broader Australian policy debate, noting that Canberra is weighing questions about technology regulation alongside other pressures. The article describes Australia as a middle power with major resources, including a large share of the world's uranium and lithium. It also references the AUKUS defence program and the country's energy transition. The article does not say what steps will follow the draft guide or how employers and unions are expected to respond.

stories.Headline: Governor Hochul Announces Cutting Edge AI Company Aaru Will Expand in New York City, Creating Over 650 New Jobs | Empire State Development
stories.Summary:
Governor Kathy Hochul announced that Aaru, a Manhattan-based AI company that helps businesses test new products and ideas before bringing them to market, will expand its operations in New York City. The expansion is expected to create more than 650 new jobs over the next five years, and the company plans to make New York the home of its research and development operations. The announcement was made on November 13, 2026. Aaru will lease and build out more than 27,000 square feet of office space near Union Square. The company currently employs about 60 people and expects its workforce to grow to more than 700.

Under the plan, Aaru will invest in the State as it grows, deepening its roots in the city where it was founded just two years ago. The company's workforce is set to grow tenfold, which Governor Hochul pointed to as evidence that New York has overtaken the San Francisco Bay Area as the nation's largest tech talent market. Hochul credited her investments in computing power, research and talent with drawing companies and jobs to the state. She said Aaru started in New York, is growing here, and is creating hundreds of well-paying jobs for New Yorkers. The governor's remarks framed the expansion as a sign that leading AI companies are choosing New York to grow.

Aaru Co-Founder and CEO Cameron Fink said the company deliberately chose to build in New York City. He pointed to the depth and diversity of local talent, the closeness to the world's largest enterprises, and the city's history of innovation as reasons for the decision. Fink also said being a New York company is central to Aaru's identity and thanked Hochul and Empire State Development for their support. Empire State Development President, CEO and Commissioner Hope Knight said the company's growth shows what innovative firms can achieve when they have the talent, resources and support they need. Knight described the expansion as an important investment in Aaru's future and said the state is helping companies scale their operations and build lasting economic opportunities.

stories.Headline: Rajnath Singh calls for stronger defensive capabilities to maintain 'element of surprise' in future warfare; launches UDAAN-developed AI applications
stories.Summary:
Rajnath Singh, India's Defence Minister, called on the armed forces on Thursday, November 12, 2026, to strengthen their offensive and defensive capabilities. He spoke at the Air Force Commanders' Conference in New Delhi, where he also launched a suite of artificial intelligence applications. The applications were developed in-house by the Indian Air Force. The launch took place amid evolving warfare and rapid technological advancements affecting the region.

The applications were developed by the IAF's AI Centre of Excellence under the Unit for Digitisation, Automation, Artificial Intelligence and Application Networking, known as UDAAN. They are deployed on the IAF's secure network and are designed to automate and expedite tasks across operations, administration and aerospace safety. The initiative marks a significant milestone in the IAF's pursuit of technology-driven transformation. Singh also stressed the need to strengthen intelligence and surveillance mechanisms and to improve integration among systems. He urged identifying potential threats before they unfold.

Singh said the Defence Forces must develop capabilities that leave an adversary no time to react or recover. He stated that surprise can manifest in conventional and electronic forms, and that operational preparedness must be enhanced. The release attributed these remarks to the Defence Minister himself. He also commended the IAF for implementing its doctrines and operational methods during and after Operation Sindoor, praising the professionalism, restraint and judgement of its air warriors.

Singh said contemporary conflicts are extending beyond traditional battlefields into non-contact domains, where missiles, drones and advanced weapon systems play a significant role. Referring to the Russia-Ukraine and Israel-Hamas conflicts, he said drones and air defence systems have emerged as critical components of modern warfare. He called on the Indian Air Force to develop dedicated doctrines and architectures for electronic, cyber and space domains. He said victory in future conflicts would depend not merely on the number of aircraft but on technological sophistication, speed of response and precision.

Singh highlighted that the Defence Forces are undergoing a transformative phase covering organisational structures, jointness and integration, and operational concepts. He noted that the changing security environment requires continuous adaptation. He also highlighted the coordinated contributions of all three Services during Operation Sindoor and said jointness must guide military planning. The articles say he urged Commanders to train air warriors in emerging technologies and to use the expertise of young recruits. On the Second Tour of Duty for Agniveers, he said the decision followed feedback from the Defence Forces.

The two-day conference was attended by the Air Officers Commanding-in-Chief of all IAF Commands, Principal Staff Officers and Director Generals. The inaugural session included Raksha Rajya Mantri Sanjay Seth, Chief of the Air Staff Air Chief Marshal Ashutosh Dixit, and Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh. Secretary for Defence Production Sanjeev Kumar and Secretary for Defence Finance Vishvajit Sahay also attended. The conference, themed 'The Year of Empowerment: Maximising Efficiency Through Decentralisation', was intended to address critical operational, maintenance and administrative issues.

The articles provide no information about specific operations or incidents that prompted the call for stronger capabilities beyond the references to Operation Sindoor, Russia-Ukraine and Israel-Hamas. They do not describe any reaction from opposition parties, foreign governments or other officials. They also do not detail how the AI applications will be rolled out beyond the IAF or what budget was allocated. The articles also leave unclear how the decentralised, efficiency-focused theme will be translated into concrete measures after the conference concludes.

stories.Headline: China's $3 billion-plus pipeline of Nvidia-powered AI data centres
stories.Summary:
Reuters has identified more than $3 billion in Chinese computing projects built around Nvidia's restricted processors, according to a report published on November 13, 2026. The findings came a day after Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive over a scandal. The review found projects ranging from China's wealthy coastal technology hubs to remote western provinces. Nvidia has said that US export controls have effectively shut it out of the Chinese AI data-centre market. The report stresses how deeply Nvidia's technology remains embedded in China's AI expansion.

A proposed 6.2 billion yuan, or $873 million, AI computing centre in Xianyou county, Fujian province, specifies Nvidia H100 chips and is seeking commercial partners. In Shaanxi province, Sinomach said a subsidiary won a contract for a 3 billion yuan computing centre specifying H100 and H200 processors. An April government prospectus in Jilin province describes a 2.26 billion yuan project combining H100 processors with Chinese-developed chips, with banks expected to finance about 80% of the investment. In Inner Mongolia, a 1.5 billion yuan development proposes installing 625 Nvidia H200 servers. In Gansu province, a 1.16 billion yuan contract awarded in July covers a centre planning about 3,072 Nvidia processors.

The report suggests these plans depend on US processors that are vulnerable to trade restrictions. Tighter curbs could cause construction delays, higher costs or redesigns around domestic alternatives. Nvidia's chief executive resigned, and Huang's departure could deepen vulnerabilities for Chinese companies exposed to potential delays and supply disruptions. The Reuters review did not establish whether the processors in the Gansu project have been delivered. Huang, who co-founded Nvidia, had been a vocal advocate of easing export restrictions.

Other Chinese facilities already use restricted Nvidia hardware, according to the review. The Wuxi municipal government in Jiangsu province said in March 2025 that a computing cluster using H800 processors had entered operation. In June, Shanghai-listed Damingcheng disclosed that a computing venture in Fujian had built an H800 cluster under a computing-services agreement originally worth 759 million yuan, which ended early. Shenzhen University bought three H100 processors in September, and US-blacklisted Northwestern Polytechnical University bought two H200 chips the following month. Demand thus extends to research institutions.

A separate Global Times editorial published on November 8 argued that US technology companies could consider deploying some AI computing capacity in China. The editorial pointed to American constraints such as insufficient electricity supply, grid upgrade delays, high construction costs, lengthy approvals and local opposition to data centres after the midterm elections. It cited China's advantages in electricity, equipment manufacturing and infrastructure planning. Some estimates in a related commentary put US construction costs at $8 million to $12 million per megawatt, against $5.5 million to $6.5 million in China. The editorial acknowledged practical limits involving national security, data protection, latency and regulation.

The Global Times commentary described the idea of "American computing, Chinese data centre" as an online joke that is little more than a joke because of Washington's securitisation of technology. It blamed continued US export controls and investment restrictions for making cooperation harder. The editorial said the two countries should move away from zero-sum competition and expand practical cooperation while jointly advancing AI governance. It also urged the United States to recognise China's strengths rather than pursue technological decoupling. Commentary on the editorial said it should not be mistaken for an official policy proposal.

Background from the articles shows that Nvidia's restricted chips have been used in China despite US curbs, and that several projects and buyers, including state-owned and university entities, rely on them. The Reuters review noted that Nvidia has said export controls effectively shut it out of this market. The Global Times editorial framed the issue around US grid and construction bottlenecks, while the Reuters review focused on the exposure of Chinese projects to trade restrictions. The articles also reference earlier reporting on Chinese purchases of restricted Nvidia chips and on the chief executive's departure.

The articles leave open whether the Gansu processors were delivered and how the Xianyou, Shaanxi and Jilin projects will be financed or completed. They do not establish how tighter US curbs will affect the projects or whether Chinese companies will switch to domestic alternatives. It is unclear whether US companies will take up the offshore data-centre idea, and the Global Times editorial was not an official policy proposal. The articles also leave open how the APEC leaders' meeting may shape these positions, and whether any cooperation on AI governance will follow.

stories.Headline: Gov't vows zero tolerance against cheating with AI glasses
stories.Summary:
The South Korean government has promised zero tolerance for cheating with artificial intelligence glasses in next week's nationwide college entrance exam. The pledge, announced on Friday, followed suspicions raised by an unusually high score in this year's certified tax accountant exam. The Prime Minister's Secretariat and the Office for Government Policy Coordination made the statements, with the Yonhap and KBS reports both covering the announcement. The College Scholastic Ability Test, known as the Suneung, is set for Thursday, November 19, according to the reports' timing.

The suspicions began when the highest scorer in the tax accountant exam's first round earned 397.5 points out of a possible 400. That person missed only one of the 160 questions, a result many test-takers consider unrealistic. Specialized personnel will be deployed to test sites to detect AI glasses during the Suneung. The government said it would dispatch additional staff and coordinate a quick response between the education ministry and regional education offices. Anyone caught faces punishment for interference with business and obstruction of official duties by fraudulent means, and loses eligibility to retake the exam for three years.

The Office for Government Policy Coordination said cheating with AI glasses is a serious issue that infringes on fair opportunities for diligent students. The office said it takes public concerns on the matter very seriously. The Prime Minister's Secretariat said it takes growing public concern about recent fraudulent acts involving AI glasses during state-run exams very seriously. The government said it will make thorough preparations for the Suneung and closely monitor exam operations until the test concludes. Students who have worked hard for the exam are the people the government says these measures are meant to protect.

Public concern has grown after recent fraudulent acts involving AI glasses during various state-run exams. The suspicion over the tax accountant result has raised worries that similar AI-assisted cheating could occur in the Suneung. Students taking the Suneung on Thursday are directly affected by the heightened monitoring at test sites. Test-takers in the tax accountant exam have also voiced doubts about the top score. The government said last month that it would take steps to catch cheaters using AI-equipped smart glasses, which indicates the problem had already been under discussion before the latest announcement.

The government said it will also seek to clear up suspicions raised in the tax accountant exam, including by requesting an investigation. If cheating is confirmed, the government said it will enforce corresponding accountability under relevant laws and regulations. The Prime Minister's Secretariat said it plans to thoroughly review how state-run exams are managed and to roll out measures against cheating with smart devices. The articles do not say when the tax accountant investigation will conclude or who will carry it out. They also do not say how many cheaters, if any, will be detected in the Suneung or how the planned review will be structured.

stories.Headline: FuelCell Energy Advances AI Data Center Power With New Testbed
stories.Summary:
FuelCell Energy said it is taking part in StabilityMax, a three-year project led by the U.S. Department of Energy's National Laboratory of the Rockies, with Argonne National Laboratory also involved. The announcement came from Danbury, Connecticut, on November 10, 2026, according to a press release distributed by GlobeNewswire. The project aims to develop and validate integrated power system architectures for artificial intelligence data centers. The company framed the work as a response to rapidly evolving electricity needs created by AI adoption. Its participation was announced under the Nasdaq ticker FCEL.

The project will develop and validate a testing and modeling framework that evaluates how fuel cells, energy storage, advanced controls and power electronics can work together. FuelCell Energy will develop a fuel cell test facility in Connecticut, creating a testbed supported by a national laboratory for evaluating integrated power solutions. The National Laboratory of the Rockies will build data center load profiles and simulation models that capture the dynamic power demands of modern computing infrastructure. Argonne National Laboratory will carry out techno-economic and lifecycle analyses to identify cost-effective deployment strategies. The initiative is intended to produce tools and insights for optimizing system designs and validating performance under realistic conditions.

The National Laboratory of the Rockies is the lead institution and is responsible for the modeling and simulation work, which it described as part of a wider effort to support energy needs of AI-enabled digital infrastructure. FuelCell Energy's Chief Product and Technology Officer, Shankar Achanta, said the project combines the company's operating experience and fuel cell technology with national laboratory expertise. Zhiwen Ma, principal investigator at the National Laboratory of the Rockies, said the project would show how integrated fuel cell systems can respond quickly to data center power needs. Ma added that such systems could limit impacts on the utility grid and on ratepayers. The laboratory's new modeling tools, planning platforms and test environments are meant to accelerate deployment of these power systems.

Eric Strayer, FuelCell Energy's Head of Global Sales, said the company is working with customers and partners deploying power solutions for digital infrastructure. He said the project will provide data and operating experience to inform future deployments as load profiles change with each new generation of chips. Analysts at Quantisnow, whose AI agent Ellis summarized the release, described the project as a research and development collaboration that reports no contract or revenue. That summary noted that the company will fund and build its share of the test facility. The release says the work is expected to affect operators of AI data centers, who face rapid swings in electricity consumption, and the utilities that supply them.

The project builds on FuelCell Energy's existing development of integrated power solutions for digital infrastructure. Earlier in 2026, the company announced a collaboration with Siemens to advance a layered architecture that combines technologies operating across different timescales. FuelCell Energy describes its fuel cell systems as generating electricity on-site at the point of use, with global deployments approaching one gigawatt. The company also states that its systems are compact, modular and quiet, with low emissions. Zacks Investment Research noted that FuelCell Energy carries a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold).

The articles do not say when the Connecticut test facility will be completed or begin operating. They also do not give the project's budget, the company's share of its cost, or any timeline for the first results. No commercial contract or customer commitment tied to StabilityMax is reported. Whether the testing will lead to orders for FuelCell Energy's systems remains unstated in the sources.

stories.Headline: AI spending helps lift UK growth to fastest since early 2024
stories.Summary:
Britain's economy grew 0.7% in the July-to-September quarter of 2026, its fastest quarterly expansion in two-and-a-half years, helped by investment in artificial intelligence. The Office for National Statistics announced the figure on Thursday, and the growth extended a strong first half of the year. Growth had been expected to slow after the Iran war began, so the result defied those predictions. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the quarterly rate, but output in September alone rose 0.2%, beating expectations of no change for the month. Annual growth picked up to 1.9% in the third quarter, the strongest reading since the fourth quarter of 2024.

Monthly GDP has now beaten consensus forecasts for the fifth month in a row and seven times in the last eight months. Rob Wood, chief UK economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, said these figures strengthened the chances of another Bank of England rate hike next month. Growth over the three months to September was the fastest since May, on a rolling basis. Growth so far this year has been the strongest since 2017, excluding the post-pandemic rebound. British growth in the third quarter was the second-fastest among the Group of Seven advanced economies, behind only the United States.

The Office for National Statistics said there was widespread strength in industries that may be related to artificial intelligence. Computer programming, consultancy and related activity made the largest single contribution to growth in the third quarter. Computer manufacturing made the biggest contribution to industrial production, which rose 4.6% in the three months to September. The economy had expanded by 0.6% in the first quarter of 2026, showing resilience in the first half of the year. Business investment, however, grew just 0.4% on the quarter, half of what economists expected, and was the weakest growth since the start of the year.

Scott Gardner, investment strategist at JP Morgan Personal Investing, said the UK economy has been relatively resilient since the conflict started, but that strength will be tested in the months ahead. He said nervousness before the autumn budget and continued uncertainty from the Middle East war are expected to weigh on confidence and activity in coming GDP readings. The Bank of England last week raised its 2026 growth forecast to 1.6%, against the 1.2% forecast by the government's Office for Budget Responsibility after finance minister John Healey's October 28 budget. The central bank attributed some of the strength to spending on AI and a small, temporary boost from Healey's fiscal plan. Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Healey welcomed the data.

The data is likely to increase pressure on the Bank of England to raise interest rates again. The central bank warned last week that inflation will near 5% in 2027, and investors see a 73% chance of a back-to-back hike in December after November's increase. Wood said that with growth and inflation both strong, he expects at least two more hikes from the Monetary Policy Committee, and that today's figures make a December hike more likely. Household gas and electricity bills are still set to rise by about 25% when the energy price cap changes in January. Britain's government has offered limited support to help families absorb the energy price shock.

Some economists expect slower growth in the final quarter of the year as higher energy prices and borrowing costs weigh on activity. There have been recent signs of weakening consumer and business demand, with retail sales volumes falling in September. Consumer confidence also suffered its sharpest month-on-month fall since April 2020 before the budget. The articles do not say how large the fourth-quarter slowdown will be or whether the Bank of England will raise rates in December. They also do not give the outcome of the autumn budget, which Gardner described as a source of nervousness for confidence and activity.

stories.Headline: Akhilesh Yadav says phones can't be trusted in AI age amid Rahul Gandhi's phone-tapping allegation
stories.Summary:
Akhilesh Yadav, chief of the Samajwadi Party, said on Friday, November 13, 2026, that phones and modern technology cannot be trusted in the age of artificial intelligence. He spoke in Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh, backing Congress leader Rahul Gandhi's claim that Prime Minister Narendra Modi had his phone tapped. Yadav also alleged large-scale manipulation of voter lists in the state. He said that anything is possible in the age of AI, referring to Gandhi's allegation. He added that a leader who is no longer alive had once spoken about their own phones being tapped.

Yadav claimed that 1.27 crore names had been removed from the electoral rolls and that votes belonging to the Samajwadi Party were being deleted. He said the BJP was preparing to bring people from Madhya Pradesh, Bihar, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand to register them as voters in Uttar Pradesh. He alleged the plan would replace votes deleted because of relocation or fraudulent registrations. He called for a durable, secure card linked to Aadhaar, and for biometric-based voting for greater transparency. He said that if a Samajwadi Party government is formed, it would introduce biometric voter cards.

Gandhi, the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha, said in a video posted by the Congress on X that the Prime Minister had his phone tapped. He challenged Modi to agree to an open, face-to-face debate and claimed proof of Modi being under the control of foreign powers was on his phone. Yadav, speaking at the Samajwadi Party's state headquarters, made his remarks before an election review meeting with assembly-level presidents of 86 reserved constituencies. Congress MP Imran Masood said the Prime Minister was scared and that the country was listening to Gandhi. The articles quote Yadav saying that the Chief Minister knows that 12.7 million, or 1 crore 27 lakh, voters had been removed from the rolls.

Yadav said voters might reach polling booths only to be told their votes were not registered there, forcing them to search for their names elsewhere. He referred to Pilibhit, where the Samajwadi Party had raised a voter list issue, after which action was taken against two Sub-Divisional Magistrates. He said the BJP would be defeated the day election dates are announced. The remarks come as both parties exchange heated jibes ahead of the 2027 State Assembly election. Masood, responding to the Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister's claim of 1.27 crore missing Hindu voters, said there was a fight between the CM and the Deputy CM.

The articles do not say whether the BJP or the Election Commission has responded to Yadav's allegations about voter lists or the planned registrations. They also do not report any formal investigation into the phone-tapping claim. Whether the Prime Minister will accept the proposed face-to-face debate is not stated. The articles do not say whether the proposed biometric voter cards will be introduced, since that depends on a future Samajwadi Party government. The date of the 2027 Assembly election is not given in the articles.
