stories.Headline: Alberta expanding use of AI technology that speeds up MRIs after successful pilot
stories.Summary:
The Alberta government has announced it will spend $14 million on artificial intelligence technology that speeds up the MRI testing process. The decision follows a pilot program that began last year and, according to the government, led to almost 12,000 more MRIs being performed. The technology is installed directly onto MRI machines in hospitals, where it improves image clarity and shortens examination times. Hospitals Minister Adriana LaGrange said a record number of MRIs were completed in Alberta last year. The province expects the technology to be installed provincewide by 2028.

Hospitals Minister Adriana LaGrange said the money will increase the province's testing capacity and reduce wait times. She described the funding as a way to build on last year's record number of completed MRIs. The government says patient data will remain safe under the arrangement. It also says the technology does not transmit individual records or information to outside networks. The announcement was made in Edmonton.

The Alberta government is the body making the spending decision and is responsible for the rollout. LaGrange, who serves as the province's Hospitals Minister, was the official quoted on the program's results and goals. The articles do not give further statements from other officials. The government's stated reasons centre on capacity and wait times for MRI patients across the province.

Patients waiting for MRI examinations in Alberta are the group the articles identify as affected by the changes. The articles give no reactions from patient groups, health professionals or opposition parties. They also provide no further details on how the technology's effects will be measured. The reported gains are limited to the figures the government itself supplied.

The articles report that a successful pilot program began in Alberta last year. They say that pilot led to almost 12,000 more MRIs being done. The articles also say Alberta completed a record number of MRIs last year. Beyond these points, the articles give no further history of the technology or of the province's MRI services.

The technology is expected to be installed provincewide by 2028, according to the articles. The articles do not say how the $14 million will be divided between sites or how the rollout will be staged before that date. They also do not say whether the government will publish results or cost figures after installation. What happens to wait times, and whether the province meets its 2028 target, is not addressed.

stories.Headline: Global powers head to Asia with trade, AI, security in focus
stories.Summary:
Global leaders are heading to Asia for a series of meetings covering AI, trade and possibly nuclear disarmament. The 11-nation Association of Southeast Asian Nations opens its final leaders' summit of the year on Sunday in Manila. French President Emmanuel Macron attends a Francophonie summit in Phnom Penh during the same period. The annual Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation conference then moves to Shenzhen, where Russian President Vladimir Putin is expected to be a key figure.

Three summits take place over five days, according to the report. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi will attend the ASEAN meeting, while US President Donald Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney will travel to both events. A proposed meeting between China's Xi Jinping, Trump and Putin may take place at APEC, though its agenda remains unclear. Xi and Trump agreed in September to set up a communication channel for AI incidents. The Philippines holds the ASEAN chair this year, and China and the Philippines are both involved in the South China Sea dispute.

Analysts quoted by AFP say Trump's recent midterm defeat will not greatly change how the region sees him. Siew Mun Tang, former head of the ASEAN Studies Centre at Singapore's ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute, said Trump still has two more years in office. Ryan Hass of the Brookings Institution expects symbolism to account for much of the summit's substance. Wang Wen, dean of Renmin University's Chongyang Institute for Financial Studies, called a breakthrough unlikely in the talks between Xi, Trump and Putin.

Trump has suggested the focus of any sit-down with Xi and Putin would be denuclearisation and ending the war in Iran. Putin has pushed for talks on Ukraine. Separately, a meeting Trump once hoped for with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un appears stalled, as Pyongyang has rejected repeated overtures. A spying scandal involving Nvidia boss Jensen Huang, who US officials have accused of sleeping with a woman they claim worked for Beijing, may cast a shadow over AI discussions at APEC.

A pause in the China-US trade war was extended through January 10 during Xi's September visit to the White House, but friction over Chinese rare-earth exports remains. Economist Harry Murphy Cruise of Oxford Economics warned that reversing existing US tariffs would require legislation that the president could veto. A separate report from McGill University's Centre for Media, Technology and Democracy found more than 3,000 AI deepfake videos drew about 20 million views in three months. The videos used the faces of real influencers, including Edmonton commentator Cole Bennett, to push content on the Alberta referendum, provincial elections and US-Canada trade tensions. Researchers identified 293 accounts in the network, and TikTok said it permanently banned the accounts named in the report.

Those behind the accounts are not yet identified, though the centre said the activity appeared to come from East or Southeast Asian time zones and some accounts were registered in China. The centre said the behaviour suggested a paid operation following workday hours. Bennett, a 29-year-old progressive pundit, said such deepfakes can be frightening because what he says is central to his brand. TikTok said it collaborates with researchers and removes more than 98 per cent of deceptive content before it is reported. Instagram had not responded to a request for comment by midday Thursday.

The centre could not determine the network's goal, and the videos do not appear to advance a single ideological agenda. Many of the most-watched videos contained false claims, including one that said Trump had issued Canada a 48-hour ultimatum over retaliatory tariffs. Those 161 videos using that script drew about 5.1 million views in total. The network also appears not yet to be earning money directly from the content. Kristina Collins, known online as Kallmekris, was among the Canadian creators whose likeness was used.

The ASEAN summit in Manila is not expected to produce a South China Sea Code of Conduct with China, according to one diplomat involved in preparations. Former ASEAN Studies Centre head Tang said the code may have lost its purpose because conditions on the ground have changed, citing militarisation of islands by China and Vietnam. Trade is expected to be a major topic at both ASEAN and APEC, though regional free-trade plans remain complicated by China-US tensions. No major changes to US trade policy are expected for the time being. The report leaves open what the deepfake network intended and who runs it.

stories.Headline: Naver clinches $1.5 bil. AI computing deal with US firm
stories.Summary:
Naver, the South Korean internet company, has signed a 2 trillion-won ($1.5 billion) computing services supply contract with a U.S. artificial intelligence inference company, its first customer for its AI infrastructure business. The deal was announced on Thursday, November 12, 2026, during the company's third-quarter earnings call, and it comes ahead of a commercial launch planned for the first half of next year. The contract covers computing services using next-generation graphics processing units, with the initial supply scheduled to begin in 2027. Naver's chief executive, Choi Soo-yeon, described the agreement as confirming real market demand and the early commercial viability of the AI factory business. Naver also said it had reported record quarterly revenue alongside weaker operating profit.

The contract covers about 20 megawatts of capacity over four to five years, according to reporting on the deal. Naver plans to expand its AI factory capacity from 55 megawatts next year to 200 megawatts by 2028. The company said its contracted data center capacity already exceeds that 200-megawatt target for 2028. Naver is in talks with more than 10 prospective customers outside Asia, including major AI model developers, for the remaining capacity. Separately, the company plans to set up a dedicated logistics subsidiary and expand its leased fulfillment centers, with investment expected to approach 1 trillion won through 2030.

Choi said the AI factory is being developed in partnership with the Canadian asset manager Brookfield and the U.S. chipmaker Nvidia. Choi said Naver was pursuing long-term contracts with major customers while widening its customer base to include global AI companies with strong growth potential. She said this would reduce reliance on individual clients and help the company seek stable, higher-margin business. Choi also said the company would seek appropriate financing and revenue structures to limit the impact of logistics spending on cash flow and earnings. Naver's chief financial officer, Kim Hee-cheol, spoke about the negotiations with prospective customers.

The company reported third-quarter sales of 3.47 trillion won, up 10.7 percent from a year earlier, marking its sixth consecutive quarterly revenue record. Operating profit fell 20.9 percent to 451.3 billion won, giving an operating margin of 13 percent, as AI-related investment and content spending weighed on earnings. Platform revenue rose 7.3 percent to 1.95 trillion won, while financial platform revenue increased 14.1 percent to 487.7 billion won. Global business revenue climbed 15.9 percent to 1.04 trillion won, driven by consumer-to-consumer businesses including Wallapop and Poshmark. Naver also plans to launch a personal AI agent app by the end of this year that can carry out tasks such as shopping and making reservations.

Naver is also planning robotic delivery services at residential complexes in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, in the first half of 2027, combining its digital-twin mapping technology with Naver Labs' Nuri robot. Choi said traffic from the AI Tab to shopping and local services has nearly doubled since its launch, with transaction value also growing. The expansion of AI infrastructure and logistics is aimed at reducing reliance on search and e-commerce as revenue sources. Naver's global business and Saudi digital-twin projects also contributed to the growth in its global ventures revenue. The company's stated plans cover the coming years, but the articles do not say how the logistics investment will be financed.

Naver has not named the U.S. customer, and the articles do not say which specific AI models will run on the capacity. The articles also do not say how much revenue the AI factory will generate once commercial services begin in the first half of next year. Whether Naver will sign contracts with the more than 10 companies it is negotiating with remains unknown from the reporting. stories.Headline: Exclusive: US-sanctioned Jinan Supercomputing Center still gets Nvidia AI products
stories.Summary:
On June 17, 2026, the China Government Procurement Network published a result announcement for an AI equipment procurement project run by the Shandong Computing Center, also known as the National Supercomputing Center Jinan. The procurement, titled "Edge Intelligent Computing Team AI Workstation and Graphics Card Procurement Project," listed Nvidia's RTX 5090 graphics cards and DGX Spark systems. Radio Free Asia reported the findings in an investigation published around November 13, 2026, alongside Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation. The report found that sanctioned entities in China were still able to obtain the company's AI chips despite U.S. restrictions. The investigation said the procurement appeared in a winning bid announcement this year, which made the center's access to the products a central question.

The center appears on the U.S. Department of Commerce Entity List, so U.S. rules would bar it from buying or using these products without a license. Exporting controlled items to the center generally requires a Commerce Department license, and without one the request is presumed to be denied. The winning bid was RMB 148,500, about US$22,000, awarded to Qiyuan Jiasu (Tianjin) Technology Co., Ltd. The procurement quantity was listed only as "one batch," without stating how many graphics cards or DGX Spark units it covered. The RTX 5090 has a standard version and China-specific versions, RTX 5090 D and RTX 5090 D v2, but the announcement did not say which one was bought. The DGX Spark is listed on Nvidia's official Chinese website, so it can be sold in China's general market, though that does not permit sales to restricted entities.

Radio Free Asia said the company's profile and rules govern the matter, but the articles do not name a specific official who answered the findings. Nvidia's chief executive, Jensen Huang, announced his resignation on Thursday amid a scandal over an alleged extramarital affair, which the report said may have been a Chinese spy plot targeting him. The U.S. government will continue to investigate Huang's involvement with Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a former executive at Singapore cloud data center company Megaspeed. Alice Huang is suspected of collecting intelligence for Beijing and helping Chinese clients obtain restricted chips. The articles report that Chris Tseng, a researcher at Taiwan's Research Institute for Democracy, Society and Emerging Technology, said current controls rely heavily on corporate self-compliance.

Tseng told Radio Free Asia that export controls travel with the item, so a license is still required to transfer these products to a controlled entity even if they reach legitimate distributors first. Sylvia Chen, an economic security policy analyst at DSET, said third-party firms cannot first buy controlled products and then resell them to the center, and that they could face legal liability. Chen said the Bureau of Industry and Security has only one export control officer in Beijing, and only 15 such officers worldwide. Bloomberg News reported that Nvidia's inventory verification reports to the U.S. government underreported about 50,000 AI chips sold to Megaspeed, valued at billions of dollars. The articles said the concern is that chips leaked into China via Southeast Asia, and that the center was added to the entity list in April 2021.

The Shandong Computing Center was established in 1976 and is affiliated with Qilu University of Technology, while the National Supercomputing Center Jinan was established in 2011. The Commerce Department listed "Shandong Computing Center" as an alias for the center in April 2021, before broader chip export restrictions began in 2022. At that time the department said seven Chinese supercomputing and chip institutions, including Jinan, Shenzhen, Wuxi and Zhengzhou, had procured U.S.-origin items to support military units and weapons programs. Qiyuan Jiasu shares identical website wording, production bases in Wuqing, Tianjin, marketing offices in Shangdi, Beijing, and client lists with Sitonholy (Tianjin) Technology. Sitonholy was an Nvidia partner from 2015 and was placed on the Entity List on April 11, 2024.

The articles say a commentator familiar with China's AI industry suspected Qiyuan Jiasu could be a new entity taking over part of Sitonholy's business after it was sanctioned. Li Houchen, a Japan-based columnist, said Nvidia would need to investigate the sales and ultimate flow of related products if that inheritance were confirmed. Public information shows only that the two companies' profiles, client lists and locations overlap, with no direct evidence yet of shared ultimate ownership. The articles do not say whether Nvidia has responded to the procurement findings or the Megaspeed reporting. They also do not establish whether the center actually received the graphics cards or systems, or whether any penalty has been imposed on Qiyuan Jiasu.

stories.Headline: China’s Jensen Huang ‘honeypot’ trap is only more reason to win the AI race
stories.Summary:
China's Jensen Huang, the Nvidia chief executive, has been at the centre of a controversy over an alleged extra-marital affair and claims that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy. Commentators and social media have turned the saga into widespread entertainment, with memes and influencer gags spreading online. The matter has also prompted questions about its effect on the frontier artificial intelligence race between the United States and China. Analysts see the episode as a potential shift in that contest, one that could influence how the two countries compete in AI development. The coverage gives the story a central place in the wider debate over AI leadership.

Huang has long been seen as a villain by many US hawks because he has argued for relaxing restrictions on the sale of Nvidia chips to China. The latest allegations have added to hawkish views about him, and the scrutiny extends to concerns over alleged corporate espionage. An HT analysis of trade data shows China has rising import dependence on commodities that are likely GPUs or related products. The United States has tried to restrict China's access to cutting-edge chips and GPUs, while China has limited rare earth mineral supplies to the US. The Pax Silica alliance, launched by the US in December 2025, is designed to ease American access to rare earth minerals.

China has denied the allegations of spying and has downplayed the controversy, as expected. The Straits Times writer argues that some pain for Nvidia could help secure the West's AI lead over China in the long run. Commentators disagree on how much China needs Nvidia's chips, and the actual evidence on that question is not clear. The HT analysis notes that the disclosure of Huang's affair is certain to add paranoia in the US AI ecosystem about a Chinese catch-up. The writer's view is that Nvidia's weakening might also spur competition and innovation.

China's trade surplus is expected to exceed a trillion dollars for a second consecutive year in 2026, according to the HT report. China released the open-source reasoning model DeepSeek-R1 in January 2025, bringing it within striking distance of leading frontier AI developers, all based in the US. A Lowy Institute report shows Chinese models are catching up fast with American models, although the US leads China in every AI field except human resources. A Carnegie China report, cited by HT, indicates China is catching up quickly with the US in skilled AI workforce. Huawei announced a new chip-design approach in May 2026 that could limit the effect of US export controls.

The articles leave open whether the constraints on chips and rare earths will matter in the long term, and whether either side will crack its challenge before those constraints become redundant. The Lowy Institute report says Huawei could design chips by 2031 with transistor density equivalent to TSMC's 2028 chips, but whether this succeeds is not yet known. Beijing countered the Pax Silica alliance with the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization earlier in 2026. The articles do not say how the allegations against Huang will ultimately be resolved or how Nvidia's position will change.

stories.Headline: AI Expert, Spelman College President’s New Book Offers a New Vision for the Future of Artificial Intelligence - Carroll County Mirror-Democrat
stories.Summary:
On November 10, 2026, Spelman College in Atlanta hosted an event to launch Spelman President Ayanna Howard's new book about the future of artificial intelligence. The book, titled REBOOTING THE MACHINES: A New Human Vision for Artificial Intelligence, was celebrated with a fireside chat, an audience question-and-answer session, and a book signing. All proceeds from the event went toward Spelman scholarships. The press release announcing the event was issued on November 12, 2026, through GlobeNewswire, and the same text appeared in other outlets. Howard's book is presented as a new vision for AI that centers human values, ethics, and diverse perspectives.

Howard draws on her experience as an AI and robotics expert, entrepreneur, and academic leader to examine how human values shape AI's future. In the book she argues that AI, including robotics, is not built with a moral center, so people must supply that moral compass if the technology is to serve all humanity. An excerpt quotes her saying that people must take stock of AI's influence on their lives to thrive in an AI-infused world. She also says society has the power both to build AI that reflects society as it is and to build AI that fosters the society people aspire to have. The book offers a practical roadmap for deciding what to demand from tech companies, what to resist, and how to build ethical human values into machines.

Howard, who became president of Spelman in August 2026, wrote the book as the author and speaker in the launch. The press release attributes the book's message to her and quotes her directly. The release does not describe any other person as responsible for the book's arguments. Its contents are presented as her own views on AI's moral foundations and its social role. The release frames the book as her contribution to the discussion, supported by the launch event.

The release says that students in higher education worry that AI will erase the futures they worked hard to build. Howard's arrival at Spelman comes during this period of anxiety, according to the release. At the launch, engineer and policy scholar Dr. Kamau Bobb and WABE's Rose Scot joined Howard in a conversation about AI's changing effect on the workforce. They also discussed the importance of diversity among AI developers, ways to address bias in new technologies, and shared responsibility for a more equitable AI future. Spelman students and the wider public are the groups the release identifies as affected by these concerns.

Spelman College was founded in 1881 and is located in Atlanta, where it has 2,700 students. The release describes Spelman as a liberal arts college focused on educating women of African descent, and it says the college leads the country in producing Black women who complete Ph.D.s in STEM fields. U.S. News & World Report ranked Spelman No. 34 among liberal arts colleges and No. 1 among historically Black colleges and universities for the 20th year. Recent initiatives include a Department of Defense designation as a Center of Excellence for Minority Women in STEM and collaborations with MIT's Media Lab, the Broad Institute, and the Army Research Lab on AI and machine learning. The release also lists notable alumnae such as Marian Wright Edelman, Rosalind Brewer, Stacey Abrams, and Tayari Jones.

The articles do not say whether a second printing, further events, or policy steps will follow the book's launch. They also do not state the book's sales figures or how much money the scholarships will ultimately receive. Readers can learn more or buy the book at www.broadleafbooks.com, and the release directs media questions to Spelman's public relations office. The articles do not describe any response from tech companies or government bodies to Howard's proposals.

stories.Headline: How it feels to battle with a flood of AI-generated complaints
stories.Summary:
A UK housing association complaint investigator has written to The Guardian, in a letter published on 13 November 2026, describing how AI-generated complaints have swamped their work. The writer says the scope of their job changed completely within a few months, after nine years in the role. They respond to an earlier Guardian article from 8 November about UK public bodies facing a flood of chatbot-written grievances. The writer says that hundreds of pages of wordy complaints are hard to sift through, and that the technical language in AI-drafted letters often confuses customers when staff speak with them in person or by phone. They argue that a human-written complaint, even one with spelling mistakes or expletives, comes from the person and gets straight to the heart of the issue.

They also describe regular complainants who send multiple, massive AI-generated complaints each month, which makes staff feel disrespected. The organisation is considering treating this bombardment as a form of harassment. A second letter, from Pete Bibby, takes a different view. Bibby says that using AI as an assistant to seek redress should not be seen as a nuisance, but as a way of extending recourse to people who lack the time or resources to pursue complaints. Bibby argues that public bodies, especially councils, should use AI with a human in the loop to work through likely legitimate complaints, whatever their wording.

Bibby also suggests that the so-called clog may reflect earlier powerlessness among people who could not express grievances before. The letters sit against a backdrop of strain on public services, and the first writer points to the case of Awaab Ishak as an example of why accessible complaints processes matter for tenants. The articles do not say whether the housing association has formally adopted a harassment classification, or what the outcome of the debate will be. The letters themselves are opinion, not reporting on a decision.

stories.Headline: Foundation Models framework
stories.Summary:
Apple has released an updated Foundation Models framework, a native Swift API for integrating large language models into apps, according to its developer site dated 12 November 2026. It gives direct access to the Apple Foundation Models both on-device and in Private Cloud Compute. Guided generation, tool calling, image understanding and Dynamic Profiles are built in, so developers do not need to add them separately. Separately, Microsoft has begun rolling out its own foundation models under its Microsoft AI program, known as MAI, according to InfoWorld. Microsoft's models are offered mainly through its Foundry platform, which the article says gives access to more than 11,000 different models.

Apple's framework now accepts multimodal prompts, so an app can pass images alongside text and reason about visual content. The Vision framework is integrated, giving the model tools such as OCR for text extraction and barcode readers, all on-device. The framework also extends to server models, including Claude and Gemini, through the same Swift API, with support for tool calling and guided generation. Developers in the App Store Small Business Program with fewer than two million first-time App Store downloads can use the Apple models on Private Cloud Compute with no cloud API cost. A new fm command line tool arrives in macOS 27, and an Evaluations framework lets developers test prompts and validate features.

Apple says any model provider can create a Swift package conforming to the Language Model protocol, which lets developers choose the right model for their app. It describes Dynamic Profiles as declarative APIs for updating a session's model, tools and instructions on the fly. Each profile carries its own model, temperature, reasoning level and toolset, and the session transcript is shared across every profile switch. Apple says the Evaluations framework is meant to give developers confidence that their app's behavior holds up before shipping. It also says the Private Cloud Compute option ensures user data is not stored or accessible to Apple or anyone else.

InfoWorld's Simon Bisson reports that Microsoft's MAI models focus on offering a lower token cost than competitors, which he says fills a gap in the market. He writes that the era of free and low-cost tokens is over, as hyperscale vendors try to recoup their multi-billion-dollar data center investments. MAI describes its approach as humanist, with a focus on safety and environmental impact. The affected users include developers who can call MAI models through existing Foundry Azure OpenAI APIs, and who can set limits on tokens used per request. Microsoft also offers a tuning service that lets customers build custom versions of the models using their own data.

Apple's framework also offers open source pieces, including a utilities package with custom skills, context management helpers and a Chat Completions client for a hosted model of your choice. A Foundation Models SDK for Python extends the framework into the Python ecosystem. Apple publishes Acceptable Use Requirements that prohibit certain uses of its models, and cites Article 53(1)(b) of the AI Act in making documentation available for AFM 3 Cloud. On the Microsoft side, Foundry started from a partnership in which OpenAI trained models on Azure infrastructure and Microsoft became the first commercial partner to use them. Its stable later grew to include Anthropic, Hugging Face, Meta, Mistral and DeepSeek models, alongside its Phi series and Cognitive Services models, and Microsoft Research has long topped benchmark tables with focused models.

Among the MAI models, MAI-Code-1.1-Flash is used in the GitHub Copilot service and MAI-Cyber-1.1-Flash in Microsoft's MDASH security system, while MAI-Thinking-1 handles the most complex applications. MAI-Code-1.1-Flash needs more than 120GB of RAM, so it is not yet small enough for Copilot+ PCs, while a Surface Ultra with an NVIDIA RTX Spark and at least 128GB of RAM should be capable. MAI-Cyber-1.1-Flash handles 90% of tasks once done by larger models and is 18% cheaper to run than version 1.0. The Maia 300 accelerator raises compute by 36%, improves high bandwidth memory performance 2.5 times, and gives roughly a 2x gain per watt, with 96 accelerators per rack. The articles leave open how much local operation would save over cloud servers, and they give no release date for the new Apple tools beyond macOS 27.

stories.Headline: Nvidia's interim CEO inherits risky AI bets and a legal mess
stories.Summary:
Nvidia's chief executive, Jensen Huang, resigned with immediate effect, the company's board announced on November 12, 2026. The departure came amid a dizzying week that also included a suspected intelligence scandal and reports of multiple extramarital affairs involving the leader of the company that has been central to the AI boom. Colette Kress, the company's longtime finance chief, agreed to serve as interim chief executive while continuing as executive vice president and chief financial officer. The board said it would search for a permanent successor and would consider both internal and external candidates.

Kress has been with Nvidia since September 2013 and previously spent nearly 25 years in finance roles at technology companies including Cisco and Microsoft. The board also named Harvey C. Jones as its first-ever chair, and he has more than 30 years of experience as an entrepreneur, technology executive and venture investor. Jones previously served as chief executive and executive chairman of Synopsys. The company said its operations, customer commitments and product roadmap are expected to continue without interruption. Nvidia also reaffirmed that it will report third-quarter fiscal 2027 results on November 17 as scheduled.

Gary Marcus, a cognitive scientist and longtime AI researcher, told NPR's Morning Edition that Nvidia has effectively become a kind of bank for the industry. He described a practice of circular financing, in which Nvidia invests in AI companies that then use the money to buy Nvidia's chips, and said OpenAI, Anthropic and CoreWeave have relied on such funding even as many AI businesses struggle to turn a profit. Marcus characterized Huang as willing to make bets of arbitrary size, while he suggested Kress, whose background is in finance, may take a more cautious approach. He also said Kress would have to deal with possible federal and congressional investigations into Nvidia's dealings involving China.

Marcus said lawmakers need answers about what information Huang may have shared with Alice Huang and why Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had not intervened earlier. He pointed to the broader stakes for an industry that depends heavily on Nvidia's financial backing. The company's own statement, by contrast, stressed continuity, with Kress saying the focus remains on serving customers, partners, developers and shareholders. Whether the new leadership changes how Nvidia backs the wider AI industry, and how the investigations unfold, were questions the reporting left open.

stories.Headline: Google’s AI glasses raise questions about enforcing biometric privacy protections
stories.Summary:
Google is entering the AI glasses market with privacy protections designed to address controversies surrounding Meta's smart eyewear. Its developer documentation leaves unanswered whether Android XR technically enforces its prohibition on facial recognition or relies on policing applications after they gain camera access. Google's intelligent eyewear, developed with Warby Parker, Gentle Monster and Samsung, became available for preorder on a Thursday, with retail availability scheduled for December 10. Google's answer combines local facial redaction, restrictions on biometric identification, limits on AI training and controls intended to prevent covert recording.

Automatic redaction blurs bystanders' faces before imagery reaches Gemini, and Google says it does not save those visuals in Gemini History or use them for training or targeted advertising. Google told 9to5Google that redaction occurs locally on the paired smartphone and that Gemini images are deleted immediately after processing. The glasses require separate camera and microphone permissions, feature an outward-facing recording indicator with tamper detection, and limit conventional video recordings to 90 seconds. Google also plans to extend its Private AI Compute technology to the devices. Its Android XR policies prohibit facial recognition, biometric identification, surveillance, real-time bystander identification, persistent eavesdropping and voice identification.

Google published its policies and says it does not save redacted visuals, but it has not established how those restrictions would be technically enforced. Its Android XR documentation describes how authorized third-party applications access the glasses' camera through a companion smartphone using standard CameraX interfaces, including ImageAnalysis. Google requires apps to follow its intelligent eyewear safety rules, but its documentation does not establish how those rules would be enforced against apps distributed outside Google Play. Gemini's facial redaction is not shown to apply to third-party applications. Equivalent third-party access through an iPhone has not been established.

The concerns center on whether glasses that can identify strangers without their knowledge could turn ordinary encounters into biometric surveillance. Google's Gemini assistant can visually analyze surroundings without illuminating the outward-facing recording indicator, a practice that has drawn scrutiny of Meta's glasses. Meta has explored adding facial recognition to its smart glasses, and a proposed class action alleges Facebook and Instagram photographs were used to develop biometric identification capabilities without appropriate consent, which the articles describe as unproven. Meta says no facial recognition feature has shipped to consumers. Google's new eyewear currently requires accounts from the U.S. or South Korea.

The articles note earlier controversies: the Texas attorney general investigated Meta's glasses over biometric privacy concerns, and Google reached a $1.3 billion Texas settlement in 2025 over location tracking, private browsing and biometric information unrelated to its new eyewear. On October 29, Senators Edward Markey and Ron Wyden questioned Meta about sensitive imagery, AI training and camera-based AI interactions, with Meta having until November 25 to respond. In May, ten Democratic senators led by Markey and Jeff Merkley demanded that DHS abandon a proposed $7.5 million initiative for biometric smart glasses in its fiscal 2027 budget. On October 13, the European Data Protection Board recommended obscuring bystanders' identities and making AI-assisted camera processing noticeable to nearby people.

Ireland's parliamentary Joint Committee on Artificial Intelligence recommended on November 10 a prohibition on smart glasses capable of covert recording without consent, citing Meta's reported facial recognition plans. That recommendation is not enacted law. The articles leave open how completely Google's controls prevent prohibited biometric identification once camera access is granted, and whether Google's safeguards were developed in anticipation of oversight by the incoming Democratic Congress. They also leave open how the restrictions would apply to government or independently distributed software, and whether bystanders should have to rely on protections they cannot independently observe or control.

stories.Headline: 'Artificial Intelligence enhances private sector competitiveness'
stories.Summary:
Qatar Chamber Chairman Sheikh Khalifa bin Jassim bin Mohammed Al Thani told the opening session of the 13th Gulf Quality Conference in Doha that quality is now an integrated corporate culture. He said artificial intelligence is a key driver of institutional performance, improving service quality, data analysis and operational efficiency. The remarks were made on 12 November 2026 at Sharq Village & Spa in Doha, under the theme "AI and Customer Service Quality." The session was attended by Minister of State and President of Qatar National Library Dr. Hamad bin Abdulaziz Al Kuwari, along with officials, experts and representatives of public and private institutions. The event was organised by the Gulf Quality Centre for Consultancy and Training as a platform for sharing AI applications that enhance customer services across Gulf institutions.

Sheikh Khalifa said adopting international quality standards and AI applications would help private sector companies, particularly SMEs, raise productivity and competitiveness. He reaffirmed the Qatar Chamber's commitment to supporting technological advancement and best institutional practices. He expressed hope that the conference would end with practical recommendations to promote innovation across the GCC. He also commended the Gulf Quality Centre for organising the event. Mohammed Al Hamad, Director of Communications at the Gulf Standardization Organization, highlighted how digital transformation and AI improve services, communication and data-driven decisions.

Mohammed Al Hamad also described the GSO's work with national standardisation committees to develop standards and technical regulations across the GCC. Mohammed Saleh Al Kuwari, Chairman of the Gulf Quality Centre and President of the conference, said the theme reflects the growing importance of modern technologies. He pointed to ISO 10004:2018, which covers monitoring and measuring customer satisfaction. He hoped the discussions would encourage companies to strengthen their commitment to international quality standards. Al Kuwari announced three new services by the Centre, coinciding with World Quality Day.

Those services are the "Mi'yar" platform, which uses generative AI to analyse customer feedback, the "Ma Qalla Wa Dalla" series of short AI-produced training films, and the "Creative Ideas Bank," managed by an AI agent. The conference's focus on customer service quality concerns institutions across the Gulf and the private sector companies that the chairman singled out. The articles identify SMEs as a group that would benefit from adopting these standards and applications. Speakers presented these tools as ways to improve services for customers in the region.

Separately, on 12 November 2026, Navatar, a Salesforce-based CRM for private equity and M&A firms, announced enhanced Salesforce Model Context Protocol capabilities in New York and London. The capabilities bring information from documents into Claude-assisted work, even when users do not know which document holds it. The supported sources are documents in Navatar CRM, SharePoint, other connected document management systems and shared drives. Professionals can verify findings, select relevant information and add it to the right CRM fields, and firms need not move documents into a single repository.

Navatar's announcement says that important deal information often sits outside structured CRM fields, such as in management presentations, meeting notes or diligence files. Without document access, a professional asking Claude about a deal may miss a relevant detail. The company says the enhanced connection lets Claude use that document information alongside CRM data, with results returned to Navatar. Navatar's Claude-native deal engine is now available for private markets firms. The company describes itself as powering private markets and investment banking firms worldwide, including private equity, venture capital and private credit firms.

The Peninsula article gives no figures on the conference's outcome, attendance, or the adoption of the AI tools by companies. The Navatar release does not say how many firms use the service or the pricing terms. Neither article reports whether the GCC recommendations will be issued or how the Mi'yar platform and other Centre services will perform. The articles also do not state whether companies in Qatar will adopt the Navatar tools. Both sources leave open how widely these AI services will be taken up in their respective markets.

stories.Headline: Scale AI Launches Singapore Legal Reasoning Benchmark with IMDA
stories.Summary:
On November 12, 2026, Scale AI and Singapore's Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) introduced SG-LegalClarify, a benchmark for testing AI on Singapore law. The benchmark tested 19 language models on 1,860 scenarios spanning 10 domains of Singapore law. It assesses both legal accuracy and whether a model asks for missing facts before answering. Scale presents it as the first research initiative under a collaboration that was formalized in April 2026 and publicly described on July 7, 2026. The project is meant to help governments check AI systems against their own laws and institutions, rather than assuming international benchmark results carry over.

The dataset begins with 1,100 English-language source questions, of which 340 are fully specified and 760 are underspecified. Each underspecified question is paired with a fully specified counterpart that contains the hidden facts. Twenty-three verified lawyers wrote the questions, and seven of them also served as reviewers, with legal experience ranging from two to 37 years and a median of six. Each question carries a lawyer-written rubric of 12,546 criteria covering issue identification, rule recall, application and conclusion. Of these criteria, 89.0% are mandatory for a substantively correct answer, and the headline results count only those mandatory items.

The researchers say that a sufficiency gate first requires each model to either answer directly or gather facts. On the fact-gathering path, a simulated user reveals hidden facts only when the model explicitly asks for them. A three-model AI judge panel, chosen by comparison with human lawyer assessments, grades each criterion by majority vote. The benchmark is designed to test a skill separate from accuracy: deciding whether a query contains enough legally material information to be answered at all. Singapore is described as a demanding test because English common law operates alongside local modifications and Singapore-specific statutes.

Scale states that Singapore's legal system draws on English common law while incorporating its own statutes and principles, so a model relying on general common-law concepts may reach the wrong conclusion. The company says governments need ways to independently assess whether AI systems perform reliably against their own laws, institutions and standards. It also notes that many existing legal benchmarks assume all necessary information has already been supplied. Scale describes SG-LegalClarify as a milestone in its collaboration with IMDA, with IMDA contributing expertise in Singapore's regulatory environment and AI governance. Scale says its own contribution is developing rigorous benchmarks and evaluating frontier models.

The results in the paper show that Claude Fable 5 led closed-book testing by satisfying 69.8% of mandatory criteria, against an average of 53.8% across models. With web search, Kimi K3 led at 77.8%, and the average rose to 63.0%, with every model improving to varying degrees. Rule recall was the weakest component, with pass rates of 43.2% without search and 56.5% with it. Without web search, about 39% of closed-book scenarios with missing facts received no clarifying question, while models asked unnecessary questions in about 28% of scenarios that already contained enough information. When facts were missing, models asked about an average of only 39% of the relevant facts identified by legal experts.

The paper also reports that, in web-enabled trials where models requested every relevant missing fact, 55.6% reached the correct legal conclusion, 32.1% reached an incorrect conclusion and 12.3% gave no conclusion. The authors identify several limits, including limited human validation of the AI helpers, differences in search-tool access across providers, and the possibility that upfront routing altered clarification behavior. They note that not every annotated missing variable is necessary to resolve an instance, so incomplete fact-request coverage does not automatically mean inadequate clarification. The paper's ethics statement says the scores should not be read as evidence that a model is safe for unsupervised legal advice.

The researchers plan to release 50% of the source questions in each category, keeping each underspecified and fully specified pair in the same split, while retaining the rest for private evaluation. Model outputs on the public split and the evaluation pipeline are also planned for release. Scale says it is also exploring further work with IMDA on agentic AI, model evaluation methods and AI safety. The articles do not say when the public subset will be released, how the private portion will be managed over time, or whether the approach will be adopted by other governments.

stories.Headline: AI agent tooling provider LangChain secures $300M investment
stories.Summary:
LangChain Inc., a San Francisco startup that makes open-source tools for building artificial intelligence agents, has raised $300 million in funding, according to a report by The Wall Street Journal on November 12, 2026. Alphabet Inc.'s CapitalG fund led the round, joined by IVP, Sapphire Ventures, GIC and DFJ Growth. The raise values the company at $3 billion. The company's best-known product is its eponymous framework, released in 2022, which cuts down the work needed to connect an agent to a large language model, attach tools and set a system prompt.

The company's portfolio includes two other open-source tools. LangGraph links multiple LangChain-powered agents into a single workflow and can insert human approval for sensitive actions. Deep Agents extends both tools with a virtual file system, a work planning tool and a feature for generating subagents. LangChain also sells a paid product called LangSmith, which stores agent versions, lets teams roll back buggy updates, compares output quality between versions and analyzes execution traces to flag and rank technical issues. After its previous funding round last year, the company said its open-source tools were downloaded about 90 million times per month, and LangSmith is used by Autodesk and Cisco Systems.

The articles say the company reportedly plans to nearly double its headcount to 850 employees by the end of 2027. It intends to hire infrastructure experts, AI engineers, salespeople and marketers to support that growth. The articles do not include a direct statement from company leadership about the round or the hiring plan, and they attribute the funding details to the Wall Street Journal's reporting. The coverage places the investment within a broader stream of large AI infrastructure deals reported the same day. The articles do not say what LangChain will do with the new capital beyond the hiring plan.

stories.Headline: Tougher curbs on AI chip sales to China likely after Nvidia CEO resigns
stories.Summary:
US lawmakers from both parties are pushing for tighter limits on China's access to advanced AI chips after media reports about former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy. Huang stepped down on Nov 12, days after the reports surfaced. The reports concerned an executive at a Singapore-based tech company whom US authorities suspect of spying for Beijing. Nvidia did not address Huang's actions in its statement, and Huang has admitted to an extramarital affair without naming the person.

Congress is weighing several Bills that would give lawmakers more control over chip exports, track advanced chips, and pressure allies to limit help to China. House Speaker Mike Johnson said on Nov 12 that a growing consensus in Congress favours new restrictions. A handful of lawmakers want to attach the proposals to the annual defence authorisation Bill, which typically attracts bipartisan support. A Senate version of that legislation already includes several of them, including the AI Overwatch Act, Chip Security Act and Match Act.

The AI Overwatch Act, proposed by Senators Elizabeth Warren and Jim Banks, would give Congress a larger role in reviewing changes to export rules, which the Commerce Department now controls largely without congressional input. The Chip Security Act would require chipmakers to track the location of advanced AI processors and notify the government if they suspect chips have reached prohibited users. The Match Act would pressure allies such as the Netherlands and Japan to restrict sales and maintenance of chipmaking equipment bound for China. The Remote Access Security Act, which passed the House in January and awaits Senate consideration, would give the Commerce Department authority to regulate Chinese firms renting Nvidia-powered computing power overseas.

Nvidia's revenue from chip sales to Chinese data centres is near zero, according to an August company statement, and the company does not expect that to change in the third quarter. The company said in July that the remote-access measure, if enacted, could have "a material impact on our business." Reuters reported on Nov 12 that Chinese AI companies are rushing to secure access to Nvidia-powered computing capacity outside China. The Semiconductor Industry Association, whose members include Nvidia, has said mandatory tracking requirements could be costly. The proposals remain under consideration, and the articles do not say when or whether they will pass.

stories.Headline: Cyclotron recognized as Data Security & Governance Microsoft Partner of the Year for Excellence in Securing the Foundation of Enterprise AI
stories.Summary:
Cyclotron, a cloud, data, and AI services firm based in San Francisco, announced on November 13, 2026 that it had been named Microsoft Partner of the Year for Data Security & Governance in the 2026 Microsoft Partner of the Year Awards. The honor is Cyclotron's sixth recognition from Microsoft and recognizes firms at the forefront of securing the foundation for enterprise AI. The awards drew more than 4,500 nominations submitted worldwide across a diverse range of categories and geographies. Microsoft announced the winners ahead of Microsoft Ignite, which is being held in San Francisco from November 17 to 20. Cyclotron's recognition comes as the company says its work helps customers adopt AI agents while keeping their data protected, labeled, and governed.

Cyclotron says its work helps organizations find overshared data, apply sensitivity labels and access controls, and build AI governance that holds as adoption grows. Its newly launched Argus Managed Compliance solution is described as a managed compliance offering that keeps an organization's AI, agents, and data aligned with regulatory and internal requirements on an ongoing basis. Argus pairs an AI engine that continuously examines Microsoft Purview policies, labels, and settings with a team of compliance experts who review each recommendation. The solution builds on Cyclotron's Microsoft Partner of the Year recognitions for Data Security & Compliance in 2024 and 2025. Cyclotron also offers AI strategy, Azure migration, custom AI platforms and agents, Microsoft Agent 365 implementation, and AI FinOps services across the AI journey.

Nicole Dezen, Chief Partner Officer and Corporate Vice President at Microsoft, congratulated the winners and finalists and said their work harnesses Microsoft Cloud and AI to deliver transformative solutions. Nathan Carlisle, Senior Director of Security at Cyclotron, said Purview provides a critical foundation for AI and agent protections and warned that an agent will find and act on sensitive data if the data foundation has not been cleaned up. Susan Moyer, Director of AI Strategy & Innovation at Cyclotron, said AI projects stall when use cases are unclear, data and governance are not ready, or people do not change how they work. Cyclotron's leaders say the company addresses those issues together, from data foundations to governance and change leadership. The statements are attributed to Microsoft and Cyclotron executives, and the release is written for enterprise customers considering AI adoption.

Organizations that deploy AI agents and copilots are affected because those tools work with whatever data a user can reach, so loose permissions, unlabeled sensitive files, and unclear ownership become exposed at the speed of a prompt. Enterprises that need to keep AI compliant as agents, data sources, and users multiply are the audience for Argus Managed Compliance. Cyclotron says its customers can adopt AI solutions and agents knowing their data is protected, labeled, and governed. The announcement also describes Cyclotron's services for organizations moving from first exploration to measurable return on investment. The release identifies Microsoft Partner of the Year honors as the basis for its claims about these outcomes, and it reports no independent measurements of customer results.

Cyclotron's earlier Microsoft recognitions include the 2025 Partner of the Year Award for Data Security & Compliance, the 2025 Microsoft Intelligent Security Association Security Excellence Award for Security Customer Champion, and the 2024 Partner of the Year Award for Compliance. It also received the 2023 Partner of the Year Award for Modern Endpoints and the 2020 Partner of the Year Award for Social Impact. The company describes itself as providing cloud, data, and AI solutions, with expertise across Microsoft platforms, Claude, and emerging AI technologies. The release was distributed through PRWeb and PRNewswire, and its media contact is Andrew Fletcher at Cyclotron, Inc. Microsoft's Partner of the Year Awards celebrate partners delivering customer outcomes through Microsoft Cloud, AI, services, and devices.

The articles give the complete list of 2026 categories, winners, and finalists at a Microsoft web address, and Microsoft Ignite will take place in San Francisco from November 17 to 20. The release does not say how many customers Argus Managed Compliance has or what results it has produced since launch. It does not state pricing or availability terms for the Argus solution. The articles leave open how Cyclotron's recognition will affect its business or client engagements in the coming months. They also do not describe the specific criteria Microsoft used to choose the Data Security & Governance winners from the nominations.

stories.Headline: Is Mark Zuckerberg's cute new AI assistant a surveillance trap?
stories.Summary:
Meta's Muse AI, billed as an 18+ productivity assistant, is drawing warnings from child safety experts who say it looks more like a toy. The concern centers on Muse Charm, a two-inch wearable with an animated avatar called Jolly, which the articles say is set to launch later. The articles report that Meta first rolled out Muse across the US and Canada in September 2026 and has since expanded it to Japan and Singapore, with India to follow. Reports cited by TechRadar suggest the company is considering Europe, with The Times saying on Monday that the UK is first in line. The articles do not confirm a release date for Muse outside the existing markets.

Muse is described as an AI agent that can carry out tasks for users, such as shopping online, booking vacations and buying groceries. The Muse Charm device reportedly has a 2-inch OLED touchscreen, front and rear cameras, microphones, speakers, 5G connectivity and USB-C charging. Users can personalize Jolly, a pink-cheeked, Labubu-style avatar, including its name, appearance, outfits and voice. Muse already has more than 1.8 million daily users across the US and Canada, according to the articles.

Critics, including the Canadian children's digital safety group The White Hatter, warn that always-on AI companions could change how people attach to machines. Cuteness researcher Joshua Paul Dale told Fast Company that cute, child-like designs stimulate pleasure before users assess risks. AI safety specialist Kavya Pearlman, a former risk advisor during Meta's Cambridge Analytica scandal, calls the toy-like design a deliberate attempt to attract younger users. Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts told WIRED the claims are a story in search of a story, saying the customization brings users joy. Meta says Muse users must provide a date of birth, and a spokesperson said age checks will be included.

Children and teenagers are the group the experts say face the most risk from Muse Charm, and the always-on microphones and ambient recording are the features raising concern. The articles also note that a physical companion would sit on a desk or be worn, keeping the device close to the user at all times. Meta's core social platforms, Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, are the company's existing products, which the article says already shape users' online social lives. The articles do not describe any specific harm that has yet occurred from Muse.

Meta has positioned Muse as a productivity tool and has said the avatar is intended to be fun and customizable. The Muse Charm hardware was described in reports as upcoming, and the articles do not give a launch date for it. The articles say Meta has yet to confirm a release date for Europe, and they do not say whether the age checks will be enforced in every market. Whether regulators or child safety groups will take action in response to these concerns is not addressed in the articles.

stories.Headline: Same Prompt, More Complete Prints: Meshy.ai Publishes Printability Benchmark for AI-Generated 3D Models
stories.Summary:
Meshy.ai published the results of a printability benchmark for AI-generated 3D models on November 13, 2026, conducted with the Advanced Digital Design and Fabrication facility at the University of Massachusetts Amherst. In an FDM print test, Meshy.ai's Make Printable feature reduced prints with major missing features or holes from 44% (11 of 25) to 8% (2 of 25). The study, which Meshy.ai commissioned and funded, used six Bambu Lab A1 printers and printed 125 parts from 25 hard-to-print prompts across five workflows. Facility staff prepared and sliced the files, printed the parts, removed supports and graded every part objectively. Facility participation does not constitute endorsement of Meshy.ai products or an audit of its software.

Make Printable repairs mesh defects and reinforces thin features for the selected size and process, and it works on both Meshy.ai-generated models and uploaded models. Three experienced 3D printing users scored each part against a five-criterion rubric, while 17 volunteers ranked the anonymous prints. Across the 100 prompts in a larger geometry assessment, models with complete, connected surfaces rose from 33.4% for raw Meshy 7 output to 98.8% after Make Printable. In the physical test, 23 of 25 Meshy 7 with Make Printable prints (92%) had no major missing features or holes, compared with 56% to 84% for three other AI 3D generators. The full whitepaper is available on the Meshy.ai blog, and Make Printable is available now as part of Print Check in Meshy.ai.

Dave Follette, Director of ADDFab at UMass Amherst, said that the study aimed to evaluate AI platforms by actually 3D printing each part on a consumer FDM printer. Jessie Bergau, 3D Printing Product and Partnerships Manager at Meshy.ai, said that users want to bring ideas to life rather than spend hours repairing models before printing. Two Meshy 7 with Make Printable prints, a six-legged insect and a long-finned tropical fish, still had major missing features or holes. The study's 25 prompts were deliberately chosen to challenge the models, so the findings should not be read as representative of all prompts. The physical test covered only FDM printing, and the company notes that future testing could extend to SLA, SLS and Full-Color printing.

On November 12, 2026, Rapidflare launched Rapidbench, a research benchmark that measures how accurately AI agents answer technical queries about electronics products. Rapidflare CEO Navanee Sundaramoorthy said general-purpose benchmarks do not show how well an agent handles queries across complex electronics catalogs. The first version tests AI agents on 116 technical product queries involving NVIDIA's Jetson and IGX platforms and partner products. The test catalog covers 2,130 products from 212 manufacturers across 54 categories. Rapidflare compared agents without tools, with web search, and with access to its structured catalog through the Model Context Protocol.

Across three runs, the tested models achieved pass rates of about 18% without tools, 49% to 60% with web search, and 88% to 94% with Rapidflare's structured catalog via MCP. Rapidflare generated the query set from its product catalog, guided by real search trends, and validated each query against the catalog. Human reviewers agreed with the automated judge's pass/fail decisions on 98% of the reviewed subset. Rapidflare CTO Vasanth Asokan said the team verified product data against manufacturer sources and reconciled conflicting specifications.

The company is based in San Jose, California, and its platform works with companies including AMD, Qorvo, Amphenol and Taoglas. Rapidflare has published the methodology, limitations and evaluation trajectories on its website so readers can examine how the results were produced. The first version is limited to NVIDIA's Jetson and IGX ecosystem and 116 queries. The articles do not say when a later version of Rapidbench will be released or whether the Meshy.ai study will be extended beyond FDM printing.

stories.Headline: The promise and peril of AI in government
stories.Summary:
Taoyuan, Taiwan's industrial hub home to 200 semiconductor facilities, is using AI to manage its fast growth under Mayor San-Cheng Chang. The city runs an AI-powered lung cancer screening program for residents over 40 with risk factors such as occupational exposure or family history. The program began in March 2023 and screened over 400,000 residents within two years. Chang previously served as Taiwan's first nonpartisan premier and held leadership roles at Google and Acer. The Post and Courier separately argues that AI's potential benefits, such as a phone app describing scenes for blind users, deserve attention alongside its risks.

Taoyuan, which is home to Taiwan's international airport and 2.2 million residents, must handle heavy truck traffic, air pollution, population growth and constant construction. The screening program detected 233 lung cancer cases, with 90% at an early stage, and saved NT$500 million, about $17 million, through AI-aided diagnostics. The software predicts cancer risk from a single low-dose CT scan without requiring additional clinical data. The city also built a system that analyzes exhaust pipe images against a database of legal configurations, and complaints about illegal exhausts fell 20% over last year. AI cameras monitor construction sites and factory chimneys, and traffic lights now shave about 10 seconds off each wait.

Mayor Chang is responsible for these projects and has been selective about which AI tools his administration adopts. He has said he will not sanction generative AI chatbots that could hallucinate. He distinguishes between machine learning that detects existing conditions and machine learning that predicts future outcomes, favoring the former. The Taoyuan administration uses AI to locate potholes and to identify wheelchair users at train station elevators so assistance can be ready. The article presents these uses as ones where AI sees what is already present without automating human decisions.

The article's author, Beth Simone Noveck, warns that predictive AI is being relied on for decisions such as sentencing, parole, credit scoring and hiring. Princeton researcher Arvind Narayanan is quoted as warning that predicting job performance or recidivism involves countless unpredictable variables. Fraud-detection systems may misclassify a struggling single parent with irregular gig income as a fraud risk. The Post and Courier editorial, meanwhile, says the public conversation about AI has been largely negative and that Democrats are taking control of Congress partly by pointing to AI's dangers. Students at the College of Charleston, including Saif Chaundry, have built an app that narrates surroundings for visually impaired users.

Narayanan identifies five ways predictive systems break down, including models that miss crucial context, systems that can be gamed, and overreliance on automated outputs. A sepsis prediction system sold by Epic was trained on national data and proved ineffective for local patient populations. The author distinguishes population-level forecasting, such as for forest fires, from judgments about individuals, which she says should be advisory and contestable rather than automated. Labor disputes in Taiwan's semiconductor industry and worries about cost and context for non-English languages also appear in the coverage. The Post and Courier argues that the federal government has declined to restrict AI development or require public disclosure of its use.

The articles leave open how Taoyuan's screening and traffic programs will be evaluated over the long term and whether other governments will adopt similar limits on predictive tools. They do not say whether the federal government will impose the restrictions the Post and Courier calls for once Democrats take control of Congress. The College of Charleston app's release and wider adoption are not described, and the outcomes of the Taiwanese labor disputes are not reported. The articles also do not say whether individual-level predictive systems will be restricted or made contestable in practice.

stories.Headline: Arctera Helps Companies Bring Business Information into Microsoft Copilot Workflows with Governance Controls in Place
stories.Summary:
Arctera, a business unit of Cloud Software Group, announced on November 12, 2026, new Model Context Protocol connectivity for Microsoft 365 Copilot from its base in San Ramon, California. The connectivity lets organizations bring enterprise information governed through Arctera into supported Copilot workflows. The capability gives employees access to more of their company's information for AI-assisted work while keeping established governance and compliance controls in place. The new connectivity is part of Arctera AI Converge, which uses MCP to link AI models with enterprise information that Arctera governs. The company said the connectivity is available now.

Model Context Protocol is an open standard for connecting AI applications with external data sources and tools. Through a custom federated connector, Microsoft 365 Copilot can reach Arctera's MCP server and interact with enterprise information governed through the platform. Organizations keep control over who can access the information, how it can be used, and how long it must be kept. The connectivity supports Arctera's Modern Compliance Intelligence strategy and builds on the Arctera Unified Platform's communications governance, compliance, and eDiscovery capabilities. Arctera's platform can capture data from more than 130 content sources and includes more than 280 AI policies.

Irfan Shuttari, product manager at Arctera, said that connecting enterprise information to Copilot requires preserving the governance controls built into that content. He said that pairing MCP connectivity with years of secure collaboration data managed within Arctera can accelerate regulatory inquiries and legal investigations while maintaining full compliance. Soniya Bopache, SVP and GM at Arctera, said that much of an organization's knowledge sits outside the workflows where employees could use it. She said the Copilot connectivity brings that information into work while preserving the governance controls businesses have established. Bopache added that leaders can get more value from information they already manage and from their AI investments.

The articles present the Arctera announcement as aimed at organizations that hold valuable information spread across systems and want their workforce to get more useful output from AI tools. Arctera is described as helping the biggest companies in the world monitor and control how their information is accessed, used and shared. Arctera was created in 2024 from Veritas Technologies. A separate article from ITWeb, dated November 12, 2026 and written by Joanne Carew for CloudZA in Johannesburg, covers AI governance for businesses. It recalls that in April South Africa's Draft National Artificial Intelligence Policy was officially withdrawn by Communications and Digital Technologies Minister Solly Malatsi because it contained fake, AI-generated academic references.

Jonathan Oaker, founder and CEO of CloudZA, advises that good AI governance starts with understanding the data a business holds and sorting it into categories. He recommends assessing AI tools by where each model gets its data, how it was trained and what access it has to business information. Oaker suggests weighing return on investment for the next six months or year and embracing Open Telemetry from day one. He says a business that cannot fail and handles identifiable data should consult a service provider or partner, and he warns that retrofitting governance later is complex and costly. Failing to consider governance can expose businesses to data breaches, legal liability and reputational damage.

The articles do not say when or how the Arctera connectivity will be adopted by specific customers, nor what results organizations have achieved with it. They also do not give pricing for the Arctera connectivity or detail how supported Copilot experiences are defined. The ITWeb article does not link its governance advice to the Arctera product. Whether Microsoft or other AI providers will expand similar connectivity is not addressed in the articles. The articles leave open how South Africa's AI policy will be revised after its withdrawal.

stories.Headline: NTT DATA becomes AI Consulting Partner of the Nitto ATP Finals
stories.Summary:
NTT DATA has become a Gold Partner of the Nitto ATP Finals, serving as Official AI Consulting Partner and Official Technology Consulting Partner, according to a release dated November 12, 2026. The 2026 tournament runs from November 15 to 22 at Inalpi Arena in Turin, Italy. The partnership gives the Japan-based technology group a global stage to show how AI, data and technology can support human potential. The company says elite tennis, which demands skill, judgment and adaptability under pressure, offers a fitting setting for that message. Through the event, NTT DATA aims to show that technology can provide deeper insight into performance and help people and organizations tackle challenges beyond sport.

NTT DATA will host a Tech Corner in Turin where visitors can see computer vision, Physical AI and advanced AI infrastructure applied to monitoring, safety, construction and humanoid robotics. The space will also house the Mental Economy Gym, powered by Formula Medicine, an Italian sports medicine and human performance company. There, guests can take on digital challenges that measure concentration, reaction and mental workload. At the Fan Village court, NTT DATA will present an on-court experience with FITP that combines cognitive and physical monitoring with AI-powered computer vision. The company frames the activity as a way to reveal previously invisible dimensions of player performance.

Kazuhiko Nakayama, President and CEO of NTT DATA Group, said that sport is ultimately human, driven by ambition, courage and determination. He argued that technology can help people see what was previously invisible and find new ways to improve. Nakayama said the company wants to celebrate human potential while showing how technology can expand what people achieve. He added that NTT DATA combines AI capabilities with deep industry expertise to help clients transform their businesses and create new value. The statement presents the partnership as an extension of the company's broader positioning.

The partnership is the latest in a series of sporting partnerships that bring NTT DATA's brand statement, "Intelligence to Impact," to life. The company says intelligence comes not only from AI and technology but also from human expertise and industry understanding. NTT DATA is a business and technology services company with more than $30 billion in revenue, serving 75% of the Fortune Global 100. It has experts in more than 70 countries and is part of NTT Group, which invests over $3 billion each year in R&D. The company describes itself as a Global Top Employer with a robust ecosystem of innovation centers and partners.

The Turin activations are intended to appeal to both spectators and corporate audiences, according to the trade coverage of the announcement. Industry reporting notes that tennis has become a testing ground for data-led analysis across officiating, broadcast coverage and training. The coverage also says the demonstrations place tools used in industrial and operational settings into a consumer-facing environment linked to measurable human activity. The announcement reflects a wider trend in professional sport, where tournaments and governing bodies use technology partnerships to enhance fan experiences and collect detailed information on athlete preparation.

The articles do not say how long the partnership will last or whether NTT DATA will sign further sporting partnerships after the 2026 tournament. They also do not report any results, attendance figures, or the financial terms of the sponsorship. The company says it will continue to build on these efforts, using sport as a platform to show how AI can enhance human potential. The articles leave open how visitors will respond to the Tech Corner and Mental Economy Gym, and whether the demonstrations will lead to any commercial outcome for NTT DATA.
