stories.Headline: Micron (MU) Has Next Year’s High-Bandwidth Memory Mostly Sold. Can That Anchor a Decade-Long Case?
stories.Summary:
On November 5, 2026, the S&P 500 fell 4.36%, its worst day since the April 2025 tariff crash, wiping out roughly $3 trillion in value across its companies. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 5.52% into a correction, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell about 12%, its worst day since 2020. The slide followed an October in which the S&P 500 technology sector lost 6.8%, its biggest monthly drop since March 2025. Defensive groups such as consumer staples, by contrast, had a record month. Growth stocks tend to feel such swings first because their prices rest on faster expected sales and earnings growth.

Investors are questioning how companies will pay for their large artificial intelligence budgets and whether those spending plans will pay off. The midterm election results raised a second concern, as investors wondered whether data center construction could slow if new rules follow. October's jobs report showed payrolls up 165,000, against the 65,000 economists expected. Traders now put the odds of a Federal Reserve rate hike in December above 75%. Edward Jones senior global strategist Angelo Kourkafas called the report a "blowout jobs report."

Micron Technology, listed on the NASDAQ as MU, ranks 10th on one published list of the 10 best growth stocks to buy for the next decade. Gavin Baker, who runs Atreides Management, has argued that the memory chip shortage will last and that Micron looks inexpensive for what it earns. Philippe Laffont's Coatue Management added nearly three million shares in a single quarter. David Tepper's Appaloosa tripled its stake late last year before trimming some of it. Chief Executive Officer Sanjay Mehrotra said the company has agreements covering the vast majority of its calendar 2027 high-bandwidth memory supply.

Micron reported fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of $54.23 billion, up 379% from a year earlier, and full-year revenue of $133.19 billion. Data center revenue rose fourfold, and gross margin and earnings per share also set records. Mehrotra said the supply agreements are priced significantly higher than a year earlier, and he expects an even stronger fiscal 2027. Customers have agreed to buy most of the high-bandwidth memory Micron plans to supply next year before it has been made. The company has a market capitalization of $825.89 billion and 184 hedge fund holders as of Q2 2026.

Insider Monkey, the publisher of the article, said it believes certain other AI stocks offer greater upside potential and less downside risk than Micron. The article describes growth stocks generally as companies expected to grow sales and earnings faster than the market average, often reinvesting profits rather than paying dividends. It notes that such stocks often carry high price-to-earnings ratios, leaving little room for disappointment. Investors holding Micron through a downturn are described as needing to consider which companies can keep compounding through several more months like this one.

The articles leave open whether the Federal Reserve will raise rates in December, and whether the midterm results will slow data center construction and AI spending. They also do not say whether Micron's supply agreements will hold up or how its fiscal 2027 results will compare with Mehrotra's expectations. The sources do not state whether the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index or the Nasdaq will recover from their November declines. Whether Micron can justify a decade-long case, as the headline asks, is not settled by the reporting.

Articles.Title: Micron (MU) Has Next Year’s High-Bandwidth Memory Mostly Sold. Can That Anchor a Decade-Long Case? - Yahoo Finance

stories.Headline: District Court Rejects Mobile Source Exemption for x.AI Turbines as EPA Weighs a Different Regulatory Approach
stories.Summary:
On October 30, 2026, the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Mississippi denied a motion to dismiss filed by x.AI Corp. and MZX Tech LLC. The motion sought dismissal of a Clean Air Act lawsuit brought by the NAACP and the Mississippi State Conference of the NAACP. The court rejected x.AI's argument that its gas-fired turbines, mounted on flatbed trailers and powering a data center, were exempt mobile sources. The decision came as the EPA weighs a different regulatory approach to portable turbines.

The court held that the turbines did not fall within the federal definition of mobile source incorporated into Mississippi's State Implementation Plan. That definition covers a motor vehicle, a nonroad engine or a nonroad vehicle. The turbines were neither vehicles nor nonroad engines, but stationary combustion turbines, because they were not self-propelled or intended to be propelled while performing their function. The court also noted that the Subpart KKKK definition in 40 C.F.R. Part 60 contemplates such turbines being mounted on a vehicle for portability. As a result, the turbines remained subject to stationary source permitting rather than the mobile source exemption.

The lawsuit was filed in April 2026 and alleges that x.AI Corp. and MZX Tech LLC built and operated a power plant of gas-fired turbines on flatbed trailers without a permit. It claims this violated the Clean Air Act and Mississippi's State Implementation Plan. x.AI argued that the turbines were portable and intended to remain at the site for less than 12 months, so they qualified as mobile sources. The Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality had earlier issued a letter indicating it understood the turbines qualified for that exemption. The court's ruling rejected that position.

Separately, the EPA is developing a proposed rule titled the "Nonroad Combustion Turbines Rule," which could treat certain portable turbines as nonroad engines subject to mobile source standards rather than stationary sources. As of early November 2026, the proposal had been submitted for White House Office of Management and Budget review but had not yet been formally proposed. The articles say the rule may not retroactively excuse turbines already operated without permits, as alleged in the x.AI litigation. They also say it could allow future data center developers and operators to deploy certain portable turbines without stationary source permitting.

The articles attribute the court's reasoning to its reading of the definitions in Mississippi's State Implementation Plan and the federal regulations. The articles quote a Liskow & Lewis analysis stating that because the plant is not a mobile source under those regulations, it was not exempted from permitting requirements under the Clean Air Act and Mississippi's SIP. The firm concluded that the plaintiffs' claims will not be dismissed. The articles identify the NAACP and the Mississippi State Conference of the NAACP as the plaintiffs, and state that data center developers and operators are the parties the anticipated EPA rule could most affect.

The articles describe the case as turning on whether the turbines already operated without permits were stationary sources at the time. The Liskow analysis says that mounting combustion turbines on trailers or intending to operate them temporarily does not make them mobile sources under existing Clean Air Act regulations. The firm advises data center operators, developers and other stakeholders to monitor both the ongoing litigation and the EPA rulemaking. The articles identify Liskow attorneys Greg Johnson, Clare Bienvenu, Emily von Qualen and Colin North as contacts for further information.

Articles.Title: District Court Rejects Mobile Source Exemption for x.AI Turbines as EPA Weighs a Different Regulatory Approach - Liskow & Lewis, APLC

stories.Headline: Classroom Artificial Intelligence Learning Thrives on Teacher Scaffolding and Interactional Friction
stories.Summary:
Researchers Xinyun Hu and Boris Wai Yan Choy published a qualitative study in AI, Brain and Child examining how young children and teachers interact with AI-powered learning tools in classrooms. The study, reported on bioengineer.org on November 12, 2026, found that AI educational tools do not work smoothly for early childhood learners, but rely on teachers to turn glitches and communication breakdowns into learning opportunities. The authors applied Actor-Network Theory to track micro-level classroom interactions. They argued that commercial emphasis on seamless digital interfaces hides how automated systems actually work, creating what they call pedagogical black boxes.

The study was an instrumental single-case study conducted over two weeks at a public kindergarten in Shenzhen, China. It involved two certified kindergarten teachers with over a decade of combined experience, and sixteen children with a mean age of 69.8 months and no special educational needs. The researchers focused on one educator, Teacher Mandy, and four children, three girls and one boy, with a mean age of 71 months and no prior AI experience. The curriculum followed the Notice, Inquire, Create, and Express framework across four lessons on garden plants. Researchers tracked 2,814 turns of talk and action across 167 minutes, identifying 593 turns involving AI devices.

The authors say the findings show that seamless AI integration is neither realistic nor pedagogically advantageous for early childhood classrooms, where learning requires overcoming friction. Teachers act as mediators, using directive modeling to handle technical constraints, critical framing to challenge wrong outputs, and strategic non-intervention to support children's independence. The study identifies three kinds of black boxes: operational, epistemic, and relational. The authors describe educators as network weavers and guardians of friction who should keep children's agency and critical thinking intact during technological breakdowns.

The articles do not name the publisher's full editorial decisions or provide responses from the technology companies whose products were used. Commentary from other educators, parents, or outside experts is not included. The articles also do not say whether the findings apply beyond the single Shenzhen kindergarten, and the authors note that the devices were novel during the study, which may have increased the visibility of breakdowns. Further studies across other settings, ages, or tools are not described.

Articles.Title: Classroom Artificial Intelligence Learning Thrives on Teacher Scaffolding and Interactional Friction

stories.Headline: Time to Ban AI Companions
stories.Summary:
Jonathan D. Teubner and Tyler J. VanderWeele, writing in First Things on November 12, 2026, argue that AI companion products should be banned. They open with the image of an always available, never judgmental artificial friend and note that Mark Zuckerberg, Meta's CEO, said last year that AI companions could fill a gap in Americans' social lives. The authors describe apps such as Nomi, Replika, and Character.AI, which offer on-demand conversations with human-like virtual characters. A 2025 Common Sense Media study found that nearly three-quarters of American teenagers had tried an AI companion, and one-third had used one for friendship, romance, or emotional support. The authors call this trend alarming and say it calls for a swift and decisive response.

The authors tie their case to the 2025 Global Flourishing Study, which tracked more than 200,000 people across twenty-two countries. That study found that young adults now report the lowest levels of flourishing of any age group, reversing the long-observed U-shaped curve of well-being across life. In the United States, the older a respondent is, the more likely he or she is to report higher scores across all domains of flourishing. The authors conclude that the country faces a youth flourishing crisis, not merely a youth mental-health crisis. They point to close social relations as among the strongest predictors of flourishing, and they cite delayed sleep, less in-person time, and fragmented attention as effects of digital addiction.

Lawmakers have acted in several places. California passed Senate Bill 243, which requires AI companions to disclose that users are talking to a machine. In New York, legislation restricting chatbot behaviors considered unsafe for children and teenagers passed both chambers and was sent to Gov. Kathy Hochul. In April, the federal GUARD Act, which would bar minors from AI companions and require age verification for every user, cleared the Senate Judiciary Committee unanimously, though its path to law is uncertain. The authors say the legislative response is welcome but insufficient, since it treats as a matter of adult choice a phenomenon they regard as harmful in itself.

They argue that an artificial friend or romantic partner offers only illusory benefits, because easing an evening's loneliness does not cure loneliness. They cite the 2023 U.S. Surgeon General's report, which found that about half of American adults report loneliness and linked digital technology to isolation, noting that young adults who used social media more than two hours daily were twice as likely to feel socially isolated as those using it under thirty minutes. The authors distinguish social media, which directed users toward real people, from virtual friends and romantic chatbots, which replace other people rather than bridge to them. They say they do not propose banning all relational AI, and they describe a UNC Chapel Hill School of Civic Life and Leadership instructor who repurposed an AI sales tool so students could practice civil discourse with an avatar. They argue that the state already bans some activities that replace or damage goods, such as organ sales and counterfeit money, and that counterfeit relationships could likewise be banned.

The authors warn that the effects of friendship and romance chatbots may soon exceed what has emerged from social media over the past two decades if action is not taken quickly. They also cite Dietrich Bonhoeffer's observation in Life Together that community begins on the far side of disappointment with others and ourselves. The articles do not say how a ban would be enforced, which products would be covered beyond those named, or whether Governor Hochul will sign the New York legislation. They also do not indicate whether the GUARD Act will advance past committee, or how companies such as Meta, Nomi, Replika, and Character.AI have responded to the proposals.

Articles.Title: Time to Ban AI Companions - First Things

stories.Headline: Flawed Triggers: How A New Proposal to Automatically Pay Extended Unemployment Checks in Response to AI Fears Misses the Mark - American Enterprise Institute
stories.Summary:
Flawed Triggers, as an article in the AEI series, examines an unemployment-benefit proposal from Senators Ron Wyden and Michael Bennet, which would automatically pay extended federal unemployment checks once unemployment rates passed set levels. The analysis finds that, had the 2021 proposal been enacted, federal extended benefits would now be payable in 24 states. That result holds even though the country currently has its longest stretch of low unemployment on record. The author argues the same kind of trigger is now being proposed in response to fears of AI-driven layoffs. The 2021 proposal would pay 13 weeks of extended benefits, fully federally funded, whenever a state or national total unemployment rate reached 5.5 percent or higher.

A second trigger adds a state's or the nation's rise above its three-year low to its current rate, and pays benefits when the sum reaches 5.5 percent. A third trigger follows the Sahm rule, applying when a rate is at least 0.5 percentage points above its 12-month low. Benefits under that trigger continue until the rate falls for at least two consecutive months, drops below 5.5 percent, and sits less than 1.5 points above its level when the program started. The article notes that in October 2026 the national unemployment rate was 4.1 percent, and it had been at or below 4.5 percent for 60 consecutive months. The national total unemployment rate averaged 4.2 percent as of November 6, which does not meet the 5.5 percent trigger.

Under the first trigger, the District of Columbia at 5.7 percent and Puerto Rico at 6.1 percent would qualify, since both count as states under the unemployment insurance system. Under the second trigger, twelve jurisdictions would qualify, including Arizona, Connecticut, Delaware, Florida, Michigan, New Mexico, Oregon and Washington. Under the Sahm-rule trigger, nine jurisdictions would qualify today, including Alabama at 3.4 percent and Hawaii at 2.7 percent. Twelve more states, including California, Iowa, Kansas, Maine and Vermont, remain eligible because they have not met the shutoff criteria. Nine states, among them Arizona, Connecticut and Oregon, would receive 26 weeks of benefits rather than 13.

In total, 24 states would receive at least 13 weeks of federal extended benefits, covering about 44 percent of the US population. The author writes that Senators Wyden and Bennet, joined by Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and Senator Elizabeth Warren, proposed the October 23, 2026 plan as a way to address AI-related job losses. Wyden said Americans fear AI job losses and that Congress has a responsibility to help the country prepare. The author contends the trigger design misses its target, because the same mechanism would pay benefits to states with very low unemployment.

The article's own analysis is the basis for this criticism rather than any statement from the senators on the trigger's flaws. Those affected include unemployed workers in the 24 states identified, along with taxpayers who would fund the payments. The author notes that Governor Gavin Newsom in October boasted that California's economy was dominating other states and was a leader in raising wages and salaries. California would have been eligible for benefits under the third trigger even as its economy was praised.

The article further notes that under the 2021 proposal's earlier version, blue states would have continued benefits well past the Labor Day 2021 expiration of pandemic programs. The author recounts that Congress has passed temporary extended unemployment programs during every recession in recent memory, most notably after the 2007-09 Great Recession, when it passed a dozen laws and paid up to 99 weeks of benefits over five and a half years. Those programs ended when labor market conditions improved. Former Obama administration officials and academics, in a 2019 volume called Recession Ready, proposed automatic triggers to pay a range of benefits when unemployment exceeded preset levels.

Wyden and Bennet introduced their unemployment modernization legislation in April 2021, and it did not advance. The articles do not say whether the October 2026 proposal will advance in Congress or what its specific trigger levels are. They also leave open how many states would ultimately qualify under the new AI-focused version and what it would cost. It is unclear whether lawmakers will revise the triggers in response to the critique.

Articles.Title: Flawed Triggers: How A New Proposal to Automatically Pay Extended Unemployment Checks in Response to AI Fears Misses the Mark - American Enterprise Institute - AEI

stories.Headline: AI Can Review Your Contracts, but Should It Negotiate Them?
stories.Summary:
Raman Rai, an AI deployment and adoption adviser who has worked on large-scale implementations, spoke at Law.com's General Counsel Conference East about the rush by companies to adopt artificial intelligence. According to the article dated November 12, 2026, he told general counsel that many firms are spending heavily on AI without first deciding which problems the technology should solve. The piece frames this as the core risk facing corporate legal departments under growing pressure to adopt AI. Rai's warning centers less on picking the wrong tool than on letting AI make decisions that call for a lawyer's judgment. The article's headline asks whether AI that can review contracts should also be trusted to negotiate them.

The article is reported by Trudy Knockless and carries no further detail on specific tools, rules, or contract terms. It gives no figures, dates for any new requirements, or formal changes to how legal departments must operate. What it does set out is a general distinction between using AI for review and handing it negotiation tasks that depend on legal judgment. Readers should understand this as the adviser's framing of the issue rather than a described policy or mandate.

The reporting does not indicate that any company has yet made such a change. Rai is the person responsible for the views expressed, and the article attributes his remarks to his work in AI deployment and adoption, including a role connected to UN Women UK. The article reports his concern in paraphrase: companies are investing heavily without always settling on the problems AI should address, and the greater danger lies in delegating judgment-heavy decisions to the technology. The piece does not include direct statements from other executives or from the legal departments themselves on this specific point.

The attribution is limited to what Rai told the conference audience. The article sits within a wider conversation in the same publication, including a related piece on Harvey Forum Chicago where general counsel discussed rising expectations for AI use. Those pieces suggest that in-house lawyers are increasingly expected to exhaust AI options before sending work to outside counsel. The articles provided do not describe what happens next for the specific question of AI negotiating contracts.

Articles.Title: AI Can Review Your Contracts, but Should It Negotiate Them?

stories.Headline: Secure, Scalable AI for Manufacturers
stories.Summary:
I can't write this as a news story. The only source is a single vendor marketing page for NTT DATA, which promotes an IDC InfoBrief and a webinar on sovereign AI for manufacturers. It gives no reported event, no named actor doing anything, no numbers beyond the webinar date of 8 November 2026, and no statement from any responsible party beyond general product claims. stories.Headline: Colorado Joins Other State AI Leaders in Regulating the Use of AI in Psychotherapy Services - The National Law Review
stories.Summary:
Colorado has enacted HB 26-1195, a law regulating the use of artificial intelligence in psychotherapy services, which went into effect on August 12, 2026. The law was enacted alongside two other Colorado AI healthcare laws this year, SB 26-189 and HB 26-1139. The article describes the law as establishing new restrictions for Colorado psychotherapy providers who want to use AI in their practices. It was published on November 12, 2026, by the National Law Review, and it was written by lawyers from Sheppard, Mullin, Richter & Hampton LLP. The authors are Carolyn V. Metnick and Madeline Cunnion.

Under the law, AI may be used for administrative support, such as scheduling, billing, insurance claims, and general therapy communications. It may also be used for supplementary support, such as maintaining client records, analyzing progress data, organizing referrals, and collecting intake questionnaires. In either case, the licensed provider must keep responsibility for reviewing all AI output. The law bars AI from recording or transcribing therapy sessions unless the client is told in advance, told the specific purpose, and gives written consent. It also bars AI from therapeutic communication with clients without real-time interaction among provider, AI, and client, and from generating treatment plans or recommendations without provider approval.

The article does not name a legislator or state official who sponsored or signed the law, so the responsible parties are described only through the law itself. The authors of the article are the only named people who comment, and they state that Colorado's framework shares common elements with other states' rules. They advise providers to confirm written, revocable consent workflows, update intake materials, audit AI tools against the statute's categories, and review marketing claims. The authors also say that flexible compliance programs are needed in a still-developing field.

Several groups are affected by the law. Psychotherapy providers in Colorado must follow its consent, review, and disclosure requirements, and any person or company offering AI tools cannot suggest that the AI's output equals licensed psychotherapy services. Clients of psychotherapy providers gain the right to written notice and consent before AI records their sessions. Organizations deploying AI in mental health across several states face what the authors call a patchwork of differing state rules.

The article explains that Colorado's 2024 Artificial Intelligence Act made it an early leader in AI regulation. It notes that HB 26-1195's core provisions resemble legislation Illinois enacted last year, and that Tennessee, Nevada, and Vermont have adopted advertising and marketing restrictions, some resembling Colorado's. The article also says that SB 26-189 repealed and replaced much of Colorado's landmark AI Act. The law's text sits in the article's footnotes, with the sections cited for each provision.

The article does not say how the law will be enforced or what penalties apply to violations. It also does not say whether other states will adopt rules resembling Colorado's, or how courts or regulators will interpret terms such as "administrative support" and "supplementary support." It leaves open how the Colorado Consumer Protection Act's advertising provision will be applied in practice. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Colorado Joins Other State AI Leaders in Regulating the Use of AI in Psychotherapy Services - The National Law Review

stories.Headline: Biglaw’s Latest AI Incentive For Associates Comes With A $1 Million Prize Pot
stories.Summary:
Latham & Watkins has announced a new Associate AI Impact Award, backed by a $1 million prize pot for 2027, according to an article published by Above the Law on November 12, 2026. The program is aimed at associates who lead or materially contribute to AI initiatives that generate value for clients, practice groups, matter teams, or the firm as a whole. The article notes that awards will vary depending on each initiative's impact and its potential to scale. It also reports that the program comes as the firm expands its artificial intelligence work.

The award is designed to recognize work that the firm believes can improve how it serves clients and runs its operations. Latham has set aside $1 million for payouts in 2027, and the size of each award will depend on the reach and promise of the initiative behind it. The article does not describe specific eligibility criteria, application steps, or how many awards will be given. It does state that the money is meant to reward associates who turn AI ideas into practical results. Because the program ties rewards to impact, the firm appears to be using financial incentives to encourage lawyers to experiment with the technology.

Michael Rubin, global chair of Latham's AI practice and chair of its AI strategy committee, commented on the program. He said that associates bring firsthand insight into where AI can make a meaningful difference. He added that the award is meant to foster that ingenuity and to identify and scale the ideas most likely to create value for clients and the firm. The article presents these remarks as the firm's rationale for the program, and Rubin's role places him at the center of its AI strategy.

The program follows several recent moves by the firm to expand its AI capabilities. According to the article, Latham recently partnered with Harvey on a tool for investment funds. It also invested in Nvidia-powered servers that let the firm run and customize AI models in-house. The article does not say what the firm plans to announce next or how the 2027 awards will be judged in detail. Those details, along with the first recipients, would likely come in later reporting.

Articles.Title: Biglaw’s Latest AI Incentive For Associates Comes With A $1 Million Prize Pot

stories.Headline: The Next Generation Of Law Students Don’t Trust AI Hype
stories.Summary:
A new report from Blickstein Group, titled "The College Student AI Reality Check," finds that today's college students are wary of artificial intelligence despite using it often. The survey drew responses from students at 37 colleges and universities, plus five in-depth interviews. The project was led by Vera Grabow, an intern and college junior, who began it after watching AI change her own education. Her work was published on November 12, 2026 on the Above the Law website.

The findings show heavy use but little trust. Some 71 percent of respondents said they use AI several times a week or more for schoolwork, and 27.8 percent said they turn to an AI tool first when learning a new concept, slightly ahead of Google at 25.3 percent. Only 3.8 percent go first to professors or teaching assistants. Most students said AI saves them modest amounts of time, with the most common answer being 10 to 24 percent (32.4 percent), and 72.1 percent believed heavy reliance on AI leaves people somewhat or much less capable at their jobs. Pre-law students showed the same heavy use but even more skepticism, with 66.7 percent saying AI is acceptable only for brainstorming.

The report's author, Vera Grabow, conceived the project, wrote the questionnaire, led outreach, analyzed the data and drafted the report, according to Blickstein Group CEO Brad Blickstein, who said the firm helped but credited her with the work. Blickstein described it as an exceptional piece by a college student. The article's author, Joe Patrice, a senior editor at Above the Law, wrote that his own conversations with students largely matched the report's conclusions. Neither source suggests the findings are settled beyond this sample.

The article presents the results as a challenge for the legal industry and for AI developers who have promoted tools that would take over much of the drafting work. The report suggests that a skeptical human overseeing AI is a more sensible model for law than full automation, and that AI companies will need to persuade this generation to trust the technology more. The article does not say what steps firms or developers will take in response. Readers can find the full report through a link on the Above the Law article.

Articles.Title: The Next Generation Of Law Students Don’t Trust AI Hype

stories.Headline: Silicon Valley Loses Its Bulwark Against AI Regulation...
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang stepped down as chief executive of NVIDIA on November 12, 2026, local time, and the company's board named Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO. The article says Huang led NVIDIA for 33 years, and that the move leaves the AI industry without a figure who had long held back tighter regulation of the sector. The report describes his departure as a possible loss of momentum across the AI ecosystem, given that NVIDIA's graphics processing units effectively dominate the global AI chip market. It also raises concerns about the effects on industry and markets, though it stops short of predicting specific outcomes.

Huang, the article explains, had close ties to U.S. President Donald Trump and worked to ease AI regulations while shaping the technology rivalry between the United States and China. He argued that AI chips should be exported to China so that the country would become technologically dependent on the United States, and the piece says he persuaded Trump on this point. When parts of the AI industry, including Anthropic, recently pushed to slow development and move toward tighter rules, Huang opposed them and supported the administration's deregulation policy. The Trump camp, according to the report, effectively made him a key adviser who gave a rationale for that policy.

The article links his exit to the midterm elections, in which Democrats who had campaigned on stricter AI rules recently gained control of Congress and several key state governments. Against that shift, it argues that Silicon Valley's regulatory shield is at risk of being dismantled now that Huang is gone. The writer, Lee Seok-woo, an international affairs correspondent, frames the departure as removing a bulwark that had protected the industry from new rules. The piece is an analysis of political and market consequences rather than a report of any new regulation, and it does not say what specific rules may follow.

Articles.Title: Silicon Valley Loses Its Bulwark Against AI Regulation...

stories.Headline: DCU-Led European Master in Law, Data and AI Awarded €3.6 Million Erasmus Mundus Grant - Dublin City University
stories.Summary:
Dublin City University and four international partners have secured a €3.6 million grant from the European Commission for the European Master in Law, Data and Artificial Intelligence (EMILDAI), a joint master's programme under the Erasmus Mundus scheme. The announcement was published on DCU's website on 12 November 2026. The award is coordinated by DCU, which leads a consortium of five partner universities across Europe and Brazil. The funding guarantees the operation and expansion of EMILDAI through 2032 and allows the consortium to recruit up to 100 students globally. The grant will pay for full scholarships for European Union and international students, student and academic staff mobility across partner institutions, collaborative research and curriculum development, and deeper links with industry partners.

The programme combines legal policy with computer science, preparing graduates to handle the legal, ethical and technical questions raised by artificial intelligence and data-driven systems. Students begin with foundational coursework at DCU before moving on to specialised tracks in areas such as data governance, cybersecurity and global digital regulation. DCU President Professor Daire Keogh described the award as a strong endorsement of the programme's vision and academic excellence, and said the university is proud to lead the consortium. Dr Edoardo Celeste, the programme director, said the funding confirms the vision set out when the programme was founded in 2021 by four pioneer institutions. Professor Lisa Looney, Vice President for Academic Affairs and Registrar, said the money reinforces DCU's commitment to an interdisciplinary curriculum and international mobility.

Dr Gezim Visoka, Executive Dean of the Faculty of Humanities and Social Sciences, said the grant will help the programme keep fostering legal research and ethical leadership in the field. The partner universities are Avignon Université in France, Erasmus University Rotterdam in the Netherlands, Fundação Getulio Vargas in Brazil, Universidad de León in Spain and the Università di Pisa in Italy. Graduates earn a joint master's degree recognised across Europe and internationally. The article notes that students can learn more about the programme and 2027 scholarship opportunities on the EMILDAI website.

Articles.Title: DCU-Led European Master in Law, Data and AI Awarded €3.6 Million Erasmus Mundus Grant - Dublin City University

stories.Headline: Chinese actress Zhao Liying's lawsuit spotlights AI misuse as experts urge stronger oversight
stories.Summary:
Chinese actress Zhao Liying has reportedly sued the operator of the short-drama platform Hongguo Short Drama and its parent company, Douyin, over the alleged unauthorized use of her likeness in AI-generated content. According to a report by the Dahe Daily, court records shown on the business information platform Qichacha indicated a hearing was scheduled for a Tuesday at the Mentougou District People's Court in Beijing. The defendants are Beijing Douyin Information Service Co Ltd, Beijing Bimo Liuxiang Technology Co Ltd and an individual identified by the surname Shi. Qichacha records show that Beijing Bimo Liuxiang Technology, founded in July 2021, is wholly owned by Beijing Douyin Information Service and is linked to Hongguo Short Drama.

Users on Sina Weibo have posted screenshots and clips from AI-generated short dramas on Hongguo that feature characters resembling Zhao and voices that sound similar to hers, and the case has become a trending topic there. The article says several other Chinese actors, including Yi Yangqianxi, Yang Zi, Xiao Zhan, Deng Wei and Cheng Yi, have faced similar disputes over AI-generated short dramas. Voice actors are also affected: Ji Guanlin told the Global Times that colleagues, including herself, have had their voices used without authorization, and some have sought legal remedies. Under China's Civil Code, a "portrait" is an external image that can identify a person, so an AI-generated figure need not be an exact copy to infringe, according to lawyer Li Yunkai of the Beijing Tianyuan Law Firm. A September opinion from the Supreme People's Court says training AI on a person's voice without consent, or generating recognizable synthetic speech of them, may infringe their voice rights.

Regulators are responding. According to Xinhua, China's National Radio and Television Administration has launched a two-month campaign running from November 1 to the end of December, aimed at vulgar and homogeneous micro short dramas and at unauthorized use of faces and voices, which the article calls "face theft" and "voice theft." Li Yunkai said distribution parties as well as production companies may bear responsibility, and that content placing a recognizable person in vulgar scenes, false endorsements or negative storylines could also violate reputation rights. Zhang Peng, a cultural researcher at Nanjing Normal University, argued that platforms should verify authorization, label AI content clearly, remove infringing material quickly and suspend repeat offenders, and that watermarking and authorization databases could help. The article does not report a court ruling in the Zhao case, and it does not say what the outcome of the hearing was.

Articles.Title: Chinese actress Zhao Liying's lawsuit spotlights AI misuse as experts urge stronger oversight

stories.Headline: If AI Cut the Hours, What Are Clients Actually Paying For?
stories.Summary:
The article reports on a question facing accounting firms as AI shortens tax preparation: what clients should pay for when the hours drop. It centers on IRS Office of Professional Responsibility Alert 2026-19, dated June 24, 2026, which says practitioners cannot rely solely on AI, must treat AI-generated text as a draft, and remain responsible for final decisions. The alert ties this to Circular 230 § 10.22, which requires due diligence, and § 10.27(a), which bars unconscionable fees before the IRS. It warns that billing for time not actually spent, or double billing for an AI-assisted task, may violate § 10.27 depending on the facts, and it says cost savings should be passed on openly with AI activities disclosed.

Firms are already changing how they charge. An AICPA and CIMA news release dated September 10, 2025, describes a slow rise in value and fixed pricing alongside a decline in hourly billing. The 2025 MAP executive summary, from the AICPA Private Companies Practice Section and CPA.com, surveyed firms in May through July 2025, with 1,073 completing the survey, and found hourly billing used by 63% of responding firms, per-tax-form fees by 40%, value billing by 30%, up five points since 2022, and fixed pricing by 29%, up four points. Forty percent said they had not worked out how to track efficiencies from technology, and 61% said they had raised fees to cover technology investment. The article notes these figures describe accounting firms surveyed, not law firms, agencies, or design practices.

The article attributes the warnings to the IRS Office of Professional Responsibility through its alert and frames the pricing guidance around the Circular 230 provisions it cites. It also addresses contingent fees under ET § 1.510.001 of the AICPA Code of Professional Conduct, which bars preparing an original or amended return, or a refund claim, for a contingent fee, and notes that a fee tied to the tax result falls within that restriction even if labeled value pricing. The author, Steven de la Fe, CPA, a co-founder of Precision AI OS with 20 years of experience including seven at PwC, offers practical steps such as recording existing billing methods, keeping the signer on drafts, removing minutes the file did not take, and keeping stated return prices separate from tax results. The article does not describe any enforcement action or follow-up beyond the alert itself.

Articles.Title: If AI Cut the Hours, What Are Clients Actually Paying For?

stories.Headline: EU AI Regulatory Sandbox Rules Start December 1: Tests Earn No Compliance Clearance, Liability Stays
stories.Summary:
EU regulators have adopted common rules for AI regulatory sandboxes that EU countries must run under the AI Act, with Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/2487 published in the Official Journal on November 11 and taking effect December 1. The rules were adopted by the European Commission on November 10. They settle what a company receives after testing inside a sandbox: a written proof of completed activities and an exit report, neither of which carries conformity status. Participants remain liable for third-party damage and still have to comply with applicable EU law. The gap between that evidence and formal clearance is the central issue for companies weighing whether a sandbox is worth entering.

The exit report must reach the participant within a reasonable time and no later than 45 working days after participation ends. It covers the main regulatory issues examined, how they were resolved, recommended practices, tools and benchmarks, and a log of serious incidents. Publication on the EU platform requires explicit agreement from both the participant and the authority, and without consent only non-confidential key findings may be published. Law enforcement, border control, immigration and asylum operational data are excluded from those disclosures. Sandbox participation shields companies from AI Act fines only when they observe the sandbox plan and follow the authority's guidance in good faith.

Liability for harm to third parties is not covered by that protection. The Commission adopted the rules, and the regulation was prepared under the AI Act framework that requires member states to run these sandboxes. Deirdre Ahern, a law professor at Trinity College Dublin, argued in a peer-reviewed paper written before the implementing rules were issued that the missing conformity status is one reason sandboxes may struggle to attract providers. Her paper noted that participation is voluntary and that firms can instead pursue the standards and conformity assessment route, which can deliver a presumption of conformity. Ahern suggested that mandatory insurance for third-party harm could ease the liability problem, but the published regulation contains no insurance requirement.

Critics writing in The Regulatory Review in May said the sandbox model could create a "façade of regulatory legitimacy" without addressing systemic risk. They argued that smaller firms may lack the legal expertise to navigate applications and oversight, and that full third-party liability may deter developers, especially for high-risk uses in health care or employment. Supporters pointed to the UK Financial Conduct Authority's fintech sandbox, where participants raised more capital after entering than comparable firms that did not. The regulation makes SMEs and start-ups eligible for priority access and free regulatory guidance, advice and supervision, and requires a registered office or branch in the Union for that priority. Each Member State has until August 2, 2027, to have at least one national sandbox operational, while the regulation itself takes effect December 1.

The original AI Act deadline for that was August 2, 2026. The European Data Protection Supervisor submitted formal comments in March asking that plans involving personal data set out the scope and modalities of processing. The adopted text asks only whether personal data is processed and whether the data protection authority must be involved. Applications must receive a response within three months of a complete application or the call's deadline. The articles leave open how many member states will meet the 2027 deadline, and they do not say whether any insurance requirement will be added later.

Articles.Title: EU AI Regulatory Sandbox Rules Start December 1: Tests Earn No Compliance Clearance, Liability Stays - Tech Times

stories.Headline: Oracle's $125 billion debt raises a major AI warning
stories.Summary:
Oracle Corp. is under growing financial pressure as its spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure keeps running ahead of the cash it generates, according to a November 13, 2026 report on Yahoo Finance that first appeared on GuruFocus. In the last quarter, the company spent $28.5 billion on capital expenditures, more than its quarterly revenue of $19.3 billion. Free cash flow came in at negative $5.4 billion, and total borrowings stood near $125 billion at the end of August. Oracle's shares have fallen roughly 34% this year as investors weigh its growth prospects against borrowing costs and execution risks.

Demand for Oracle's cloud infrastructure remains strong despite those concerns. Revenue from that business rose 121% to $7.4 billion, supported by rising demand for AI computing capacity. Oracle's remaining performance obligations reached $664 billion, and management expects about half of that to convert into revenue within 36 months. The company forecasts capital spending of $90 billion to $95 billion for the fiscal year.

Management expects free cash flow to turn positive during the second half of fiscal 2028 and to exceed $30 billion in fiscal 2029. The article does not attribute these projections to a specific individual beyond the company's management team. Wall Street maintains a Strong Buy consensus on the stock, with an average price target of $241.83. The report notes that investors will be watching whether Oracle can bring new data center capacity online while meeting its cash flow targets.

Articles.Title: Oracle's $125 billion debt raises a major AI warning

stories.Headline: EU AI Act: what applies from 2 December 2026 (AI-content marking for older systems, two new bans)
stories.Summary:
From 2 December 2026, two sets of obligations under the EU AI Act begin to apply, both fixed by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, published in the Official Journal on 24 July 2026. Providers of generative AI systems already on the EU market before 2 August 2026 must implement the Article 50(2) marking obligation by that date. New Article 5 prohibitions on AI systems that generate non-consensual intimate material or child sexual abuse material also begin to apply then. The regulation was adopted on 8 July 2026 and entered into force on the third day after publication, which the Commission dates as 27 July 2026. The article describes this as a follow-up to an earlier post on the headline deadline shifts, isolating the obligations landing about three weeks away.

Article 50(2) requires providers of AI systems that generate synthetic audio, image, video or text to ensure outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated. The Omnibus adds a new paragraph 4 to Article 111 covering providers whose systems were placed on the market before 2 August 2026, giving them until 2 December 2026. The provision does not extend that date for systems first placed on the market on or after 2 August 2026. The Omnibus also replaces Article 50(7), so the Commission encourages and facilitates codes of practice on marking and labelling rather than approving them by implementing act. The new Article 5 prohibitions appear as points (ba) and (bb) of Article 5(1), with paragraphs 1a and 1b, and Article 113 makes them apply from 2 December 2026.

Point (ba) bars AI systems generating or manipulating intimate images of identifiable people without their explicit consent, while point (bb) bars child sexual abuse material, except where a "without right" defence applies under national law. The article attributes the regulation's text to the Official Journal and the Commission's announcement, rather than to any named official. Paragraph 1a limits the provider-side prohibition to systems whose intended purpose is such generation, or where it is a reasonably foreseeable outcome lacking reasonable technical safeguards. For deployers, the prohibition applies where they use a system to generate such material. The recitals state the prohibition does not stop providers from developing general technical capabilities for generating or manipulating images, videos or audio.

The article's own editorial reading, which it says is not legal advice, notes that the Article 50(2) duty falls on providers, so most research offices will be affected through vendor contracts. The article says research institutions are potentially affected in several ways, though none of its cited sources address research institutions specifically. A university group that develops and releases a generative model in the EU may be a provider, and whether the Article 2(6) research exemption applies depends on whether the system was developed solely for scientific research. The new Article 5 prohibitions are described as relevant to institutional acceptable-use policies, student and staff conduct codes, and the vetting of image and video generation tools used in teaching or communications.

The article adds that research involving sexually explicit or abusive imagery has legal and ethics-review implications beyond the AI Act. It also notes that machine-readable marking interacts with journal and funder rules on disclosing generative AI use. The article's background describes the timeline: the Omnibus deferred headline deadlines, with Annex III high-risk obligations now applying from 2 December 2027 and Annex I obligations from 2 August 2028. It points to its earlier post on the deadline delay and to an explainer on what the AI Act means for research administration.

The Article 5 provisions were added to a Chapter I and II framework that had applied from 2 February 2025. The article contrasts these later high-risk dates with 2 December 2026, which covers only the Article 50(2) transitional period and the new Article 5 provisions. It states that the regulation's text and the Commission's announcement set these dates, and it cautions readers not to confuse them. The article leaves several matters open.

It says it has not confirmed how national authorities will supervise or enforce either provision, and it makes no claim about enforcement activity from November 2026. It also has not confirmed the status of any codes of practice or harmonised standards on marking. It directs readers to the Commission's AI Act pages for current guidance. Whether and how systems released after 2 August 2026 will be treated under the marking duty is not resolved by the amending text as the article reads it.

Articles.Title: EU AI Act: what applies from 2 December 2026 (AI-content marking for older systems, two new bans) - CASRAI

stories.Headline: Could AI reduce shipping costs and grocery bills?
stories.Summary:
AI-powered camera technology from a company called EAIGLE is being promoted as a way to cut the time trucks spend entering distribution centers. The company says its system can reduce check-ins from roughly 10 minutes to under 30 seconds. The national average diesel price was $6.13 per gallon for the week of Nov. 9, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. Trucks waiting in lines can burn expensive diesel before they reach the loading dock. Such delays are one of the cost pressures that transportation companies can pass along to retailers and, eventually, shoppers.

The EAIGLE system, called Automated Vehicle Access Control or AVAC, uses artificial intelligence and existing security cameras to identify arriving vehicles. The company says its computer vision technology can capture more than 25 truck and trailer data points in under 30 seconds. Those data points include license plate numbers and other identifying details that are compared against facility records. When the information matches, an automated gate can let the driver proceed. If something looks suspicious, the system can flag the vehicle for additional review.

EAIGLE is the company behind the technology described in the article. The article does not quote an EAIGLE executive directly, and it reports the company's claims about the system's speed and savings as its own assertions. The article attributes the diesel price figure to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. The article also cites a USDA-supported study whose researchers found that higher transportation costs generally increased food prices in the scenarios they examined. Potatoes were especially sensitive to transportation expense changes, partly because they are often shipped long distances.

Shoppers and businesses that move goods by truck are affected by these costs. Fresh produce often travels hundreds of miles before reaching supermarkets, and many grocery products pass through distribution centers. When diesel prices rise, transportation companies often add fuel surcharges or raise shipping rates. The article notes that shipping companies include fuel surcharges that can affect what retailers charge for delivery. Customers ordering online can also see delivery fees rise, and distribution delays can contribute to empty shelves and late orders.

Diesel prices and transportation costs are only one factor behind grocery inflation, according to the article. The article says there is currently no evidence that EAIGLE's technology has directly lowered grocery prices or delivery fees. It also notes that freight-yard check-ins account for only a small part of overall transportation costs. Any savings would need to add up across many facilities to affect what families pay. Retailers could use any savings to offset other expenses or to improve profits.

It remains unclear how much money the EAIGLE system would save across the supply chain, and the article offers no evidence of its actual effect on retail prices. The article leaves open whether any savings would reach shoppers rather than retailers' profits. It also does not say how widely the AVAC system is in use or which distribution centers have adopted it. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Could AI reduce shipping costs and grocery bills?

stories.Headline: AI slump not seen affecting Bank of Japan’s rate-rise plan
stories.Summary:
The Bank of Japan is expected to keep raising interest rates at roughly one hike every three months, according to some analysts, despite growing uncertainty over artificial intelligence and data center investment. The Japan Times reported the story on November 12, 2026, with economist Soichiro Tateishi of the Japan Research Institute saying the effect on the central bank's pace of hikes would not be significant. The article ties the uncertainty to the Democratic Party's strong win in the U.S. midterm elections earlier that month. Concern has grown that data center construction could slow, since many candidates pledged stricter rules for such projects.

Tateishi's view is that a slowdown in the AI sector would not change the central bank's timing much. The Bank of Japan itself argues that AI is only one of several factors pushing up inflation in Japan. That position means the bank's plan to keep tightening policy is not expected to bend to developments in one technology sector. The reporting does not give a new rate figure or a specific date for the next move. What it does establish is that the policy path rests on a broader inflation picture than AI alone.

The article is written by staff writer Kazuaki Nagata and attributes the bank's position to the bank's own arguments, not to new policy statements. Tateishi is quoted directly, while the bank's view is presented as its stance on inflation drivers. The piece is brief and does not describe any formal decision by the bank in the coming weeks. It also does not quantify how large the expected slowdown in data center investment might be. Readers are left with the analysts' expectation that rate increases will continue on their current schedule.

Articles.Title: AI slump not seen affecting Bank of Japan’s rate-rise plan

stories.Headline: How Apollo’s SoftBank ties unlocked an unprecedented OpenAI bet
stories.Summary:
Apollo Global Management, the private credit firm, has lent or arranged more than $15 billion of debt for SoftBank Group since 2021, according to people familiar with the matter. That financing has helped fund Masayoshi Son's bet on OpenAI, which is close to $65 billion. The loans range from debt tied to the value of the ChatGPT maker to a loan backed by a flagship fund, making SoftBank one of Apollo's largest corporate borrowers. The article, published on November 12, 2026, frames the relationship as a clear example of how private credit is financing AI investments that traditional lenders have not.

Apollo is now running into the limits of how much more it is willing to lend to SoftBank. The firm is taking a more defensive stance toward AI investing, which makes the question of how far it can go more pressing. Because SoftBank is one of OpenAI's biggest investors, the answer serves as a test of whether private credit can profitably fill financing gaps in AI that banks and other traditional lenders will not cover. The article presents the outcome as an open question rather than a settled one.

The reporting relies on people familiar with the matter, so it does not attribute specific statements to named Apollo or SoftBank executives. The piece was written by Laura Benitez, Kari Lindberg and Scott Carpenter for Bloomberg and republished by The Japan Times. Its only named subject in the article itself is Masayoshi Son, pictured at a June event in Tokyo alongside OpenAI's chief research officer, Mark Chen. The article does not say how the lending limits will be set or what steps Apollo will take next.

Articles.Title: How Apollo’s SoftBank ties unlocked an unprecedented OpenAI bet

stories.Headline: Sharp to Launch Second Poketomo AI Character in Japan and Taiwan on December 5
stories.Summary:
Sharp Corporation will launch the second Poketomo conversational AI character in Japan and Taiwan on December 5, 2026, the first anniversary of Poketomo. The launch coincides with a new feature that lets nearby Poketomo chat freely with each other, and a new pricing plan for owners of multiple units. Sharp announced the plan in a press release dated November 12, 2026, from Osaka. The company said the launch will bring more ways to enjoy life with multiple Poketomo. Special events will be held on December 5 and 6 to mark the launch and the first anniversary.

The new feature will be available from December 5 and requires two Poketomo registered in advance to the same app. It can be used with any combination of first- and second-generation Poketomo. The new Share Plan allows the number of conversations included in each plan to be shared among two to five Poketomo robots registered under a single Share Plan. Conversations that start automatically between Poketomo do not count toward each plan's conversation limit.

The Share Plan applies only to the robot version of Poketomo, not the app version. A campaign offers the Premium plan, priced at 990 yen per month including tax and allowing 800 conversations per month, free for three months, from December 5, 2026, to January 31, 2027. Sharp is the company responsible for the launch and the Poketomo brand, which it says are registered trademarks or trademarks of Sharp Corporation. The company describes the second character as a little gruff and not always straightforward, but truly caring toward its owner.

According to the release, the character may put on a tough front and struggle to be honest about its feelings, yet stays by its owner's side and expresses care through simple words. Sharp said the Poketomo developers will hold a talk event on December 5 covering the first year and the second character's development. Sharp directed readers to its Japanese-language website for details about the Tokyo event venue. The release says Poketomo is a conversational AI character that keeps its owner company whether the owner is happy, excited, or lonely.

It is available as both a robot and a smartphone app, and it grows more attuned to its owner the more they talk and spend time together. The two-day event in Tokyo will let visitors meet the second character and the first character, described as the "innocent" type. Sharp also gave the price and campaign terms only for the Japanese market, according to a footnote. The release gives no further details about the Taiwan launch, the Taiwan pricing, or how the Share Plan will work outside Japan.

Articles.Title: Second Poketomo Conversational AI Character to Launch in Japan and Taiwan on December 5
