stories.Headline: Could the Voter Backlash Against A.I. Actually Help the Economy?
stories.Summary:
The artificial intelligence boom has powered the U.S. economy through tariffs, war and uncertainty, but it has also pushed up prices, raised borrowing costs and fueled fears of a financial bubble. In last week's midterm elections, Americans signaled that they do not think that trade-off has been worth it. Voters overwhelmingly backed ballot initiatives aimed at reining in data center development, and elected governors and legislators who promised to do the same. The shift is reported in an article published by The New York Times on November 12, 2026, with a source article dated November 9.

The articles do not specify the exact text, numbers or thresholds of the ballot initiatives or legislation involved. They describe the newly empowered Democrats' challenge as addressing voter concerns without derailing the economy. Many economists are optimistic that slowing the rapid pace of A.I. infrastructure buildout could make it more sustainable, even with some short-term hardship. Gina Hinojosa, the newly elected Democratic governor of Texas, has said she wants data center projects to benefit communities rather than stop them entirely.

Gina Hinojosa, named as the newly elected Democratic governor of Texas, is among the A.I. skeptics who won office last week. The articles attribute to her the position that projects should benefit their communities, not be halted altogether. Other officials who won office are described only generally as skeptics who promised to rein in data center development. The articles do not provide further direct statements from policymakers in Washington.

The articles say the mere suggestion of scrutiny in Washington has rattled both Silicon Valley and Wall Street. Those sectors enjoyed two years of lax regulation under Republicans' watch, according to the article. Financial markets whipsawed in the days after the 2026 election, showing how narrow the path is. The articles do not identify specific companies or investors affected beyond these broad sectors.

The articles give the background that the A.I. boom has coincided with tariffs, war and economic uncertainty, and that it has raised prices and borrowing costs. They note that fears of a financial bubble that could burst to devastating effect have accompanied the boom. The articles also state that Republicans held the federal regulatory posture during the two years of lax oversight that preceded the election. The article's preview indicates it is a partial view, with the full text unavailable.

The articles leave open whether newly empowered Democrats can address voters' concerns without derailing the economy. They do not say what specific policies lawmakers will adopt or when. They also do not say how financial markets will respond over the coming months, or whether the buildout will in fact slow. The full article content was not available to confirm further details.

Articles.Title: Could the Voter Backlash Against A.I. Actually Help the Economy? - The New York Times

stories.Headline: 1 UCL Claim Could Freeze Frontier AI: Lawsuit [2026]
stories.Summary:
The nonprofits sued the five AI developers in San Francisco on November 12, 2026. Four groups, Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen, Heat Initiative and The Alliance for Secure AI, filed the complaint. They asked a judge to stop OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Meta and SpaceX from building anything more capable than their current systems. No judge has ruled on the request, and nothing has been frozen. The suit has not reached a hearing, and no case number has been confirmed.

The plaintiffs want an order barring development or deployment of more advanced models until the systems can be shown to be under adequate human control. The legal basis is California's Unfair Competition Law, a state law against unlawful, unfair or fraudulent business practices. The complaint names ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude among the products at issue. Reports describe a 63-page complaint, and the injunction is the main remedy sought. No damages figure has been confirmed in the case.

Brendan Steinhauser, CEO of Alliance for Secure AI, said executives building these systems have warned for years that their frontier models pose catastrophic risks. He said the companies keep developing AI they admit they cannot reliably control. A spokesperson for the plaintiff coalition, whose name the release does not give, called for a freeze on frontier AI development until the technology is under control. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is cited in coverage saying the company does not understand how its AI creations work.

The defendants have not given a substantive public reply in the sources reviewed. The complaint alleges that AI systems have bypassed safeguards and accessed computer systems without authorization. It raises risks to public health, safety and property. The plaintiffs rely on the labs' own safety research and promotional claims as evidence.

Coverage of the suit says the defendants are the five largest frontier AI developers. Reporting notes that the lawsuit is a shift from voluntary corporate commitments toward state-level enforcement, though that framing comes from one outlet. In March 2023, an open letter called for a six-month pause on training systems more powerful than the leading model of that time. Labs did not pause after that letter.

Since then, AI policy has produced transparency and incident-reporting rules, along with lawsuits over copyright, privacy and patents. This filing is the first reported to seek a development freeze under a consumer-protection law. Reporting says no hearing date is set, and it is unclear whether the plaintiffs will seek emergency relief. Whether a court will accept the statute as a basis for the requested order remains open, as does how it would define "more advanced" and "adequate human control."

Articles.Title: 1 UCL Claim Could Freeze Frontier AI: Lawsuit [2026] - shattered.io

stories.Headline: AI needs the kind of federal regulation that has made air travel safe [letter]
stories.Summary:
The Wright brothers made their first powered airplane flight on Dec. 17, 1903, near Kill Devil Hills and Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. Orville Wright piloted the flight, which covered 120 feet over the ground and lasted 12 seconds. Federal regulation of flight later led to the 1958 creation of what is now the Federal Aviation Administration. That agency manages more than 5.3 million square miles of U.S. airspace through a layered system of control.

The system has three main tiers that work together. Airport traffic control towers handle ground movement on runways and taxiways along with takeoffs and landings near the airport. Terminal radar approach control systems guide aircraft during arrival and departure, up to roughly 10,000 to 17,000 feet, and often serve several regional airports at once. Air route traffic control centers oversee planes as they cross states and time zones. FAA rules and regulations, published in hundreds of pages and documents, direct how these systems are built and run.

In a letter to the editor published Nov. 13, 2026, Dennis Dezort of Marietta argues that artificial intelligence should be governed by a similar framework. He writes that AI today is at roughly the same stage the Wright brothers' airplane was in 1903. He says that systems and rules should be designed now to govern the technology. The letter appeared in LancasterOnline's opinion section and does not describe any proposed legislation or agency action.

Articles.Title: AI needs the kind of federal regulation that has made air travel safe [letter] - LancasterOnline

stories.Headline: Why Are Games Hiding Their Blatant AI Usage If They Think It's Totally Cool And Fine And The Future
stories.Summary:
Luke Plunkett, writing for aftermath.site on November 12, 2026, asks why video games are hiding their use of AI when developers apparently consider it acceptable and the future. He says he will not discuss the Big Walk controversy here, focusing instead on games that use AI-generated assets without disclosing it. Steam's AI disclosure policy, rewritten in January 2026, requires developers to disclose any AI-generated content "consumed by players," such as visuals, sound and writing. Plunkett says the number of undisclosed games on Steam, especially in his own recommendations, is getting out of control. He describes strategy and management games he has installed only to find blatant AI imagery, including Napoleonic officers with odd buttons and space miners wearing nonsensical goggles.

Plunkett argues that the lack of disclosure is maddening, since developers who value AI for cost-cutting and time-saving should be proud of it. He suggests the studios hide it because they know players dislike it and want to avoid criticism. Disclosure matters to him because it lets him decide whether to spend his time and money on a project. He says that searching store pages and the first few hours of playtime to verify a studio's honesty is exhausting and places an unwanted burden on consumers. He writes that he has twice reported on major games he had been enjoying until he found AI-generated material in them.

Plunkett, co-founder of Aftermath, presents himself as a consumer who does not want to support the technology, and he says concealment is worse for him than obvious AI slop games. He says platforms could do more, and that Valve enforcing its own AI guidelines would be a start. He frames the issue as one of trust, arguing that he should be able to make an informed choice. The articles say a huge number of gamers hate AI in games and will make purchasing decisions on that basis. Plunkett's article links to related coverage, including the Big Walk controversy and a January 2026 policy rewrite.

The related headlines show the wider debate: an IGF juror reportedly declined to vote for any game using generative AI, and Big Walk apologised that its LLM usage may not meet others' standards. Danbooru, an anime art site, was taken down by a malicious pull request seemingly powered by LLMs and has since returned. The articles do not say whether Valve will enforce its guidelines, nor how many games on Steam currently go undisclosed. They also do not state whether any studio named in the piece will change its disclosures.

Articles.Title: Why Are Games Hiding Their Blatant AI Usage If They Think It's Totally Cool And Fine And The Future

stories.Headline: AI Agent Emily Books, Bills and Refills for MUSC Health
stories.Summary:
MUSC Health, the health system of the Medical University of South Carolina, now routes patient calls first to Emily, an artificial intelligence agent built on SoundHound AI's platform. Emily has supported more than 2.2 million patient calls since MUSC Health deployed it in 2024, SoundHound said in a July announcement. That month, the system added its retail and specialty pharmacy phone lines to Emily's responsibilities. Before Emily, the call center was open only from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., and the system wanted round-the-clock support.

Emily started with two tasks, confirming and canceling appointments, and now answers all 92 of MUSC Health's patient access phone lines. Rescheduling and Spanish-language calls came next, according to HealthTech HotSpot. Emily now handles 25% of the system's patient calls, and staff answer the rest faster while fewer callers hang up. Patients who want a live person can still reach one. Emily is also integrated with the system's Epic electronic health record, so a changed appointment updates the patient's record automatically.

Emily also answers billing questions and helps patients pay a bill, and it can handle a caller's appointment and payment in a single call. For pharmacy callers, Emily can request a prescription refill, give a real-time status update and route the caller to a pharmacy team when needed. Crystal Broj, chief digital transformation officer at MUSC Health, said the technology must be secure, reliable and able to responsibly handle sensitive patient interactions. Broj cited patient frustration and workforce pressure as reasons for the change, according to HealthTech magazine.

Customer service is the most common use of AI among healthcare firms, with 60% using it for customer service chatbots, according to a PYMNTS Intelligence report. That report is based on a March survey of 60 senior technology executives at U.S. enterprises with at least $1 billion in annual revenue, 20 of whom work in healthcare. Spending is rising, with 60% of healthcare firms planning to increase AI budgets over the next 12 months. Obstacles remain, however, as 30% named system integration challenges and the same share named data quality issues as top barriers.

Articles.Title: AI Agent Emily Books, Bills and Refills for MUSC Health

stories.Headline: The Bank of Nvidia just lost its banker — here’s where the AI trade is exposed
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of Nvidia and left its board on Thursday, effective immediately, after reports of three affairs, one involving an alleged Chinese spy. Colette Kress, the company's chief financial officer, became interim CEO, and Nvidia still plans to report earnings on Tuesday. Nvidia's stock fell to its lowest level in more than a year, briefly sitting about $2 trillion below its October record before recovering to a loss of roughly 4% at the close. The selling was uneven across the AI trade. Nebius and CoreWeave, cloud companies that rent out Nvidia chips, took the heaviest losses, while Broadcom and AMD each rose more than 5%.

Analysts tie the pattern to Huang's role as a financier of the AI boom. Nvidia holds stakes in companies including Intel, SpaceX, CoreWeave, Coherent and Safe Superintelligence, bought $3 billion of Meta's stock offering, and has pledged up to $10 billion to Anthropic ahead of its IPO next week. It also holds a $30 billion stake in OpenAI and has a preliminary deal to invest as much as $100 billion more. Many of those companies buy Nvidia chips in turn. By Yahoo Finance's count, Nvidia's latest quarterly filing lists about $530 billion in commitments and guarantees, including roughly $65 billion to rent back cloud capacity and a guarantee of up to $105 billion on OpenAI's Ohio data center leases.

Liz Thomas, chief market strategist at SoFi, said these circular relationships have been a subject of discussion for most of the past year. Kress, who signed off on many of the deals as CFO, now decides how many more to make. The article describes several pressure points: the OpenAI guarantee pays out only if OpenAI defaults, a downturn that sank OpenAI would likely also hit Nvidia's sales, and Nvidia's receivables reached $63 billion last quarter with collection times rising to about 60 days from 45. The value of Nvidia's largest public stock holdings has also fallen by more than $20 billion since June, led by Intel. Nvidia's balance sheet offsets some of this, with about $99 billion in cash and securities against $33 billion of debt at the end of July.

The article notes that money for the AI build-out was already getting harder to find, since CoreWeave's chief executive said the company won't borrow without collateral at current rates. Savita Subramanian of BofA said large tech companies are now issuing more stock than they buy back. Nvidia's earnings report on Tuesday will show whether Kress stands behind the guidance and commitments and whether customers are paying on time. Thomas framed the question for the coming week as whether the market can survive without positive results from Nvidia.

Articles.Title: The Bank of Nvidia just lost its banker — here’s where the AI trade is exposed

stories.Headline: Banks need sovereign AI, but not as expected
stories.Summary:
Vikram Bharwani, CTO for banking and financial services in the UK and Ireland at NTT DATA, wrote on November 13, 2026 that every major bank will need sovereign AI. He used that term not to mean a bank-owned frontier model or large GPU capacity, but the ability to use powerful AI while keeping control of what it learns and the decisions it supports. He said banks now face the question of who controls the institutional knowledge that AI systems absorb from them. He noted that the Bank of England and the UK's Financial Conduct Authority found in 2024 that 75% of responding firms used AI, up from 58% in 2022.

Bharwani drew on Satya Nadella's description of the "reverse information paradox," in which a buyer gives away its knowledge in order to use what it bought. In a bank, that knowledge includes a credit officer's corrections, a fraud analyst's rejected leads and the reasons behind decisions. He stated that enterprise providers often protect submitted data from training shared models, but the risk is that a bank's evaluations, feedback and workflow logic become tied to one platform. He argued that this knowledge layer is more valuable than the model itself and should survive a change of model supplier. He also said that data residency alone does not confer control.

Bharwani set out practical tests of sovereignty: whether a bank controls its data, can explain decisions, retains what the system learns and can keep operating when something fails. He said an agent's permissions, network access and spending limits should sit outside the model, with critical actions requiring approval and a means to stop them. He said the FCA expects firms to apply existing duties and senior accountability to AI, and he proposed a "decision passport" recording inputs, permissions, policy and model versions, tool actions, human interventions and the final explanation. He illustrated this with a mortgage for an applicant with irregular income, where the underwriter should see conflicts and assumptions and a declined customer should receive a clear reason and a route to review.

Bharwani also said that learning from appeals, arrears and complaints should be tested in a sandbox before affecting live systems, and that lending data may reflect past exclusions. He said the same principles apply to fraud, customer service and operational resilience, and that the test is outcomes such as fewer avoidable referrals, lower false positives and better customer experiences. He advised banks to own their data, knowledge and evaluations, to change models without losing context, and to keep a tested fallback for critical services. He suggested starting with one material process and measuring whether AI improves its outcomes, and he warned that junior underwriters need supervised exceptions to keep their judgment. He concluded that a bank can rent a model but cannot rent accountability.

The article does not report any response from regulators, banks or customers beyond the FCA expectations and the survey figures cited. It also does not name any specific bank or affected customer group beyond the general references to borrowers, applicants and customers. Bharwani's piece was published on the NTT DATA website, and it promotes an IDC InfoBrief on sovereign AI for banking and financial services sponsored by NTT SATA. The article gives no timetable for when banks must adopt such controls. It also leaves open how the FCA would enforce its expectations, and it gives no figures on the cost or timing of building the systems it describes.

Articles.Title: Banks need sovereign AI, but not as expected

stories.Headline: AI's $600 billion debt rush could push up borrowing costs across economy: Howard Mark
stories.Summary:
Oaktree Capital Management co-founder Howard Marks has argued in his latest memo that the artificial intelligence boom is becoming large enough to affect the cost of borrowing across the whole economy, not just stock valuations. He points to global AI-related debt issuance of nearly $600 billion this year, citing Goldman Sachs data. The figure covers bonds issued by hyperscalers, project financing for data centres, and borrowing by other AI-linked companies. Marks estimates that AI could need an average of $1 trillion in new capital each year in the coming years, with hundreds of billions of dollars potentially still coming from debt markets.

Marks applies the economic idea of "crowding out," usually used for government borrowing, to corporate AI spending. In his view, hyperscalers are rate-insensitive borrowers that may compete aggressively for the world's savings. They cannot easily pause infrastructure spending because of higher financing costs without risking their position against rivals, so they may become willing to pay more to secure funding. CNBC's analysis, as cited in the article, shows hyperscalers rising from about 1% of issuance in the $15 trillion US investment-grade bond market to roughly 10% in two years. Marks also notes they are now drawing on cash reserves and current cash flows while borrowing more, and lenders must weigh what happens if leverage rises, depreciation accelerates, or AI revenues lag capital spending.

The article attributes these views to Marks, who is described as measured in his assessment. He does not dismiss AI as an illusion and expects it to transform companies and economies, but he separates the technology's potential from the economics of financing it. He argues that much of the investment case currently rests on belief rather than demonstrable economics, since it is unclear whether AI will generate enough value to sustain compute prices that deliver adequate returns. He also flags circular transactions in which chipmakers, hyperscalers, AI labs and data-centre developers invest in, lend to and buy from one another, which makes it hard to judge whether demand is independent. Reuters has reported that banks and credit investors are scrutinising data-centre lease terms, service obligations and conditions under which large customers could cut commitments.

The article presents these concerns as a reason for investors to look beyond headline revenue growth and ask who ultimately pays for the computing capacity being sold. It states that this does not establish the AI build-out is unsound. Marks's warning implies that bond yields, spreads, collateral values and refinancing risks will reflect the sector's borrowing, and that equity valuations will reflect the same belief. For the wider economy, the article concludes that the result could be a higher cost of capital. The articles do not report any specific next steps or outcomes beyond these projections.

Articles.Title: AI's $600 billion debt rush could push up borrowing costs across economy: Howard Mark

stories.Headline: AI is coming for consulting’s billable hours — and its graduate pipeline
stories.Summary:
AI is putting pressure on the consulting industry's traditional model of charging clients by the hour and relying on large numbers of junior graduates. According to a CNBC report published on November 12, 2026, clients increasingly want firms to deliver measurable outcomes rather than billable time. Automation is also taking over research, analysis and presentation work that junior consultants have long handled, which raises questions about how they will build experience. Svilena Tzekova, global head of consulting at KPMG and based in London, told CNBC that the knowledge once at the core of consulting work is now far more accessible, so clients expect more. She said part of her firm's advisory business has largely disappeared because anyone can now reach that level of advice quickly.

The industry has not yet settled on how to price the new work, she said, because procurement departments still compare firms by headcount and hourly rates. AI also brings added costs, including computing power and fees charged by AI providers based on how much text their models process. Smaller, AI-native consultancies say they are better placed for this shift. Emiko Caerlewy-Smith, head of investor relations at London-based challenger firm Elixirr, said her company has never billed on a time-and-materials basis and expects clients to pay for fixed deliverables. She said Elixirr helped a global insurer build an AI-based motor insurance platform, and that it took the firm six months to get its data into a form its AI models could fully use.

She argued that large firms with tens of thousands of staff will find that kind of change far harder to make quickly. Established firms are rethinking roles and training in response. Claire Trachet, a former Deutsche Bank dealmaker who now runs her own advisory firm, warned that junior staff may lose the chance to build professional judgment if AI handles the foundational work. Paul Goodhew, EY's London-based global assurance innovation and digital leader, said AI can now prepare first drafts of work that junior auditors once did by hand, and EY is creating roles such as data delivery professionals and product managers. Tzekova said KPMG will not stop graduate recruitment but expects junior consultants to take on more responsibility earlier, while Caerlewy-Smith said traditional firms must redeploy staff to new tasks or the pyramid model will stop working.

Articles.Title: AI is coming for consulting’s billable hours — and its graduate pipeline

stories.Headline: Is Big Law ‘AI Gaslighting’ Us?
stories.Summary:
Big Law firms have made a string of large announcements about artificial intelligence, some involving hundreds of millions of dollars, and a commentary published on artificiallawyer.com on November 12, 2026 asks whether these gestures amount to "AI gaslighting" of clients. The author questions whether the firms genuinely intend to change how they practice or whether their management is simply misreading the moment. The piece argues that if heavy spending on AI produces no clear benefit for clients, with outputs that are unchanged, priced the same or higher, and delivered the same way, the investment is hard to justify. It floats several explanations, including that the spending is a membership fee of doing business, an expensive marketing exercise, or a way to cut firms' own costs.

The author sets out ways firms could show clients real value from AI. Firms could reduce the cost of some or all of a matter, which can be measured and shared, especially on time-based or fixed-fee work. They could also show faster completion of transactions, perhaps with a table tracking where time was saved and how that supported a deal's closing, and might even charge a speed bonus. Harder but more important, the author suggests firms could show where AI surfaced insights or arguments that changed the direction of a matter, and over long relationships, how it reduced risk, such as fewer escalations in employment cases.

The author concedes that demonstrating risk reduction is difficult, since clients only feel it when something goes badly wrong. The piece calls for firms to share hard numbers in the way they share profit and revenue figures with legal media. The article's central criticism is aimed at the large firms, which the author says have been prominent in funding legal AI but have not yet made clear to clients what they gain. The author notes that the louder and grander the announcements, the less clear it is how clients benefit.

The author also praises Big Law's legal work in general and says the sector should continue. The author does not describe any formal response from the firms named or any regulatory action, and the articles provided do not say what the firms have said in reply. The closing thought predicts an irony: in-house legal teams and small to mid-size firms that bill on fixed or no-win, no-fee bases may end up changing how they operate and reaping the tangible benefits of AI. The commentary offers no timetable or further developments beyond that prediction.

Articles.Title: Is Big Law ‘AI Gaslighting’ Us?

stories.Headline: For insurers, the AI bill gets bigger after the pilot
stories.Summary:
Insurers are raising their AI budgets and becoming more selective about which projects they take beyond the pilot stage, according to an article published November 13, 2026, by Insurance Business. The piece reports that once a tool enters daily use, the cost of protecting customer data and monitoring its output can determine whether it is worth rolling out across the company. Chris Raimondo, EY's global and US insurance consulting leader, is the main source for this reporting. Coverage draws on several surveys to show that spending is rising across the sector.

KPMG's US insurance practice reported this year that 90% of the insurance executives it surveyed said their companies had increased AI budgets from the prior year. A separate Celent survey of 44 North American property and casualty insurers found that the average respondent expected overall IT funding to rise nearly 10% in 2026, with AI and supporting data among the priorities. Deloitte's 2027 insurance outlook, published November 12, found that only seven of 35 insurance technology leaders rated the returns on their AI investments as high or very high. Deloitte also said operating costs could become more variable as insurers use different models and as usage grows.

Raimondo said the conversations he has with carriers have shifted past early trials, with clients now asking how to run AI securely at scale and what return they will get. He said insurers see the opportunity but recognize that the path is more complex and likely requires more investment, so they will be more selective about which opportunities get funding. He also said that moving a tool into regular use forces an insurer to decide who can access the data and how to reconstruct what happened if an output is questioned. In his view, the industry needs proper investment in governance, safety and security while also needing to operate at a more profitable baseline.

The article adds that adoption has moved faster for employee productivity tools and AI features built into software staff already use, such as claims systems, while custom agents remain more often the subject of experiments. Raimondo expects agents to act more independently in internal IT, but he expects people to keep working alongside them in underwriting, pricing and claims servicing, where errors can affect what a customer pays. A 2026 WTW survey of 59 P&C insurers in the US and Canada found that 16% were using AI to support human underwriters, and 60% planned to prioritize that use by 2028. Raimondo also said that the closer the technology gets to the core insurance value chain, the higher the bar for automating it. More to follow.

Articles.Title: For insurers, the AI bill gets bigger after the pilot

stories.Headline: Fake content, false impression: Pennsylvania’s AI ad disclosure law takes effect December 21
stories.Summary:
Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro signed SB 806 on October 22, 2026, creating the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act, also known as Act 99 of 2026. The law takes effect December 21, 2026, making Pennsylvania the third state after New York and California to require disclosures for certain AI-generated advertising. Unlike those states, Pennsylvania's law does not focus on synthetic performers. It applies only when AI content creates a false consumer perception. The article's author, a Reed Smith counsel, argues that advertisers should already avoid such ads because misleading advertising is illegal everywhere.

The statute requires that an advertiser not create or disseminate an ad using synthetic content in a way that misleads consumers about the nature, origin, or authenticity of what is being sold, unless a clear and conspicuous disclosure is included. Synthetic content means an image, video, audio clip, or text that has been significantly modified or generated by AI, though text-only content is excluded. The law does not define false consumer perception, so the author expects Pennsylvania to borrow the FTC framework on whether a message is likely to mislead a reasonable consumer and whether it is material. A required disclosure must state that the ad contains AI-modified or AI-generated content, appear the first time the content is shown, and appear in the same medium. The law also sets penalties of up to $3,000 per violation, plus attorney fees and costs, enforced by the Attorney General or district attorneys.

The author notes that the statute has no knowledge requirement, since the final bill removed "knowingly, recklessly or willfully," so advertisers may be liable for the messages they release. The author argues the disclosure cannot cure an ad that is misleading at its core and that adding one could be read as an admission of deception. The author's view is that the law's practical use will be as an added tool for prosecutors against deceptive AI ads already vulnerable under other laws, and that "violation" is undefined, so exposure could grow quickly across high-volume campaigns. The article compares the three state laws, noting that New York's law has a knowledge requirement and California's and Pennsylvania's do not, and that Pennsylvania has the broadest coverage. It recommends eliminating deception rather than designing a disclosure, reviewing routine AI uses, and tightening oversight of agencies and vendors.

Articles.Title: Fake content, false impression: Pennsylvania’s AI ad disclosure law takes effect December 21 - Reed Smith LLP

stories.Headline: How CUBE Is Transforming Global Regulatory Compliance with AI
stories.Summary:
CUBE, a regulatory technology company, is extending its AI software by placing its regulatory intelligence directly inside the platforms businesses already use. Its Powered By technology lets software providers access CUBE's regulatory data and AI agents without having to collect, organise or maintain the underlying information themselves. The latest example is Thomson Reuters, which has integrated CUBE's technology into CoCounsel Legal. The article says the integration gives corporate legal teams and international law firms access to regulatory information across more than 150 countries and could reach up to one million legal professionals.

Through this integration, CoCounsel Legal users can research laws, rules, guidance and regulatory developments alongside Westlaw, Practical Law and Reuters content. CUBE has also published internal benchmark findings comparing its regulatory intelligence agents with two leading AI models. The evaluation, conducted in August 2026, involved 13 regulatory queries covering the UK, Spain and the UAE. According to CUBE, its agents identified three to four times more essential regulatory material than the competing models, and six to 17 times more regulatory guidance, codes and supervisory material, depending on the model. The article notes these results come from CUBE's own evaluation rather than independent testing.

Ben Richmond, Founder and CEO of CUBE, said the company aims to be the regulatory data infrastructure that the world can trust and that delivering regulatory intelligence at the point of need is the future of the industry. Thomson Reuters said its subject matter experts assessed how CUBE's content would complement its existing resources before the integration. Its representatives said that global coverage and quality were both essential to them and that CUBE met both requirements. The article also says CUBE has spent 15 years building a database covering more than 12,000 issuing bodies across 750 jurisdictions, validated by 250 subject matter experts and processing more than ten million data points each year. CUBE adds that 24 of the world's 29 Global Systemically Important Banks already use its regulatory intelligence.

Articles.Title: How CUBE Is Transforming Global Regulatory Compliance with AI

stories.Headline: Banks Face Agentic AI’s Twin Tests: Customer Authority and Internal Costs
stories.Summary:
Banks are facing two linked pressures as artificial intelligence agents move from answering questions to taking action. On one side, customers may delegate financial decisions to agents, raising legal questions about consent and accountability. On the other, banks deploying their own agents may face runaway computing costs that erode expected savings. A WilmerHale client alert and a Reuters report on McKinsey's Global Banking Annual Review describe both problems.

The compliance issue starts with whose instructions a bank is carrying out. WilmerHale's analysis, focused on the U.K. Financial Conduct Authority framework, separates authenticating an agent from establishing its authority. Software may legitimately access an account yet make a transfer or investment beyond the limits the customer intended. Under the U.K. Payment Services Regulations, payment authorization depends on payer consent through an agreed procedure, and strong customer authentication is a separate requirement. Banks therefore need to consider how authority is established, restricted and withdrawn, and when customers must approve further action.

Those concerns help explain the caution across the industry. Reuters reported that most banks currently block external agents from authorizing transactions within their systems. Demand nevertheless appears substantial, since McKinsey surveyed 46,000 retail banking customers worldwide. Among AI users, 72% said they would allow a banking agent to perform one financial task, though they would cap autonomous approvals at $500. The consultancy expects widespread customer use of agents within three years.

Delegation also complicates financial crime monitoring and disputes. WilmerHale describes an agent choosing payment methods, currencies or intermediaries that individually seem reasonable but collectively produce unusual activity. Existing anti-money-laundering and sanctions obligations still apply, so banks must separate legitimate automation from fraud or evasion. When a customer disputes a transaction, ordinary records may not show whether the agent followed its instructions, so WilmerHale suggests banks consider what evidence they need, including permissions and action histories.

Banks' own agents raise a separate cost problem. Reuters reported McKinsey's warning that token spending, the units underlying AI processing charges, could easily reach 20% of banks' total labor costs. Some banks have assigned oversight to teams called AI FinOps, and agent-to-agent communication makes earlier usage controls less effective. As a result, banks are becoming more selective, favoring applications with stronger expected returns and asking whether added revenue justifies higher AI spending. The two pressures could compound, since customer agents might shift deposits into higher-yielding alternatives while banks absorb the costs of their own automation.

Articles.Title: Banks Face Agentic AI’s Twin Tests: Customer Authority and Internal Costs

stories.Headline: Kansas School District Deploys ZeroEyes AI Gun Detection
stories.Summary:
Ulysses USD 214 in Kansas has deployed ZeroEyes gun detection software as part of a wider school security investment. The Grant County district serves about 1,400 students and employs 225 staff members across its four school buildings. Funding came through the Kansas Safe and Secure Firearm Detection Grant Program, which the state attorney general's office administers. The rollout was reported by Campus Security Today on November 13, 2026, with the article written by Chelsey Arries.

The district's broader package includes controlled building access, upgraded cameras, school mapping and reunification planning. Under the system, the software flags potential firearms and sends images to a continuously staffed ZeroEyes operations center for human review. When reviewers confirm a threat, they alert school officials and law enforcement with the firearm type, a visual description and the latest known location. The company says those alerts can reach responders within seconds of detection. The articles do not describe how often the system has flagged a threat or any incident that has prompted an alert.

ZeroEyes, the vendor, is the party that describes how its system operates and what its response timing is. The articles attribute the district's grant-funded deployment to the state program and quote no district official on the purchase or its goals. The reporting also does not say whether the district plans to expand the system or evaluate its results. The article is a short news item, and the surrounding page lists unrelated security and cyber stories.

Articles.Title: Kansas School District Deploys ZeroEyes AI Gun Detection - Campus Security Today

stories.Headline: South Korean billionaire Jay Y. Lee's Samsung starts $900 million AI chip plant
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics, led by South Korean billionaire Jay Y. Lee, has broken ground on a $900 million plant to package high-bandwidth memory chips at its Onyang campus in Asan, South Chungcheong province. The company also raised its planned investment in the country's central Chungcheong region to 144 trillion won, or about $107 billion. Lee attended the groundbreaking, where he recalled that the site was bare hills and unpaved roads 40 years ago. The report was published on November 12, 2026.

The new facility will handle advanced packaging for HBM, the stacked memory chips that sit beside processors in artificial intelligence servers. Packaging has become a bottleneck in AI chip supply, because each stack requires several layers of memory to be bonded and tested before it ships to customers such as Nvidia Corp. Samsung plans to turn the Onyang site into a hub for advanced chip packaging. The higher figure builds on a July plan by Samsung group companies to invest about $90 billion in the region over the coming years for chips, displays and batteries. That earlier program already included new HBM packaging lines.

Lee, 58, became chairman of Samsung Electronics in October 2022 and is the grandson of company founder Lee Byung-chul. He is the son of the late chairman Lee Kun-hee, who turned Samsung into the world's largest memory chipmaker. Since taking over, Lee has spent heavily to defend the company's lead in memory and to expand its contract chipmaking business. Forbes ranks him as South Korea's richest person, with a fortune built mainly on his family's stakes in Samsung affiliates.

Samsung has been working to regain ground in HBM after trailing domestic rival SK Hynix Inc. in the early stages of the AI boom. Earlier this year it began mass shipments of its sixth-generation HBM4 chips to Nvidia. SK Hynix has announced its own packaging investments in the same region. Figures in the report were converted at 1,340 won to the dollar.

Articles.Title: South Korean billionaire Jay Y. Lee's Samsung starts $900 million AI chip plant - Billionaires.Africa

stories.Headline: Lafayette City Council rejects proposed new downtown AI bar - KATC
stories.Summary:
Lafayette City Council members voted late on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, to reject a proposed high-tech bar in downtown Lafayette. The decision came amid concerns about safety in the downtown area. The owner had planned to use artificial intelligence bartenders to staff the club. Entrepreneur Quintin Borel had hoped to open a bar called "Plush" in the former "Bliss" cocktail lounge. He said it would use technology to change the patron experience.

Under the plan, bar-goers would scan a barcode and order a drink from their seats. A machine would make the cocktail, and a server would deliver it to the customer. Borel said the system would reduce disturbance and traffic movement, allowing him to organize the venue as he wanted. He said his focus was the satisfaction of the guests themselves. The articles give no further terms, dates or figures for the proposal.

Borel defended the concept, saying it added convenience and kept the flow of customers orderly. The Downtown Development Authority's board approved a resolution a couple of weeks earlier asking the council to vote no. Kevin Blanchard, the authority's CEO, said weekend conditions after midnight downtown were not safe. He said the area had seen a lot of chaos and violence on the streets for some time. Blanchard said the authority had raised that concern for a while.

The articles do not describe how other residents or businesses reacted to the vote. They also do not say how the rejection affects Borel's plans beyond his intention to open Plush. Blanchard's remarks focused on weekend nights after midnight, and the articles do not name any specific incidents. The articles say the downtown area has faced ongoing safety concerns, which the Development Authority has cited in opposing the bar. The articles give no further background on the council's earlier handling of the proposal.

It is not yet known what Borel plans to do next. The articles do not say whether he will appeal the decision, revise the concept, or seek another location. They also do not state whether the council will consider similar proposals in the future. The articles leave open how the downtown safety concerns will be addressed.

stories.Headline: Cohesity Expands Cyber Resilience and AI Data Capabilities for Microsoft Environments
stories.Summary:
Cohesity, a company that describes itself as a leader in AI and data security, has expanded its data protection and resilience capabilities across the Microsoft ecosystem, according to a PR Newswire release datelined Singapore on November 13, 2026. The announcement covers Azure, Microsoft 365 and DevOps environments, and it also extends to AI and analytics through an integration between the Cohesity Gaia Catalog and Azure Databricks. Recent innovations span cloud, productivity and DevOps environments, the company said in the release. Cohesity's chief product officer, Vasu Murthy, framed the work as giving customers greater confidence in their systems and data as AI becomes more central to their businesses. The Azure enhancements add protection for Azure Blob Storage, Azure Data Lake Storage and Azure Kubernetes Service, with application-consistent backups and granular recovery for Kubernetes resources.

Azure Government support now includes Azure SQL Database, SQL Managed Instance, PostgreSQL, MySQL, Table Storage and Cosmos DB. Preview access covers GitHub repositories and complete Azure DevOps organizations, including pull requests, boards, wikis and pipelines, with an isolated, immutable copy option. Microsoft 365 recovery adds threat scanning across Exchange, SharePoint and OneDrive, along with protection of the Preservation Hold Library and metadata preservation across OneDrive, SharePoint, Teams and Groups. The integration with Azure Databricks lets organizations publish curated datasets as an external data source, while the underlying data stays in Cohesity Data Cloud. Cohesity is the party responsible for these capabilities, and its chief product officer, Vasu Murthy, said organizations depend on more applications and data than ever, making resilience across those environments increasingly critical.

Murthy said the company's work with Microsoft is focused on giving customers greater confidence in the systems and data they rely on. The company also said the work creates new opportunities to put that data to work as AI becomes more central to the business. The release does not attribute any further statements to other executives. The release frames the Gaia Catalog integration as a way to find, curate and publish enterprise data into Azure Databricks without new extract, transform and load pipelines. It describes Gaia Catalog as building on an existing integration with Microsoft 365 Copilot, which lets employees query enterprise data in natural language.

The company says role-based and file-level access controls ensure responses reflect existing user permissions. Customers relying on Microsoft environments are the audience the release addresses, including public sector deployments that use Azure Government. Cohesity says it is trusted by customers in more than 140 countries, including two-thirds of the Global 500. Cohesity was founded as a provider of data protection and has positioned itself as the leader in AI and data security, according to its own release. The company says its Cohesity Data Cloud is backed by industry leaders such as NVIDIA, Amazon, Google, IBM, Cisco and HPE.

The release also says Cohesity is certified as a Great Place to Work in multiple countries. The company has invited attendees to visit booth 5215 in the Microsoft Ignite Hub at Moscone Center in San Francisco. The Dark Reading article that appeared alongside the release covers a separate subject: Commvault's SHIFT 2026 conference in Nashville, Tennessee. Cohesity will present a session titled "Build resilience and recover Microsoft operations after compromise" on Thursday, November 19, from 10:45 to 11:10 a.m. PT at Microsoft Ignite 2026.

The session will cover a cyber resilience framework for Microsoft 365, Azure, Active Directory and Entra ID. The release does not say whether the DevOps preview will become generally available or when, and it gives no pricing. It also does not describe how customers will adopt the new Microsoft 365 governance features beyond the capabilities named. The articles leave open how the new capabilities will perform in customer deployments.

stories.Headline: China's trade surplus soars past US$1 trillion as AI boom powers exports - CNA
stories.Summary:
China's exports jumped 35.2 per cent in October from a year earlier, customs data released on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, showed, extending a surge driven largely by the global race to build artificial intelligence infrastructure. Because of that strength, China's trade surplus reached US$1.04 trillion over the first ten months of the year, topping the US$1 trillion mark for a second straight year and arriving a month earlier than it did in 2025. Imports also climbed sharply, rising 41.6 per cent in October, which was faster than economists had expected. One Caixin report put October exports at US$412.3 billion and imports at US$307.1 billion, leaving the monthly surplus at US$105.3 billion, down from September's record of US$133.6 billion.

The figures point to Beijing's growing dependence on overseas demand to prop up an economy weighed down by weak household spending and a long property slump. Sluggish domestic demand has pushed Chinese automakers to seek buyers abroad, and domestic vehicle sales fell for a twelfth straight month even as car exports kept growing. Analysts warned that the AI-driven boom could sharpen trade frictions with major partners, including the European Union, which has agreed with Beijing to limit Chinese hybrid vehicle exports over the next few years. Caixin noted that much of the export growth reflected rising prices rather than higher shipment volumes, and that AI-related chip exports rose sharply even as overall shipment volumes fell slightly.

Economists and analysts pointed to the risks ahead. Joe Peissel, lead macroeconomist at Trivium China, said the risk of additional tariffs and other trade barriers would stay elevated in 2027 as Chinese manufacturers keep expanding overseas. Macquarie analysts said the outlook depends on how long the AI boom lasts, and they expect exports to accelerate further in the fourth quarter before slowing from the first quarter of 2027. China has also extended a trade truce with Washington by two months, though it tied any expansion of its purchases of US farm goods to the implementation of an agreed reciprocal tariff-reduction arrangement. The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit is set for Shenzhen next week, where Xi Jinping and Donald Trump are expected to meet for the third time this year.

stories.Headline: Kazakhstan-linked hackers used AI to steal Tajik government documents, researchers say
stories.Summary:
A hacking group linked to Kazakhstan used an artificial intelligence agent to steal more than 2,000 national security-related documents from Tajikistan, according to a report published on Wednesday by the Singapore-based cybersecurity company CloudSEK. The firm said it found the operation after the attackers accidentally left a server exposed to the internet. The group, which researchers call Silent Lynx, relied on Hermes, an open-source framework for autonomous AI agents, and the data CloudSEK recovered shows the hackers began reconnaissance around mid-August before breaking into Tajikistan's electronic document system a couple of weeks later. The server also held more than a dozen gigabytes of material, including stolen government files, hacking tools and records of how the agent was used.

According to CloudSEK, the hackers configured the agent to act as an offensive security expert, and it handled reconnaissance, data collection and the erasing of traces from compromised systems. The agent was also set up to run certain potentially destructive commands without additional approval, and the operator issued instructions in Russian through a Telegram bot, which let them direct it from a phone. The AI models behind the system were mainly developed by the Chinese company DeepSeek. Once inside Tajikistan's systems, the group used the credentials of a single railway employee to log into the national platform that ministries use to exchange official correspondence, then built tools to download large volumes of files, including thousands sent to or processed by the Defense Ministry in 2026. The stolen material also reportedly touched the National Guard, the State Committee for National Security and the State Investment Committee, and information about more than 100 government organizations.

CloudSEK said it assessed with medium confidence that Silent Lynx has ties to Kazakhstan, pointing to Russian-language communications and test connections from a residential internet provider in the country. The company's findings align with earlier assessments that the group is probably based there, though they do not establish any link to the Kazakh government, and Kazakh and Tajik officials did not respond to requests for comment. The researchers also found evidence of a compromised server supporting Uzbekistan's Smart Forestry initiative and malicious files posing as official Turkmenistan documents that were created in October, which suggests another phishing campaign was being prepared. Silent Lynx, also known as Cavalry Werewolf and YoroTrooper, has been active since at least 2022 and has previously targeted government and diplomatic bodies across Central Asia, Russia and Europe. Efforts to reach the group were unsuccessful, and the researchers did not determine whether the Turkmenistan attacks succeeded.

stories.Headline: Databricks Launches New Always-on Genie: Autonomous AI for Complex Enterprise Work
stories.Summary:
Databricks announced on November 11, 2026, the second generation of its Genie product, which it describes as an always-on, autonomous agent for enterprise work. Employees can give Genie a goal and trust it to keep work moving on its own. Genie takes ownership of the work, delegates to subagents when needed, tracks progress, and follows up on missing inputs. It also reaches out when a person needs to make a decision. A new inbox highlights what needs attention, and Genie emails users when they are away.

The new Genie runs in the background using its own compute and can handle both daily tasks and larger responsibilities, such as keeping a quarterly forecast on track. Users share a goal and clear boundaries, and Genie manages the task while asking for input when needed. Each new alert arrives as its own unread email, and updates go to the same thread so the inbox does not fill up. Every action stays within Unity Catalog permissions and Unity Gateway approval rules and budgets, and is fully auditable. Genie Search gives people and agents one governed way to find information across the lakehouse and business apps, and Databricks now offers 100+ connectors for key business apps.

Databricks is the company behind the announcement, and the articles quote Ali Ghodsi, its co-founder and CEO. Ghodsi said Genie has made him a 10x more productive CEO and that it no longer waits for him to ask. He said Genie keeps up with his inbox, preps him for meetings, and runs in the background, returning only when it needs a decision. He credited Genie's knowledge of how the company works, including what it means by revenue, which numbers are official, and who can see what. The articles state that Genie operates within a company's existing Databricks environment and is governed by Unity Catalog and Unity Gateway.

The articles say enterprises now expect AI to take real tasks off their plates, and that much of the knowledge needed for complex projects lives across multiple platforms or in people's heads. They say an enterprise assistant can handle this only if it knows the business, can reach the systems teams use, and follows correct permissions and access controls. Genie Ontology, described as an agentic ontology, captures a company's horizontal context, including definitions, metrics, people and processes, and keeps it current as the business changes. Marketers, customer success teams and executives are given examples of tasks they can ask Genie to monitor or report on. The articles describe Genie as built for how companies actually work.

The articles state that Genie Ontology is the layer that supplies business context to Genie's actions. They do not describe a prior generation's limitations in detail beyond noting that Genie is now autonomous and always-on. They also describe Genie Search as expanding enterprise search across tools such as Google Drive, Jira and Confluence without moving or copying content. Ontology Manager, expanded Genie Ontology sources, live governed artifacts, and expanded Genie Agents are listed as additional capabilities. The articles add that Genie can be used through web browsers, mobile apps, email, and collaboration and AI tools including ChatGPT, Claude, Microsoft Copilot Cowork, and Grok Bot.

The articles do not say when the second-generation Genie will be generally available or what it costs. They do not report independent evaluations or customer results beyond the CEO's statement. They also leave open how the autonomous features perform in practice and how decision requests will be handled in large organizations. The articles give no further timeline for the Ontology Manager, expanded connectors, or the new MCP connectors for Atlassian, Google Drive and GitHub.

stories.Headline: Can HMRC look into your AI chat history?
stories.Summary:
From May, HMRC is set to gain new powers to scrutinise the use of large language models in preparing self-assessment tax returns. The change is part of the Budget Bill, which is expected to become law at the end of May, and it would let the tax authority demand computer records from third parties such as AI platforms, as well as personal data from taxpayers themselves. The power would be used to check whether enough tax has been paid, and the articles describe it as an update to existing information powers rather than a blanket inspection of chatbot conversations. Anyone who fails to respond could face a £300 fine, and taxpayers who fail to report inaccuracies could be liable for up to £3,000. HMRC has said it can only request information where it already has a lawful basis to do so.

The articles point out that completing a tax return is a demanding task, which is why millions of self-employed people and higher earners have turned to AI for help. Government concern is that some of these users may be leading themselves into paying too little tax. HMRC can only issue "Schedule 36" notices, demanding information, when it can show a reasonable need. One article notes that the government has said safeguards are in place and private data will not be compromised. Meanwhile, the Budget Bill also gives the tax authority separate powers to recover debts directly from bank accounts from July 2029.

Seb Maley, chief executive of the tax insurance provider Qdos, said HMRC was making sure it isn't left behind as more people and businesses use AI for their tax affairs. Anne Strickland of the Taxpayers' Alliance campaign group warned that demanding private chatbot data would be a deeply intrusive overreach, and argued that the tax authority already has sweeping powers. David Stirling of Mint Wealth advised people to assume their chatbot workings could one day be scrutinised. An HMRC spokesperson said the change reflects how tax information is now stored digitally and that it is not about going through everyone's use of large language models.

The debate comes as the government works to recover an estimated £59.2 billion owed in the 2024/2025 tax year, which the articles present as part of Labour's broader effort on unpaid tax. The articles suggest that the new powers will not automatically give HMRC access to anyone's full chatbot history, but they leave open the possibility that such records could be requested. Critics argue the proposal goes too far in intruding on privacy, while HMRC maintains that its requests will be limited and lawful. The articles do not say how often such requests are expected or how the safeguards will work in practice.

stories.Headline: Harris County wants to expand AI in government. Could your personal information be at risk?
stories.Summary:
Harris County is considering a new artificial intelligence policy that could expand how county government uses AI, though commissioners pulled the item from their Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026 agenda. The discussion was expected at the commissioners' meeting, but no new date has been set. The county already approved an AI policy in November 2024, and officials are now weighing a more comprehensive replacement. Experts have raised concerns about taxpayer spending, data privacy and accountability as the county moves forward.

The proposed update would replace the 2024 policy and strengthen countywide standards for cybersecurity, data privacy, responsible AI use and oversight. County officials recommended May 2027 as the implementation target so departments have time for employee training and guidance. The proposal has not been approved. In March 2026, commissioners approved $425,000 in supplemental funding for contractor resources supporting AI compliance, governance and implementation. That amount does not represent the county's total spending on artificial intelligence.

The county's Universal Services Department developed the update after commissioners directed it on Jan. 8, 2026, to create a more comprehensive policy. The department says the new policy ensures alignment with enterprise architecture, cybersecurity, data privacy and responsible use principles. Harris County first introduced generative AI guidelines in October 2023 before approving the countywide responsible-use policy in 2024. The county's Universal Services Department is responsible for the drafting work described in the agenda documents.

Dr. Dorothy Jiang, an associate professor at the University of Houston's Bauer College of Business, says AI can ease routine paperwork and help residents in multiple languages. She warned that employees might paste residents' personal information into free tools the county does not control. Jiang recommends that county data go only into county-approved tools, that vendor contracts bar training on county data, and that independent audits check compliance. RaSheem Barnett, CEO of Emagine Reality, says governments must weigh full costs and define the problem before buying technology.

Both experts stressed that the department using an AI tool is responsible for its outcomes, the same as if an employee had made the decision. Jiang believes residents should be told when AI is involved in decisions affecting them and should have a simple way to challenge errors. Barnett says a person should be able to override AI recommendations and that residents need a clear path to a county employee. Residents, who would be affected by any misuse of their personal information, can attend Commissioners Court meetings and ask which departments use AI.

The county's AI policy discussion came up in the same period as a separate agenda item on Hurricane Harvey recovery projects, which commissioners also planned to address on Nov. 12. The Texas General Land Office granted a one-year spending deadline extension in September, moving the CDBG-DR project deadline to February 2028 and the CDBG-MIT deadline to March 2029. Texas Land Commissioner Dawn Buckingham had warned that unspent funds would be reclaimed. Harris County also planned to consider 24 jobs supporting violence prevention programs HART and RISE.

The articles do not say when commissioners will revisit the AI policy, nor whether the proposed update will be approved. They also do not say whether the recommended safeguards from experts will become requirements in the final policy. It remains unclear how the county will address the full cost of its AI programs beyond the $425,000 already approved. Residents can find meeting agendas and public comment information through the Harris County Commissioners Court website, where the existing policy remains in effect for now.

stories.Headline: Rackspace and Together AI Announce Strategic Agreement to Support Enterprise AI Inference
stories.Summary:
On November 10, 2026, Rackspace, which trades on NASDAQ as RXT, and Together AI announced an initial multiyear strategic AI infrastructure agreement from San Antonio. Under it, Rackspace expects to provide and operate dedicated NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 infrastructure to support inference workloads run by Together AI, which calls itself the AI Native Cloud. The infrastructure will be connected with NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet networking, and Together AI will run its managed cloud platform on top of it. Deployment is planned for 2027, subject to the satisfaction of certain conditions set out in the agreement. The companies also signed a separate, non-binding letter of intent to explore a joint go-to-market approach for enterprise-focused AI solutions.

Rackspace expects to provide and operate the dedicated NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra infrastructure, including the associated power, liquid cooling, networking and storage. Together AI expects to supply the managed cloud platform, including access to open source models, inference optimizations and developer tools. Rackspace plans to run the deployment on dedicated GB300 NVL72 systems in a purpose-built, liquid-cooled facility, supported by NVIDIA networking. The parties expect to evaluate additional security, governance and compliance controls for future offerings, depending on end-customer requirements and agreed configurations. Under the letter of intent, Together AI would supply inference, while Rackspace would add infrastructure, platforms, solutions and forward-deployed engineering expertise to serve enterprise customers.

Gajen Kandiah, Rackspace's chief executive, said enterprise AI needs more than access to compute, since success depends on running it reliably and delivering sustained value. He said that requires deep infrastructure and engineering expertise combined with operational accountability, and that Rackspace brings more than 25 years of experience operating complex enterprise environments. In his view, the agreement lets Rackspace apply that experience to the dedicated infrastructure behind Together AI's inference platform, and he said it advances the company's aim to be the operator of the full enterprise AI stack. Vipul Ved Prakash, founder and chief executive of Together AI, said scaling in the enterprise needs infrastructure that can grow with the company's ambitions while delivering the performance and reliability customers expect. He said Rackspace brings the infrastructure engineering and operational expertise to support that growth, and that Together AI looks forward to exploring further opportunities together.

Raj Mirpuri, NVIDIA's vice president of global AI clouds and infrastructure ecosystem, said enterprises need infrastructure that turns AI advances into services they can deploy at scale. He said NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra will let Rackspace and Together AI run inference workloads efficiently and bring the next wave of enterprise AI services to market. Rackspace intends to build a repeatable model to support AI platform companies, systems integrators and enterprises as they scale AI infrastructure while keeping control of their technology and customer relationships. The companies said Rackspace's experience in regulated industries, and across private cloud, hyperscaler and edge environments, may let them evaluate deployments that bring Together AI's cloud closer to enterprise data and workloads. Any such configurations, including data residency, security and compliance features, would depend on the specific offering and customer arrangement.

Rackspace says its approach to scaling AI infrastructure is to seek contractual commitments for dedicated capacity and to manage the related financing and capital commitments. The aim is to align them with expected customer demand and the useful life of the underlying hardware. Effective November 6, 2026, Rackspace entered a share purchase agreement with an investor group led by Voss Capital, LP, providing for an aggregate $66 million private placement of its common stock. The company expects to use the net proceeds for general corporate purposes, working capital, capital expenditures and growth capital, including funding for GPU-related initiatives. Rackspace describes itself as an NVIDIA Cloud Partner and as the operator of the full enterprise AI stack.

Rackspace expects to seek separate financing for buying the NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 systems and says it is in active discussions with potential lenders. No definitive GPU financing commitment had been obtained as of the date of the release, and the company said there can be no assurance it will be obtained on acceptable terms or at all. Rackspace's obligations to proceed with the deployment are subject to that financing condition and other conditions in the definitive agreement. Any joint offerings under the non-binding letter of intent would depend on further agreement between the parties and on applicable customer requirements. The availability and characteristics of any joint configurations, including data residency, security and compliance features, remain undetermined and would be set by the specific offering and customer arrangement.

stories.Headline: CoreWeave (NASDAQ: CRWV) Blowout Quarter Signals Robust AI Infrastructure Demand, Lifting Nasdaq 1.6%
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave, listed on the Nasdaq as CRWV, reported record quarterly revenue of $3.66 billion on Wednesday, November 11, and the results lifted the broader market. The company also raised its full-year 2026 revenue outlook, which eased worries that corporate demand for computing capacity might not justify the heavy spending required to build it. Its shares jumped 24.71% during the session, and the stock has risen 52% since it went public in 2025. The results gave a lift to technology stocks as well, with the Nasdaq Composite climbing 1.60% to close at 25,466 after declines caused by Tuesday's inflation concerns. The S&P 500 gained 1.29% to finish at 7,618.

The rally was concentrated in technology and semiconductor names rather than spread evenly across sectors. Micron Technology rose 11.89% as chipmakers recovered from losses earlier in the week. Nebius Group closed 15.44% higher and Applied Digital finished up 7.37%, as investors reassessed the near-term earnings potential of companies tied to AI infrastructure. The article describes CoreWeave's report as a confidence reset for a part of the market that had been pressured by valuation worries and doubts about how long AI-related capital spending could last.

The story frames the gains as a reaction to that single catalyst. Several risks remained after the rally, according to the article. The 10-year Treasury yield kept moving toward the 5% level, which the piece notes has historically created headwinds for growth stocks. Higher yields raise the discount rate applied to future earnings, which can leave richly valued technology shares more exposed if the upward drift continues.

The article also questions whether the gains reflect broad market strength, since they were confined to a narrow group of AI and semiconductor companies. The article's author, David Prior, a senior reporter at the Foreign Policy Journal, presents CoreWeave's results as having restored credibility to the AI trade for now. He says investors will be watching whether that momentum holds as macroeconomic pressures build. The piece does not specify any further scheduled events or outcomes beyond that.

stories.Headline: Rescale Expands Agentic Digital Engineering with Customizable AI Agents for R&D Teams
stories.Summary:
On Nov. 10, 2026, Rescale, a San Francisco digital engineering platform company, announced new agentic digital engineering capabilities that let R&D and engineering teams customize AI agents to their own standards. The announcement went out through PR Newswire, and Tech Times reported it on Nov. 11. The release says the tools bring agentic AI into engineering work where every result must be reviewable and traceable. Its centerpiece is a set of Agentic Projects, which give engineers a way to customize agents and build reusable agentic workflows. Rescale presents the package as an engineering-specific harness, meaning the structure and context that govern how agents operate and keep humans in the loop.

Teams can define each Agentic Project with its own context, skills, tools and guardrails, share projects across teams, and retain approved learnings through project memory. Expanded engineering intelligence capabilities connect data across requirements, design, simulation, test and process systems into foundational knowledge graphs. As agents execute workflows, the platform generates project-specific work graphs that provide traceability and capture learnings. Rescale Desktop extends the platform to engineers' local machines, and expanded Model Context Protocol connectors cover Rescale's ecosystem of engineering applications, including availability on the Claude and Codex directories. Rescale Edison, the platform's AI assistant and agent orchestrator, now has persistent memory, so engineers can describe their intent in natural language.

For AI physics, a new dataset creation agent turns simulation data into training-ready datasets, while Auto Tune, guided pre-processing, uncertainty quantification and a local design explorer add further tools. Jacob Surber, Rescale's vice president of product, said customers build aircraft, vehicles and reactors, so the supporting agents must deliver reliable results. He described Agentic Projects as providing context that grows with every iteration, and called the launch a material step toward an engineering harness built for how these teams actually work. Kairos Power and the Department of Energy's Manufacturing Demonstration Facility at Oak Ridge National Laboratory built a digital agentic scaffolding on the platform with support from Rescale AI developer engineers. Ed Blandford, Kairos Power's chief technology officer and co-founder, said the company depends on quick learning cycles of designing, building and testing.

He added that agents managing setup, execution and reporting leave his engineers free for judgment and rigor. Ryan Dehoff, the facility's director, said Rescale gives industry engineers and lab researchers a digital environment for working side by side, and that agents let Oak Ridge's expertise scale beyond its facility. The release says agents exercised thermal, flow and shielding simulation and reporting workflows for the reactor cavity and bioshield plug designs, with engineers approving each agent action. Oak Ridge is encoding its simulation and additive manufacturing expertise in agents on the platform so engineers can adopt advanced methods to address industry challenges. For high performance computing administrators, new cluster performance metrics show where execution slows and why jobs are waiting.

A new priority score weighs wait time, job size and resource usage to help teams allocate resources fairly. Tech Times pointed out that an audit trail records what an agent did and who approved it, but does not by itself show that the underlying model is valid for the job. It advised teams to ask what each approval step actually checks, how surrogate predictions are rechecked against full simulations, and what outside AI assistants can reach through the connectors. The work is part of a collaboration to test advanced manufacturing and construction methods for Hermes 2, which the release describes as Kairos Power's 50-megawatt fluoride-salt-cooled reactor. Tech Times reports that Hermes 2 is Kairos's demonstration plant in Oak Ridge, Tennessee, where ground was broken on April 17, 2026, and that Kairos says it will deliver up to 50 megawatts of electricity to the Tennessee Valley Authority grid.

The release does not say whether the 50 megawatts is thermal or electric, though Kairos describes it as electric output, and Kairos has targeted 2030 for power production. Kairos reported on Sept. 4 that it had tested modular precast concrete shielding in a reduced-scale mockup of the Hermes 2 reactor cavity, with the facility supplying 3D-printed forms. Rescale's own release notes date several of the new pieces earlier than the announcement: Agentic Projects to Oct. 26, the Edison rename to Oct. 19, Rescale Desktop to Nov. 5, and uncertainty quantification and the dataset agent to Nov. 6. The company describes itself as backed by investors including NVIDIA, Sam Altman, Jeff Bezos, Paul Graham, Peter Thiel, Microsoft, Hitachi and the University of Michigan. Kairos Power projects that agentic workflows built from past simulations could raise end-to-end simulation analysis efficiency by up to 3x while preserving the data traceability required for regulatory compliance.

Tech Times stresses that this threefold gain is a projection, and that the release gives no measured figure for the workflow. The article also notes that Rescale's May 12 release cited a 1,000x increase in simulation speed and a 90% reduction in full-stack simulation costs, with no baseline, sample size or timeframe stated. The release says the new capabilities across agentic digital engineering, AI physics and intelligent HPC work together as organizations adopt AI-first operations across their product development lifecycles. Organizations can learn more about the new capabilities at rescale.com, though the excerpted articles do not say when Kairos or Oak Ridge expect measured results.
