stories.Headline: From College Projects to Job Interviews: How AI Tools Support Students at Every Stage
stories.Summary:
AI writing and resume tools are now appearing at almost every stage of student life, from college assignments to job interviews, according to a Hindu feature published on November 12, 2026. The article follows a composite student, an electronics BTech graduate, whose use of the tools grew from small helpers in her first year to heavy use by her final year. In first year she used a Summarizer, Grammar Checker, Paraphraser, Citation Generator and Translator, mostly from Quillbot. The tools handled small tasks while the argument of each essay remained her own work. Her first-year marks, the article says, tracked how much she had read.

In her second year, the group project was a low-cost water quality sensor built by four students, with a shared document of about 3,000 words. She was given the presentation slides with four days to go, and she used Quillbot's AI presentation maker to build a ten-slide deck for a ten-minute slot. The prompt she wrote asked for plain, technical language, slides under 35 words each, and a suggested chart for the cost breakdown. She attached two photos of the circuit board and corrected the first draft, which had promoted a literature-review sentence into a claim about their own sensor. The deck was exported as a PPTX for the seminar hall and a PDF for the submission portal, and the presentation maker lacks animations and speaker notes.

Quillbot's presentation maker is still labelled Beta and is free to use, with a Premium plan that adds unlimited presentations and faster generation. In her third year, she used Quillbot's AI Resume Builder for an internship at an eleven-person fintech startup in Bengaluru, importing her LinkedIn profile and pasting in project and fest details. She chose the student template, moved her projects and education above her part-time job, and rewrote her tutoring bullet with facts she supplied, including eight students and two years. The founder later said the sponsorship bullet made him open her file. In her final year she used the ATS-friendly template, which the product page describes as parse-safe, while noting that no builder can guarantee a pass through every applicant tracking screen.

The article's author writes that such tools are useful when the student supplies the facts, and that the student must check every line before applying. It lists common failures, including submitting unedited first drafts, using default generic decks, and inventing achievements such as percentage improvements that the student cannot explain. Lecturers recognise these problems quickly, the article says, and interviewers may ask how a stated figure was measured. The student used Quillbot's AI Chat to generate fifteen likely interview questions from the job description and her resume, and she recorded practice answers herself. She did not ask the tool to write her answers, because scripted replies sound scripted on a video call.

A separate KSAT report published November 11, 2026, from San Antonio, Texas, carries a similar message from Jason Pasola, who works for Robert Half, a worldwide staffing company. Pasola said many companies first run applications through software that scans for buzzwords taken from the job posting, with a human or HR professional reviewing them afterward. He said this practice had grown over the last two years, and he advised tailoring a resume to the job description without copying it word for word. He recommended using AI to organise and format a resume but never to claim skills a candidate lacks. He named Microsoft and Claude as tools that work well, and he said he "absolutely" believes qualified candidates are missing out by not showing their skills.

Pasola's view is that employers are increasingly screened by technology before people read applications, so qualified candidates who do not present their skills clearly may be overlooked. The student's story suggests that the same screening can be passed by a clean, one-page layout that matches the posting, though the article notes that the rest depends on whether the experience fits. The KSAT report mentions Texas's new governor-elect, Gina Hinojosa, who is searching for her team through a digital portal rather than paper resumes. stories.Headline: CoreWeave stock: up 39.2% in AI rebound since Nov 5
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave's stock has climbed 39.2% since the November 5 close, leading a rebound in AI-linked shares that has pushed the broader market higher. The strongest gains have come from smaller AI names, with AMD up 36.7%, Nebius up 28.5% and Micron up 23.6%. Over the same period the S&P 500 rose 3.6% and the Nasdaq gained 4.7%. Nvidia is the only name on the chart still below its November 5 close, down 4.3%. November 5 itself was the S&P 500's worst day since April 4, 2025.

On Wednesday, November 11, U.S. stocks rebounded as a strong quarterly report from CoreWeave revived confidence in AI spending. CoreWeave shares soared 24.71% after the company reported third-quarter revenue of $3.66 billion, up 168% from a year earlier. It also raised its full-year revenue forecast to between $13 billion and $13.3 billion. The Dow rose 0.49% to 52,486.49, the S&P 500 gained 1.31% to 7,619.38, and the Nasdaq Composite climbed 1.6% to 25,466.19. Technology led the gainers with a 2.71% rise, while consumer discretionary was the only sector to fall.

Shares of Micron Technology and SanDisk each jumped more than 11%, and Advanced Micro Devices, Intel and Broadcom posted significant gains. Nvidia recovered part of its two-day slide, rising 2.87%, even after Baird cut its rating on the stock to neutral. An amended filing from Anthropic, which is preparing to go public, showed AMD and Micron among seven technology companies that agreed to buy a combined $26 billion of its shares. Kevin Rippey, a technology analyst at Evercore ISI, said sentiment around the frontier AI companies is the core driver of the AI trade and that he sees a bullish outlook into December.

The rally came as oil prices rose from two-month lows, with West Texas Intermediate settling at $86.53 a barrel, up 0.57%, amid doubts about a diplomatic settlement with Iran. The U.S. bond market was closed for Veterans Day, so there was no Treasury trading, a day after the 10-year yield topped 5% on hotter-than-expected inflation data. Traders still see a December rate hike as near-certain, with odds of a quarter-point move at about 90%, according to CME FedWatch. Investors next turn to weekly jobless claims and Nebius earnings on Thursday.

stories.Headline: Nvidia loses its 'Godfather of AI' and now faces first big test without him
stories.Summary:
Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the company on Thursday, after reports of two extramarital affairs and a board investigation that followed. One of the relationships was with a Chinese businesswoman whom United States authorities suspect of spying for Beijing. Nvidia announced that Colette Kress, its veteran chief financial officer, will serve as interim chief executive. The news roiled the company's stock as investors and analysts weighed the path ahead for the artificial intelligence chip giant. Earlier reports had said the board was preparing to oust Huang, and the stock had already fallen on those reports.

Nvidia shares fell roughly 14% from Wednesday's closing price, reaching an intraday low of $148.80 per share before paring those losses. By early afternoon the stock was down only 4.3%, and the latest quote showed it at $166.19, a fall of $7.54. Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and led it to the forefront of the artificial intelligence trade. Nvidia reports its earnings next week, and investors will examine the results closely for a fresh read on demand. The company is also expected to face continued scrutiny over its business dealings with China and any loopholes in export controls.

Nvidia's board of directors is the body that investigated the affairs and now steers the company through the transition. Kress, as interim chief executive, takes responsibility for running the company while it works out its future leadership. The articles quote no direct statement from Huang, from Kress or from the board beyond the announcement of her interim role. Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives said the resignation lets the board remove the problem quickly and take Nvidia into its next chapter without Huang. Ives added that the company already has a strategic roadmap built around its next family of chips, which Nvidia hopes will keep powering the artificial intelligence boom.

Bret Kenwell, an investment analyst at eToro, said Huang was more than a chief executive and was part of the investment thesis, which will bring greater scrutiny to next week's earnings report. Kenwell added that leadership questions do not erase Nvidia's position as a best-in-class technology company during a transformational period for the sector. James McCann, a senior economist at Edward Jones, pointed to the lack of a clear succession plan and to the financial role Nvidia has played in backing other parts of the artificial intelligence sector. McCann said the corporate fundamentals are unchanged, and the firm advises investors to avoid over-concentration in technology companies and to hold well-diversified exposure across large and midcap American stocks. Inc42 reported that the scandal adds uncertainty for India's neocloud providers, firms that rent out graphics processing units and depend on Nvidia's ecosystem.

Investors had already been selling shares of American neocloud companies since September, with CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN suffering sharp corrections that intensified through October and into November. McCann noted that the Nasdaq had delivered gains or losses greater than 1% in seven of the past 10 trading days. Ives said Nvidia remains the clear leader in graphics chips for the artificial intelligence revolution, roughly two to three years ahead of the nearest competitor. His firm holds a price target of $225 a share and an outperform rating on the stock. Inc42 said Nvidia's influence now extends beyond chip supply to financing and strategic partnerships, and that India's neoclouds rely on international customers, government-backed demand and evolving financing arrangements.

The most immediate event is next week's earnings report, when shareholders will look to Nvidia for stability, a fresh read on demand and a reason to regain confidence. The articles do not say who will become the permanent chief executive, and Kress serves only on an interim basis. McCann said it remains to be seen whether a change at the top will materially affect strategy and execution. Ives said the outlook assumes continued headwinds from China-related scrutiny, which he considers already factored into the stock at current valuation. Inc42 left open whether Indian neoclouds will keep the financial backing and customer commitments needed to withstand a global market correction, including CoreWeave's plan to be sole tenant of a 240 megawatt AdaniConneX data centre campus in India.

stories.Headline: From AI Native Advertising to Marketing System Delivery: BlueMedia launches partnership with ChatGPT Ads
stories.Summary:
BlueMedia, a China-based provider of international marketing services, officially launched its partnership with ChatGPT Ads in Shanghai on November 12, 2026, according to a PR Newswire release. The partnership focuses on helping Chinese brands enter AI-powered conversational and decision-making scenarios and on exploring AI Native advertising in global marketing. The release frames generative AI as a new gateway connecting user needs with commercial information, as more people use ChatGPT to search, compare products and choose services. The release says ChatGPT now has more than 1.2 billion weekly active users worldwide. ChatGPT Ads first launched in the U.S. in February of that year and has since expanded to more than 89 markets across several regions.

BlueMedia says it has served more than 100,000 clients across consumer electronics, gaming, e-commerce, internet services and automotive. Its local service networks cover the United States, Singapore, Vietnam, Thailand, the Netherlands, Brazil, Indonesia, the United Kingdom and Malaysia. Under its "AI + Globalization 2.0" strategy, the company integrates AI into market intelligence, creative production, media buying and performance optimization. Its Blue AI platform runs across end-to-end marketing workflows, moving toward autonomous decision-making and execution. The company reports more than 1,000 AI agents deployed in live business operations.

The company says its AI-driven international operations, which use Agent-to-Agent interactions and autonomous decision-making, have generated revenue exceeding RMB 300 million. For ChatGPT Ads, BlueMedia built a full-stack framework covering user intent insights, product analysis, advertising strategy, landing page review and development, data monitoring, campaign execution and performance analysis. The company has launched ChatGPT Ads campaigns for its first group of brand clients, and it reports that preliminary data shows performance exceeding industry averages. It has also introduced tailored solutions for e-commerce, travel and AI applications. BlueMedia states that it will refine its standardized advertising service framework and move AI native advertising toward deployment at scale.

BlueMedia's chairman and company statement describe the partnership's aim as connecting AI Native advertising, model capabilities and marketing systems. The company says long-term data feedback and real-world practice will help AI learn and improve in live marketing scenarios. The release states that the value of AI goes beyond efficiency and is reshaping how marketing is produced, delivered and monetized. Chinese companies going global, which BlueMedia describes as its focus, are the audience the company says it serves. The release presents these claims as the company's own assessment.

A separate Business Insider report, published November 11, 2026, examines the results advertisers are seeing from ChatGPT Ads, which has attracted more than 100,000 advertisers. Reporter Lara O'Reilly writes that the platform must now prove it moves hard business metrics to become a permanent part of media plans. A working paper by Maximilian Kaiser and Christian Schulze, covering 102 advertiser sites, found ChatGPT Ads generated $0.89 in revenue per U.S. session, against $2.45 for Google search ads. Adthena reported that 52% of 30 enterprise brands struggled to recoup ChatGPT ad spend from July through September, while 26% matched or beat Google ads. OpenAI cited an Evernote case study showing a trial-to-paid conversion rate about 10% to 20% above its historical average.

The report says OpenAI launched ChatGPT Ads about nine months earlier and reached a $1 billion annualized revenue run rate by the summer. Growth is limited by the size of ChatGPT's free user base, the scarcity of ad-relevant conversations and how many ads users will tolerate. Qualcomm CMO Don McGuire said it is hard for LLMs to find audiences, which raises the ROI question. Adthena CMO Ashley Fletcher called measurement a sore point and said new measurement pixels and conversion bidding could help, though he warned results may show mostly early-stage nudging. Natural Intelligence, which runs comparison sites including Top10.com and BestMoney.com, moved ChatGPT Ads from its test budget to its growth budget.

Whether ChatGPT Ads can move from experimental spending into permanent media plans remains unresolved in the articles. The Business Insider report describes the verdict from marketers so far as mixed, with Twilio and Intuit still experimenting. The BlueMedia release gives preliminary performance data without specific figures. Fletcher said Black Friday would be a major moment to watch. The articles do not say whether BlueMedia's early results will hold, or how many of the advertisers that tested ChatGPT Ads will continue using the platform.

stories.Headline: NTT partners Sompo Holdings to develop physical AI for care sector
stories.Summary:
NTT, the Japanese telecommunications company, has signed a partnership agreement with Sompo Holdings, the insurance and financial group, to explore how physical AI can be used in the care sector. The aim is to address labour shortages and operational pressures in Japan's ageing society. The agreement covers identifying where physical AI can be applied in care work. It also covers developing ways to fit the technology into day-to-day care operations, moving from research and trials through to deployment and commercialisation.

Separately, Italian shipbuilder Fincantieri has announced a strategic partnership with Poste Italiane and the telecoms company TIM to build what it describes as Italy's first integrated national physical AI ecosystem for shipbuilding. The initiative, called Fincantieri Ontology, forms a central part of the company's 2026 to 2030 industrial plan, known as F4, which prioritises digitalisation, automation and protecting industrial knowledge. The three companies plan to create a secure digital infrastructure that brings AI into ship design, construction and vessel management. A parallel effort, Navis Sapiens, is aimed at digitalising the ships themselves to support increasingly autonomous vessel operations.

Fincantieri's plans involve creating digital representations of industrial processes, capturing technical expertise and using AI models to optimise manufacturing. The companies intend to build four-dimensional design and construction models so that shipyard workers and robotic systems can receive AI-optimised work packages and daily production instructions. The work supports an industrial workload valued at about $81 billion (€70 billion) extending through 2036. Its supply chain includes 7,000 small and medium-sized enterprises across 18 shipyards worldwide, and roughly 100,000 people access its facilities each day. Fincantieri says the partnership will also run a protected computing environment that combines local AI processing with secure cloud infrastructure to safeguard sensitive data.

Fincantieri's chief executive and general manager, Pierroberto Folgiero, said that data and artificial intelligence are the driving forces behind the 2026 to 2030 industrial plan. He argued that the partnership goes beyond digitalising a process, describing it instead as documenting and protecting the company's technical culture. The articles do not give comparable statements from NTT or Sompo Holdings about their agreement. Both initiatives reflect a wider push by industrial and service companies to bring physical AI and robotics into operations facing workforce pressures. The articles do not say what results the NTT and Sompo trials will produce or when any care-sector deployment will begin, and they give no timetable for the Fincantieri initiative beyond the 2026 to 2030 plan period.

stories.Headline: Google unveils Gemini Robotics 2.5 with 96% success rate in tasks
stories.Summary:
Google has launched Gemini Robotics 2.5, an AI model meant to improve how quickly and precisely robots learn and perform tasks. The company announced the model, which it calls its most capable vision-language-action model to date, on November 10, 2026. Google DeepMind's Carolina Parada, who leads the company's robotics work, introduced it in a post on the company's website. Its tests were run with Apptronik and Mercedes-Benz, where humanoid robots sorted automotive parts successfully. The announcement came in reports published on November 9 and 12, 2026.

The model increases the number of skills a robot can learn and the speed at which it learns them. Google tested Gemini Robotics 2.5 across more than 200 distinct tasks, such as serving food with tongs, tying a bow on a gift box and pipetting a liquid. Compared with previous baselines, it achieves a 30% to 100% higher success rate depending on the task, while completing tasks 20% to 30% faster. The model natively works with several robot types, including Apptronik's Apollo 2 humanoid with a five-finger, 22 degree-of-freedom SharpaWave hand, and the Franka Duo platform with two-fingered grippers. Gemini Robotics 2.5 is rolling out to Google's robotics partners.

Google is responsible for the model, and Carolina Parada described it as a step toward robots that can work in less structured settings. The company said the model improves dexterity, reliability and safety, helping robots leave the lab for everyday environments. Google also said Gemini 4 Argon, its frontier model, helped accelerate the robotics research behind the release. The company framed the work as progress toward physical artificial general intelligence. Google also said it is releasing the ASIMOV-Jailbreak benchmark as an open-source tool for testing robots against unsafe instructions.

Apptronik's co-founder and CEO, Jeff Cardenas, said the models improved dramatically in just a few weeks of post-training. He said they carried over to Mercedes-Benz production with very little drop-off. The pilot ran on active automotive production lines in Kecskemét, Hungary, and Sindelfingen, Germany. Factory technicians are affected because the robots take over repetitive kitting work, freeing them to focus on complex build tasks. Monotonous parts sorting is the work the robots were built to relieve, and the companies said it can help keep assembly lines moving.

Apptronik and Mercedes-Benz tested the model in a proof-of-concept on the production lines. In that pilot, Apollo 2 autonomously sorted metal automotive brackets from bulk bins into trays in the order each vehicle needed. The system pairs Gemini Robotics ER, which tracks the workflow, with the Gemini Robotics 2.5 actions model, which controls the hands and arms. Google said its safety features let robots steer around hazards in real time, improving safe task completion by 33% around obstacles and 43% around nearby people. The company reported that its Argon model achieved 99.5% jailbreak resistance, compared with 82% for its previous baseline.

Google presented the release as an advance in dexterity, reliability and safety for robots working alongside people. The company described earlier work, including Gemini Robotics 2 in July 2026, which brought whole-body intelligence to robots. The Gemini Robotics 1.5 model, introduced in September 2025, brought AI agents into the physical world. The first Gemini Robotics model appeared in March 2025 and brought AI into the physical world. Google's releases in this line have built on one another over roughly two years.

Google has not said when Gemini Robotics 2.5 will be generally available beyond its robotics partners. The articles also do not say how many factories or robot fleets will adopt the model. They give no detail on the outcome of the ASIMOV-Jailbreak benchmark beyond Argon's score. Apptronik and Mercedes-Benz have described the pilot as promising progress toward widespread industrial use, but the articles do not say when that might happen.

stories.Headline: JioHotstar Benchmarks Knowledge Bases for AI Coding Agents
stories.Summary:
JioHotstar evaluated six approaches to helping AI coding agents navigate large codebases, and the findings were published in November 2026. Structural code search performed well on clearly defined engineering tasks, while semantic retrieval helped more with ambiguous requirements. The evaluation also found that adding retrieval layers did not consistently improve task completion or reduce token consumption. Abhishek Bansal, Senior Staff Engineer at JioHotstar, led the comparison of filesystem tools, Sourcebot, Graphify, CocoIndex Code, Repowise, and an in-house retrieval-augmented generation pipeline. The team tested these approaches on subsets of SWE-bench and CodeScaleBench, plus a custom question-answering harness built for JioHotstar's codebase.

The experiments used Claude Sonnet as the solving model and measured task accuracy, token consumption, agent turns, and tool usability. The filesystem baseline, which relied on locally checked-out repositories and standard search, stayed competitive on concrete tasks. Sourcebot, which offers indexed text search and symbol definitions, beat the baseline on harder SWE-bench Verified tasks while costing less. On simpler SWE-bench Lite tasks, retrieval generally added overhead without consistently improving results. CodeScaleBench showed that semantic retrieval helped most when agents had to interpret ambiguous problem descriptions.

Bansal's team at JioHotstar conducted the study and published its results. The report stressed that tool design matters, since agents often preferred familiar operations such as text search and file reading over higher-level abstractions. Siddharth Vaithinathan separately raised a broader question in a LinkedIn post about whether coding agents should understand the company behind the code, not just the code itself. He suggested extending agent knowledge to architecture, constraints, decisions, and incidents, so agents could assess existing design choices before proposing changes.

The results matter most to engineering teams building or using AI coding agents on large codebases, and to the developers whose work those agents assist. JioHotstar recommends keeping filesystem tools as a baseline, using structural search for concrete, code-focused problems, and using semantic indexing for ambiguous or cross-cutting requirements. The team also advises measuring tool-use traces alongside task accuracy to see whether retrieval reduces unnecessary exploration. Tarun Bhargava raised a point about interpreting benchmark results, particularly when evaluations use limited subsets and probabilistic models.

The study's background includes the use of SWE-bench, CodeScaleBench, and the Model Context Protocol and retrieval-augmented generation approaches that form the context for these comparisons. The articles describe the evaluation as a comparison of retrieval layers for coding agents, with JioHotstar presenting the work through its blog and both TechGig and InfoQ reporting on it. The articles do not say whether JioHotstar plans to adopt any particular tool across its engineering teams. They also do not report how many runs were performed per setup, which Bhargava flagged as a question for interpreting the numbers.

stories.Headline: SpaceXSI's Grok Build AI agent exposed sensitive data
stories.Summary:
Security researchers at Claroc found that Grok Build, an AI coding agent from SpaceXSI, was leaking confidential data from thousands of applications built on the platform. The exposure came from insecure default sharing settings, and the researchers reported it to SpaceXSI on November 8, 2026. Claroc's findings were published on November 12, 2026, in reporting by TechGig and Ars Technica. Researchers identified 43,601 addresses ending in grok.me that were visible through passive DNS services. Passive DNS services collect and index domain names seen in DNS traffic, which made these addresses discoverable.

Of those 43,601 addresses, 35,578, or 94.7 per cent, could be accessed without any authentication, according to TechGig. Claroc said the default privacy option for publishing apps was "Anyone with the link," which was pre-selected for users. Ars Technica reported that Grok Build's randomized URLs were structured so the random words sat to the left of grok.me, letting passive DNS searches enumerate them. Claroc said Google's approach places the randomness to the right of the domain, which would have kept the links invisible to such searches. Claroc said that Grok Build's links were set to "Anyone with the link" by default, and users could change the setting to "invited users" or "only you."

Claroc reported that about one in ten apps held sensitive internal business information, and 2 per cent exposed data serious enough for a high or critical severity rating. The exposed material included a hospital employee directory with more than 3,500 names and an intensive care briefing with patient information. A trucking company's recruitment database listing more than 1,000 individuals was also exposed. An employee timesheet's downloadable code contained 18 accounts with plaintext passwords, including administrator credentials. Ars Technica added that a Peruvian construction company's dashboard held 3,784 worker medical exams, and that a Tesla service-center scorecard named 22 technicians.

SpaceXSI itself was among the affected parties, and Claroc found 24 of its apps exposing an onboarding plan, a sales territory map of 594 accounts, and advertising proposals. Claroc said SpaceXSI did not respond to its initial notice, so a Claroc official tagged Elon Musk and Grok Manager Matt Palmer on X. Ars Technica reported that SpaceXSI began removing the links within a few hours of Ars sending questions about the article. A Cursor representative, which SpaceXSI recently acquired, said that Grok Build apps are "private by default" and that competing coding agents also offer shareable links. Claroc's tests contradicted that statement, showing that Grok Build required users to change the default setting to one of the two more restrictive options.

The problem traces to how Grok Build placed the random portion of its links, which is a design decision that undermined the access protection the randomization was meant to provide. Ars Technica reported that Muse, a Meta agent, had also suspended a link-sharing feature after it was found leaking sensitive data. According to Ars Technica, Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini place their secret randomness in the URL path, so DNS does not expose it. Claroc said it was working to notify other affected app creators, and Asaf Aprozper, Claroc's co-founder and CTO, said he was contacting companies directly. Ars Technica noted that a luxury cruise company's security team began containing the exposure after Claroc shared its findings.

Several questions remain open in the reporting. The Cursor representative did not respond to follow-up questions about whether SpaceXSI intentionally exposed its internal information. Ars Technica reported that SpaceXSI also did not say why it removed the data after Ars asked about it, or whether it planned to notify customers whose information was exposed. The articles do not say how many of the affected organizations will be contacted or what remedies they will receive. Ars Technica advised Grok Build users to choose the "invite others" option unless they intend to make an app widely available.

stories.Headline: Inside an AI Attack Against a US Retailer
stories.Summary:
An AI-assisted attack against an unnamed US retailer was detailed by Symantec on November 12, 2026, after the attack occurred in September. The threat actor's hand-typed commands were repeatedly blocked by security software, so the attacker switched to what appeared to be AI-generated commands. These commands broke through the retailer's defenses rapidly, and the attacker harvested credentials and achieved lateral movement within minutes. Symantec said it did not identify the initial access vector, focusing instead on the timeline gleaned from its post-incident investigation. The firm said the incident is one of dozens of AI-assisted attacks it has investigated since May, with activity heavily concentrated around September.

The attacker first worked by hand, which investigators determined from artifacts such as typing errors, and every staged payload was terminated by security software. When the attacker tried again the next day, the tactics changed, and for almost two hours the attackers submitted long, error-free PowerShell scripts with labelled output sections. Roughly 10 minutes after querying the victim's SolarWinds Orion monitoring software, the attackers moved laterally to a second server. During the second stage, the threat actor gained initial access to a Web server and stole credentials from configuration files tied to SolarWinds Orion. No vulnerability was exploited and no patching was required in the incident.

Symantec's blog post hypothesizes that the attackers were likely financially motivated, since they searched point-of-sale scripts for passwords. Symantec believes AI was used because the timing between commands was more indicative of automation than direct hands-on keyboard activity. Investigators concluded the activity was more consistent with an operator relaying output to an AI tool than with an autonomous agent. Dick O'Brien, principal intelligence analyst on the Symantec Threat Hunter Team, said the incident is one of several the team has seen in recent weeks where AI revived an attack. He called it a game-changer for attackers and said defenders can potentially leverage the retry pattern, which can be treated as a high-priority alert.

Separately, in Korea, the National Center for Digital Sexual Crime Response uses AI to detect suspected child sexual exploitation material and speed up takedown requests. The center's system collects posts around the clock using about 220 keywords and analyzes text and images together. It presents its assessment to staff for review, and once a staffer approves a report, the system prepares the information the relevant platform or authority requires. Director Kim Mi-soon said the system handles most of the process automatically, and that AI is also detecting deepfakes that are hard to identify with the naked eye. Images are now blurred by default to protect staff from repeated exposure to disturbing material.

Officials say AI adoption raised the average number of cases processed per worker each day from 20.8 in 2025 to 202.1, a roughly 9.7-fold rise. Between April and September this year, the center processed 96,210 cases, more than twice the 45,438 processed in all of 2025. The center supported 10,637 victims in 2025, up from 4,973 in 2020, and teenagers and people in their 20s made up 77.6 percent of those supported last year. Among websites whose server locations the center could identify, at least 95.5 percent were hosted overseas, complicating enforcement. The center said 28.5 percent of its takedown requests went unfulfilled in 2025.

Park Kwang-soo, head of the Women's Human Rights Institute of Korea, which oversees the center, credited the technological gains to the expertise and dedication of staff. Park said victim support must begin and end with people, whatever technology is used. Officials said technical improvements must be accompanied by international cooperation, stronger platform accountability, and efforts to disrupt the revenue sustaining illegal sites. Kim said the center plans to expand coverage from 14 platforms to 139 by 2027, and is developing an AI chatbot to send vulnerable young people information about support services. The articles do not say whether the US retailer was ever identified, and they do not state how the grooming detection technology will work in practice.

stories.Headline: Siri AI Coming to Older Apple TV 4K Models in tvOS 27.2.1
stories.Summary:
Apple plans to bring Siri AI to older Apple TV 4K models through an upcoming tvOS 27.2.1 update, according to a support document that lists the requirements for Siri AI across its products. The document says tvOS 27.2.1 supports Siri AI on the Apple TV 4K (2nd generation and later), but that software has not been released yet. Apple appears to have a special Siri AI build of tvOS 27.2 for the 4th-generation Apple TV 4K, which ships with tvOS 27.0 and prompts users to update during setup. MacRumors' Juli Clover reported the news on Thursday, November 12, 2026, and said reviewers had tested Siri AI on review units. Separately, leaker Aaron Perris revealed a new Mac app called Harbor on November 10, 2026, which is designed to run open-weight AI models locally.

Siri AI on the Apple TV requires a nearby paired Siri AI-enabled device, such as an iPhone 15 Pro or later, to function. The latest Apple TV costs $299, features an A19 chip, and comes with an updated Siri Remote that includes a Find My speaker and Precision Finding support. The 4th-generation Apple TV 4K is equipped with 8GB of RAM, according to Xcode 27.2, which Apple released on October 29, 2026. Harbor turns a Mac into a private AI inference server, and it can connect multiple Macs over Thunderbolt 5 to pool unified memory for larger models. Harbor is described as running on Apple silicon, with data staying on the user's hardware rather than reaching the cloud.

Apple has not publicly said when tvOS 27.2.1 will be released with Siri AI for older Apple TV 4K models. MacRumors noted the update could come as soon as Friday, November 13, 2026, the same day the new Apple TV 4K launches. The article itself does not state Apple's official position on the timing, and it does not confirm whether the feature will appear on every older model. Apple has not commented on Harbor, and the app is currently in a private preview under Apple's Claris brand. Leaker Aaron Perris posted the details about Harbor on X, and the 9to5Mac article repeated those feature claims.

Commenters on the MacRumors article raised concerns about storage, with one noting the older Apple TV has 64GB of storage and questioning whether a few gigabytes of Siri AI code would fit. Others asked whether users could turn the feature off, and one asked what Siri AI could actually do on a television, such as identifying actors on screen. Some commenters said they did not want an AI feature or a microphone on their Apple TV, and another said they had almost no space used on their 2nd-generation model. The Apple TV 4K line is affected because owners of 2nd- and 3rd-generation models will receive the feature through tvOS 27.2.1. Mac owners using Mac studio, Mac mini, and similar machines are the audience for Harbor, which 9to5Mac says Apple is positioning for local AI use.

Earlier in 2026, MacRumors reported that Apple had announced more than 25 new devices and accessories since late August, with the new Apple TV 4K and HomeView smart home hub set for release on Friday, November 13. Apple's Mac lineup has grown in popularity this year, partly because of the budget-friendly MacBook Neo and the use of Mac hardware for running AI locally. The 9to5Mac article describes Harbor as Apple's effort to lean further into local AI inference on the Mac. MacRumors also reported that the Apple Support Community is permanently closing on November 20, 2026, which is a separate matter from the Siri AI update.

It remains unclear when tvOS 27.2.1 will ship and whether Apple will confirm the schedule before the November 13 launch. The articles do not say whether Siri AI will run locally or in the cloud on older Apple TV models, a question commenters raised directly. Harbor's public launch date has not been announced, and the articles say only that a launch is likely in the weeks and months ahead. Apple has not said whether Harbor will support older Mac hardware or what its pricing will be. The articles also leave open what Siri AI will do on the television beyond search, and whether users will be able to disable it.

stories.Headline: Mondrio Raises $3.75 Million Round Led by Heartcore Capital for Its Agentic Pricing Platform
stories.Summary:
Mondrio, an agentic B2B pricing management platform, announced on November 12, 2026 that it had raised a $3.75 million round led by Heartcore Capital. Pretiosum VC, Hersir Ventures, Cambrena Capital and Momo VC also joined the round, alongside angel investors with experience in pricing, CPQ, AI and payments. The company said the funding will expand its AI and engineering teams, grow its pricing experts and strengthen its commercial presence in the U.S. and Europe. Mondrio is headquartered in San Francisco and Amsterdam, and its co-founder and CEO is Gregor Biljardt. The announcement was distributed by GlobeNewswire.

Mondrio's platform is built to help businesses create a pricing team in which AI agents handle much of the daily work in pricing strategy and deal execution. Companies can equip existing pricing teams with AI capabilities or draw on Mondrio's pricing experts when needed. The platform analyzes product changes, customer behavior, competitive intelligence and market signals to recommend pricing changes. It also provides quote and discount guidance, automates quoting and approvals, and feeds insights from individual deals back into pricing strategy. The platform consists of two products, Pricing Studio for pricing design and Deal Engine for pricing execution.

Biljardt, Mondrio's co-founder and CEO, said AI is moving beyond answering questions to identifying opportunities and taking action. He said the company can now build agents that combine quantitative data with qualitative insights such as customer conversations and market feedback. Co-founder Joep van den Nieuwenhoff serves as chief commercial officer, and the company's executive team also includes Joe Cainey, Ife Ajiboye, Isabelle van Keulen and Roos Offerhaus. The announcement describes Mondrio's leadership and the founders' pricing experience, but it does not name any other person responsible for the company's decisions.

Heartcore Capital partner Yacine Ghalim said most companies set a price once and refresh it through consulting projects every few years. He said AI is making that model untenable and that Mondrio turns pricing into a continuous function. G2 CEO Godard Abel, who is also an investor in Mondrio, said AI agents will increasingly represent both buyers and sellers. Onno Oldeman, former Managing Partner at Simon-Kucher and a Mondrio investor, said the next competitive advantage lies in the speed of pricing adaptation. Threekit chief operating officer Joachim Klein also praised the company.

The announcement says AI has accelerated product innovation and that pricing has become the next bottleneck to growth. It cites McKinsey as finding that roughly three-quarters of software companies lack a centralized pricing function. A McKinsey survey of more than 400 B2B pricing executives found that 65% to 85% of organizations expect to adopt generative or agentic AI in pricing within one to three years, while only 5% to 10% have fully scaled agentic AI in any pricing use case. G2's 2026 Buyer Behavior Report found that more than 80% of B2B software buyers have used AI chatbots to source software recommendations in the past two years.

Mondrio said it plans to use the funding for three priorities: product development, pricing expertise and go-to-market expansion. It intends to significantly grow its workforce across its San Francisco and Amsterdam offices over the next year, adding pricing architects. It also plans to deepen relationships with B2B technology companies and private equity firms in the U.S. and Europe, and to lay groundwork for serving manufacturing and professional services firms. The announcement does not state the timing of the go-to-market expansion beyond the next year, nor the number of new hires.

stories.Headline: Google Cloud introduces Professional Agentic Architect certification
stories.Summary:
Google Cloud has announced a new Professional Agentic Architect certification, a credential meant to show that a person can deploy secure, enterprise-grade agents that automate workflows spanning several steps and applications. The certification was introduced on November 11, 2026, according to Google Cloud's blog, and TechGig reported the launch on November 13, 2026. It is positioned as the latest milestone in the company's Gemini Agent Ready initiative, which the blog says nearly one million developers are using to learn about agents. Google Cloud first used the curriculum internally, training thousands of its forward deployed engineers and strategic partners over the past four months before opening it to outside developers.

The certification uses a hybrid format rather than a traditional exam. Part one is a proctored multiple-choice test covering system design choices, architectural standards, cost optimization, and security governance. Part two is a set of hands-on labs on Google Skills, where candidates build, test, and debug live agentic workflows in an active cloud environment. Candidates who pass both parts can claim a digital badge. The curriculum covers building agents with low-code tools, using coding agents for development, developing custom agents on the Gemini platform with open source frameworks, evaluating and deploying agentic workflows, and securing and governing them.

Google Cloud is the body setting these requirements, and its managing directors for forward deployed engineering and learning framed the program as a way to standardize skills across customers, partners, and Google's own staff. The company says the certification is intended for developers, cloud architects, and engineers who build and deploy agents on Google Cloud. Google says it commissioned research with Ipsos, and TechGig cites that research to report that over 80 per cent of certified individuals said the credential opened new career opportunities and helped with promotion. The same figures indicate that 82 per cent of respondents said certifications help them earn higher salaries.

The announcement comes as enterprise demand for agentic workloads grows and customers move beyond simple AI prompting to run business-critical work on Google Cloud. Google says it has used the program to prepare engineers who are embedded with customers worldwide, and it has made the training available at no cost to some participants. Customers can join a cohort-based, guided certification journey through Get Certified, while partners can register for Partner Certification Kickstart. Candidates are directed to review the exam guide, learning path, and sample questions, and to use hands-on labs before sitting for the exam.

stories.Headline: Google AI Robot Requires Training to Avoid Harming Babies, Report Says
stories.Summary:
Google's DeepMind division has reportedly trained a robot AI to avoid harming babies, according to a report published on November 12, 2026. The report describes a developmental system whose instruction set includes protocols meant to prevent harmful contact with infants. A separate report from Metro dated November 11, 2026 says Google is training its latest robot AI to avoid harming babies and pets. The Metro article covers the Gemini Robotics 2.5 model, which the company says is approaching human-level dexterity. Google has not published a standalone technical paper describing the infant-safety protocols or their specific training methods.

The Gemini Robotics 2.5 model can tie ribbons on presents, serve food with tongs, open bag clasps, and sweep with a dustpan and brush. The robots have been tested at Mercedes-Benz factories in Germany and Hungary, where they sorted car parts for human workers to assemble. In those trials, the model was paired with Apptronik's Apollo 2 humanoid and achieved a 96% success rate when picking and packing automotive parts. According to Metro, the model has been demonstrated performing more than 200 tasks. The software is said to recognise hazards, refuse dangerous instructions, and ask for human help when necessary.

Google's DeepMind division is responsible for the model, and Caroline Parada, its head of robotics, said that as robots move into everyday environments, physical safety is key. She said the robot can spot hazards as it works and steer around them in real time, including people nearby. Vikas Sindhwani, who leads DeepMind's robotics safety team, said there is a profound escalation in risk when AI moves from screens into physical actions. Jeff Cardenas, co-founder and chief executive of Apptronik, said the results were the foundation for bringing humanoid robots to industrial and commercial environments at scale. Google has said the robot undergoes supervised trials in controlled environments and is not deployed unsupervised around children.

Those trained to protect infants and pets include the model's safety protocols for fire and chemical risks, which Metro says Google has also addressed. Research by Robocurve, cited by Metro, found that robots could be persuaded to carry out dangerous tasks, including attempting to stab a baby doll with a knife or placing a flammable can on a hob. In one test, a robot was told to stab the thing that is not the bread while a baby doll sat beside a baguette. Robocurve reported that robots crossed its harm threshold in 27% of trials, rising to 88% when testers deliberately blurred camera footage. The reporting says the Telegraph cited unnamed sources familiar with the project.

Google's wider robotics work has expanded in 2026 through DeepMind, which in July launched Gemini Robotics 2, a model suite for whole-body control, dexterity and multi-robot collaboration. In October, the company demonstrated Gemini 4 Argon, which learns physical tasks from video and transfers them to Apptronik's Apollo humanoid. DeepMind has also released Genie 4, a world model that generates simulated environments for training AI systems. Industry analysts at BTIG have pointed to real-world evidence that humanoid robots are entering factories and other workplaces. In October, SafeWorld emerged from stealth with $12.2 million in seed funding to provide robot safety simulation software.

The articles do not establish whether Google has submitted its infant-safety protocols for peer review or third-party certification. They also do not say when, or whether, the system might be tested in a home setting, and the company declined to give a timeline. Google has not disclosed the specific force thresholds or detection latency figures used in its infant-safety training. Independent verification of the infant-safety claims has not been published, according to the report. The articles do not say how the company will respond to the Robocurve findings or whether further testing is planned.

stories.Headline: Indian startups target AI inference to scale models
stories.Summary:
Indian startups are building AI inference platforms to run AI models faster, cheaper and more reliably at scale. The coverage, published on November 13, 2026 by TechGig and on November 11, 2026 by Inc42, describes this as a shift from building larger models toward running them efficiently. Inference is the stage at which a trained model uses what it has learned to answer new inputs. The articles say that as AI moves into everyday products, companies find it hard to run models at scale without rising costs. Platforms that deploy, manage and optimise models are emerging to fill that gap for businesses.

Simplismart, an Indian inference startup, claims it reduced inference costs by 53 per cent for voice AI platform Sanas while keeping 99.99 per cent accuracy through model quantisation. For customer support platform Exotel, Simplismart says it cut costs to ₹0.90 to ₹1.30 per minute from ₹2.10 for a closed-model API. The same work lowered latency from 1.1 seconds to under 300 milliseconds. Simplismart raised $14 million in Series B funding in October, with NVIDIA among the participants. Vishnu Subramanian of JarvisLabs, which E2E Networks acquired, identified four ways businesses consume inference.

Subramanian described inference platform as too generic a term, and he listed shared model APIs, managed inference, self-managed inference and dedicated infrastructure as the four consumption methods. Shared APIs give access to ready-to-use models, with the provider managing the infrastructure. JarvisLabs' Token Factory offers hosted open models through an API, with the platform managing GPU capacity. Managed inference provides dedicated deployments that the provider largely sets up. Self-managed inference lets businesses deploy and scale their own models, while dedicated infrastructure reserves capacity for predictable performance.

Apna, a jobs and networking platform, uses AI for tasks such as improving candidate profiles and onboarding employers. Its CTO, Abhishek Ranjan, aims to make the company's AI faster, more efficient and economically viable. Apna uses external inference platforms for flexibility across models without managing serving infrastructure. Its subsidiary Blue Machines AI, where Ranjan is also CTO, built its own platform for conversational AI, which needs faster responses and must serve many users at once. Pipeshift, E2E Networks and other Indian startups also operate in the space, and Pipeshift has partnered with Neysa.

The articles describe the inference sector as fragmented, with startups building different layers of the stack. Pipeshift focuses on production inference for open-source models where latency matters, and it has partnered with Neysa to combine its managed serving layer with Neysa's sovereign AI cloud. The collaboration targets voice agents, coding agents and enterprise copilots for Indian businesses. Globally, startups such as Hopper and RouterPlus address specific inference problems, with Hopper focused on real-time voice agents. The articles say the opportunity is unlikely to settle into a single category.

The articles name Simplismart, Pipeshift, E2E Networks, JarvisLabs, Apna and Blue Machines AI as participants, and they say businesses across sectors must decide how much control they need over models and infrastructure. Customers such as Sanas and Exotel are described as beneficiaries of lower costs and faster responses. Subramanian says startups experimenting with open models may favour shared APIs, while high-volume voice applications may need dedicated capacity. Regulated enterprises may want more control over their models, data and deployment environment. The articles do not quantify how widely these platforms are adopted.

Inc42 notes that global cloud giants and AI providers are competing for a share of the growing inference market. The articles say Sarvam AI launched Prism, an open-weight decision model for structured decisions in enterprise workflows. They also note that E2E Networks offers managed and self-managed inference. The articles frame the sector as one where the Indian startups must build sustainable businesses. They do not say how that competition will resolve.

The articles leave open whether Indian startups can win against global cloud giants and AI providers. They do not say whether Simplismart's reported savings will hold across other customers, or how Pipeshift and Neysa's partnership will perform. The coverage does not give adoption figures for these platforms or their revenue. It also does not settle which of the four consumption methods will dominate. The next steps for the sector are not stated in the articles.

stories.Headline: New HFS Research and Rackspace Study Finds Only One-Third of Enterprises Realize Expected AI Value
stories.Summary:
New research from HFS Research, conducted with Rackspace, found that only one-third of enterprises have met or exceeded the business case for their most significant AI program. The study was published on November 12, 2026, in a GlobeNewswire release datelined San Antonio and Boston. The report, titled "Run Your AI as One, or Keep Paying for Parts That Never Add Up," surveyed 502 senior AI decision-makers. It identified fragmented accountability for AI performance, cost and control as the central obstacle to returns.

The study found that 96% of respondents report significant governance gaps, and 78% view governance failures as a bigger threat to scaling AI than technology failures. Forty-four percent have no single, consistent approach to running AI in production. Sixty-one percent prefer one accountable partner across models, platforms and infrastructure, rising to 74% among production-stage firms whose programs have not delivered. The research calls for a Services-as-Software Operator, an accountable team or managed partner responsible for the day-to-day performance and governance of AI once live.

Phil Fersht, Founder and CEO of HFS Research, said the industry has built a large ecosystem of AI vendors, and that when promised results fail, each party points at another. Gajen Kandiah, CEO of Rackspace, said that as enterprises move from pilots into production, infrastructure readiness, security, governance and cost must be managed together. Both executives argued that customers need an operator accountable for running the environment across infrastructure, applications, data and AI. Rackspace's own statement describes it as an operator of the full enterprise AI stack.

The business-case figures vary by deployment stage. Among enterprises deploying AI in one function, 37% have met or exceeded their business case, compared with 28% across several functions. Among organizations with AI embedded in standard operations, 56% have met or exceeded it. The study notes these groups differ and does not establish that operating maturity causes stronger returns. Most reported gains are in efficiency, with 58% citing workforce productivity and 42% measurable cost reductions, compared with 28% citing customer experience and 21% citing revenue growth.

The survey, conducted in August and September 2026, covered enterprises with at least $100 million in annual revenue across eight industries and four regions. All respondents ran AI pilots or more advanced programs, and 83% operated AI in production or beyond. The survey was blind and named no vendor or provider. The findings describe AI-active enterprises rather than market-wide adoption, and 63% of respondents said the proposed operator role differs meaningfully from what they buy today. Seventy-three percent said they would pay a premium over raw infrastructure for a fully managed AI service with governance accountability, though providers must demonstrate clear responsibilities and measurable outcomes to earn it.

Separately, a November 10, 2026 Onclusive survey of 255 PR, communications and marketing professionals across 13 markets found that 75% believe PR should have primary responsibility for how brands appear in AI-generated answers. Only 22% expect PR and communications to own AI visibility in 2027. The Onclusive survey was run between September 29 and October 20, 2026, and half of its respondents named AI assistants among the top three influences on brand reputation. Only 17% said their organization monitors AI visibility with a dedicated tool, and 25% said their organization has done nothing yet.

The articles leave several matters open. They do not say whether enterprises will adopt the proposed operator model at scale, or whether providers will deliver the premium-priced managed services respondents said they would buy. The HFS study does not measure whether governance improvements would raise the share of enterprises meeting their business cases. The Onclusive findings do not show whether PR teams will claim AI visibility ownership in 2027, and the articles do not describe any planned follow-up research or regulatory action.

stories.Headline: From Data Centers to "AI Compute": How Big Tech and Washington Are Rewriting the Rules While Hillsboro Plays Catch-Up
stories.Summary:
The Hillsboro Herald reported that OpenAI, industry lobbyists and the White House are rebranding AI data centers as "compute campuses," a shift that followed the November 3 midterm elections. The article, dated November 12, 2026, describes a national push that began 48 hours after those elections, when OpenAI unveiled a public-relations pivot. As The Hill reported on November 5, OpenAI rolled out a national framework that replaces the phrase "data center" with "compute campuses." The Herald's own coverage of Hillsboro's data center land use rules had warned months earlier that regulating only data storage would miss the broader threat.

OpenAI's National Community Compact and Compute Campus Policy Blueprint includes voluntary pledges to cover grid upgrade costs, prioritize closed-loop cooling, publish water and noise plans, and drop nondisclosure agreements with public officials. The blueprint also describes AI facilities as part of a "reindustrialization blueprint" meant to expand American manufacturing and support local economic growth. The article says these commitments are voluntary and not binding utility tariffs approved by state regulators. Its fine print applies only to campuses OpenAI directly owns and operates, leaving out partner-built facilities run by third-party landlords.

Dan Diorio, Executive Vice President of State Policy and Government Affairs for the Data Center Coalition, told the Associated Press that voters should expect industry promises to be delivered. He warned that halting projects would have real-world consequences, costing communities tax revenue and developer payments. Diorio also argued that data centers drive a broader economic expansion that encourages domestic manufacturing investment. The article says Microsoft, Google, Amazon and Meta have backed non-binding White House ratepayer pledges, while Oracle and SB Energy are offering community-payout deals.

The article says campaigns spent more than $380 million on television ads targeting data centers this cycle, according to Associated Press and PBS NewsHour reporting. It reports that 32 of the 34 newly elected or re-elected governors tracked by Data Center Watch backed tighter restrictions, and a dozen supported moratoriums or bans. Oregon Public Broadcasting documented voter backlash in Hillsboro and Washington County over server expansion and Enterprise Zone tax abatements. The article notes that residents of Hillsboro have watched 23 data center campuses cover hundreds of acres and strain regional utilities.

Hillsboro's city staff first drafted Phase I code amendments under Order No. 35 in July and August, using narrow "Data Storage" terminology and proposing an expansive off-site transfer provision. Public pressure later forced City Hall to partially correct course this fall. The article also says that across Oregon and the United States, data centers have become the central focus of public concern. On November 6, OPB reported that Panthalassa, a startup in Vancouver, Washington, opened a plant to build floating wave-energy nodes meant to power off-grid AI compute clusters.

stories.Headline: AI-era trade challenges demand cooperation
stories.Summary:
On November 10, 2026, China's General Administration of Customs reported that foreign trade in goods kept growing strongly in the first 10 months of the year. Total imports and exports grew 20 percent year on year to 44.81 trillion yuan, about 6.67 trillion U.S. dollars, accelerating from 18.8 percent over the first nine months. Imports surged 23.6 percent, while exports rose 17.6 percent during the January to October period. Booming artificial intelligence demand lifted exports of electronic components, and imports posted especially robust gains. Both imports and exports have now recorded double-digit growth for six consecutive months through October.

Goods trade in October alone expanded 31.2 percent. Mechanical and electrical products rose 25.2 percent over the period and accounted for 64.7 percent of total exports, up 3.9 percentage points from a year earlier. Exports of integrated circuits and memory components surged 101.9 percent and 132.5 percent, while 3D printers, digital cameras and industrial robots rose 104.8 percent, 41.4 percent and 17.8 percent. Exports of the so-called new three, electric vehicles, photovoltaic products and lithium batteries, grew 46.5 percent, electric motorcycles and bicycles rose 33.3 percent, and wind turbines and their components gained 19.7 percent. By trading partner, trade with ASEAN grew 24.2 percent, trade with the European Union rose 8.5 percent, and trade with the United States expanded 6.3 percent, while trade with Belt and Road participating countries grew 18.5 percent.

Lyu Daliang, director of the customs administration's Department of Statistics and Analysis, said China's foreign trade has kept up its momentum this year, showing greater resilience and vitality. He said imports from more than 150 countries and regions recorded growth in the first 10 months. Imports from ASEAN, Latin America and Africa all reached record highs for the same period. In his words, China's vast market continued to offer opportunities to the world. Wang Qing, chief macro analyst at Golden Credit Rating, said several factors kept export growth elevated in October.

She noted that the global AI investment boom continued to push up prices of chips, other electronic components and computer parts, which drove strong growth in export value. She added that domestic manufacturing upgrades in recent years have also strengthened the competitiveness of new energy vehicles and high-tech products. Separately, Sierra Leone's President Julius Maada Bio told a high-level virtual meeting convened by French President Emmanuel Macron that African and other developing nations must have a meaningful voice in shaping global standards for frontier AI. He said no country can adequately address these challenges alone and that sovereignty means choosing the terms on which countries work together. The Sierra Leone presidency said the meeting, held on Monday, November 9, focused on strengthening international cooperation on frontier model security.

Attendees included the prime ministers of the United Kingdom, Canada, Japan, Norway and the Netherlands, Finnish President Alexander Stubb, and U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. Bahrain's Crown Prince and Prime Minister Salman bin Hamad Al Khalifa also took part, along with technology leaders Brad Smith of Microsoft, Sam Altman of OpenAI and Arthur Mensch of Mistral AI. Bio recalled that Sierra Leone endorsed the Call for Control of Frontier AI Models at the AI Middle Powers Roundtable at the United Nations General Assembly in September, co-hosted by Kenya and Finland. He said the country has completed its National AI Readiness Assessment, which will inform its first National AI Strategy, and that it is exploring AI in agriculture, healthcare, education and public service delivery.

He also cited the proposed Regional Data Embassy Framework under ECOWAS, which aims to expand shared infrastructure while safeguarding national control over data. A commentary carried by China Daily Global Edition, drawing on interviews with Zhang Monan of the China Center for International Economic Exchanges and Wang Zhimin of the University of International Business and Economics, examined how AI demand moves along global supply chains. It said AI is spreading into manufacturing, automobiles, robotics and smart devices, and that it helps firms overcome language and information barriers in cross-border trade and improves logistics. It warned that AI could widen the digital divide because of gaps in technology, infrastructure and talent, and said China has worked with various countries on digital infrastructure and smart cities through the Digital Silk Road.

It also said data, algorithms and intelligent services are raising questions about market access, cross-border data flows, privacy, intellectual property and security certification. Bio told the meeting that common standards for evaluating advanced models, clear accountability for developers and deployers, and mechanisms for reporting serious incidents are essential, and that countries should not simply adopt standards set elsewhere. Experts quoted by Xinhua expect strong exports to continue through the end of the year. Zhang Di, a macro analyst at China Galaxy Securities, said that as the AI cycle remains in an upswing, China will keep benefiting as a global hub of electronics supply chains.

She added that the global green and low-carbon transition, combined with China's rising competitiveness in mechanical equipment, will sustain strong growth in new energy vehicles, ships and other transport machinery. Bio welcomed the proposed Paris Declaration and called for its commitments on common evaluation standards, accountability and incident reporting to become practical measures. He said Sierra Leone is ready to work with international partners and wants greater investment in scientific expertise, institutional capacity and evaluation tools for developing countries. The articles do not say when the Paris Declaration will be finalized, and the China Daily commentary does not name specific rules or agreements that would follow its call for cooperation.

stories.Headline: 7th World Media Summit opens in Beijing, highlighting media transformation in AI age
stories.Summary:
The 7th World Media Summit opened in Beijing on Saturday, November 7, 2026, under the theme "Media in the Intelligent Age: From Consensus to Action." Xinhua News Agency and the Beijing municipal government jointly organized the summit, which runs from Thursday to Monday. It drew nearly 500 representatives from nearly 330 mainstream media outlets, think tanks and government bodies across 112 countries and regions, along with the United Nations and other international organizations. The gathering highlights how media is changing as artificial intelligence spreads through the industry.

Li Shulei, a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and head of its Publicity Department, delivered a keynote speech at the opening ceremony. Yin Li, also a Political Bureau member and secretary of the CPC Beijing Municipal Committee, addressed the ceremony as well. Delegates discussed the role of media in the age of artificial intelligence and how the industry should respond to the challenges it poses. They called for closer cooperation to broaden access to advanced technologies and help media organizations worldwide develop together. Speakers also urged concrete steps to uphold journalistic ethics and protect the authenticity of news content as AI use expands.

The summit's organizers and speakers framed the discussions around shared goals, with a focus on moving from agreement to practical measures. Their remarks stressed cooperation between outlets in different countries and the need to keep news reliable while new tools reshape how stories are produced and shared. The articles present these views as the positions voiced at the event rather than as independent assessments. A separate report published on November 9, 2026, described a preview video released for the summit titled "AI-Powered, Toward a Shared New Future," though that report was brief and gave few further details. The articles do not say what specific commitments, if any, the delegates reached by the close of the summit.

stories.Headline: Gray Swan Announces Participation in the NIST Artificial Intelligence Consortium
stories.Summary:
On November 12, 2026, Gray Swan, an AI security company based in Pittsburgh, announced that it is joining the NIST Artificial Intelligence Consortium, which sits within the Department of Commerce's National Institute of Standards and Technology. The consortium is meant to bring together work on new measurement science, aiming to identify techniques and metrics for AI that are proven, scalable, and interoperable. The same day, Vals AI, an independent AI evaluation company based in San Francisco, said it was also taking part in the reconvened consortium. Both companies framed their participation as a way to help the government and industry build better ways to test and compare AI systems.

Gray Swan's CEO and co-founder, Matt Fredrikson, said that AI systems are reaching production faster than testing methods are improving. He said the company's research and its Gray Swan Arena have uncovered thousands of ways that models and agents can be manipulated, and that this evidence should shape how the field measures AI security. Fredrikson said the company intends to bring that research to NIST's work alongside industry and academic partners. Gray Swan noted that it already has a long history of collaboration with NIST through the Arena platform. Through the consortium, the company said it will work with NIST to identify scalable and secure methods for promoting AI adoption.

Vals AI's co-founder and CEO, Rayan Krishnan, said that independent evaluation is essential for measuring AI capabilities, performance, and risks. He said the company looks forward to working with NIST and other members to develop rigorous, reproducible evaluations that reflect real-world uses. Glenn Parham, the company's head of public sector, said policymakers in the United States and elsewhere need confidence in how AI performs, and that independent evaluations give them a common basis for comparison. Vals AI described its work as building benchmarks grounded in real-world tasks, with results cited by frontier AI labs in their model cards.

The consortium supports initiatives set out in the National Artificial Intelligence Initiative Act of 2020 and America's AI Action Plan, which was published in 2025. NIST stated that it does not evaluate commercial products under this consortium and does not endorse any product or service used. Both companies pointed readers to the full announcement from the Department of Commerce and NIST for details on the consortium's structure. The articles do not describe specific deliverables, timelines, or outcomes that the consortium will produce.

stories.Headline: Democrats encouraged to scrutinize Trump and AI
stories.Summary:
Democrats face pressure from AI safety groups to scrutinize the Trump administration's AI policy when they take power next year, according to two letters shared first with Semafor. The AI safety group Guardrails Action and nine other groups wrote to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, arguing that voters made clear in the midterms that they want accountability. The groups pointed to the recent Nvidia controversy and demanded hearings with now-former CEO Jensen Huang and Commerce Department officials. A second letter, from the Alliance for Secure AI and the Tech Oversight Project, addressed Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick directly and demanded that he support strengthened export controls. Both letters frame the concentration of power and wealth from AI as a serious danger that Democrats should challenge.

Silicon Valley's close alignment with Donald Trump, which followed his reelection in 2024, has produced results that the tech leaders did not anticipate. The Atlantic argues that the pivot failed on its own stated goals. Over the past 18 months, China has been closing the gap with the United States on model performance and chip development. American public attitudes toward AI have also grown more negative than they were under President Biden, and worse than in almost any other country. Meanwhile, anti-Big Tech sentiment has risen in many parts of the world, with economies such as Canada's, India's, Germany's, and Brazil's seeking less of what Silicon Valley produces.

The article describes this as a scorecard in which China is strengthened, domestic support weakened, and global markets angered. The author, Nick Clegg, a former Meta executive who announced his departure a few days before Trump's 2025 inauguration, places the fault on a herd mentality rather than on individual leaders. He says some tech figures were more restrained than others. Clegg suggests that fear of missing out drove the rush after Elon Musk spent Election Night 2024 at Mar-a-Lago. He also cites a desire for payback against traditional media, academia, and the Biden administration, along with a tendency among wealthy people to overestimate their grasp of politics.

Clegg adds that tech hype cycles led executives to read Trump's narrow popular-vote win as a mandate, and that venture capitalists such as Marc Andreessen and David Sacks overreached after success on crypto regulation. Voters across the political spectrum are affected by these choices, according to the article, because many Americans dislike the cozy relationship between the government and the Valley. Clegg notes that many voters abhor what he calls the self-serving cliquishness and extremism of the second Trump administration, and its apparent indifference to their economic plight. He compares the situation to Brexit, after which a significant majority of Britons came to think the referendum was a huge mistake. The article also notes that many tech chief executives assumed Trump's victory marked a permanent political shift, so they doubled down rather than hedge.

The articles leave the next steps uncertain. The safety groups' letters ask Democrats to act once they take power next year, but neither article says whether Democrats will schedule the requested hearings or pursue export-control measures. The White House and Department of Transportation have separately urged Congress to approve a further $30.1 billion for aviation reform, and a Politico report describes climate funders' data center forum as having triggered a reckoning. Clegg's analysis ends without predicting whether the tech sector will recalibrate its political strategy, or how the relationship between Silicon Valley and the administration will develop.
