stories.Headline: Public funds ploughing cash into AI will 'own' megatrends shaping economy
stories.Summary:
Sovereign wealth funds and public pension funds are pouring money into artificial intelligence and infrastructure, and a PwC report released on Thursday, November 12, 2026, projects that state-backed investors will reshape the economy. Sovereign wealth fund assets are expected to rise nearly 50% to $22.4 trillion by 2030, up from about $15.2 trillion. Public pension assets are forecast to climb to $36.3 trillion from about $27.6 trillion, and central bank assets to about $20.9 trillion from about $17.3 trillion. The report, which analysed the world's 350 largest public investors, was reported by Reuters and carried by CNBC Africa.

The report says these investors have moved from passive stakes to what it calls principal investors that originate deals themselves and take controlling positions with operational roles. Eric Janson, PwC's global private equity and principal investors leader, said these investors no longer rely only on external managers. Assets are becoming concentrated in a small group, with the top 10 institutions holding about 41% of combined sovereign wealth and pension assets and the top 50 holding 77%. The report says a few dozen large institutions are positioned to set the tone, adding that they will enable, accelerate and own the megatrends shaping the global economy.

In 2025, state investors channelled roughly $66 billion into AI and digitisation, and most of it went to the United States, while flows to China slipped to around $4 billion. The report found Gulf state funds were tilting hard toward the US, pointing to pledges from Qatar's QIA and Abu Dhabi's MGX and ADIA. Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund was an exception, cutting foreign allocations to roughly 20% from a peak near 30% as it shifts toward a domestic focus. The article does not describe any formal rule or requirement that these shifts impose on governments or institutions.

The release was issued by DGEN Technologies Corp., which describes itself as a Vancouver-based technology company. stories.Headline: Forget Nvidia. Anthropic is the AI trade’s litmus test
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, is preparing an initial public offering that could raise as much as $90 billion, with trading expected to start next Thursday. The move comes as Nvidia Corp., the sector's most valuable company, faces a leadership crisis after co-founder Jensen Huang admitted to an affair with a woman that US officials reportedly believe to be a Chinese spy. Bankers are weighing plans to raise the price, and the order book is already multiple times oversubscribed. Chip stocks have steadied after last week's sharp selloff. Traders are betting a successful debut can offset the negative headlines around Nvidia.

The IPO matters because the AI labs have depended heavily on Nvidia to back their computing deals. Huang has championed vendor financing, which supports nascent AI labs and data-center developers. Two months ago, Anthropic signed a $35 billion cloud-computing deal with Nvidia-backed neocloud Lambda, and Nvidia, rather than Anthropic, holds the lease on the data center. Once public, Anthropic could use an at-the-market offering, private placements or convertible bonds to raise money directly. The article says it may not receive an investment-grade rating right away, but it would gain more room with loan bankers if its shares trade alongside other mega-caps.

Asian suppliers are especially exposed. South Korea's SK Hynix, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. and Japanese test-equipment maker Advantest all rely on Nvidia for a substantial share of their sales. If Nvidia's dealmaking slows or financing for computing hits a snag, these firms could be forced to cut their earnings outlooks. The article notes that a financing channel opening for the labs themselves would benefit the whole semiconductor supply chain. For now, investors are giving the AI trade the benefit of the doubt.

The writer frames the listing as a test of whether the sector can rely on public capital markets rather than a few large backers. US-based tech firms have raised at least $220 billion from follow-on equity offerings so far this year, according to Bloomberg data, and companies have been selling convertible bonds throughout 2026. The article argues the AI industry would no longer need its own central bank if public markets embrace a major pure-play frontier lab. It adds that Anthropic must first deliver a smooth public debut before that baton can be passed.

stories.Headline: Rising Ai Costs Leading To Model Swapping Capgemini Finds
stories.Summary:
Capgemini Research Institute surveyed senior executives at large organisations and found that AI spending is pushing companies to swap models for cheaper alternatives. Of those polled, 59% said their AI expenditure had been significantly above expectations or budget, with the overrun averaging 24%. Many are turning to open-weight large language models, which can be up to 15 times cheaper than proprietary models from frontier labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic. Nearly three in five organisations plan to expand their use of open-weight models, according to the findings published on 12 November 2026. The average price gap is smaller than that extreme figure, but tokens for open-weight models still cost 87% less than those for closed models.

Usage data from the LLM platform OpenRouter supports this trend, showing that open-weight models handled 72% of traffic in September but accounted for only 27% of spending. The article suggests this willingness to switch models raises doubts about how durable the competitive advantage of frontier providers is. Their lead over open-weight rivals is measured in weeks or months, and only a small number of use cases need cutting-edge capabilities. The models are also largely interchangeable for many tasks. Capgemini further found that most organisations struggle to see the full financial impact of their AI deployments.

Only about a third of the executives surveyed could estimate indirect costs such as oversight and governance. Half admitted that AI spending had been approved without adequate visibility of full costs or proper consideration of expected business outcomes. Computing's own research found similar concerns, with AI costs rising up IT leaders' agendas as providers stop offering cheap and freemium licences in an effort to recover heavy infrastructure spending. In response, some vendors are building platforms that switch automatically between models based on cost and capability. Rich Radley, VP of field engineering at Databricks, said many customers now realise that a model six months old can perform as well as a frontier model, pointing to the company's Unity Gateway platform.

Databricks' research found that retail organisations are the most likely to use multiple model families, with 83% using two or more. Nagy Nagy, head of data at Compare the Market, told Computing that his AI decisions weigh cost, the match between capability and use case, and the risk of vendor lock-in. He said the company might use a model from OpenAI one day, Anthropic the next, and possibly Kimi as well. The article presents this flexibility as the direction many organisations are moving in.

stories.Summary:
Amplitude, the analytics company, has built a proactive product agent called Wave that helps teams turn product insights into shipped improvements, and an OpenAI article published on November 12, 2026 describes how it works. Amplitude says Wave is roughly 80% powered by OpenAI models, including GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Luna, and GPT-Image-2.5 Flare. Teams give Wave a product area along with the goals and metrics they want to improve. Wave brings together Amplitude data, session replays, customer feedback, and code to identify and prioritize opportunities. When an opportunity is ready, teams can send it to coding agents, including Codex, with a technical plan and acceptance criteria.

Amplitude estimates that Wave can help teams ship product improvements in 1–2 days, down from roughly a month. Wave uses GPT-6.1 Sol for the opportunity manager and deep investigations into code and data. GPT-6 Luna handles frequent, lower-cost tasks such as scanning code and running small evaluation checks. GPT-Image-2.5 Flare generates product mockups using screenshots from session replays as visual references. In one evaluation, GPT-6.1 Sol had a mean model cost of $1.28 per dispatch for the Data Science Agent, compared with $2.63 for another leading model.

Spenser Skates, Amplitude's CEO, said that AI can now find useful work the company never thought to assign it. He said OpenAI's models can investigate a problem, write and run code, and use the results to decide what to try next. Amplitude says it chose its models by evaluating quality, latency, and cost for each task. Skates said OpenAI gave the company both strong reasoning models and smaller, faster models. Amplitude presents the article as an account of its own product work and its own test results.

Amplitude's Jacob Newman, Principal AI Product Manager, described Wave as a unified platform with agents that comb through session replays, analytics, and code to find opportunities. The company tested Wave on its own homepage, where generic suggestion cards were meant to help users start a conversation with an AI agent. In a sample of 100 session replays, 80 users typed their own questions and only 12 selected a suggestion. Wave proposed personalizing the cards and produced a technical plan, after which a coding agent made the change and Amplitude A/B tested it. Eric Carlson, Senior Principal AI Engineer at Amplitude, said the result showed how small, ignored changes can increase feature adoption in unexpected ways.

In the readout Amplitude shared, messages sent through homepage suggestion cards rose 160% relative to control after one day. The article says Wave analyzes session and analytics data and then develops recommendations with a proposed fix, technical plan, and acceptance criteria. Most teams send bug fixes straight to coding agents, while new features and larger bets receive a human review. Among customer-launched experiments, flags, and guides, one in four went live the same day Wave surfaced the opportunity. Half went live in under four days, and two in three went live within a week.

The article says Wave is in beta with customers across industries, and it describes the company as a mid-market technology firm in North America. Amplitude has long helped teams see how people actually use their products, and the article presents Wave as the next step in that work. Amplitude's evaluation of GPT-6.1 Sol for the Opportunity Investigator found a model cost of $1.34. The article reports that GPT-6.1 Sol scored 4.06 out of 5 overall, compared with 3.62, 3.52, and 2.94 for three alternatives. It also had the fastest median investigation time, at 54 minutes.

Skates says the ambition with OpenAI is to make self-improving products the way companies build software. He expects teams to delegate more investigation and implementation work to agents as OpenAI's models improve at reasoning and coding. Amplitude says agents are already finding and delivering improvements in its own product while the team works on other priorities. The article does not say how many teams are using Wave or what changes will come with a general release. It also does not describe how the results will hold up outside Amplitude's own homepage and evaluations.

stories.Headline: AI is turning Apple’s app review process into a nightmare for developers
stories.Summary:
AI-generated apps are overwhelming Apple's app review process, leaving iOS developers waiting weeks for approval. An estimated 10 to 20 new iOS music apps reach the market every day, since AI lets anyone vibe code their own apps and AUv3 plugins. Developers say the review process has become erratic, with some apps stuck in review or rejected even after appeals. The articles describe this as a nightmare for many developers, who face months of delays on work they have spent months building.

To publish an iOS app, a developer must join the Apple Developer Program, which costs $99 per year. Every app, whether a synthesizer, effect, game or utility, must pass Apple's review, which checks that the app meets requirements including security standards. Apple's App Review guidelines say the process works around the clock and typically reviews at least 50% of submissions in less than 24 hours and 90% in less than 48 hours. Before the surge, submission to release took 24 to 48 hours, and sometimes a few days. Developers say the typical review took a day or two.

Apple's App Review process is the body that reviews these submissions and decides on rejections. The articles do not quote an Apple statement on the delays, so Apple's position is not given. Developers who have been affected describe automated rejections that they say do not respond to their explanations. The articles also note that Apple has not directly answered appeals made to the App Review Board.

Several developers, including AudioThing, Igor Vasiliev, Sugar Bytes and others, say their new apps have been stuck in review for weeks with no updates. Pittsburgh Modular released its Microvolt 3901 synth as a VST on October 27th, but the iOS version arrived only on November 12th, despite a planned simultaneous release. Unfiltered Audio's Sinusoidal Run Rhythm was rejected four times, and Michael Hetrick said Apple seems to be using AI for automated reviews. The app is now out in audio-only form, while its MIDI version is still unreleased. Marek Dendes's CRUX Synth has been rejected four times, and he says he has had no real help from his contacts at Apple.

The articles report that the delays hit cross-platform releases and livelihoods hardest, since developers planned simultaneous launches and some have spent months on their apps. One developer, Igor Vasiliev, saw his HollowTone app stuck in review for weeks. AudioThing's Materia took 25 days to be approved after one rejection, and its Seconds, made with Hainbach, has been in review for 29 days and counting. Some developers say their enthusiasm has faded and that they doubt things will return to how they were. A commentator also argues that the loss of music-app coverage since Apple ended its affiliate program has left small indie developers without advertising budgets.

The articles describe the iOS platform as a place where developers have long built music tools, and they note that media outlets focused on music apps have largely disappeared because the work was no longer financially viable. Apple ended its affiliate program years ago, which the articles say left media outlets unable to cover iOS meaningfully. Written coverage of iOS music apps is now rare unless the apps come from major names such as Roland, Korg or Moog. The articles also say the flood of new apps has made it harder for good apps to get noticed.

The articles do not say whether Apple will change its review process or how quickly the backlog will clear. It is also unclear whether the stuck apps, including CRUX Synth and Sinusoidal Run Rhythm's MIDI version, will be approved. The articles do not state whether Apple has responded publicly to the developers' complaints. It remains open whether Apple will reach out to iOS developers in person again, as the articles say it did early on. More to follow.

stories.Headline: AI Comic Drama Boom: Why Ordinary People Get-Rich-Quick Dreams Can’t Ride the Trend
stories.Summary:
The AI comic drama boom has drawn many ordinary people toward get-rich-quick hopes, but the articles say the reality is far harsher. Feedback from practitioners shows that playback revenue for AI comic dramas has fallen sharply since the start of this year. A company head told China Newsweek that revenue per 10,000 views fell from over 100 yuan to 30 to 50 yuan by May. Creators are now warned that the trend does not guarantee profit, even as promotional messages keep promising quick success.

DataEye Research Institute reported that 221,900 new AI dramas and comic dramas were launched on Douyin in the first half of this year. Only 1,055 of them exceeded 100 million views, about 0.48 percent of the total. Using 50 million views as a break-even reference, DataEye counted 2,886 works, roughly 1.3 percent. Individual creator Xingyu Shinyo said her 12-episode work cost 1,715 yuan to make and earned only 19.64 yuan after one month. Its revenue was 3.97 yuan per 10,000 views.

Fu Peng, an economist with Xinhuo Group, said nearly all AI comic dramas had suffered losses over the past three months. He estimated that buying traffic accounts for 80 to 90 percent of total cost when creators promote their own work. Computing power adds about 10 percent, and the final profit left for the project is only about 5 percent. He likened creators to digital tenant farmers working for platforms, arguing that AI has not changed the platforms' bidding and revenue-sharing logic.

Fu Peng's cost figures apply mainly to self-funded promotion, and the articles note that they do not fully match platforms such as Fanqie. On the Changdu platform under Fanqie, creators deliver finished films after obtaining IP authorization, while distributors choose products, pay for traffic and share revenue based on promotional conversion. Hongguo's latest policy, announced on November 12, sets a minimum guarantee of 15,000 yuan for S-level AI scripts, none for A-level scripts, and no cooperation for B-level scripts. Xiaoguogege, creator of The Little Carpenter from Anhui, said his low-end drama earned 1.5 yuan per 10,000 views while high-quality work earned 12 yuan.

Pan Luan, a media practitioner, advised that people with experience in shooting, editing, self-media or novel promotion could try the field on a small scale, while those without such experience should not join blindly. Zhang Hansheng, chief planner of Travel to Song Dynasty with Weapons, said AI equality only means equal access to models, not an end to creative barriers. He warned against selling AI comic dramas as a course that makes money easily. The articles report that Xiao Tianle, a junior at Soochow University, earned over 3 million yuan, but his team produced hundreds of comic dramas in under a year, with only one real hit.

Training institutions promote AI comic drama courses priced from 9.9 yuan to tens of thousands of yuan, often claiming zero-foundation mastery within three days. The articles say basic tool operation differs from producing works independently, which requires long practice. Investment promotion providers sell franchises, production systems and computing power packages. Entertainment Voice reported that a Hubei consumer paid 59,800 yuan to a Jinan network company for a regional agent system, which turned out to be public internet resources. Some intermediaries recruit creators under the banner of platform orders and then pass production costs and rework risks down through layers of subcontracting.

stories.Headline: WorkBuddy & Codex Drive AI Competition to Task-Centric Delivery: Reliability as the Non-Negotiable Hard Threshold
stories.Summary:
WorkBuddy and Codex are pushing AI competition toward task delivery, where reliability has become a hard threshold, according to an article published by 36Kr on November 12, 2026. The piece, drawn from a WeChat article by the Yiou Think Tank with author Zhu Luman, argues that the evaluation unit of AI office work is turning into a task that can be checked and accepted on completion. It contrasts asking an AI to explain how to make a business analysis with asking it to read sales tables, calculate metrics, generate charts and deliver a report. The article says users now judge products by whether the task is completed, not only by whether the answer is excellent.

The article describes WorkBuddy as a product that treats local file operations, autonomous planning and result delivery as core capabilities. In an official practice example for business analysis, users supply an Excel or CSV file, specify metrics and time ranges, and the product reads the data, performs statistics and generates charts or reports. Codex, first released in 2025, handled code reading, command execution and test runs, and in June 2026 OpenAI disclosed that knowledge work such as reports, spreadsheets, presentations and research analysis had been added. In August, OpenAI opened Codex's execution loop as an integrable Harness that other applications can use.

The article attributes these developments to product teams and their platforms rather than to a single new model. Tencent's WorkBuddy page and OpenAI's Codex materials are cited as the sources describing these capabilities. The article argues that a "domain expert" label on a task does not by itself show an independently trained vertical model, since professional capability can come from general models, task descriptions, materials, tools and execution control working together. Its authors present model specialization as only one of several implementation methods.

The article reports that general models have grown better at following instructions, handling long documents and calling tools, which reduces the need for separate processing logic per task. It traces the technical context to 2018 early GPT research on pre-training followed by fine-tuning, to GPT-3 in 2020 completing tasks from in-context descriptions and examples, to 2020 RAG research adding external retrieval, and to a 2024 Berkeley BAIR summary of "composite AI systems." It notes that RAG, fine-tuning, workflows and agents developed in overlapping periods rather than replacing one another. The article also says that Dify added a Human Input node in March 2026 and that Salesforce's Agentforce documentation separates deterministic logic from model reasoning.

Those affected include enterprise users whose contracts, inventories and business records change daily and cannot wait for retraining, and developers choosing between retrieval, training and workflow design. The article states that the choice between retrieval and training depends on whether a shortfall comes from missing information or from unstable task performance. It adds that long tasks lasting dozens of minutes, with file changes and tool failures, need systems that track completed steps and resume after errors. Anthropic's engineering practice for long-running tasks, using progress files and version records, is cited as one approach.

The article points to research on reliable agents, including Nature's Paper2Agent and Science's Biomni, which it says focus on runnable, verifiable systems. It also cites a 2026 ICML study of 15 models that found recent capability gains produce only small reliability improvements. The article concludes that a single accuracy figure cannot capture repeated runs, input changes and failure consequences, and that task quality, repeated-run performance, manual review and total cost should be observed together. The articles do not say what specific products will ship next or how competitors will respond.

stories.Headline: Viral Hit Game Gets AI-Plagiarized Just One Week After Exploding in Popularity
stories.Summary:
Jade Scratch Scratch, a mobile-style game from Sleepless Game Studio, went viral after its Demo was released on May 16, 2026. Within days, the game's creator, Penpen, saw its core gameplay copied. By May 20, a pirated version had appeared on the market, and the copying spread further over the following months. Developers say AI tools are making such copying faster and cheaper than ever.

According to the articles, copying works through two methods, both driven by AI tools. Some copiers obtain a game package, feed it to AI to reverse engineer, and reproduce a near-identical copy. Others need only a trailer or gameplay video, which AI can use to rebuild the game through Vibe Coding. Copies often appear on Douyin, Google Play and Roblox as mini-games. In October this year, over 41% of the more than 7,100 games at Steam Next Fest were marked as AI-assisted, and 28% were fully AI-generated.

Penpen says the studio's submitted entry was uploaded to a game jam platform as a downloadable package, so anyone could access its source code. The organizer cannot protect every game's data, and the team lacked time to add protections during the tight schedule. Developer Jupiter the Sorcerer says small teams can only add minor obstacles, and that the effective defense, moving core logic to a server, is costly and requires ongoing maintenance. Penpen has called on others to stop joining game jams.

Developers say the threat reaches far beyond one studio. Indie developer Liangshui, a former programmer, said he extracted a game model with ChatGPT in about ten minutes in June. Jupiter estimated that a two-hour AI session cost between 55 and 60 US dollars, or about 5 dollars with a subscription. Liangshui said a team of seventy or eighty people usually needs nine to ten months to build a game, while one person using AI may need no more than a month. Liangshui now releases only demonstration videos, not demos or trial versions.

Penpen's studio has tried to protect its rights through platform reporting, which he describes as complicated and slow. Proving ownership on Douyin required company qualifications, ownership proof and release screenshots, a process of about two weeks. The studio applied for software copyright, which takes a month, but a pirate's registration came through only one day after its own. Copiers often replace art and music after a takedown request, and on Steam a pirate filed a counter-notice demanding a lawsuit in the United States.

Developers affected include Penpen's Sleepless Game Studio, Freya Holmér, creator of a Tetris variant, and the makers of Escape the Walls and Bills Must Be Paid. Anthropic tried to restrict Claude's Opus 5.5 and Claude Code tools from reverse engineering old games, but many developers reported that the limit also blocked legitimate users. Chinese copyright law protects expression but not ideas, methods or gameplay, which judicial practice often classes as ideas or systems. The articles say Penpen's studio cannot afford tens of thousands of yuan in litigation fees, and that the studio's future remains uncertain. It is not clear whether the Steam lawsuit will proceed or whether pirated copies will be removed.

stories.Headline: AI Pinpoints Pathogenic Cells from DNA – Google AlphaGenome 2 Unlocks New Drug Targets for Diabetes and Cancer
stories.Summary:
Google DeepMind has released AlphaGenome 2, a new-generation model that predicts how DNA mutations act in specific cell types and which genes they affect. The model is presented as a way to trace the root causes of diseases and find more accurate drug targets for conditions such as cancer and diabetes. The announcement was reported by 36Kr on November 12, 2026, with the Chinese outlet QbitAI listed as the original source. The model was trained on data from 68 types of tissue and more than 107 million cells, covering both human and mouse cells. In a test covering 28 types of immune cells, its recall rate for identifying key causal variants reached 30 percent, compared with 16 percent for the previous generation after fine-tuning with single-cell data.

Its ability to judge whether a variant strengthens or weakens gene activity rose from 23 percent to 43 percent. The article says the model can adapt to new single-cell data without retraining and can predict DNA methylation. Google CEO Sundar Pichai framed the work around the idea that cells share the same DNA blueprint but read it differently, so a variant may matter only in one cell type. The article also quotes Sarah Teichmann, a professor at the University of Cambridge and co-founder of the Human Cell Atlas Consortium, who praised the model's ability to work with small numbers of cell samples.

The piece presents these statements as enthusiasm about the tool rather than as independent validation of its clinical value. In one example, the article says James Lee's team spent a year and a half of experiments to link a DNA variant in a "gene desert" to over-activation of the ETS2 gene in intestinal immune cells, linked to inflammatory bowel disease. According to the article, AlphaGenome 2 reproduced the key finding through calculation in about half an hour. The model is available for non-commercial research through an API and an interactive Colab tutorial, and Google plans to add it to its Agent toolbox and to Google Antigravity as AlphaGenome 2 Skills.

Articles.Title: AI Pinpoints Pathogenic Cells from DNA – Google AlphaGenome 2 Unlocks New Drug Targets for Diabetes and Cancer - 36Kr

stories.Headline: How Founders Select Top Experts for AI Transformation: Avoid Treating Tool-Only Users as Core Leaders
stories.Summary:
Founders undergoing AI transformation often make a hiring mistake: they hand operational problems to an AI-savvy hire and expect that person to solve everything alone. An article published by 36Kr on 13 November 2026 used an example from a private gathering in Hangzhou on 23 October, where an AI transformation expert named IS described an e-commerce owner who hired a skilled IT specialist. Every time that specialist tried to schedule a meeting with business leads, they ignored him. When asked what AI meant to the company, the owner said it was a matter of survival, and IS pointed out that the survival task had been given to someone on the job for only two months. The article argues that many founders, including those with annual revenue of hundreds of millions to over a billion yuan, fail to set priorities or define responsibilities.

Another AI transformation expert, XD, described a project that started before the 618 shopping festival, when the company needed more advertising creatives. The existing shooting and editing team had limited capacity and inconsistent quality, and expanding it would have required more hires and spending. XD's team included himself as operation lead, internal and external content experts, and a dedicated AI junior specialist. Their workflow covered analysing data, grading creatives, and generating scripts and storyboards. After a week or two, the process still failed because no one oversaw the links between steps, such as whether the AI understood the product and its differences from competitors.

XD personally re-ran the workflow, breaking each step into human inputs, AI outputs, and the standards results had to meet before moving on. Creatives meant to build product awareness were judged differently from those meant to drive conversions, and humans decided which metrics applied. Hard-to-edit materials were assigned to humans and easy-to-edit ones to AI. One night at about 11 PM, XD told the execution team group that he had worked out the full feasible workflow. During the 618 festival, the workflow reportedly raised advertising ROI by about 25 percent and increased creative supply by about 30 percent without additional headcount.

XD also granted performance exemptions during the trial period and prepared incentives in advance. Creatives that underperformed in ad delivery were not penalised under the old assessment rules, while good results were to be rewarded. The article notes that many business owners overlook this, since employees exploring new workflows must carve time from existing work while old performance indicators still apply. A founder asked XD whether the boss must personally validate workflows, and XD answered that consultants with on-ground implementation capability can run one or two projects first, but the founder must set overall strategy, select the first task, allocate resources, and resolve cross-departmental conflicts. The article states that organisational problems are often mistaken for a lack of talent, and that companies need different talent at different stages.

The article's authors, identified only as the contributor 张美吉 and the 36Kr platform, state that the views belong to the author and that 36Kr provides only information storage services. They recommend pairing people with rich business experience, who make judgments, with fast learners and strong doers, who deliver results, rather than loading every requirement into one "AI lead" role. They also suggest that companies with annual revenue between 100 million and 3 billion yuan reassess their teams to identify who can set standards, run workflows, and lead the original team. The article says such hires should be measured by whether they have delivered tangible results and whether their methods can become capabilities the company keeps. The article does not report any response from the e-commerce owner, and it gives no further details on how the new roles would be structured or how their results would be measured over time.

stories.Headline: AI Computing Power Rent-Collecting Business: Undergoing a Transformative Sea Change
stories.Summary:
Zhou Yong, a computing power landlord with tens of billions of yuan in orders, began reaching out to key clients after the end of the second quarter of this year to strike a rarely seen deal. He replaced a long-standing fixed cabinet rental fee for GPU computing power with a revenue-sharing scheme tied to the call volume of AI Tokens. Economic Observer reporters interviewed several upstream and downstream enterprises in the computing power industry chain and found that many service providers had adopted similar practices. Some providers cut the fixed service fee by about 10% in contracts while raising the Token revenue share by more than 200%. Public information showed that during this year's "Double 11" promotion, top live streamers sold nearly 100,000 large model Token monthly cards in half an hour.

Under the new model, the guaranteed minimum fee is cut, and the excess Token output above an agreed threshold is divided according to an agreed proportion. In one example, a customer's annual rigid computing power spending of about 120 million yuan falls to 108 million yuan. Zhou Yong's company calculated that if the customer's inference call volume rises steadily, its annual comprehensive income could rise by 20% to 50% over the original fixed rent scheme. If call volume stays below baseline for a long time, however, its annual revenue could drop by up to 10%. The arrangement has been piloted since the first quarter of 2026 between leading domestic providers and large model and Agent application makers, and it has not yet reached small and medium-sized customers or training orders.

Zhou Yong said the change amounts to a reconstruction of the internal revenue structure of long-term orders, in which the provider gives up part of its fixed return in exchange for a share of the downstream inference growth. Wang Daowei, head of Token business at a listed South China provider, said his company now includes share clauses in new contracts. One project type uses MaaS joint operation profit sharing, with the provider supplying computing infrastructure and the model maker supplying model capability, while another type sells Tokens directly with an annual guaranteed minimum plus pay-as-you-go billing for overseas orders. Wang Daowei added that more than one peer is running similar pilots, though their degree of disclosure varies. Customers gain lower upfront rigid costs, while providers gain a deeper binding to the customer's business.

Customers are shifting toward enterprise Agents and industry large models, whose call volumes are growing quickly, while general casual chat grows more gently. A procurement head at a leading cloud vendor said this demand shift is pushing customers to reduce upfront fixed costs and pushing providers to share the benefits of inference growth. The person in charge of computing power at a leading large model company said his firm runs a hybrid architecture, with its own cluster handling stable core work and external computing power for elastic expansion. A business person at a leading domestic AI chip maker said assessment now focuses on how many Tokens each hardware unit actually outputs and the cost of a single Token. A bank financing manager said such projects carry notably higher risk than ordinary manufacturing, so banks raise risk premiums and demand combined credit enhancement.

The articles leave open how widely the sharing model will spread, since Wang Daowei said it is not yet at a comprehensive inflection point and predicted traditional long-term rental will still dominate ordinary customers and training businesses. They also leave open whether hardware output will meet expectations, because the chip iteration cycle runs about 1.5 to 2 years while accounting depreciation may reach 3 to 4 years and commercial life is often shorter. Zhou Yong said shared revenue depends on the delivery and acceptance of computing power units and customer activity, and that risk is shared in both directions. The bank said its first repayment source is downstream real business cash flow, though the articles do not say how banks will weigh these factors in practice.

stories.Headline: Absurd "Made in India" AI Model Exposed as Repackaged Qwen3.5: Huge Fiasco Uncovered, Even Forcing AI to Claim "Originates from India"
stories.Summary:
The Indian AI company 169Pi released Alpie Seed 9B on November 8, a multimodal reasoning model with 9 billion parameters. It accepts text, image and video input, supports a 262K context window, and was promoted as able to run offline on workstations, laptops and smartphones. The company presented it as a new achievement for India's AI research field, timing the promotion around the Diwali festival. Shortly after release, developers examined the configuration files and found that the model's base was Alibaba's Qwen3.5-9B.

The model's architecture, tokenizer vocabulary and weight structure were found to be highly consistent with Qwen3.5-9B. The team reported using supervised fine-tuning with DoRA, adjusting parameters such as the attention layers and feedforward networks. A second stage used GRPO reinforcement learning across seven reward dimensions, including answer correctness, hallucination penalty and answer length. That stage ran on 8 NVIDIA H100 GPUs for 3,034 training steps, consuming about 3,472 GPU hours. The Chat Template also contained an identity_policy instruction telling the model to say it was developed by 169Pi and came from India.

Developers who criticized the project argued that the identity prompt was a deliberate attempt to present the model as Indian-built. Netizens on X, including a user identified as "Dongxi NLP," said the model was effectively a tribute to Qwen3.5-9B. Some commenters said open-source fine-tuning was acceptable but that the original authors' work should be acknowledged. Others argued public criticism was too harsh, since many startups fine-tune open models and such post-training work has its own value. The debate centered on whether the project can fairly be called independently developed Indian technology.

Independent developer Satyajit published a technical analysis on November 9 comparing the Safetensors files of both models. He sampled and compared all 760 tensors and ran full hash verification and value-by-value decoding on some of them. His results showed that Alpie Seed retains the original Qwen3.5-9B architecture, and that parts such as the visual encoder and word embedding layer remain unchanged. The changes were concentrated in some attention layers and feedforward networks, so the parameter share actually altered was not high. His article concluded the model is a post-trained derivative, not a foundation model trained from scratch in India.

On November 9, 169Pi issued a statement admitting that Alpie Seed was developed from Qwen3.5-9B and not pre-trained from scratch by its team. The company acknowledged the contributions of the Qwen team and the open-source community, and said it had not sufficiently highlighted the model's origin in earlier promotion. It said its work focused on post-training and engineering optimization, and that running a multimodal 9B model on CPUs, laptops and phones required substantial engineering. 169Pi said it would clearly mark the technical origin in future introductions and was exploring developing its own foundation model. The model is released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Whether the company will change the identity_policy prompt or remove the India-origin claims from the model was not reported in the articles. The articles also do not say whether 169Pi plans to build its own foundation model or when that might happen. How much the post-training work improved Alpie Seed's benchmark results over Qwen3.5-9B is not addressed. The articles do not report any formal response from Alibaba or the Qwen team. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Absurd "Made in India" AI Model Exposed as Repackaged Qwen3.5: Huge Fiasco Uncovered, Even Forcing AI to Claim "Originates from India" - 36Kr

stories.Headline: CopilotKit Releases OpenBot 1.0: An MIT-Licensed, Self-Hostable AI Coworker With Built-In Governance
stories.Summary:
CopilotKit released OpenBot 1.0 on November 9, 2026, an agent workspace published under the MIT license that can be self-hosted. The company positions it as an alternative to vendor-locked AI coworker products, letting customers choose their own models, agents and infrastructure. Every action a Bot takes is checked against a policy before it runs. The release was reported by MarkTechPost on November 12, 2026.

Each Bot runs inside its own container with a dedicated Chromium browser, its own logins and files, and access only to the tools a user has granted. Every browser click, file write, tool call and component passes through a single gateway that evaluates a CEL policy and writes an audit record before acting. Deny rules take precedence over allow rules, and a malformed rule causes the action to be refused rather than permitted. The workspace supports single sign-on through Google, Microsoft Entra and Okta, along with SAML and OIDC, plus SCIM sync for users and groups. Administrators can set per-Bot tool grants, approval routing for sensitive work, spend limits, and a full audit trail with SIEM export.

CopilotKit, the team behind the AG-UI protocol, is the party responsible for the release. The article says the company designed the product so organizations keep control of their data and rules instead of ceding them to a vendor. The article also states that the platform supports eight agent frameworks listed on the company's site, including Claude Agent SDK, OpenAI Agents SDK and LangChain, and several more in the repository. For models, teams can use OpenAI, Claude, Gemini or Grok through existing subscriptions or API keys, as well as open models such as Kimi, DeepSeek, Qwen, Nemotron and Mistral.

For companies, the platform deploys through a single Helm chart onto AWS EKS, Azure AKS, Google Cloud GKE or any Kubernetes cluster. Personal use is free and runs locally. The business tier, OpenBot for Business, costs up to $29 per active user per month, with a 5% charge applying only to model spend above $5,000 per month. An Annual plan adds air-gapped deployment and 24/7 support, and forward-deployed engineers help teams roll it out. Early access is listed for iOS, Android, Slack and Microsoft Teams, and the article gives examples such as support ticket triage, expense review and operations workflows.

Articles.Title: CopilotKit Releases OpenBot 1.0: An MIT-Licensed, Self-Hostable AI Coworker With Built-In Governance

stories.Headline: Can Nvidia’s Self-Developed Protégé Become the Savior of AI Trading?
stories.Summary:
After a sharp selloff in AI computing stocks, CoreWeave, a U.S. computing power rental company, released its third-quarter 2026 financial report after U.S. market hours on November 10, Eastern Time. The report showed revenue of 3.66 billion U.S. dollars, up 168% year on year, and the company raised its full-year revenue guidance. Global AI computing stocks rebounded sharply on November 11 after the release. The Nasdaq had fallen 5.3% in October and dropped another 5.52% on November 5, its largest single-day decline since April 2025.

The report's figures exceeded earlier guidance in several areas. CoreWeave's revenue rose by more than 1 billion U.S. dollars from the previous quarter, above the top of its guidance range. Adjusted operating profit reached 379 million U.S. dollars, against a guidance range of 200 million to 260 million U.S. dollars. The company raised full-year revenue guidance to 13 billion to 13.3 billion U.S. dollars. Its on-hand orders were about 132.5 billion U.S. dollars as of the end of September 2026, up 138% year on year.

CoreWeave's chief executive, Michael Intrator, said on the conference call that computing power demand is growing faster than the industry can deliver the infrastructure. He said the effective demand the company receives equals ten times the capacity it can offer before the end of 2027, and that capacity through 2027 is almost sold out. Intrator argued that AI is spreading across industries faster than new computing capacity is entering the market. CFO Nitin Agrawal said cash flow from existing customer contracts is enough to repay the corresponding debt.

Analysts and investors reacted to the report in different ways. A communications analyst at a South China brokerage told the Economic Observer that revenue and profit both beat market expectations. That analyst said the report gave a clear boost to sentiment after computing stocks had fallen for more than a month. Market participants still hold differing views on whether CoreWeave can become the savior of the AI trade. The stocks most affected include CoreWeave, NVIDIA, Zhongji Xuchuang and Eoptolink, and South Korean and Chinese Taiwan markets also rose.

The selloff followed a run of negative news from early October. OpenAI's reported annualized revenue of about 50 billion U.S. dollars was below earlier expectations of nearly 70 billion. Free cash flow at Amazon, Alphabet and Meta was negative in the third quarter of 2026. CoreWeave's debt was close to 47 billion U.S. dollars at the end of September, and some of its bond yields rose above 16% in early November. The Democrats won control of the Senate and House on November 3, and UBS estimated that about 30% of new U.S. data center capacity expected by 2028 could be affected by possible construction suspensions.

The articles leave several questions open. It is unclear whether CoreWeave's demand and pricing trends will hold, since the company said prices are still rising after entering the fourth quarter. It is also unclear whether the expected 9 billion U.S. dollars in customer prepayments and deposits over the next three months will arrive as planned. CoreWeave said it would not raise funds through the unsecured bond market at current yields. The articles also do not settle whether computing power is overbuilt, and they note that the next customer-linked loan is expected to cost 7% to 7.5%.
