stories.Headline: Chinese AI Project Scouts Spies in Taiwan Chip Industry
stories.Summary:
The Chinese government is reportedly running an AI-powered Big Data mining program that tracks ethnic Chinese people abroad, according to documents leaked to the China watchdog NetAskari. The report was shared with Dark Reading and Sky News UK ahead of publication on November 12, 2026. In some cases, the program has helped design influence operations aimed at high-ranking individuals in the artificial intelligence industry. The articles say the system scrapes social media and public sources, feeds the results into machine learning algorithms, and produces intelligence for officials in Beijing.

Its main purpose appears to be influence operations, both at home and abroad, run by the United Front Work Department. The leaked material includes a report titled "Profiles of Ethnic-Chinese Leading Talent in the Chip Field, Their Circle Characteristics, and Work Recommendations." That report names executives of the Taiwanese AI company Skymizer, high-performing students at a top Taiwanese research university, and an AI research center director at Microsoft. It also recommends using non-official groups such as hometown associations, alumni associations and professional societies to build relationships with these people. The system generating the reports is called the Overseas Chinese Affairs Big Data Platform, and it is housed in a 500-square-meter Big Data laboratory at Jinan University in Guangzhou.

The articles attribute the program to the Chinese Communist Party and its United Front Work Department, which the leaked documents describe as the body behind the platform. NetAskari's analyst described the platform as a worldwide dragnet that uses open source intelligence and Big Data analysis to find potential collaborators and affiliates. The analyst said the goal is extending the Communist Party's influence abroad and creating a China-friendly environment in other nations' political, economic and social settings. The articles say the platform scrapes Instagram, Facebook and X, along with Weibo and WeChat, with the scrapers run on machines located in foreign countries behind rotating proxy networks. The leaked document says this obfuscation is meant to prevent the collection system from being traced and discovered.

The analyst said the concern reaches beyond the Chinese diaspora, arguing that the operations could affect ordinary citizens in the United States and Europe even if they have no personal ties to China. The articles say the people targeted may not know they are being singled out by a foreign state. The analyst described the expansion of such work as made possible by remote methods that do not depend on a physical presence abroad. The articles also note that many of the affected people are ethnic Chinese working in the semiconductor and AI industries.

The articles place the program within a broader context of Chinese state activity against the chip industry. On November 8, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang emailed his staff admitting to an affair with Alice Huang, a Ministry of State Security agent whose activities were separately exposed. The articles say Alice Huang redirected Nvidia semiconductors to China, where they are banned, and passed intelligence from the CEO to the Communist Party. The articles describe the United Front Work Department as taking a less dramatic approach to breaching Taiwan's semiconductor industry. They also say that the leaked documents contain only references from 2021 about how machine learning and natural language processing fit into the system.

The articles leave open whether modern large language models have been added to the platform, and they do not say how far its reach extends beyond the documents seen. They also do not report any response from the Chinese government or from the named companies and individuals. What happens next is unclear from the articles, which offer no details on further disclosures, investigations or policy steps. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Daylight Lands $80 Million for AI-Powered Security Operations
stories.Summary:
Israeli-American cybersecurity startup Daylight has raised $80 million in a Series B funding round, bringing its total funding to $120 million. The round was led by Goldman Sachs Alternatives' Growth Equity, with additional support from Okta Ventures, Bain Capital, Craft Ventures, Vintage Partners, and Maple Capital. The article was published on November 12, 2026. The company was founded in 2024 and has headquarters in New York and Tel Aviv. Daylight has built Aura, an AI-native platform that hunts for, analyzes, and contains cyber threats in real time.

The platform combines AI automation with human expertise to build, run, and customize agents that handle daily security operations according to each customer's workflows, risks, and priorities. Customers can choose a fully managed service, a co-managed arrangement, or support from forward-deployed engineers. Daylight also covers the AI platforms organizations use, offering protection against prompt injection, risky MCPs, and rogue AI-driven activity. CEO and co-founder Hagai Shapira said that as AI agents become more capable, they will change how threats are detected, investigated, and contained, with expert security engineers governing and improving those operations. He described the company's model as one that pairs the speed and scale of AI with the judgment and oversight of human experts.

Shapira said the company is building the foundation for a new era of security operations. The article does not name any other person as responsible for the funding or the platform. The company plans to use the new money to speed up platform development, expand its security and technology teams, grow its presence in the United States, and enter new markets in the EMEA and APAC regions. The article places the funding within a wave of similar security startup rounds it links to, including Bay, which raised $50 million to control what enterprise AI agents can do. The article does not say what the next steps or timelines are beyond these plans.

Articles.Title: Daylight Lands $80 Million for AI-Powered Security Operations - SecurityWeek

stories.Headline: IDC InfoBrief | Sovereign AI for Insurance
stories.Summary:
This is a thin story: a marketing page for an IDC InfoBrief on sovereign AI for insurers, dated 12 November 2026, with no reported event, named official, or regulatory change beyond the brochure itself. The page is published by NTT DATA, which promotes the InfoBrief and its AI Factory offering. The article states that a new IDC InfoBrief explores how sovereign and private AI can help insurers scale AI securely across underwriting, claims, fraud detection and compliance. It also notes a webinar held on 3 November 2026. The brief is described as covering how insurers can move AI from pilots to production while protecting sensitive data and keeping governance, explainability and regulatory compliance in place.

The page lists four topics: transforming underwriting and claims with secure AI, strengthening fraud detection while protecting sensitive data, building trust through explainability and auditability, and scaling AI with AI Factory approaches. The article does not name any requirement, deadline, dollar figure or percentage, and it does not name an IDC analyst. The only attribution is to IDC research and to NTT DATA as the publisher. Responsibility for the content rests with NTT DATA, which hosts the page and offers the download form, and IDC, whose research is cited.

The page presents the material as guidance and invites readers to request the InfoBrief by filling in a contact form. It does not describe any findings or conclusions in detail, so the claims about what the research shows cannot be verified from this text. Related items listed on the page include an agentic AI blog post from 14 October 2026, a 2026 global AI report for insurance dated 9 June 2026, and a report on fast-tracking insurance from 3 September 2026. stories.Headline: Unstructured Data Governance: A missing foundation for agentic AI at scale
stories.Summary:
Enterprise data governance has long centered on structured data such as tables, fields, models, lineage, quality rules, access controls and ownership. NTT Data published an article on 10 November 2026 arguing that generative and agentic AI are now pushing organizations to govern unstructured content too, including documents, presentations, emails, contracts, policies, conversations, images, audio and video. The article frames this as a missing foundation for agentic AI at scale. It says much of an enterprise's knowledge and context lives in this unstructured material, and most of it was never created or managed with AI consumption in mind. The core governance principles still apply, but the question has shifted from whether an employee can open a document to whether an AI system can discover, interpret, combine and use it.

The article says the governance capability stack must expand as information moves from rows and columns to documents. Cataloging becomes repository discovery and content inventory, while profiling extends to OCR, transcription, parsing and multimodal inspection. Classification grows to cover topic, entity and sensitivity detection, and lineage extends to documents, chunks, embeddings and AI responses. Data quality adds readability, structural integrity, semantic consistency, extraction accuracy and relevance to the intended AI use case. The article also describes a continuous operating model with four stages: visibility, understanding, control and qualification, and activation through search, analytics, RAG, assistants and agents.

The article is an NTT Data publication and does not attribute its arguments to a named individual, so responsibility rests with the company. NTT Data says it has worked on assets and accelerators built around this problem, which evaluate unstructured content across semantic quality, visual and structural quality, and compliance and risk. These produce a quantitative assessment and a disposition that acts as an AI-readiness gate. The company describes its Company Brain concept as a persistent enterprise context layer that brings together data, knowledge, business meaning, decisions, policies and operational context. The article states that it promotes NTT DATA's AI services and provides contact and career links.

The article's audience is enterprises that are deploying generative and agentic AI, and it says those organizations face risks if unstructured content is poorly governed. It warns that outdated documents, conflicting versions, permissions not carried into AI retrieval, missing semantics and absent provenance can each lead agents to reason over the wrong context or expose information users could not access directly. It notes that a chatbot retrieving an incorrect policy may give a wrong answer, while an agent using the same policy could start a workflow, modify a system or recommend an action. The article identifies organizations that connect the largest number of documents to an LLM as less likely to succeed than those that turn information into trusted, governed and machine-usable context.

The article offers no sales figures, adoption statistics or survey results, and it does not name any enterprise customers or independent experts. It does not report any specific incident, regulatory action or legal requirement that prompted the piece. It does not specify how the AI-readiness gate or the Company Brain is priced, deployed or measured. It also does not state what tooling standards, if any, exist across vendors for carrying permissions into embeddings and retrieval indexes. Those points remain unaddressed in the article, which ends by inviting readers to learn more about NTT DATA's AI services.

stories.Headline: NTT develops physics-based AI to improve robot handling of variable loads
stories.Summary:
NTT, the Japanese telecom company, has developed a physical AI technology that lets robots predict possible load collapses and dropped objects before they carry out a task. The initial application planned is automated airport baggage handling. According to the article published on November 12, 2026, the technology is still in its early stage. The system relies on a world model that pairs a video generation model with a proprietary physics control adapter. It estimates physical properties of objects, including their position, orientation, velocity and mass.

It then applies equations of motion to forecast how those objects will behave during different handling motions. The article's full details on the specific figures and thresholds are behind a registration wall, so they cannot be reported here. The article attributes the work to NTT and does not name individual engineers or executives. It describes the company as the developer and presents the technology as a way to make robots more reliable when the loads they handle vary in weight and shape.

Beyond the airport baggage use case, the excerpt available does not say what other applications NTT intends to pursue. The available text does not describe competing efforts, prior results, a timeline for commercial deployment, or any next steps beyond the planned airport trials. Readers seeking those details would need the full article. This is a breaking story based on limited available text, so more to follow.

stories.Headline: ServiceNow (NOW) Expands AI Operations Reach With New Autonomous Solution
stories.Summary:
ServiceNow (NYSE: NOW) and Kyndryl have widened their partnership to launch an AI-powered autonomous operations solution. The new offering pairs Kyndryl's managed infrastructure expertise with the ServiceNow AI Platform for automating IT operations. It is now available to enterprise customers through the ServiceNow Store. The announcement was reported by Simply Wall St on November 12, 2026. The article presents the launch as a partnership expansion rather than a standalone product release.

The solution runs Kyndryl Bridge data through the ServiceNow AI Platform and gives customers predictive issue detection and automated fixes. According to the article, this positions ServiceNow as a control layer for complex IT environments rather than only a helpdesk tool. The launch aligns with the company's push into agentic AI workflows. The article also notes that more AI agents acting on live infrastructure raise exposure to AI platform security flaws. Competitors, including Microsoft and other ServiceNow partners, sell their own automation offerings.

The article names ServiceNow and Kyndryl as the parties behind the expanded partnership, and it does not attribute any direct statement to either company's executives. The piece is written by Sasha Jovanovic, an equity analyst at Simply Wall St, and it frames the deal as a test of the broader AI thesis for ServiceNow. The author describes the main requirement for that thesis as continued growth in AI annual contract value, security and risk workflows, and mid-market products. The article also cites a $157 fair value estimate for ServiceNow and mentions the integration of Armis and Veza as an additional factor. Those figures come from the publisher's own narrative tools, not from the companies.

The article does not give any financial terms, pricing, deal size, or timeline for future releases of the solution. It also does not describe what, if anything, the companies plan next beyond general availability through the ServiceNow Store. The piece ends by framing the investment question as whether the existing ServiceNow story about AI-driven workflows and security at scale is credible. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Shares of AI cloud operator Nebius drop 16%+ despite strong quarterly results
stories.Summary:
Shares of Nebius Holdings NV, an artificial intelligence cloud operator, fell 17% on November 12, 2026, after the company released its third-quarter financial results. The results themselves beat expectations, with adjusted profit and revenue both coming in above forecasts. The drop was attributed in part to a full-year forecast that came in below the consensus estimate. Some reporting also suggested the sudden departure of Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang may have contributed, since Nvidia is an investor in Nebius.

Nebius raised its full-year capital spending guidance to $27 billion, which CNBC reported is $4.15 billion above what Wall Street had expected. Its plan to invest between $40 billion and $45 billion in data centers next year also exceeded the consensus estimate by a wider margin. The spending is linked to a shift away from colocation facilities, since about 90% of the company's infrastructure is currently in rented data centers. The next 2 gigawatts of computing capacity will be mostly powered by data centers the company operates itself. Nebius also expects full-year revenue at the low end of its $3 billion to $3.4 billion target range, below the $3.37 billion analysts expected.

Founder and Chief Executive Officer Arkady Volozh said the company remains focused on building a healthy, profitable business for the long term. He said Nebius will keep investing in capacity and infrastructure, in its platform and products, and in its team. The company swung from a $100.4 million adjusted loss a year earlier to a $90.9 million adjusted profit, or 31 cents per share, against analysts' expected loss of 69 cents per share. Revenue rose 517% year over year to $980.8 million, well ahead of the $907.5 million consensus.

Growth was driven partly by Token Factory, a service for running open-source AI models that launched a year ago and is nearing a "multi-hundred-million-dollar run rate." Nebius signed $12 billion in contracts in the three months ended September 30, including multiyear deals with Snowflake Inc. and Databricks Inc. The company uses customer prepayments to finance data center projects, and says prepayments received in the quarter exceeded capital expenditures. That ratio is expected to decline as data center spending ramps up. For 2027, Nebius forecasts revenue of $12 billion to $13 billion.

Articles.Title: Shares of AI cloud operator Nebius drop 16%+ despite strong quarterly results - SiliconANGLE

stories.Headline: Nebius Crashes 20% as Jensen Huang Shock Rocks AI Stocks: One ETF Is Having a Field Day
stories.Summary:
Shares of Nebius Group fell nearly 20% on Thursday, November 12, 2026, while the Tradr 2X Short NBIS Daily ETF (NBIZ) rose roughly 39%, making it the day's top-performing fund. The sell-off followed weaker-than-hoped forward guidance from Nebius and a broader wave of selling across U.S. AI infrastructure stocks. That wave was triggered by the sudden resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on the same day. The article describes NBIZ as a leveraged vehicle designed to deliver twice the inverse of Nebius's daily performance.

Nebius reported third-quarter revenue of $980.8 million, up 571% year over year and above analyst estimates of about $907.5 million. Even so, the company cut its 2026 revenue guidance to $3 billion to $3.2 billion, trimming the top of its earlier $3.4 billion forecast. The revision followed delays in bringing some third-party data center capacity online, now expected in the first half of 2027. Nebius also raised its 2026 capital expenditure forecast to about $27 billion, up from $20 billion to $25 billion, with spending projected at $40 billion to $45 billion in 2027. The company still expects 2027 revenue of $12 billion to $13 billion and aims to reach pre-tax break-even by year-end.

The article attributes the earnings disappointment to Nebius itself, while linking the broader sell-off to Huang's departure from Nvidia. It notes that Nvidia's strategic and financial ties to neocloud companies made its leadership change a concern for investors. Shares of CoreWeave fell sharply and IREN also came under pressure, according to the article. The piece presents these moves as a reaction to uncertainty about the sustainability of AI infrastructure spending rather than as an explanation given by any company.

The article points out that NBIZ targets twice the inverse of Nebius's daily return, not its cumulative performance, so over several sessions its returns can diverge from a simple doubling of the inverse move. Management reportedly said customers are already seeking computing capacity for 2028. The article also notes that Nvidia ETF holdings are now being scrutinized because of Huang's exit. Beyond that, the article does not describe any further steps.

stories.Headline: Nebius Bets $40B on Customer-Funded AI Cloud Expansion
stories.Summary:
Nebius, the former Yandex cloud unit, is pushing ahead with a $40 billion AI infrastructure expansion that relies on customer prepayments and loans instead of traditional equity or bond sales. The plan was reported in an article published by The Tech Buzz on November 12, 2026. Delays at a Microsoft data center project that Nebius is involved with have already raised questions about the approach. Shares of the company tumbled 10% just days before the report after it delivered disappointing 2026 guidance. The company is betting that the capital crunch hurting its competitors can be avoided.

The neocloud model asks GPU clients to pay months or years in advance for capacity that does not yet exist. Nebius takes that cash, secures additional loans against the guaranteed revenue stream, and then orders Nvidia H100 chips and builds facilities. The articles say Nebius has not disclosed which customers are providing prepayments or how much of the $40 billion will come from loans versus advance payments. The company also announced news of a massive capital expenditure surge alongside its weak guidance. The expansion would be roughly ten times larger than anything the company has attempted before.

Nebius is the company responsible for the expansion, and the articles report that it is pursuing this financing strategy. The company's pitch to investors is that customer prepayments are a more sustainable funding source than debt markets, which can freeze during downturns. The articles report that the company's logic is that it does not depend on bond buyers or venture capitalists if it already holds the customer's money. Nebius has not publicly addressed the Microsoft data center delays in the articles. The articles present its strategy as a bet that critics are wrong or premature.

Tesla CEO Elon Musk warned of "guppy-level death" for hundreds of GPU providers, which the articles say triggered a selloff across neocloud stocks. Musk argued that most of these companies are too small, too leveraged, and too dependent on a single customer or use case to survive consolidation. CoreWeave, a GPU cloud provider that has used debt-fueled buildouts, has delivered impressive revenue growth but raised concerns about leverage. S&P Global Ratings revised Meta's outlook to negative over worries that AI infrastructure spending is outpacing free cash flow. Customers that pay upfront and any investors holding Nebius shares face the consequences if capacity is delivered late.

The articles say Nebius is a startup that spun out of Yandex less than two years ago. Meta recently announced a $25 billion bond sale to fund its AI infrastructure, and SoftBank is reportedly considering a $50 billion investment in Malaysia for AI and data centers. Hyperscalers have long used capacity reservation agreements to lock in revenue, but Nebius is extending that practice further. CoreWeave has tested a similar model, and Dropbox spent $350 million acquiring Tigris Data to power its AI developer tools. Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon has said investor appetite for AI infrastructure remains strong despite market volatility.

The articles say the outcome will show whether customer-funded AI infrastructure is viable. If Nebius delivers capacity on schedule and keeps prepayment customers satisfied, the model could become a playbook for neoclouds without cheap debt. If delays continue and customers demand refunds, the sector could face a reckoning over growth strategies. The articles do not say which customers are paying in advance, how much of the $40 billion is covered by loans, or how the Microsoft data center delays will be resolved. They also do not say whether Musk's prediction will come true for companies like Nebius.

Articles.Title: Nebius Bets $40B on Customer-Funded AI Cloud Expansion - The Tech Buzz

stories.Headline: How AI tools are quietly reshaping working conditions in hospitals - Association of Health Care Journalists
stories.Summary:
Health care organizations are deploying artificial intelligence tools in a largely unregulated environment, and panelists at the Association of Health Care Journalists' 2026 Fall Summit in Los Angeles warned that the tools could harm clinicians and other workers. The discussion, reported by Farah Yousry and published on November 12, 2026, featured Sukhbir Singh, D.O., a hospitalist and board member of the Union of American Physicians and Dentists, and Mishal Khan, Ph.D., a senior researcher with the Technology and Work Program at the UC Berkeley Labor Center, with Barbara Feder Ostrov, editorial director of Medscape, moderating. Tech companies and health system executives have promised that generative AI, which summarizes clinic visits and writes chart notes, will ease burnout and administrative load. Singh said that promise has not matched daily reality for physicians.

Singh said clinicians must review, correct and sign AI-generated chart notes, which keeps full legal liability with the physician and adds a layer of mental work. He said administrators treat the resulting time savings as efficiency gains, using them to assign larger patient panels and reduce support staff. He also described how electronic medical records track metrics such as patient length of stay, discharge times and physician chart usage, which he called a "productivity ratchet" that keeps raising the bar for doctors. Khan said nurses and other staff face risks from AI tools and algorithms that are often untested and unregulated, and that employers increasingly use data-driven systems that affect wages, working conditions, gender equity and collective bargaining. She cited digital staffing platforms that have nurses bidding for shifts through algorithms that adjust pay based on worker data, and she said some automated sepsis systems can strip nurses of decision-making authority, leading to de-skilling and alert fatigue.

The panelists also described a gap in federal oversight that has prompted action at other levels. Some nursing groups are drafting their own workplace AI "bill of rights," and California has passed a law barring employers from making employment decisions without human oversight, with a forthcoming ban on workplace monitoring in restrooms and on neural data collection. Pending Illinois nursing legislation would bar AI from automating core clinical duties such as triage, care planning and discharge, and other states are moving to make it illegal to advertise AI chatbots as licensed health care professionals. Khan argued that "human in the loop" requirements are insufficient, since clinicians under pressure can turn them into corporate rubber stamps, and she called for new labor standards for the 21st century. The article also lists reading for reporters, including research from MIT Sloan, JAMA Network Open, Annals of Emergency Medicine, the AMA and the OECD, and notes that the full panel recordings are available on the AHCJ website.

Articles.Title: How AI tools are quietly reshaping working conditions in hospitals - Association of Health Care Journalists

stories.Headline: Nebius Deal Prepayments Exceed Capex as Colocation Delays Shift Revenue
stories.Summary:
Nebius Group reported third-quarter 2026 revenue of $980.8 million on November 12, 2026, up 571% from a year earlier. Customers had committed more than $12 billion in contract value since the start of the quarter. Delays at third-party data centers also pushed some expected revenue into 2027. The company's shareholder letter said prepayments on Q3 agreements covered more than 100% of their associated capital spending, up from 50% to 60% in the second quarter. Expected payback on comparable one-to-three-year contracts improved to one year and seven months from one year and ten months.

The core Nebius AI Cloud business made up about 99% of group revenue. Roughly $325 million of the quarterly total was non-recurring revenue from the first phase of an asset-light rollout, in which partners fund capacity using Nebius's architecture and platform. Adjusted EBITDA, a non-GAAP measure, was $465.8 million, while the GAAP net loss from continuing operations narrowed to $37.5 million. Purchases of property, equipment and intangible assets totaled about $7.3 billion, mainly for GPUs, hardware and data center expansion. Because that spending is so large, the improved prepayment terms are central to how the build-out gets financed.

Delivery dates at several third-party colocation sites moved into the first half of 2027, including the remaining New Jersey tranches. Nebius expects to have delivered more than half of the New Jersey capacity contracted with Microsoft by the end of 2026, with the rest due in the second quarter of 2027. The company said the contracts remain in place and affected customers have been informed. Following the delays at DataOne, Nebius is scaling Bloom Energy fuel cells to serve as the site's main power source, and it said its owned sites were on time or ahead of schedule.

As a result, Nebius now expects 2026 revenue at the low end of its $3.0 to $3.4 billion range. Its 2026 capital expenditure forecast rose to about $27 billion from $20 to $25 billion. The initial 2027 outlook calls for pre-tax breakeven in the fourth quarter and $40 to $45 billion of capital spending for more than one gigawatt of new capacity. Management expects customer prepayments and investment-grade asset-backed financing to cover 75% to 85% of that spending. Nebius's 2027 breakeven target therefore depends on turning these commitments into operating capacity on the revised schedules while arranging the remaining financing.

Articles.Title: Nebius Deal Prepayments Exceed Capex as Colocation Delays Shift Revenue - Unite.AI

stories.Headline: Nebius says customer prepayments now cover its AI build-out costs
stories.Summary:
Nebius Group, the Amsterdam-based AI cloud infrastructure provider listed on NASDAQ as NBIS, said in its Q3 2026 shareholder letter, released November 12, 2026, that customer prepayments on contracts signed during the quarter now exceed 100% of the related capital expenditures. That is a sharp change from the prior quarter, when prepayments covered roughly 50% to 60% of associated capex. The company credited better customer terms, including longer commitment periods, larger upfront payments, and higher pricing that tops $25 million per megawatt annually. Nebius also said the payback period on its investments shortened to about 1 year and 7 months, down from 1 year and 10 months in Q2.

The company is spending more, not less. It raised its 2026 capex guidance to about $27 billion and expects $40 billion to $45 billion in 2027, aimed at adding more than 1 GW of new capacity. Most of that future spending is expected to come from customer prepayments and asset-backed financing tied to investment-grade contracts. Q3 revenue reached $980.8 million, up 571% year over year and ahead of analyst expectations, but Nebius now expects 2026 revenue at the low end of its $3 billion to $3.4 billion range, which it attributed mainly to delays in third-party capacity. It projects 2027 revenue of $12 billion to $13 billion, and it has a contracted backlog above $40 billion, including a Microsoft deal valued between $17.4 billion and $19.4 billion.

According to the article, Nebius framed the prepayment shift as a route to relying less on expensive debt and said it targets pre-tax profitability by late 2027. Shares nonetheless fell between 16% and 23% after the report, amid broader sector volatility. The article's analysis notes that the stock reaction reflects the sharp rise in capex guidance alongside the lower end of the 2026 revenue range, and it points to concentration risk given the size of the Microsoft contract within the backlog. Going forward, the article says investors should watch whether prepayment coverage stays above 100% on new contracts, whether third-party capacity delays clear before the 2027 revenue target, and whether the payback period holds, with the late-2027 profitability goal sitting behind all three.

Articles.Title: Nebius says customer prepayments now cover its AI build-out costs - Crypto Briefing

stories.Headline: Nebius shares slide as revenue guidance weakens and AI spending rises
stories.Summary:
Shares of Nebius Group NV, the AI cloud company listed on NASDAQ under NBIS, fell 16% to $130.50 in pre-market trading on Thursday, 12 November 2026. The drop came despite a third-quarter earnings beat, as weaker revenue guidance and higher spending outweighed the results. Revenue rose 571% year on year to $980.8 million, above analysts' consensus of roughly $907 million. The company reported a loss of $0.13 per share, compared with analysts' expectations of a $0.72 loss and a $0.50 loss a year earlier.

Management now expects 2026 revenue at the bottom end of its $3 billion to $3.4 billion guidance range, against analyst expectations of about $3.35 billion. The downgrade follows delays to third-party computing capacity, now scheduled for the first half of 2027 rather than before the end of 2026. The contracts behind that capacity remain in place, which suggests the problem is timing rather than lost demand. Nebius also pushed its annual recurring revenue target, which had been $7 billion to $9 billion by December, back to February, when it now expects more than $7 billion. Its 2026 capital expenditure forecast rose to about $27 billion from $20 billion to $25 billion, and it projects another $40 billion to $45 billion in 2027.

Management attributed the higher spending to capacity for 2027, particularly at its own data-centre sites. The company expects prepayments and asset-backed financing against contracts with investment-grade customers to cover 75% to 85% of its 2027 capital expenditure. It forecasts 2027 revenue of $12 billion to $13 billion and targets pre-tax breakeven in the fourth quarter of that year. Investors are weighing questions about financing needs, possible shareholder dilution and how quickly new infrastructure will produce returns. The articles describe the sell-off as investors looking past the quarter toward execution, financing and profitability risks in the expansion.

Articles.Title: Nebius shares slide as revenue guidance weakens and AI spending rises - Yahoo Finance UK

stories.Headline: Fermi gets $200 million hyperscaler prepayment for 600 MW and ends TensorWave lease
stories.Summary:
Fermi said on Thursday, November 12, 2026, that an undisclosed investment-grade hyperscaler has committed about $200 million up front to advance an initial 600 megawatts of power capacity at Project Matador, its private-grid data center campus in the Texas Panhandle. The customer signed a $200 million prepayment agreement and a $15 million early construction and site development agreement, with capacity beginning in 2027. The two companies are still finalizing a $90 million purchase of structural steel and building materials that Fermi bought in advance. That purchase would let the customer use long-lead materials to speed construction of multiple data center buildings on the site. The deal is not yet a lease, and the parties continue to work toward a definitive long-term lease.

The same release disclosed that Fermi's first announced tenant is gone. Fermi and TensorWave terminated the Data Center Lease and Services Agreement they signed in August 2026, and the AMD credit support agreement tied to it is also terminated. That lease covered 222 megawatts with about $6.5 billion of contracted revenue over an initial 15-year term. Fermi's investor presentation shows the 600 MW reserved for 2027 by a major hyperscaler, out of up to 925 MW it could deliver that year. The release gives no reason for the termination.

Fermi's chief executive, Lee McIntire, said the company's headstart in speed to power is a key reason an investment-grade hyperscaler has signed up for 600 megawatts and committed more than $200 million up front. He said that if Fermi converts its pipeline of prospective customers into leases, it would completely fill its 2.2 gigawatts of current capacity. Fermi said the customer is making financial and development commitments ahead of finalizing a lease because it wants access to power within its delivery timeline. Texas Tech University System, Fermi's landlord, remains committed to the project, according to the release.

Chancellor Brandon Creighton said Texas Tech remains firmly committed to the success of Project Matador. Fermi's third-quarter net loss was $141.6 million, or $0.22 a share, compared with $346.8 million a year earlier. General and administrative expense was $142.2 million, including $65.8 million of non-cash stock compensation and $21.5 million of financial advisory fees settled in stock. Capital spending was $133.4 million in the quarter and $759.5 million over nine months, bringing net property, plant and equipment to about $1.67 billion.

Debt, net, rose to $958.4 million, while cash and restricted cash fell to $315.5 million from $408.5 million at the end of 2025. Fermi has no revenue, and the presentation lists $1.2 billion of financing commitments. In October, AMD signed a credit support agreement backing the 222 megawatt phase-one TensorWave lease, which Fermi called a key milestone toward securing project financing. At that time, the two companies also set a framework for up to 650 megawatts of expansion.

Fermi said then that closing the TensorWave lease and AMD's obligations were subject to conditions. Thursday's release says only that both agreements are terminated, and Fermi still has no binding long-term revenue contract on the campus. Fermi scheduled a conference call for 9 a.m. ET on Thursday to discuss the results.

Articles.Title: Fermi gets $200 million hyperscaler prepayment for 600 MW and ends TensorWave lease - MLQ.ai

Shares of ESDS Software Solution, E2E Networks and other artificial intelligence-related companies in India extended their gains on Thursday, following a sharp recovery in global technology stocks after a recent selloff on Wall Street. stories.Headline: E2E Networks Expands Data Centre Capacity For AI Computing Demand
stories.Summary:
E2E Networks has announced an expansion of its data centre capacity to meet rising demand for AI computing and cloud workloads. The company is adding 12.8 MW of capacity, which will raise its total to 27.4 MW, according to the source alert. The article notes that this figure is not independently verified. Q2 FY27 revenue reached ₹223.8 crore, up 411% year-on-year. EBITDA margin expanded to 76.6% in the same quarter. Q2 FY27 net profit reached ₹72.7 crore, up 32.5% from ₹58.6 crore profit before tax in Q1 FY27. The article links the capacity addition to strong financial momentum over the same period. It describes E2E Networks as positioning itself as a key domestic infrastructure partner for India's AI mission. stories.Headline: What the OpenAI Incident Reveals About the U.S. 'Frontier' Model and China’s Open-Weight Alternative - Monthly Review
stories.Summary:
On October 6, 2026, Sifted reported that the United Kingdom was examining whether training frontier artificial intelligence models could be illegal under existing laws. The article said the question arose because frontier AI development may involve risks that current UK rules do not clearly address. It explained that the legal uncertainty could affect companies working on the most advanced systems. The report did not name a specific incident but framed the issue as a general regulatory problem. It suggested that developers might face legal exposure without clearer guidance.

The October 15, 2026 press release from Alice said that Alice, Inflection AI, and AI21 had collaborated to show that NVIDIA Nemotron open models could be trained for frontier safety. The work used Alice’s safety data to post-train the models for company-specific safety and security policies. The release said the collaborations demonstrated that powerful open models could be aligned to safety requirements without losing capability. It named NVIDIA Nemotron as the model family involved and Alice as the provider of the safety data. The announcement was made from New York and dated October 15, 2026.

Alice said the results showed a path to responsibly deploying customizable AI. Inflection AI and AI21 were described as the partners that post-trained the NVIDIA Nemotron open models. The release stated that the collaborations focused on aligning the models to company-specific safety and security policies. Alice presented the work as evidence that open models can meet frontier safety challenges. No direct quotes from individual executives were included in the press release.

The Sifted article indicated that the UK legal question could lead to new regulatory clarity or enforcement action in the future. The Alice release did not describe any next steps beyond the demonstrated collaborations. Together, the articles suggest that open-weight models are being positioned as an alternative to closed frontier systems. The press release framed the Alice work as a practical demonstration rather than a regulatory response. Neither article stated what specific legal or policy changes would follow.
