stories.Headline: AI in Arbitration: Institutional leaders at Dubai Arbitration Week 2026 discuss how arbitral
stories.Summary:
The Dubai Arbitration Week 2026, organised by the Dubai International Arbitration Centre (DIAC), runs from 9 to 13 November 2026, bringing the global arbitration community together for panels, workshops and networking. During the week, a panel titled "AI Center Stage", hosted by Jus Mundi and Al Tamimi & Company, examined how arbitral institutions are adopting, implementing and regulating AI. The discussion covered confidentiality and data security, how far AI may assist arbitrators, and the need for common guidelines. Dr. Hassan Arab, Regional Head of Dispute Resolution at Al Tamimi & Company, opened the discussion with introductory remarks. Mr. Alexandre Vagenheim, Vice President of Jus Mundi, moderated the panel, which he said would focus on institutions themselves rather than on counsel and arbitrators.

The panel included Mr. Robert Stephen of DIAC, Ms. Dalia Hussein of the Cairo Regional Centre for International Commercial Arbitration (CRCICA), Mr. Khaled Elgarhe of the Qatar International Centre for Conciliation and Arbitration (QICCA), Mr. Arno Janssens of the Singapore International Arbitration Centre (SIAC), Mr. Karam Farah of the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC), and Ms. Khushboo Shahdadpuri of Al-Tamimi. Panellists also considered whether institutions need standards on AI use and how far AI-driven processes could affect the legitimacy of arbitration. Dr. Arab said the use of AI had become an established reality, so the question was how far tribunals and institutions should rely on it. Vagenheim identified three themes: current institutional use, the regulatory framework and convergence of approaches, and future strategies.

Mr. Stephen said case management automation was an immediate application, covering workflow, procedural timelines, notifications and deadlines. He said an integrated case management system could handle an arbitration from registration of a dispute to the final award, reducing repetitive work and costs. He described how arbitrators can receive several differing document bundles from the institution, the parties and the electronic presentation of evidence provider, and suggested a single secure repository would keep annotations confidential. He also said DIAC could cover 16 languages, and that AI could support translation, real-time transcription and natural language search of its website. Ms. Hussein said CRCICA is close to completing case automation, expected to be implemented by the beginning of 2027, and uses AI internally for research, reporting and case statistics.

Mr. Stephen warned that AI raises serious concerns about sensitive information, data breaches and unauthorised access, and said institutions must ensure providers keep infrastructure secure. He cited DIAC's ability to move data to Europe because of recent regional conflicts. Ms. Hussein said CRCICA is still training staff and assessing appropriate use before applying AI to arbitrator appointments, conflict checks and award scrutiny. The panel's discussion is aimed at arbitration users and institutions in the region and beyond, as they face the same questions about confidentiality, reliability and fairness. Dr. Arab noted that the use of AI would continue to generate disputes and legal questions.

Dr. Arab referred to a construction award issued through an AI arbitrator by the American Arbitration Association (AAA), reported by the Global Arbitration Review, and raised doubts about whether such an award would be correct and satisfy the parties. Vagenheim said the AAA has expanded its AI Arbitrator initiative beyond construction to other industry cases involving documentary records. Dr. Arab also cited concerns over undisclosed AI use before the Qatar Financial Centre Court and the Abu Dhabi Global Market. He further mentioned a Dubai Court of Cassation decision upholding a university's rejection of a student's thesis after it was found to contain AI-generated material and fake sources.

The panel's discussion continues through the rest of the week, which ends on 13 November 2026. The articles do not report what conclusions the panel reached on common guidelines or institutional standards. Whether CRCICA's appointment and award-scrutiny applications will proceed, and when, remains open. The articles also do not say whether the AAA's AI Arbitrator initiative will expand beyond its announced scope.

Articles.Title: AI in Arbitration: Institutional leaders at Dubai Arbitration Week 2026 discuss how arbitral - SCC Online

stories.Headline: Why So Many AI Prototypes Never Make It Past the Database
stories.Summary:
Dave Page, CTO at pgEdge and a Postgres Core Team member, argues in an SD Times article published November 12, 2026, that many AI prototypes never reach production because nobody deliberately designs their databases. He recalls starting with PostgreSQL around 1997 at a UK social housing provider, where he was head of IT, and choosing version 6.3.2 so tenants could view rent accounts online without per-user licensing costs. He notes that coding agents and app builders now often provision databases automatically, using default settings wherever a demo runs fastest. Such databases are frequently created without review from experienced DBAs, who must check access, failover, backups and recovery. Page says experienced DBAs were scarce even before agents arrived, so unreviewed databases can outnumber the people qualified to review them.

Page writes that prototypes often fail in production because the database was never built for real traffic, reliability or deployment flexibility. He warns that a region chosen at project creation may not cover where server logs go, since by default Postgres logs statements that trigger errors, including duplicate values in unique constraint violations. Logs can therefore hold sensitive data and be sent to wherever the model is hosted, outside the region the business defined. He says regulated businesses must pay attention to this, while test-data proofs of concept do not. He adds that problems such as poorly designed queries stay hidden until a system holds millions of rows rather than a few hundred.

Page places responsibility on developers using AI agents and says the answer is the same discipline that makes the agents useful. Teams should spend time before any code exists debating the design with the model until there is a spec and implementation plan. Production requirements, such as keeping customer data and backups in named regions or losing no more than five minutes of writes, should be defined alongside features. Those requirements should stay central during testing and auditing before a prototype reaches production. Page also says that someone who knows the database can audit whether the requirements are met.

Page states that not every prototype needs expert review, since many demos hold only test data and can stay as they are. He advises taking a moment to prepare before loading sensitive data into any database. He says AI agents make demos simple to build yet just as easy to progress far without anyone considering database design. His recommendation is to decide on the database deliberately while the application is still small enough to change. He also says teams should follow the same practices they use for code and have someone who has run that database technology in production review it before release.

The article gives Page's background as creator of pgAdmin and as having over 28 years of Postgres development experience. It also says that Postgres has added features continually for three decades, with every release bringing major changes that DBAs must learn. The article itself is the only source provided, so it gives no further reporting on affected organizations, adoption figures or any response from vendors. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Why So Many AI Prototypes Never Make It Past the Database - SD Times

stories.Headline: Google outlines no-downtime AlloyDB AI embedding upgrade
stories.Summary:
Google has published guidance on upgrading the vector embedding models used in AlloyDB AI without taking production databases offline. The approach is aimed at teams running semantic search and other vector workloads on live systems, and it describes moving from one embedding model to another while still serving user queries. It relies on in-database model access, automated embedding generation, PostgreSQL functions and concurrent index creation. The guidance was reported on November 12, 2026. Because embeddings from different models cannot be compared directly, switching models normally means re-embedding existing data, rebuilding indexes and changing query logic.

In the example Google gives, a production table of product reviews moves from text-embedding-005, which produces 768-dimensional vectors, to gemini-embedding-001, which produces 3,072-dimensional vectors. The process starts by adding a new vector column sized for the replacement model, then enabling auto-embeddings so the database backfills vectors in the background. AlloyDB AI can generate embeddings at up to 3,000 per second and tracks changes to source rows. Teams can choose transactional mode, which updates embeddings as data changes but adds write latency, or manual mode, which marks changed rows for scheduled batch refreshes. The migration example uses manual mode.

In one benchmark on a 10,000-row table, lowering max_parallel_requests from 400 to 20 cut the longest concurrent writer wait from 5.1 seconds to 0.39 seconds, while raising total backfill time from 5.2 seconds to 7.6 seconds. Google recommends checking for missing embeddings and validating new vectors against fresh model calls before switching traffic. It also says teams should test application behaviour, since retrieval results can shift sharply between models. In Google's internal tests, the top-10 nearest-neighbour results from the two models overlapped by only 31%, so ranking, filtering and evaluation logic may need review.

The process also builds a new ScaNN index on the replacement column concurrently to avoid blocking writes. Google says ScaNN builds were up to 10 times faster than HNSW on open-source PostgreSQL, and in tests on 100,000 rows a 3,072-dimensional ScaNN index took about 50 seconds while an HNSW index using halfvec took seven to 13 minutes. For the final switch, Google outlines two patterns. One uses an atomic column rename and a query function so applications need no code changes, which supports blue-green deployment but not per-query canary testing.

The other uses PostgreSQL session variables and a set-returning function, which allows canary releases and traffic splitting and quick reversion. The atomic rename pattern does not work with transactional auto-embeddings because managed triggers refer to fixed column names. Google also warns of storage and latency costs: single-row update median latency rose from about 37.5 milliseconds to roughly 191.0 milliseconds during migration, then settled near 172.0 milliseconds after cutover, and storage per row grew from about 4.5KB to about 13.3KB, implying roughly 133GB for a 10-million-row table's new column plus about 6GB for its index. After cutover, teams can clear and drop the retired column, which in Google's 100,000-row tests reclaimed 381MB of TOAST space for later upgrades.

Articles.Title: Google outlines no-downtime AlloyDB AI embedding upgrade - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Docebo launches AI agents & knowledge search for learn
stories.Summary:
Docebo has launched Docebo Knowledge and Docebo Agents for customers using its Learn platform, with the rollout reported on 13 November 2026. The new knowledge search layer and AI agents are designed to draw on learning records, skills data and approved company information held in systems such as SharePoint, Confluence, Google Drive and Slack. The launch comes as businesses increase spending on AI tools while still building the systems needed to manage skills, knowledge and workflow context. Docebo cited its 2027 Skills Intelligence Report, which found many businesses are adopting AI faster than they are establishing those foundations.

Docebo Knowledge lets employees search training material and connected business systems from one interface. It indexes content from Docebo's own platform, including SCORM and xAPI packages, and returns answers, procedures, videos and source links drawn from approved material. Users can move from an answer to a related course, certification, practice exercise or workflow, and the system keeps the permissions set in each connected source so people see only what they are authorised to access. Four pre-built agents are available at launch, covering course creation from source material, learner support, post-course reinforcement through practice, and content sourcing from third-party providers. A no-code tool also lets customers set an agent's goal, instructions and permitted actions without writing software code.

Docebo says more than 50 customers in transportation, retail, distribution and food service took part in pilots and saw early signs of time savings. An international electronics distributor reduced manual content curation by about five hours a month for each administrator, while a global restaurant operator saved store managers about 10 hours a month on training follow-up and had its Tutor Agent handle 25% of frontline training questions. A retailer that recruits 2,500 new employees a year built its own onboarding agent, which it expects to save sales managers between one and two hours per new hire. Administrators can decide which agents operate, who may use them and which actions need human sign-off, and every action is logged under existing permissions. Customers can also track AI credit usage to monitor costs, and through Model Context Protocol they can connect the system to Microsoft Copilot, ChatGPT and Claude so employees can search content, check progress and enrol in courses without opening the Docebo platform.

Alessio Artuffo, President and Chief Executive Officer at Docebo, said organisations are beginning to manage both their staff and the software agents working alongside them. He argued that both need trusted knowledge and an accurate picture of skills, and described the platform as now built on that foundation. He said the agents take on manual work that has slowed learning teams, aiming for less time on administration and more capability where it counts. The articles do not describe further rollout plans or next steps beyond the launch itself.

Articles.Title: Docebo launches AI agents & knowledge search for learn - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: SPUSD Nov. 10 Board Meeting | AI Policy Adopted, Strategic Plan Approved & $46 Million Bond Authorized
stories.Summary:
The South Pasadena Unified School District Board of Education met on November 10, 2026, and adopted its generative AI policy, approved a new three-year Strategic Plan, cleared the sale of up to $46 million in Measure SP bonds, and ratified raises for teachers and staff. The meeting began with a closed session and reconvened in open session at 6:30 p.m. All five board members attended, along with the student board member, and longtime member Dr. Michele Kipke delivered her final board report. The board approved two student-related settlement agreements in closed session by 5-0 roll call votes, with no public comment offered on those items. Every action item with a recorded vote passed unanimously, and the board's approval of the policy package followed public comment that began at the October 13 meeting.

Public speakers offered the board feedback before the vote, with several parents urging stricter limits than the policy contains. Board Policy 0441 on generative artificial intelligence, first presented on October 13, blocks generative AI on student devices unless a teacher explicitly assigns it. Student use must be disclosed, and existing plagiarism and academic integrity rules apply to it. The policy was part of a package of new and revised board policies approved at the meeting. Parents who spoke asked for additions including age-appropriate guidelines, clear expectations for independent work at home, evaluations that measure what students learn, and a commitment to revisit the policy as research emerges.

The board also approved a new three-year Strategic Plan, developed over several weeks, including two special board meetings and input from the spring 2026 Local Control and Accountability Plan survey. The plan sets four goals, covering future-ready students, relational and restorative school communities, recruitment and retention of staff, and long-term financial sustainability. The board cleared the way to sell up to $46 million in Measure SP bonds, which the plan says will upgrade and modernize campuses, improve physical security and energy efficiency. The board also ratified raises for teachers and staff. Board members said the AI policy reflects community values and was strengthened by public feedback, and one called it "a beginning" rather than an ending.

Members said the policy covers student use on any device, requires disclosure of student AI use, and applies existing plagiarism rules. They said teachers are working on changing assignments, such as writing essays in class, so AI does not become a tool for cheating, and that AI should not be used to grade student work. One board member said district staff spent hours writing code to turn off Google's Gemini after it appeared on district accounts. Another described a teacher exercise in which students completed writing prompts themselves, then compared their work with generative AI answers and concluded they did not want to use it. Board members said the policy will be revisited as the technology changes.

Dr. Martinez-Miller asked that the district make the actions under the plan more explicit. Parent Alyssa Misinga, whose child is an SPHS senior, said she is not against AI, Chromebooks or cell phones but opposes introducing them at too young an age. Sophie Ellsberg, a parent of an Arroyo Vista first grader, said the policy does not go far enough but that the board took public comment to heart. Nick Ellsberg called the changes a step in the right direction but asked that the teacher-assigned exception be removed unless a benefit is demonstrated.

Dr. Sadie Jefferson, who leads the Los Angeles Unified School District's education foundation, called the teacher-permission exception a loophole and urged a uniform block until peer-reviewed research shows academic benefits. Andrew Adjemovich, a parent of three Arroyo Vista students, said large language models are shortcuts to thinking in the classroom. Heather Bland urged the board to use policy to encourage human connection. The speakers' comments affect the students, parents, teachers and staff of the district's schools, including Arroyo Vista, Marengo and South Pasadena High School.

Articles.Title: SPUSD Nov. 10 Board Meeting | AI Policy Adopted, Strategic Plan Approved & $46 Million Bond Authorized - South Pasadena News

stories.Headline: V2 AI appoints Arseny Chernov to lead Singapore push
stories.Summary:
V2 AI, a data and AI consultancy, has appointed Arseny Chernov as Director, Forward Deployed Engineering - Applied AI, to strengthen its leadership team in Singapore. The appointment was reported on 12 November 2026 by IT Brief Australia. The move comes as the firm expands across Asia-Pacific and builds out its regional hub in the city-state. Chernov will support operations in Singapore and South-East Asia, working with customers and internal technical teams.

His work will cover AI architecture, forward deployed engineering, and secure multi-agent workflows. The role is aimed at helping companies move AI projects out of pilot stages and into live business use. The articles note that many organisations struggle with data, governance, and infrastructure when they try to scale systems across larger operations. Chernov's focus will be on the security, governance, and operational constraints that tend to emerge at that point.

Chernov previously served as Regional Director for ASEAN, Korea, and Greater China at HashiCorp, where he led regional technical teams and worked on AI-native security and governance. Before that, he spent more than five years at Google in senior technical and engineering roles across Asia-Pacific and the US, including work on Google Payments and early generative AI projects. He also led Partner Solutions Architecture for Asia-Pacific and Japan at Databricks. At Databricks, he was the company's first hire in Singapore and built a regional network of more than 50 strategic technology partners.

In a statement, Chernov said organisations are moving past AI experimentation but need strong data foundations, robust architecture, and co-design with security and governance teams to reach reliable enterprise solutions. V2 AI's leadership, speaking through a company representative named Williams, said the appointment reflects the technical and operational demands shaping the regional AI market. Williams said Chernov's experience would strengthen the Singapore team and its ability to help organisations move from AI ambition to implementation. V2 AI was founded in 2023 and operates across Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane, Perth, Singapore, and Kuala Lumpur.

Articles.Title: V2 AI appoints Arseny Chernov to lead Singapore push - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: The AI licences are live. Why hasn't the work changed?
stories.Summary:
Organisations across Australia and New Zealand have already switched on AI tools such as Copilot, ChatGPT and Claude, yet many teams have not changed how they work. Glen Maguire, founder of Matrix AI Consulting, writing for IT Brief Australia on 13 November 2026, says most of his recent calls come from firms that have already adopted AI. In those cases IT has approved the platform and staff have attended one or more webinars, but senior managers are now asking why usage remains low. Maguire says the common answer from staff, "I don't know what I'd use it for," rarely explains the problem alone.

A CPA Australia survey of 1,679 accounting and finance professionals across six markets found that 88% of Australian and New Zealand respondents' businesses use AI, but only 11% have it deeply embedded. Australia and New Zealand ranked last of the six markets for broad integration. Maguire argues that licences and logins show whether people can use AI, but not whether it has changed how work is done. He uses the Prosci ADKAR model, covering awareness, desire, knowledge, ability and reinforcement, to diagnose stalled rollouts, and he says many programmes neglect motivation, practical skill and reinforcement.

Maguire says three things must work together: purpose, permission and practice. Generic examples, such as summarising an email, rarely motivate staff, so tasks need to match real jobs. Employment Hero found 37% of New Zealand workers feel guilty using AI at work, which Maguire says suggests workplace attitudes matter. He says the most effective uptake comes from in-person workshops built on an organisation's own workflows, where people complete an AI-assisted version of a real task. MyHR reported that just 5.7% of AI-using employers have an AI policy, and Maguire says policies are often too vague to guide daily decisions.

Maguire places responsibility on several groups. He says the CIO owns technical assurance and enablement, including the platform, security, data controls and integration into existing systems. HR, he says, builds staff capability and confidence and handles consultation, while business leaders must own workflow changes and their results. Managers, in his account, identify suitable tasks, give staff time to experiment, set quality expectations and say where AI adds risk or little value. Maguire notes that Australian work health and safety rules require employers to manage the psychosocial risks that poorly handled change can create.

Maguire says the people affected are employees whose tasks are changing and whose confidence and job security depend on how change is handled. He describes a clinician whose administrator had watched generic AI videos that left her more confused and wary; after a personal session built around her own tasks, she built and deployed two Copilot agents that have lifted her productivity. He says higher usage is not automatically better, because organisations can gain active users while producing more rework, exposing sensitive information or applying AI to decisions it should not touch. He recommends measuring changed workflows, output quality, rework, time saved, staff confidence and incidents rather than logins.

The article is an opinion column and does not report any new formal change, deadline or regulatory action. It does not say how many organisations will reach deeper integration in the coming year, nor which governance measures the CPA Australia or MyHR research companies plan to follow up with. Maguire ends by suggesting leaders test whether they can name three workflows where AI is improving outcomes, explain safe-use rules and identify an accountable business owner. The article does not say what follow-up, if any, will address those gaps.

Articles.Title: The AI licences are live. Why hasn't the work changed? - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Virtana launches AI agent war room for IT incidents
stories.Summary:
Virtana has launched Agentic Observability Enterprise Management, a system that coordinates AI agents from different enterprise platforms during IT incidents, according to an IT Brief Australia report published on November 12, 2026. The product is designed to bring together agents that would otherwise work in isolation. It arrives as companies run growing numbers of AI agents across IT service management, cloud, security and software development systems. Those agents are increasingly expected to connect when an incident spans several areas.

The system uses the Model Context Protocol and the open Agent2Agent protocol to bring agents from third-party platforms into what Virtana calls an agentic war room. Virtana says the platform draws on more than 25,000 operational signals across applications, infrastructure, cloud and AI environments. It combines those signals with its System Dependency Graph to map relationships between systems, trace root causes and assess business impact. Companies can start with a recommendation model, move to approval-based remediation and later allow agents to act alone on defined classes of incidents.

Every action stays subject to enterprise policy controls and is auditable, including records of agent activity, token consumption and operating cost. Paul Appleby, Chief Executive Officer of Virtana, described the launch as part of a wider shift toward autonomous IT operations. He said the future belongs to enterprises whose agents understand the whole business and can work together on problems no single agent could solve. Amitkumar Rathi, Chief Product Officer of Virtana, contrasted traditional war rooms, which can take hours to assemble teams and coordinate fixes, with agent-based rooms that assemble, share intelligence and disband in milliseconds.

He said the two protocols give agents enterprise-wide intelligence and let them discover and act together as a governed workforce. The release responds to a fragmentation problem that the article ties to research from Salesforce, which found that the average enterprise runs 12 AI agents and that half operate in silos. Virtana is relying on open protocols rather than asking companies to replace existing tools, so enterprises can bring in agents from platforms they already use. The product is available now to select customers, and general availability is planned for the first quarter of 2027.

Articles.Title: Virtana launches AI agent war room for IT incidents - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Can fuel cells meet the power demands of AI data centers? Feds invest in Danbury company to find out - News-Times
stories.Summary:
A FuelCell Energy company in Danbury, Connecticut, is taking part in a three-year federally funded project to test whether fuel cells can supply electricity to AI data centers. The project, called StabilityMax, was announced in a release on November 10, 2026, and reported by the News-Times on November 13, 2026. The company said that as AI adoption accelerates, data centers are driving unprecedented demand for electricity and creating rapid fluctuations in power consumption. Under the project, FuelCell Energy will develop a fuel cell test facility in Danbury, serving as a national laboratory-supported testbed for evaluating integrated power solutions for AI data centers. The goal is to understand whether fuel cells can handle these demands while limiting impacts to the utility grid and ratepayers.

The project will model and validate configurations that combine fuel cells, batteries and power electronics against realistic data center demand. The National Laboratory of the Rockies will develop data center load profiles and simulation models, and Argonne National Laboratory will complement this work with techno-economic and lifecycle analyses. Those analyses aim to help identify commercially appealing deployment strategies and cost-effective approaches. The project is led by the U.S. Department of Energy's National Laboratory of the Rockies, with Argonne National Laboratory also participating. Details such as the amount of federal money involved were not disclosed.

FuelCell Energy reported 425 employees worldwide last year, most of them at its Danbury headquarters and its Torrington manufacturing plant. FuelCell Energy presented the project as an effort to optimize fuel cell-based systems for the changing demands of AI infrastructure. A company director of communications, Kathleen Blomquist, said the project is not about whether fuel cells can power data centers, stating that they can. Zhiwen Ma, a principal investigator at the National Laboratory of the Rockies, said integrated fuel cell systems can rapidly respond to data center power needs while limiting impacts to the grid and ratepayers.

Shankar Achanta, chief product and technology officer at FuelCell Energy, said the insights gained will help optimize system designs and validate performance under real-world conditions. Danbury Mayor Roberto Alves praised the company's participation as a strong example of innovation and expertise rooted in Danbury. The announcement affects the Danbury community, where the company is headquartered near the Bethel border, and the utility grid and ratepayers whose costs and reliability the project is meant to protect. Public concern about energy use by data centers has made headlines across Connecticut and the region.

In October, a developer proposed reinvigorating a 1.3-million-square-foot office structure in Danbury by bringing in a data center powered by fuel cells. Fuel cells make electricity from fuel and air without burning that fuel, and they already power commercial and industrial facilities. FuelCell Energy also operates a power plant on Triangle Street in Danbury. The project runs for three years, and the articles do not say when the Danbury test facility will be built or begin operation.

The articles do not disclose the federal funding amount or the cost of the facility. Results on performance, cost and effects on the electric grid are expected from the work, but the articles do not describe any findings yet. The articles also do not say whether the October proposal for a fuel cell-powered data center in Danbury will proceed. How the project will affect the company's staffing beyond keeping levels the same is not described further.

Articles.Title: Can fuel cells meet the power demands of AI data centers? Feds invest in Danbury company to find out - News-Times

stories.Headline: Your AI agents are ready for business. Is your business ready to own them? - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
As AI agents take on more decision-making inside companies, a Nov 12, 2026 ETCIO opinion piece by Manu Swami argues that businesses need stronger governance over them. The article says that McKinsey research found 80% of organizations have encountered risky behaviour from AI agents. It notes that enterprise architecture has long kept applications executing, people deciding and governance setting boundaries, but agents are changing that balance. Agents can interpret objectives, access enterprise systems, execute transactions and adapt their actions. The article says companies are therefore delegating elements of business judgment to software rather than merely automating tasks.

The author says businesses should define the extent of autonomy given to AI agents, with routine low-risk actions handled within predefined limits. Higher-stakes decisions involving financial exposure, regulatory obligations or irreversible consequences should require stronger safeguards or human approval. The piece gives a procurement agent resolving an invoice discrepancy as an example, where access to information does not confer authority to approve a price variance. It describes a customer service agent recommending a refund amount that must be checked against approved limits before processing. The article also says that even correctly configured agents must be continuously validated, since models evolve, tools change and business policies are updated.

Responsibility, the article says, must stay with the business, while IT, security and responsible AI teams build and maintain the controls. Using its examples, it says customer service should set boundaries for acceptable dispute resolutions, and Finance should determine what an agent can approve in financial exceptions. The author summarizes this division as the business owning decisions, technology enabling controls and governance providing oversight. Manu Swami is identified as Chief Technology Officer at Sonata Software, and the article notes that its views are the author's and that ETCIO does not necessarily subscribe to them.

The article states that agents are no longer merely automating tasks but taking on delegated judgment, which affects enterprises that deploy them and the teams that own their outcomes. It says enterprises must establish intended authority at deployment and validate exercised authority at runtime. Monitoring should show what an agent is doing, whether it stays within its authority and what impact its actions have. Important decisions should be traceable and, where stakes are high, independently reviewed, and an agent should not check its own work. Continuous assurance should test failure scenarios, adversarial behavior and edge cases, with mechanisms to restrict permissions, require human intervention or suspend execution.

The background the article gives is the traditional division of enterprise architecture described above, and the fragmented governance in which identity systems manage access, security platforms enforce controls, observability tools monitor execution and business functions remain accountable for outcomes. The article says the missing piece is the connection between these controls and the business authority an agent exercises. It frames AI maturity as how much business-critical work an enterprise can safely delegate while keeping control and accountability, rather than how many agents are deployed. The article says governance must be able to intervene, not just monitor, as AI begins to act rather than advise.

The article does not say what specific governance rules any company has adopted, nor what regulators or standards bodies will require. It also leaves open how the reversal or rollback of agent actions would work in practice across different systems. It gives no timeline for when businesses should implement these controls. The piece ends by stating that the advantage will come from building enough trust and control to extend greater autonomy where it makes sense, without saying how that threshold should be set.

Articles.Title: Your AI agents are ready for business. Is your business ready to own them? - ET CIO

stories.Headline: HUMAIN and Infra Sign SAR 2.5B AI Data Centre Deals
stories.Summary:
HUMAIN and Saudi Arabia's National Infrastructure Fund, known as Infra, signed two financing agreements totalling up to SAR 2.5 billion (about $667 million) in Riyadh on November 8. The deals are the first funded commitments under a SAR 4.5 billion (about $1.2 billion) AI data centre programme announced at the World Economic Forum in Davos in January. The agreements came one week after Aramco completed its acquisition of a 49 percent stake in HUMAIN. Arab News and Zawya reported the signing, and enterprise AM and PIF and Aramco press releases were cited for the surrounding details.

The first agreement provides up to SAR 1.1 billion (about $293 million) for graphics processing units representing roughly 25 megawatts of IT load. The second allocates up to SAR 1.4 billion (about $373 million) for substations, transmission lines and grid connections. According to Arabian Business, the grid infrastructure is designed to accommodate up to 1 gigawatt of future IT capacity. The Davos framework was described as non-binding at announcement, with terms to be finalised tranche by tranche as projects reach financial close. The 25 megawatts funded here is a fraction of HUMAIN's announced NVIDIA capacity, which The National News said leaves most of that capacity without disclosed project financing.

The articles identify HUMAIN and Infra as the parties behind the deals. PIF and Aramco own HUMAIN jointly, with PIF holding 51 percent. Aramco's stake was acquired through a transaction closed on November 1, in which it contributed about SAR 9.9 billion (about $2.6 billion) in cash and AI assets, including SCAI, a PIF-owned AI company. Tareq Amin, HUMAIN's chief executive, said at a PIF Private Sector Forum in February 2026 that Saudi Arabia has everything required to become the largest AI token exporter. The articles do not give a direct statement from Infra on the November 8 signing.

Infra, formally the National Infrastructure Fund, aims to mobilise private investment by bringing data centre projects to financial close, according to enterprise AM. It absorbs early-stage capital risk by buying GPUs and building substations, so commercial operators find working hardware and grid connections. Both parties to the deals are sovereign entities, and no private co-investor in the programme has been publicly announced. The articles say the power envelope is the larger of the two deals and addresses a bottleneck in which facilities cannot draw load until grid connections are live. The kingdom has also approved power and water tariff increases for 2027 as its industrial base expands.

HUMAIN has set a target of 3 gigawatts of AI data centre capacity by 2030 and more than 6 gigawatts by 2034, according to The National News. Saudi Arabia's national goal, announced at LEAP 2026 in February, is 6.9 gigawatts of total data centre capacity by 2034. HUMAIN's expanded NVIDIA partnership at GTC Berlin in October 2026 covers about 84 megawatts, around 27,000 GPUs. Phase 1 calls for 14 megawatts of Blackwell systems from the fourth quarter of 2026, and Phase 2 adds 70 megawatts of Vera Rubin infrastructure from June 2027. Elon Musk's xAI and Amazon Web Services are named as major compute customers, and HUMAIN and Microsoft agreed in August 2026 to integrate its ALLAM Arabic-language models into Microsoft products.

Washington approved sales of up to 35,000 advanced NVIDIA chips to HUMAIN on the condition that Chinese frontier AI models not be trained on its compute, CNBC reported in November 2025. HUMAIN's Arabic model M3 is built on an open-source base from the Chinese startup MiniMax, according to Rest of World. Tencent Cloud has invested $150 million in the kingdom and Huawei has planned a $400 million cloud-region investment, according to Asia Times. The articles do not say how strictly Washington will enforce its conditions or whether Chinese open-source models will remain accessible to Gulf firms. They also do not say when Phase 2 will reach final agreement or whether further tranches of the Davos framework will be funded.

Articles.Title: HUMAIN and Infra Sign SAR 2.5B AI Data Centre Deals - https://houseofsaud.com/

stories.Headline: Exponentia.ai Certified as Best Firm for Data Scientists
stories.Summary:
Exponentia.ai has been certified as a Best Firm for Data Scientists by Analytics India Magazine, as reported on 12 November 2026. The certification draws on structured feedback collected directly from the firm's data science professionals and assesses how well the company builds an environment where technical talent can grow and contribute. AIM's programme independently analyses survey responses across workplace culture, access to leadership, collaboration, learning opportunities, and the substance of the analytical work delivered. The recognition reflects how the organisation supports its data science teams rather than how it presents itself externally. Exponentia.ai, which describes itself as an AI acceleration partner for enterprises, works with clients in CPG, manufacturing, BFSI, MedTech and healthcare.

The article says the firm structures its data science work around measurable business impact across the full lifecycle of AI initiatives, from solution design through production deployment and ongoing operations. Client engagements have reportedly delivered 93 per cent pricing prediction accuracy and 67 per cent reductions in development cycles. The firm's focus on agentic AI puts its data scientists on problems such as agent orchestration and LLM validation, using proprietary tools including AIXponent and GenTrust, an AI governance and validation platform. Data science teams work close to consulting, engineering and client-facing functions, which gives practitioners a broader view of client strategy. Learning is described as part of the working rhythm rather than confined to scheduled training.

Three Exponentia.ai leaders are quoted praising the culture. Juhi Gianani, Senior Engineer, Data and AI, says the firm fosters learning, innovation and collaboration and encourages ownership. Vaibhav Agarwal, Value Delivery Lead, says the recognition reflects a culture that nurtures talent and empowers individuals to grow. Tushar Anand Gupta, Value Delivery Partner, says the team's opportunity to turn complex business problems into measurable customer impact is what sets the firm apart. The article also notes that AIM's certification programme is a benchmark that companies join to gather employee-led insights and review practices supporting long-term technical capability.

The article does not say how many employees responded to the survey. The article places the certification within India's competitive data science talent market, where employers increasingly compete on the quality of problems, the speed of technology adoption and whether data scientists are treated as strategic contributors. It presents the certification as a record of what employees have said about working at the firm. The article does not describe any further steps, announcements or changes tied to the recognition.

Articles.Title: Exponentia.ai Certified as Best Firm for Data Scientists - Analytics India Magazine

stories.Headline: Space Tech Startup Astrome Bags ₹64 Cr RDI Fund for AI Satellite Network
stories.Summary:
The Technology Development Board (TDB), under the Department of Science and Technology (DST), has signed an agreement to provide ₹64.05 crore to Bengaluru-based space technology startup Astrome Technologies under the Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) Fund. The money will support the development of an indigenous artificial intelligence-powered electronic intelligence (AI-ELINT) satellite constellation. The project is estimated to cost ₹128.11 crore, and TDB's assistance is structured as optionally convertible debt. The report was published by Analytics India Magazine on November 12, 2026.

The constellation will consist of microsatellites weighing about 50 kg each, operating in low Earth orbit. Each satellite will carry an ELINT payload designed to detect and analyse signals across a broad frequency range, along with inter-satellite communication links that let the satellites exchange information. AI-based ground processing software will handle the collected data. The network is meant to provide wider geographic coverage and more frequent observations of areas of interest as more satellites are added. The project also aims to raise the underlying technologies from Technology Readiness Level 4 to Level 9 through engineering, integration, testing and validation.

The TDB Secretary, Rajesh Kumar Pathak, said that through the RDI Fund the board supports Indian enterprises working on frontier technologies that can strengthen the country's strategic technology capabilities. An authorised representative of Astrome Technologies told DD News that the funding would accelerate the integration of technologies for the programme. The article places the award within India's growing private space sector, citing Bengaluru-based GalaxEye, which has secured a US patent for the core technology behind its OptoSAR imaging system, and Digantara, which has partnered with Singapore's DSTA on satellite tracking tools using AI-driven analytics. The article does not say when the satellites will launch or what the next milestones are.

Articles.Title: Space Tech Startup Astrome Bags ₹64 Cr RDI Fund for AI Satellite Network - Analytics India Magazine

stories.Headline: LatentView Analytics Certified as Best Firm for AI Engineers
stories.Summary:
LatentView Analytics has been certified as a Best Firm for AI Engineers by Analytics India Magazine (AIM), according to an article published on 12 November 2026. The recognition rests on structured survey responses from AI practitioners inside the company, which ask how well employers help engineers grow, experiment, and deliver results for clients. AIM's programme evaluates employee feedback on workplace culture, leadership, learning and development, cross-functional collaboration, and the day-to-day nature of AI work. The certification reflects how engineers describe their own experience rather than how the firm markets itself. The article presents it as evidence of a practice built on technical depth and closeness to clients.

The article says LatentView encourages AI engineers to pursue new ideas, shape their own learning paths, and develop pilots in areas that interest them. Leadership is described as supporting experimentation rather than limiting staff to defined delivery work. Engineers work on large-scale machine learning problems across global industries, taking statistically rigorous solutions from concept to production. The article also describes career development at several levels, from early-career practitioners to senior engineers who lead teams building enterprise-grade solutions.

It notes that senior staff are given scope to shape data strategy and develop future talent. Aravind Balasubramanian, an AI Engineer at LatentView, is quoted saying the firm gives people room to explore and build new solutions, backed by supportive leaders and a hands-on culture. Rajesh Krishnan, Associate Director of the Software Development and Data Science Centre of Excellence, is quoted saying the collaborative culture lets staff build scalable solutions while exploring emerging technologies. The article credits AIM with running the programme, and it attributes the employee insights to the workers themselves.

LatentView itself is presented as the firm that participates in and is recognised through the programme. The article places the certification within a market where AI engineers often find their career progress stalls once they reach a certain level of seniority, which it describes as a meaningful point of difference for LatentView. It notes that AIM's certification serves as a benchmark for organisations building high-performance AI teams, and that companies take part to review practices that support long-term technical capability. The article is a feature published on AIM's own site and does not report any follow-up action or future event.

Articles.Title: LatentView Analytics Certified as Best Firm for AI Engineers - Analytics India Magazine

stories.Headline: LTM Integrates AI Tool to Fix Quantum Computing Errors on IBM
stories.Summary:
LTM, a technology services company, has added its AI-powered Quantum Error Mitigation capability, called AI-QEM, to IBM's Quantum Functions Catalog. The company said it was the first global systems integrator to publish a function in that catalogue. According to the company, users with eligible IBM Quantum access plans can apply AI-QEM directly within their Qiskit workflows. The announcement was reported on November 12, 2026. The company's own description of the tool is the basis for the details below.

The capability uses AI models to learn error patterns specific to each device and to estimate corrections through classical post-processing. LTM says this improves result accuracy without requiring additional quantum processing unit time, repeated circuit executions or extra qubits, which some conventional error mitigation techniques need. The company tested the tool on IBM Quantum computers across circuits of different sizes and complexities, including experiments involving more than 100 qubits. It did not disclose how much accuracy improved or offer comparisons with other error mitigation methods. IBM's listing describes the function as using circuit, backend and observable characteristics to learn correction factors and to mitigate noisy quantum expectation values.

Scott Crowder, Vice President of IBM Quantum Adoption and Business Development, said in a statement that the AI-QEM function will let users mitigate errors faster and with fewer resources as they develop algorithms and applications. LTM, which was formerly known as LTIMindtree, had earlier joined the IBM Quantum Network as its first Indian global systems integrator. Other providers in IBM's catalogue offer related tools, including Q-CTRL's AI-driven error suppression, Qedma's QESEM function and Algorithmiq's tensor-network approach. The articles present LTM's function as distinctive mainly for its efficiency, a claim the company made without published accuracy figures.

Articles.Title: LTM Integrates AI Tool to Fix Quantum Computing Errors on IBM - Analytics India Magazine

stories.Headline: How Enterprises Are Matching AI Workloads With The Right Models And Infra
stories.Summary:
Inc42 hosted a leadership roundtable titled "Powering AI Workloads at Scale," held in partnership with Oracle, to examine how enterprises are moving artificial intelligence from experiments into production. The session was moderated by Sameer Dhanrajani, CEO of 3AI and AIQRATE, and featured speakers from Data Sutram, Oracle, Fluid AI, Spintly and PhroneticAI (AvenuesAI). The discussion covered how companies can match workloads with suitable models and infrastructure, manage AI economics, and build systems that adapt as the technology changes. The article was published on November 12, 2026.

The panel addressed how enterprises can scale AI reliably and economically across different workloads. Companies must decide where compute is needed, which models suit each use case, and how much performance each application actually requires. Speakers said the focus has shifted from getting an answer to delivering it sustainably at the right cost. Enterprises are also evaluating different GPUs for inference, and open-weight models are gaining traction as token consumption rises. Some workloads can run on dedicated AI clusters while higher-end compute is reserved for applications that need it.

Ravi of PhroneticAI described the transition as two phases, first choosing the right intelligence and then putting it to work at scale. Thangavelu of Data Sutram said enterprises must confirm they have used the right models to derive correct outputs. Aggarwal of Fluid AI said the larger opportunity lies in using AI to reinvent products, citing Fluid AI's work with Forbes on an AI avatar of Warren Buffett. That experience was initially meant to run for two weeks but stayed on Forbes for three years.

Saravanan of Oracle said the infrastructure challenge cuts across BFSI, government, manufacturing and IT/ITeS companies seeking to scale AI adoption. He said enterprises are unwilling to expose core data to external models, which is pushing larger organisations toward dedicated GPU environments within controlled data boundaries. Parkar of Spintly said his company deploys models on smaller hardware for facial recognition, QR code detection and anomaly detection, applications that need low latency on relatively low-cost devices. Parkar also pointed to shortages of neural processing units and constraints around data centre capacity, cooling and power.

Aggarwal said some organisations have invested heavily in AI models only to see newer models make those investments less relevant within a short period. He argued for architectures that can adapt rather than lock enterprises into one model, and said enterprises should be able to switch between frontier, open-weight and smaller models without rebuilding. Ravi said enterprises need visibility into which agent makes which decision, what data is consumed and which models are exposed. Thangavelu urged enterprises to build a repeatable harness around individual use cases, and the article's text on this point is cut off.

Articles.Title: How Enterprises Are Matching AI Workloads With The Right Models And Infra - Inc42

stories.Headline: Satellite+ai | Tag | techmonk
stories.Summary:
Google's Project Suncatcher prototype satellite generated its first artificial intelligence response in orbit on October 30, using a data centre-class Tensor Processing Unit. The achievement was reported in a TechGig article published on November 3, 2026. The article describes it as an early test of the company's research into running AI workloads in space. Beyond that core result, the source material offers few further details about the test itself.

The article does not give figures for the processor's performance, the length or nature of the response, or the duration of the test. It also does not say whether the satellite will run further tests, or what changes, if any, the result requires for the project. Much of the rest of the page is taken up by unrelated promotions for TechGig events, including an IndiaAI Challenge, an Ericsson event, DevNext 2026 and a responsible AI masterclass. Those listings have no bearing on the satellite test. The available information is therefore limited to the single milestone and its stated purpose.

Google is the company behind Project Suncatcher, and the article identifies the prototype as its satellite. The article does not quote anyone from Google or describe any statements the company made about the result. It also does not name the individuals or teams that carried out the work. Responsibility for the test is thus attributed only to the company and its project as a whole.

The wider context the article offers is limited to the idea that running AI workloads in space is a research direction Google is pursuing. The article presents the October 30 result as a step in that effort rather than a finished capability. Based on the text provided, there is no stated timeline for next steps or announced commercial plans. Anything beyond this would require further reporting, so this is treated as a breaking story: More to follow.

Articles.Title: Satellite+ai | Tag | techmonk - TechGig

stories.Headline: Preparing CAS teams for AI: Moving beyond software training
stories.Summary:
Michael Ramos, managing partner of MRA Learning, writes in an Accounting Today column dated November 12, 2026, about preparing CAS teams for AI. He describes watching a vendor demo in which an AI agent, prompted by an accountant to create a month-end payroll accrual and post the journal entry, requested source files and prepared a work program. The agent flagged missing general ledger accounts, which the accountant fixed, and paused for approval before posting. Ramos estimates that on a real client the process might take 15 minutes. He says the demo impressed him, but it led him to ask whether accounting staff are ready for this work.

The column does not describe any new rule, regulation or reporting requirement with figures, dates or places. It presents a demo scenario and recommended planning steps instead. Ramos argues that CAS staff need analytic, judgment and decision-making skills to evaluate AI-generated work programs and entries. He asks whether a staff accountant could reliably review that payroll entry and its workpapers. He also questions whether accountants who have never prepared such entries will be able to evaluate AI work on more complex tasks in the future.

Ramos writes that AI disrupts the on-the-job training model in which less-experienced accountants learn through repetitive tasks, review notes and feedback from supervisors. He says AI agents are taking many of the tasks that once served as staff training. He notes that this change affects all team members, raising questions about which judgments move down to junior staff and which become the responsibility of managers and seniors. He argues that firms must therefore rely more on formal classroom learning to build judgment. He adds that abstract concepts such as judgment are best taught by grounding them in the firm's actual work.

Ramos recommends that firms first define their AI-enabled workflow and identify where the agent acts and where professionals decide. He advises piloting the workflow on an actual client, choosing a team of experienced people who have room in their schedules and a client with reasonably clean books and an engaged contact. During the pilot, he suggests documenting how staff use expertise to evaluate AI output, what they check, and where the agent erred. He says firms can begin designing training once they can describe information flow, likely errors, controls, decision points and reviewer tasks. The column does not state how many firms have adopted these practices or what outcomes they have achieved.

Articles.Title: Preparing CAS teams for AI: Moving beyond software training - Accounting Today

stories.Headline: AI isn't a tool. It's a hire.
stories.Summary:
AI isn't a tool. It's a hire. This opinion piece by Ahmad Tamimi, co-founder and CEO of Pennix, was published by Accounting Today on November 12, 2026. Tamimi argues that most accounting firms have treated AI as something a person must open, prompt and operate, which limits its value on recurring work. He proposes instead that firms manage AI the way they manage a new employee, with defined responsibilities, training, boundaries and regular review.

The piece is framed as analysis from a practitioner rather than a news report of an event. To test the idea, Tamimi ran a comparison with a tax firm that handles individual and corporate filings, using real and messy client documents. The firm's staff took just over 84 minutes of combined administrator and preparer time to complete intake on the files tested, and downloading and renaming one client's documents averaged 10 minutes and 37 seconds. The AI, given the job rather than step-by-step prompts, classified and filed the same documents in 32 seconds and, by 1 minute and 47 seconds, had also checked them against the checklist, drafted a client email and summarized the figures. Tamimi says this was roughly 98% less time than the staff took before review.

He stresses that the people were reassigned rather than eliminated, with administrators checking classifications and preparers deciding which missing items to raise. Tamimi's central point is that firms should decide in advance what the AI handles alone, what it escalates and what a person must approve. In the experiment, every client email was approved by a preparer and every missing-item call was made by a person. He also argues that success should be measured across the whole process, including review, corrections and exceptions, rather than by speed alone. The article does not describe any regulatory response or further steps by the firm, and it presents the hiring analogy as a way of judging AI on results under supervision.

Articles.Title: AI isn't a tool. It's a hire. - Accounting Today

stories.Headline: LITEON Showcases Cloud-to-Edge AI Innovation and NVIDIA MGX Platform at electronica 2026
stories.Summary:
LITEON Technology used electronica 2026, held November 10 to 13 in Munich, Germany, to show off its cross-portfolio technology, under the theme "LITEON Powers AI." The company's press release, dated November 13, 2026, presents products spanning AI data center power, connectivity and Edge AI. Its AI power lineup supports NVIDIA MGX and OCP Open Rack V3 architectures across rack-level power delivery, energy backup and near-chip power conversion. At rack level, the company displayed a 110kW Power Shelf for the NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 architecture, along with a 72kW Power Shelf in a 1U design.

The company also highlighted the NVIDIA 800 VDC power architecture through an interactive virtual rack with 330kW, 880kW and 1.2MW configurations. Its high-power Capacitor Backup Unit is meant to support power resilience, and near-chip products such as Intermediate Bus Converters, Voltage Regulator Modules and high-efficiency Power Bricks are intended to reduce conversion losses in dense AI computing. On the enterprise and industrial side, LITEON showed Common Redundant Power Supplies rated at 800W and 2,000W, high-power PoE Injectors, DIN Rail power supplies from 12W to 960W, and medical power solutions. The release describes these as serving diverse edge applications.

On the connectivity side, the company presented O-RAN Radio Units supporting FR1 and FR2 bands and an AI-RAN solution built on the NVIDIA AI Aerial platform. It also debuted a Fixed Wireless Access solution following its integration of U-MEDIA, alongside small cells, Ethernet switches and Wi-Fi Access Points. For intelligent edge work, LITEON showed AI-powered security cameras and AI Boxes that perform local inference for smart buildings, healthcare, retail and industrial automation. The release presents these offerings as covering infrastructure from high-density data centers to edge applications, and it does not say when any of the products will reach the market.

Articles.Title: LITEON Showcases Cloud-to-Edge AI Innovation and NVIDIA MGX Platform at electronica 2026

stories.Headline: PIXTA and ByteDance, Partnership Launched to Advance Anime From Production Through Distribution, Video Generation AI "Seedance" and Short Anime Platform "Anipops" Connect
stories.Summary:
On November 13, 2026, PIXTA, the company that runs the short anime streaming platform Anipops, announced a partnership with ByteDance to advance AI-made anime from production through distribution. The companies are linking ByteDance's video generation AI, Seedance, with Anipops so that anime can be made with Seedance and then shown to viewers on Anipops. The announcement was published through the PR Times press release service, with the Japanese original dated November 13, 2026 at 16:00 Japan time. The partnership involves four joint efforts that the two companies say will bring creation and distribution together. Both firms will jointly approach creators, production studios and media companies to expand AI anime made with Seedance and released on Anipops.

Anipops will also widely seek original works and collaborations from companies and creators who hold intellectual property such as manga, novels or characters, and will offer Seedance benefits to partners whose details will be proposed individually. The companies will further share works and production case studies made on Anipops. Anipops itself offers Japanese-origin series with English subtitles, with the first few episodes of each series free, then per-episode charges of 50 yen in Japan or 0.50 dollars overseas, or weekly and monthly plans. PIXTA's president, Daisuke Komamata, said the company was built on connecting talent with people who need it, and that the partnership joins Seedance as a creation tool with Anipops as a place to deliver works.

ByteDance account executive Kai Adachi described AI as one tool among many that lets creators realize their ideas, and said the collaboration aims to bring creators' works to new fans overseas. The press release also notes that demand for Japanese anime is rising, with the overseas market reported at about 2.1 trillion yen in 2024 and the whole anime industry at about 3.8 trillion yen. Seedance was made public on July 31, 2026, and Anipops was launched as a creator posting site in March 2026 before being rebuilt as an overseas service in August 2026. The release does not give a timetable for the first AI anime works from the partnership.

Articles.Title: PIXTA and ByteDance, Partnership Launched to Advance Anime From Production Through Distribution, Video Generation AI "Seedance" and Short Anime Platform "Anipops" Connect

stories.Headline: As AI reshapes the workforce, boards face a governance challenge, says Deloitte Global Survey
stories.Summary:
Deloitte's Global Boardroom Program published a survey on 10 November 2026, finding that many organizations are still developing the workforce strategies and governance practices needed as AI reshapes jobs, operating models and culture. The research, released from New York, found that only 16% of respondents say their organizations have an established strategy for addressing the workforce impact of technology transformation. The survey drew on 806 board members and C-suite executives across 53 countries. Deloitte also conducted in-depth interviews with 15 board chairs and directors for the research. The findings suggest that many organizations still treat technology transformation and human capital as separate governance matters.

Nearly half of respondents, 49%, say their boards do not consistently include human capital considerations in discussions about AI and technology transformation. Forty-nine percent also report limited or no oversight of how investments are split between technology infrastructure and workforce enablement, while only 12% report full oversight. Productivity is the workforce outcome boards discuss most often, cited by 42% of respondents, well ahead of attracting and retaining employees at 15%. Nearly half of respondents, 46%, are concerned about the quality and sufficiency of human capital data they receive, and 38% lack confidence in current HR and IT structures. Board knowledge and experience was cited by 62% as the most important factor for strengthening oversight.

Deloitte Global Chair Anna Marks said AI is prompting many organizations to reimagine their business models, with wide-ranging effects on skills, careers and workplace cultures. She argued that boards and management teams should consider technology and talent strategies together in a cohesive approach. Prof. Dr. Arno Probst, leader of the Deloitte Global Boardroom Program, said many boards are still adapting their oversight practices to a world where technology and talent are increasingly inseparable. Lara Abrash, Chair of Deloitte US, said boards should ask management whether employees understand how their work is changing and have a voice in shaping that change. The article does not name any separate employer or regulator responsible for the survey beyond Deloitte's own leaders.

The survey's respondents identified several workforce risks as the greatest opportunity for strengthened governance, including skills gaps at 54%, data integrity or misinformation at 47%, and loss of human judgment and critical thinking at 40%. Employees, boards and management teams are the groups the article identifies as directly affected by these changes. The research also points to the rise of AI agents and automation, which the article says will require boards to seek greater clarity on accountability, workforce readiness and safeguards. The survey's authors state that workforce concerns are increasingly linked to technology decisions at the board level. The article does not give further detail on how these groups have responded to the findings.

Deloitte's report sets out three steps boards can take, namely embedding workforce strategy in AI transformation, making culture a regular agenda item, and investing in continuous learning on technology and human capital. The Deloitte Global Boardroom Program presents these steps as practical measures for boards to keep pace with AI-driven change. The article notes that the survey was conducted across 53 countries and that the findings focus on board-level governance rather than individual company actions. Deloitte describes itself as providing professional services to nearly 90% of the Fortune Global 500 and thousands of private companies. The article gives no earlier survey results or prior reporting to compare these findings against.

The article does not say whether boards will adopt the recommended steps or how quickly organizations will change their governance structures. It does not specify what workforce strategies companies will develop next, nor how their outcomes will be measured. It also gives no timeline for follow-up research from the Deloitte Global Boardroom Program. Whether committee mandates and reporting lines will change in response to the findings is not addressed. The article ends without indicating what further releases or data Deloitte plans to publish on the subject.

Articles.Title: As AI reshapes the workforce, boards face a governance challenge, says Deloitte Global Survey - Deloitte

stories.Headline: The AI Reality Check: KPMG’s Christian Peo on What Financial Leaders Need to Know Before Year-End
stories.Summary:
KPMG US Vice Chair of Audit and Assurance Christian Peo used his keynote at the Corporate Financial Reporting Insights (CFRI) 2026 conference on Day 2 to tell financial leaders that AI may already be in their close process. Peo, who has nearly 30 years of auditing experience and is a former SEC accounting fellow, called AI a revolutionary technology for financial reporting. He said that its benefits will take time and effort to realize. Between walkthroughs earlier in the year and interim testing this fall, KPMG auditors have regularly found AI in financial reporting processes that management had not identified. Peo described two ways it enters: through service providers' ERP, payroll and valuation features added by routine patches, and through individual staff switching from spreadsheets to AI models.

In one example, a spreadsheet lookup control was replaced by an AI model that produced the right answer, but the change had not been identified. For companies with a December 31 year-end, Peo recommended asking about AI use at every level, including staff-level control operators, before the books close. He advised looking for evidence that has changed or disappeared, reviewing ERP and application updates for embedded AI, checking legacy RPA bots and scripts, and contacting service providers about whether AI features are active and covered by their SOC reports. When AI is found, companies should determine whether it changes the process, the control or the information used in a control. Peo also cautioned that many AI products perform well on demo data but fall short on live data, so vendors should be tested on a company's own data.

He added that the operating model, not the technology, was the hardest part, and that KPMG bundled smaller engagements into single blocks so that time saved on them could be redeployed. Peo said that KPMG rebuilt its intern training around AI fluency, covering the evaluation of data inputs and model outputs and the spotting of hallucinations. He said interns grasped client workflows significantly faster under the new approach, and that the firm is shifting first- and second-year assignments toward evaluating outputs. Peo described the SEC and PCAOB as asking the right questions and engaging directly with firms on new technology. He expects regulators to look toward a framework similar to COSO, possibly with changes to audit evidence requirements.

He encouraged attendees to study FEI's AI Framework: Internal Control Over Financial Reporting Whitepaper, which FEI's Committee on Corporate Reporting developed. The SEC is also examining AI disclosures for consistency across earnings releases, earnings calls and periodic filings, and generic claims such as being an "AI leader" need verifiable support. Peo addressed audit fees directly, saying that a new tool typically adds hours in its first year on an engagement, breaks even in the second and produces savings in the third. Because of that two- to three-year lag, he said few firms can currently claim higher margins from technology. Over time, he expects downward pressure on audit fees, though the size of that change remains to be seen.

Near term, companies are spending significantly less of their own people's time supporting the audit. The articles say registration for CFRI 2026 remains open to FEI Members and Nonmembers, with on-demand access and a CPE-accredited replay available December 1–3 for up to 21 CPE credits. The program also features keynotes from Mastercard Chief Economist Michelle Meyer and SEC Chairman Paul Atkins, along with updates from the SEC, FASB and PCAOB. The articles do not say how the expected fee reductions will be sized or when they will materialize.

Articles.Title: The AI Reality Check: KPMG’s Christian Peo on What Financial Leaders Need to Know Before Year-End - Financial Executives International
