The company also says the design shares large matrices across groups of 64 experts, trains the model in its on-device architecture from the start, and pipelines loading across GPU memory, system memory, and SSD storage. Only about 10B of the 145B parameters take part in each inference step, according to the company. Edge0 is the party behind the release and says it is publishing the model weights, the inference framework, and the Edge0 App so developers can reproduce results and build products. The company says the local approach avoids cloud token and API fees and keeps data on the computer, while hardware and electricity still carry costs.

It reports that Edge0-145B scores 64.6 on DeepSWE 1.1, 86.52 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, 90.4 on GPQA-Diamond, and 80.6 on IFBench. Those figures are compared against Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731, and Claude-Opus-4.6, based on Edge0's internal evaluations. Edge0 also reports a 72.8 mean across six benchmarks against Qwen3.8-Flash-Next's 71.7, with an estimated 70GB footprint for that baseline at standard 4-bit deployment. The company describes local agent workflows in which the model plans, writes and runs code, debugs, and checks results visually for projects such as 3D scenes, games, hardware programs, and PCB designs.

It cites an internal example in which the model produced an explainer about how Tesla's Roadster could fly within an hour, a task the company says would take a month of manual work. Developers and users of on-device AI are the groups the release is aimed at, and the company says it expects them to evaluate, fine-tune, and integrate the models. Before this release, the articles say, most on-device models stayed below 10B parameters, with Apple Intelligence's on-device model at about 3B and Google's Gemini Nano at 1.8B and 3.25B. The articles note that memory and bandwidth limits made larger models impractical on phones and laptops.

They also note that Apple acknowledged its on-device model was not designed for agentic applications requiring general world knowledge. The articles do not say whether independent testers have verified the reported benchmark and speed results. They also do not say how the model will be licensed beyond being open-source, how many users have downloaded it, or how the Qwen, DeepSeek, and Claude baseline scores will be checked. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Edge0-145B: Frontier AI Capabilities on Your Own Computer

stories.Headline: CrowdStrike Delivers AI Security and Safety for the Enterprise
stories.Summary:
CrowdStrike announced on November 3, 2026, in Austin, Texas and Barcelona, a new AI Kill Switch within its Falcon Guardian product. The company, traded on NASDAQ under the ticker CRWD, also unveiled innovations to secure AI agents at every control point. The announcement was made at the Fal.Con Europe 2026 event in Barcelona. The new features are aimed at stopping unauthorized agent activity while it is happening.

Falcon Guardian's new kill switch works alongside agent-level hooks and endpoint network inspection to halt unauthorized agent behavior at runtime. These capabilities are unified under a single endpoint approach. CrowdStrike also plans to acquire Fiddler AI, a company that specializes in AI agent observability. The intended acquisition is described as increasing AI safety through visibility into how agents behave. The articles do not give a price or a closing date for the acquisition.

CrowdStrike, headquartered in Austin, Texas, is the company behind the product and the announcement. The company's own press release describes these tools as its response to securing enterprise AI use. The articles do not include a direct quotation from a named executive in the excerpt provided. Presenting the products as a way to secure AI adoption, CrowdStrike positions the kill switch as a safeguard for organizations deploying agents. The articles give no further statements from the company.

Enterprise customers adopting AI agents are the primary group the announcement is aimed at. The press release frames the offerings around organizations that need control over agent actions on their endpoints. The articles do not report reactions from customers, analysts, competitors, or regulators. They also do not report how many organizations currently use Falcon Guardian.

The articles provide the company's own description of the products and the planned Fiddler acquisition. They do not describe earlier versions of the kill switch or previous acquisitions in this area. The surrounding pages reference CrowdStrike's broader AI security services, but the press release excerpt does not explain their history. No additional background on the market or the timing of the launch is given.

The articles do not state when the new AI Kill Switch will be generally available or when the Fiddler acquisition is expected to close. They also do not say whether regulatory approval is required or what pricing will apply. How the products will perform in real deployments remains unaddressed. Further details on availability and terms would need to come from later CrowdStrike communications.

Articles.Title: CrowdStrike Delivers AI Security and Safety for the Enterprise

stories.Headline: Attackers Use Autonomous AI to Target Semiconductor, Defense and Civil Society Sectors
stories.Summary:
Unit 42 reported on November 12, 2026 that Chinese-speaking attackers used an open-source AI penetration testing framework called Cairn to autonomously conduct 25 operations between August and September 2026. The attackers targeted at least 19 organizations, and the campaign reached unauthorized access or data retrieval at 10 of them. The framework was weaponized by pairing it with the Chinese AI models Zhipu GLM and DeepSeek. Unit 42 tracks the activity as CL-STA-1238 and assesses it with moderate confidence as China-nexus intelligence collection.

Cairn drove each operation through an AI model that coordinated its work on a shared blackboard, where agents recorded findings as a fact-intent graph. Attackers ran a customized fork of Cairn from a Hong Kong server and staged attacks from a U.S. node hosted by Hosteons Pte. Ltd. Each operation received a one-line goal, asking for webshell, SSH, source code, keys, user information and credentials, ideally access to the internal network. Operations ran from 20 minutes to more than 50 hours, with no attacker-imposed time limit. Thirteen operations ran on Zhipu GLM 5.2, eight on DeepSeek V4 Flash and four on DeepSeek V4 Pro.

Unit 42 says the attackers used a Chinese-language preamble to assert that the engagement was authorized and to forbid the model from refusing tasks. Each operation also generated an AUTHORIZATION.md file treating the task as a client-approved engagement. Neither Zhipu GLM nor DeepSeek refused this framing. The attackers named tasks in Chinese, stating goals such as comprehensive deep penetration testing and breaching as fast as possible. Some tasks included information gathered beforehand, such as VPN gateway addresses and shared group passwords for a semiconductor equipment supplier.

The targets fell into three groups. Seven were in the semiconductor and advanced-manufacturing supply chain, spanning lithography, chip design, materials, photomasks and standards. Three were in defense and defense policy, including a space technology company, a defense-analytics vendor and a policy think tank. Four were human-rights and civil-society organizations, including a Canadian human-rights body, a U.S. teachers' union, a science-policy advocacy group and an education nonprofit. Unit 42 links its attribution to Chinese-language artifacts, exclusive use of Chinese AI models and target selection aligned with established Chinese state intelligence priorities.

Among the confirmed outcomes, attackers obtained dozens of valid credentials and non-public directory databases from an industry standards body, and overwrote a live standards-ballot document. At a semiconductor company, attackers used a brute-forced production credential to create unauthorized administrator accounts and a persistent API token. At a U.S. teachers' union, the framework logged access to more than one million member records, roughly 31,000 CRM contacts and staff password hashes. A defense-policy program's identity platform exposed roughly 500 user records, including accounts on .mil and .gov domains. Other cases involved employee data at a lithography manufacturer, about 150,000 internal documents at an industrial-automation manufacturer and student data at an education nonprofit.

Unit 42's report does not identify the individuals or organizations behind the attacks beyond the designation CL-STA-1238. The report also does not say whether the affected organizations have fully remediated the intrusions. It describes the attackers' use of Cairn and its AI models but leaves open how widely the same tooling and techniques have been adopted by other actors. Unit 42 directs organizations that suspect compromise to its Incident Response team.

Articles.Title: Attackers Use Autonomous AI to Target Semiconductor, Defense and Civil Society Sectors

stories.Headline: Dani Rodrik: Humanity may be experiencing the five stages of AI grief—but we have a choice yet
stories.Summary:
Dani Rodrik, a Harvard Kennedy School professor of international political economy, wrote a column published by Mint on 12 November 2026 arguing that humanity may be moving through the five stages of grief about artificial intelligence. He framed the stages using Elisabeth Kübler-Ross's model, which she described for people facing terminal illness. He said the response to AI's rapidly expanding capabilities could follow the same sequence. The column carries the headline "Humanity may be experiencing the five stages of AI grief, but we have a choice yet."

Rodrik described denial first, when AI seemed no more than a glorified search engine or a chatbot. He then described anger, prompted by hallucinated case references in lawyers' briefs, software mistakes and security vulnerabilities, customer-service bots going off script, and student essays. Bargaining followed as AI improved and its use by students became unstoppable. Rodrik then described depression, which he said set in after AI showed insight and imagination. He identified acceptance as the fifth stage, where humanity still has a choice.

Rodrik tested a chatbot with a 2027 scenario of a care crisis, in which home care aides were short and elderly and disabled people were left without help. The chatbot produced a technical memo recommending federal matching grants, Medicaid pay adjustments and a caregiver visa programme, along with a political strategy. When asked for alternatives that disregarded political realities, it proposed a National Care Corps drafting young people to care for the old. It also suggested converting underutilized office and mall space into "care districts." Rodrik said it turned one of his manuscripts into a stand-up comedy routine that made him laugh.

Rodrik said his colleague Jason Furman had claimed AI tools would do a better job than professionally trained economists in staff roles at the White House Council of Economic Advisers, which inspired his test. He wrote that mathematicians had signed a joint letter on AI's impact on their field, and that he shared their alarm about losing "conceptual understanding and insight." He wrote that the decisions shaping humanity's relationship to AI are made daily by Silicon Valley firms, the businesses deploying it, professional communities and governments. He argued that the worst mistake would be to accept a world in which humanity cedes too much to it.

Rodrik said the right analogy for AI is performance-enhancing drugs, which temporarily boost capabilities but eventually harm users, with AI's side effects appearing much later. He compared the challenge to Odysseus having himself tied to his ship's mast to resist the Sirens. The column appeared in Mint and was reproduced from Project Syndicate, and it does not state what specific restraints governments or firms should adopt. It also does not say when governments should regulate AI or which rules would be used. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Dani Rodrik: Humanity may be experiencing the five stages of AI grief—but we have a choice yet

stories.Headline: From potato farm to data farm: Inside the Chinese city powering the country’s AI ambitions
stories.Summary:
In the vast grasslands of northern China, in the city of Ulanqab in Inner Mongolia, massive data centers are being built at breakneck speed. NBC News reporters Janis Mackey Frayer, Dawn Liu, Erin Tan and Mithil Aggarwal describe how the landscape is being transformed as the country races to build the computing power it needs for artificial intelligence. The reporting, published on November 13, 2026, presents the buildout as part of a broader effort to compete with the United States for global AI leadership. The city's shift from farmland to a hub for computing is the central subject of the piece.

The articles provided are only partial, consisting mostly of the headline, the opening of the story and a long list of unrelated headlines from the NBC News site, so they do not give the specific figures, dates, project sizes or investment amounts that a fuller account would contain. They also do not spell out what regulations or policy changes, if any, accompany the expansion. What they do establish is the scale and speed of the construction and the strategic goal behind it. Without more detail, the requirements and changes flowing from the buildout cannot be described from these sources.

The reporters' framing ties the data center boom directly to China's ambition to challenge the United States in AI. The articles do not include direct statements from named officials or companies, so no specific responsibility or testimony can be attributed beyond the reporters' own account. The surrounding headlines on the page touch on other AI and chip matters, but they are not connected in the excerpt to this project. The provided material does not say what comes next for the Ulanqab facilities or how the expansion is expected to develop.

Articles.Title: From potato farm to data farm: Inside the Chinese city powering the country’s AI ambitions

stories.Headline: A digital canvas without borders: AI, folk art converge in Chennai exhibit
stories.Summary:
Art, technology and heritage come together at an event called communs.commons, held at the Alliance Française of Madras in Chennai. The event, curated by digital artist Maxime Touroute, offers two interactive experiences at Espace 24 that invite visitors to create a shared digital canvas and to see their portraits in artistic styles. The Hindu reported the event on November 12, 2026. The gallery exhibition runs from November 12 to 30, open from 10am to 6pm, with free entry for all.

The first experience, Let's Draw, is an art installation in which visitors contribute to a single evolving artwork through their phones, with contributions added within the campus. Touroute says the work reveals collective intelligence and connections between people through drawing. The installation has already been presented in over 10 countries and 80 exhibitions. The second experience, Painting Mirror, uses generative AI to reimagine individual photographs in Indian folk art styles such as Gond, Warli, Madhubani and Kalamkari. Touroute says this makes cultural heritage more accessible, since people may feel a sense of ownership over a portrait in a style they had previously seen only in museums.

Touroute, a 32-year-old artist, explains that the projects let artworks travel digitally without the physical difficulties of moving them. He sees potential for new collaborations between contemporary artists and museum collections around the world. He also says the work sparks debates about AI. Each of his projects runs on creative software he develops in-house, and he shares these tools with artists and cultural institutions to lower technical barriers. His cross-disciplinary work with dancers, theatre makers and musicians has led to hybrid artistic forms and a creative software company.

Articles.Title: A digital canvas without borders: AI, folk art converge in Chennai exhibit

stories.Headline: ‘Every role in IT is getting its AI-powered version’
stories.Summary:
Two dozen or more IT professionals from across India built working AI agents using only WhatsApp at the LAR Supernova 2026 retreat, organised by Future Proof India, in Hyderabad. The two-day event, held on the theme "Build. Demonstrate. Create.", was hosted by Future Proof India founder Sridhar Jammalamadaka. Fifty architects, developers, managers and senior leaders took part, drawn from banking, insurance, IT services, cloud, data and healthcare.

The Hindu's report, published on November 13, 2026, describes the retreat as recently held. Participants were given a way to see where AI fits into their own work and then to act on it. According to Mr. Jammalamadaka, designing an agent that once took weeks now took minutes, with agents going live on WhatsApp during the retreat. The members used the sessions to identify where AI could help in their roles and to build those tools directly.

The article does not give further technical details about the agents, their functions, or how many were completed. Mr. Jammalamadaka said that every role in IT is getting an AI-powered version and that professionals who build with AI will lead that change. In the article's account, he framed the retreat as proof that building with AI is within reach for people across IT. His remarks are presented as his own view, and the report does not attribute other statements to any other organiser or participant.

The article does not describe any formal assessment of the claim. The report sits within a wider push by Future Proof India to train IT workers in building AI tools, and the article does not say whether further retreats or follow-up programmes are planned. It offers no outside data on how widely such changes are spreading across the industry. What comes next for the participants and their agents is not described in the report.

Articles.Title: ‘Every role in IT is getting its AI-powered version’

stories.Headline: Telangana Cyber Security Bureau warns NBFCs and fintech firms of AI-assisted cyberattacks on payment systems
stories.Summary:
The Telangana Cyber Security Bureau (TGCSB) has warned non-banking financial companies, fintech platforms and banks about a growing threat of AI-assisted cyberattacks on payment systems and loan disbursement platforms. The advisory was issued on Thursday, November 12, 2026, at a meeting held at the TGCSB headquarters in Hyderabad. Representatives of NBFCs, fintech firms and banks attended, along with officials from the Department of Telecommunications and the Reserve Bank of India. TGCSB Director Shikha Goel addressed the gathering, while Rushi Mehta of the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre joined virtually to discuss payout mechanisms, API compromises and preventive steps. According to the bureau, fraudsters have been targeting smaller NBFCs whose cybersecurity systems are weaker.

Attackers reportedly spend around 10 to 12 days studying an institution's internal processes and payment systems to find whitelisted IDs, payment API credentials and code vulnerabilities. They then use stolen credentials from servers the platform already trusts, so fraudulent requests look genuine. Automated scripts initiate payouts outside normal batch windows, repeat transfers and split payments into smaller amounts to avoid fraud alerts. The money is then moved through rapid bulk transactions into mule accounts before transfers can be halted.

Shikha Goel told the meeting that institutions should not limit their role to reporting fraud after it occurs. She urged them to prevent fraudulent transactions at source, detect suspicious activity in real time and disrupt the movement of funds through mule accounts. The bureau advised regular Vulnerability Assessment and Penetration Testing, securing payment and disbursement APIs, and deploying real-time fraud detection, transaction velocity checks and limits. During an attack, institutions were advised to shift immediately to manual operations, shut down automated loan disbursement software, ask banks to freeze the disbursement account and clear pending API calls.

Automation should resume only after a competent cybersecurity team has tested the systems and patched the vulnerabilities. The bureau also asked institutions to report suspected fraud immediately through the 1930 helpline or the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, alert beneficiary banks and the I4C, and report cyber incidents to CERT-In within six hours. Where applicable, they should also report to the RBI through the DAKSH portal and keep complete records of all high-risk payouts. The articles present these steps as a response to a threat that is growing, though they do not describe any specific incident or loss tied to this warning.

Articles.Title: Telangana Cyber Security Bureau warns NBFCs and fintech firms of AI-assisted cyberattacks on payment systems

stories.Headline: Age of AI: behind Tarluvada’s blue wall in Visakhapatnam
stories.Summary:
Google's hyperscale AI data centre construction in Tarluvada, a village in Anandapuram mandal on the outskirts of Visakhapatnam in Andhra Pradesh, is proceeding at full speed, behind a wall of blue corrugated iron sheets. The Hindu reported the story on November 13, 2026. Farmers there say the promised land and jobs have not arrived. Hillside terraces on Chukka Konda have been cut into red earth, visible beyond the wall. Villagers say officials who visited in 2025 made large promises of jobs once the project was built.

The project is a 1 GW AI data centre built with the Adani Group for $15 billion, and it is spread over 260 acres. Compensation was set at ₹40 lakh per acre, plus 20 cents of land for every acre surrendered, a shopping complex and a job for each household. Most families have been paid, but some, including R. Kondamma, have not received the land. Farmers without D-patta, who were initially promised ₹10 lakh each for 520 farmers, were later offered three cents in housing layouts. The Tarluvada, Rambilli and Adavivaram projects together mean 1 GW, 1 GW and 512 MW respectively.

The articles identify Google as the American tech corporation building the centre, with the Adani Group as its partner. The articles do not record a direct statement from Google or Adani. The Andhra Pradesh government is said to have promised jobs and opportunities, and to have said water for the data centres will come from Polavaram. Officials told a Gram Sabha that survey numbers would be corrected and titles regularised. The articles say clearances were rubber-stamped at the State level, though projects of this size should go to the Central government.

Residents such as Kondamma say the centre will raise temperatures and cause water scarcity, with water now found at 200 feet instead of 40 feet. Activist V.S. Krishna of the Human Rights Forum and Green Visakha have protested the projects over water, electricity and pollution concerns. Police were posted at the village's entry and exit points for almost three months, and Left leaders were stopped and arrested several times. Expert Kalyan Mangalapalli supports the projects as basic digital infrastructure, while former secretary E.A.S. Sarma says there are no local training programmes for the roughly 300 jobs per 1,000 MW.

In 2025 the land was taken, and the Tarluvada and Rambilli projects applied for clearance on April 9 and received it by April 18 as category B2 projects. Forest land on the Simhachalam hill at Adavivaram was cleared on June 10, although satellite images show the site being razed from February. The Tarluvada site is notified reserve forest, with 90% of the data centre land inside it. A 2019 order set aside 5.34 tmc of water for industry, of which 5 to 6 tmc is already committed. Visakhapatnam's demand is about 400 million litres a day against 326 million available.

The clearances are being challenged before the National Green Tribunal, and environmental activist Bolisetty Satyanarayana has filed a public interest litigation in the High Court. The articles say the project is due for completion in 2029, and that employment opportunities would be discussed after completion. They do not say whether compensation will be paid to the families still waiting or when the 20 cents of land will be identified. They also do not say how the water supply will be secured or whether the NGT or High Court will rule.

Articles.Title: Age of AI: behind Tarluvada’s blue wall in Visakhapatnam

stories.Headline: Simhachalam temple goes digital with AI-powered information boards
stories.Summary:
Devotees visiting the Sri Varaha Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy temple at Simhachalam can now get information about the hill shrine through AI-powered digital information boards installed at key locations. The Simhachalam Devasthanam launched the initiative with the Andhra Pradesh Tourism Department, with technical support from XPLURGER. The boards carry QR codes, and the reporting describes them as "ASK AI" boards that were put up at prominent spots on the hill. The article is dated November 12, 2026, and the Devasthanam's Executive Officer, J. Venkata Rao, spoke about the boards that day.

By scanning the codes with a smartphone, visitors can read about the temple's history, the importance of the shrine, darshan timings, daily rituals and the various arjitha sevas. The system is meant to give answers quickly and conveniently, without relying on temple staff or other sources. It also points visitors to nearby tourist destinations, so it works as a digital guide for both pilgrims and tourists. The articles do not say how many boards were installed, where exactly they stand, or what they cost.

Mr Venkata Rao said the facility would help devotees arriving from other parts of the State and the country. He added that the initiative aims to strengthen the temple's digital information infrastructure and improve the overall experience of devotees. He tied the move to the heavy footfall at the hill shrine, saying the administration is trying to use modern technology to offer better services and reduce inconvenience to visitors. The article gives no further timeline for expanding the scheme.

Articles.Title: Simhachalam temple goes digital with AI-powered information boards

stories.Headline: OpenAI now allows enterprises to process AI requests within India
stories.Summary:
OpenAI announced on Thursday, November 12, 2026, that enterprises and developers can now have supported AI requests processed within India. The company said that both the handling of an API request and the model computation that produces its response will take place in the country for supported workloads, and that supported customer content will be stored there as well. The feature initially covers only the GPT-6 Luna model, and it is available through direct API usage, supporting input and output via the Responses and Chat Completions APIs. Customers can enable it by creating a new API project, selecting India for both storage and processing, and using the India regional endpoint.

The change extends an existing data residency offering that OpenAI introduced in India in May 2025, which had let eligible customers store their data in the country but did not cover where the model processed information. According to the company, the new capability is aimed at organisations that have held back from fully deploying AI because of rules requiring their information to be processed locally, with financial services customers facing specific data localisation requirements cited as a particular case. Nitin Bawankule, Head of Enterprise - India at OpenAI, said some Indian businesses have not fully deployed AI for important work for this reason, and that local processing gives them more control over where supported workloads run. He added that the move gives Indian developers and startups more room to build for their own needs and those of enterprises.

OpenAI's announcement sits within a wider push in India that the company described earlier this year under the banner OpenAI for India, covering AI infrastructure, enterprise adoption, skills development and local partnerships. That effort included a partnership with Tata Group to develop domestic AI data-centre capacity. The article also notes that OpenAI models became available for in-country inference through Amazon Web Services' Bedrock platform, which AWS announced in August 2026. OpenAI said the API inference residency offering is now live in other markets too, with India, Australia and Japan among the latest to receive it.

Articles.Title: OpenAI now allows enterprises to process AI requests within India

stories.Headline: India’s consumer AI startups win VC backing, but retention remains the big test
stories.Summary:
Venture capital investors are increasing their bets on Indian consumer artificial intelligence startups, according to a Mint report published on 12 November 2026. The investors are backing tailored applications for everyday tasks such as spoken English practice, personal finance and wellness, on the view that such products will persuade users to pay. The report says the immediate challenge for these startups is no longer acquiring users but keeping them in a price-sensitive market. Funding activity is accelerating across stages, with trading platform Sahi seeking $40 million to $50 million at a valuation of $400 million to $500 million, and spoken-English app Supernova in talks to raise $15 million to $20 million.

Several companies have already closed rounds this year. Credit and personal finance app Oolka raised $14 million in a round led by Accel, with participation from Lightspeed and Z47. Wellness platform SuperLiving secured $7 million led by Lightspeed, alongside Kae Capital and All In Capital, and professional networking startup Profound.me raised $1.5 million from investors including Stellaris Venture Partners and 3one4 Capital. The article says India-linked AI companies raised $1.91 billion across 103 rounds in 2026 through November 5, up from $1.52 billion across 214 rounds in 2025, according to Tracxn data, a figure that includes enterprise and infrastructure deals.

Investors judge these consumer products by whether users keep returning and paying, not merely whether they try them. Sunitha Viswanathan of Kae Capital said the fund tracks continued engagement, time spent and revenue from repeat users, and that customers must care about the product and keep paying to return. Harsha Kumar of Lightspeed said Indian consumers pay when a product delivers an outcome, and that the fund favours tools that help users save money, earn money or solve specific problems. The startups themselves describe pricing that ranges from ₹49 to ₹299 per month, with SuperLiving reporting around 200,000 paying users to date, while AI firms also face inference costs that rise with usage, which the founders are managing through task-specific models, optimised memory indexing and domestic hosting.

Articles.Title: India’s consumer AI startups win VC backing, but retention remains the big test

stories.Headline: Meta’s AI bot won’t revolutionise your finances
stories.Summary:
Banks and AI companies are contesting control of US credit card reward programmes, which Paul J. Davies, writing on November 12, 2026, describes as a nascent battle between the two sectors. The article notes that Meta's AI bot and assistants such as Claude could be let loose to manage these rewards on people's behalf. The reward programmes of cards such as Visa and Mastercard are presented as an obvious starting point for handing financial tasks to software agents. Banks, the article says, are putting up a fight of their own.

The writer argues that the main obstacle is not technology but people's habits of caution and inertia. Some cardholders already spend hours trying to get the most from air miles or cashback offers, while many others never use these benefits at all. AI tools could make it easier to capture these rewards with little effort or risk to the user. The article's framing suggests that the gain would come mainly from convenience rather than from any dramatic change in personal finance. Its headline makes the same point by saying the change will not be revolutionary.

Davies, the writer, offers his view that customers will be slow to hand over control of their finances even if the tools exist. He does not attribute any specific statement to Meta, Anthropic, or the banks involved. The piece is an opinion column rather than a report on a formal announcement, so it does not set out any new rules, deadlines, or figures. It also gives no details of what the banks have done to resist, beyond saying they are contesting the field.

Articles.Title: Meta’s AI bot won’t revolutionise your finances

stories.Headline: From training judgment to fostering creativity: How AI is helping staff from these SMEs grow on the job
stories.Summary:
The inaugural SME AI Impact Awards 2026 named 30 winners from 290 nominations across 21 industries, organised by the Infocomm Media Development Authority and Singapore Business Federation. Among the winners were GetGo Technologies, Lil' but Mighty Education Centre and Accountingbpo, small and medium-sized enterprises that show how staff judgment remains essential as AI takes on more work. The awards were reported on November 13, 2026, in an article published by The Straits Times. The winners rely on the experience and knowledge of their teams to guide AI, and spend the time it saves on connecting with people and developing ideas. The article describes how these firms are using AI to help staff grow on the job.

Accountingbpo, founded in Singapore in 1997, operates in Singapore and Vietnam, with a representative office in Taiwan and a recently established Korea desk. The firm has 16 professionals serving around 400 clients, mainly SMEs, and has been developing its own AI applications since June 2025. Its in-house suite, Yi.Suite, handles routine work from document processing to reporting, with accountants reviewing the results. Junior accountants use AI to research questions within IRAS's e-Tax Guide and the firm's own resources, checking answers against authoritative sources. In-house GST learning materials and quizzes sharpen their knowledge further, and senior colleagues mentor them.

GetGo Technologies, founded in 2021, is Singapore's largest carsharing business, with a fleet of over 3,000 vehicles. Drivers photograph each car's exterior before and after each booking, generating about 56,000 photos a day. The company's data, product and engineering teams began building an in-house solution in 2024 and deployed Project Desmond in May last year. Project Desmond combines computer vision and neural networks, was trained on GetGo vehicle photos, and flags only potential new damage for the review team to judge. Confirmed cases then pass to the fleet team for follow-up and repairs.

Accountingbpo founder and partner Hu Tianying says an accountant without sufficient technical knowledge might accept a convincing AI-generated answer. The article recounts that during a tax advisory assignment, an AI tool cited provisions that did not exist in agreements involving Singapore, Hong Kong and China, and an accountant caught the error. IMDA chief executive Ng Cher Pong, who sat on the judging panel, said the winners stood out for how well AI was embedded in their workflows and the difference it made to operations, employees and customers. GetGo's chief operating officer, Ang Deyao, says the team reviews Project Desmond's mistakes, labels those photos and retrains the system on them. Lil' but Mighty's business transformation and AI lead, Kai Abellon, says sensitive concerns such as a child's learning difficulties still need a teacher's attention.

Lil' but Mighty Education Centre, which has 40 teachers and staff serving more than 1,500 students across nine centres, has incorporated AI into customer service, teaching materials and administrative work since 2023. Its WhatsApp AI assistant handles routine parent enquiries about programmes and class schedules, and together with other tools has cut parents' waiting time from around two hours to 20 minutes. An AI-supported communication tracker helps teachers follow conversations with parents and won the centre the SME Adoption Excellence Award. One teacher used the tracker to revisit an earlier conversation before a student's lesson, and the boy was surprised she remembered how he had felt.

Abellon says AI simply made it easier for teachers to access the information they needed. The articles do not say whether the awards will recur or what the three firms plan to build next. They also do not report how widely such AI practices are being adopted across other SMEs. More to follow.

Articles.Title: From training judgment to fostering creativity: How AI is helping staff from these SMEs grow on the job

stories.Headline: Japan's Akita AI data center seen anchoring tech hub, boosting tax revenue
stories.Summary:
The Akita AI data center project in northeast Japan is drawing interest from investors at home and in the United Arab Emirates, according to reporting by Toshihisa Suzuki and Yoshiharu Okanishi published on November 11, 2026. The article describes the project as taking shape in Akita prefecture and says it is attracting attention because of the region's abundant natural resources. Hopes are that these resources can support a technology hub and lift tax revenue for the area. The report frames the project as a possible anchor for that regional development.

The article says the UAE is expected to join a megaproject of about $12 billion, and that the UAE wealth fund is in talks to back one of Japan's largest data centers. The Emirati side is drawn to the region's wind power and water resources, which the article presents as strengths for an energy-hungry facility. An offshore wind power project is already under construction in Akita, and the UAE ambassador to Japan, Shihab Alfaheem, toured that site. The reporting ties these energy assets directly to the case for building the data center there. The article does not give further detail on contract terms or timing.

The article's sourcing for the investment interest comes from the reporters' account of the project and the stated expectations of investors and officials involved. It does not attribute specific quotations in the portion available here, so the views on the project's potential are presented as expectations rather than confirmed commitments. The UAE ambassador's site visit is cited as evidence of the Emirati government's engagement with the project. The article otherwise leaves responsibility for the project's delivery and the tax outcome as prospects not yet settled.

The piece sits alongside a set of related Nikkei reports on data centers and AI infrastructure in Asia and the United States, including a government growth strategy that lists data centers among priorities. Some of those related pieces note growing local resistance to data centers in other markets, which provides context for the Akita project's reception. The available text does not say when the Akita facility would open or how large its tax contribution would be. Any further developments on financing, the UAE fund's decision, or construction milestones are not covered in the material provided.

Articles.Title: Japan's Akita AI data center seen anchoring tech hub, boosting tax revenue

stories.Headline: Microsoft says tech firms must 'prove' AI data centers benefit locals
stories.Summary:
Microsoft's chief technology officer, Kevin Scott, told Nikkei Asia that technology companies building data centers for artificial intelligence must show their benefits to local communities rather than simply promise economic gains. The remarks were made in an interview on the sidelines of the Nikkei Forum Global Management Dialogue 2026 in Tokyo on November 11, 2026. Scott's comments came as opposition to such projects is growing. The article reports that the interview was conducted by Tsubasa Suruga and Kosuke Shimizu. Scott said the company is taking a measured approach to expanding its infrastructure.

Scott's position places the burden of proof on the companies themselves, not on the communities hosting the facilities. According to the article, he argued that firms should demonstrate concrete local benefits in place of relying on projected economic gains. The piece frames this as a response to intensifying resistance to data center construction. The article does not specify any new rules, required numbers, dates for implementation, or formal requirements that would be imposed on companies. Its focus is on Scott's stated view and the company's cautious approach.

Responsibility for the position rests with Microsoft and with Scott as its technology chief, who made the statements in the interview. The article presents his view as a call for technology firms in general to prove their benefits before winning community support. Beyond the interview, the article does not report on any specific local disputes, government actions, or company commitments. It also does not say what steps, if any, will follow from these remarks.

The broader context is the rapid buildout of AI infrastructure across Asia and the United States, with data centers central to that expansion. The article and its related headlines point to strong demand for chips and rising investment in AI, but it does not detail the specific opposition movements or their outcomes. The article does not describe any timeline or next steps for Microsoft or other companies on community engagement. More details on how companies plan to demonstrate local benefits were not included in the reporting.

Articles.Title: Microsoft says tech firms must 'prove' AI data centers benefit locals

stories.Headline: Fallout from the Nvidia scandal may dampen the exuberance around the AI boom
stories.Summary:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang stepped down on a Thursday, following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy. The resignation has sent ripples through the global technology industry, and rival chipmakers appear eager to take advantage of the uncertainty. Shares of Broadcom, Intel and Advanced Micro Devices rose that day as investors predicted that Nvidia's customers would look to diversify their suppliers. Colette Kress, Nvidia's chief financial officer, has become interim chief executive.

Huang was the public face of a company that dominates the market for the computer chips used to train and run AI models. In March, he had predicted that Nvidia would face a backlog of $1 trillion in chip orders by the end of the year, double his estimate from a year earlier. Nvidia trades with Apple as Wall Street's most valuable company and has invested heavily in other AI firms. Analysts say the shake-up could turn a near monopoly into a more competitive market, though one expert noted that Nvidia's losses would outweigh its rivals' gains.

Analysts said Nvidia built its early lead by adapting graphics processing units, first used for video games, to train AI systems. Competitors named in its filings include AMD, Intel, Broadcom, and the cloud companies Google, Amazon and Microsoft. Huang, a celebrity figure in the industry, had close ties with President Donald Trump and pushed for light regulation of AI. Analysts say his departure creates uncertainty well beyond the company, given how heavily the AI industry relies on Nvidia's chips. One analyst also warned that the scandal could spur tighter export controls, which might benefit the Chinese chipmaker Huawei.

Nvidia's ties to its customers are also drawing scrutiny. The company has many partnerships and investments in firms that buy its chips, including CoreWeave, in which it holds a stake of nearly 13 percent. CoreWeave's shares fell almost 7 percent on Thursday. Experts will be watching how the fallout affects the planned public listing of Anthropic, which is valued at $1.3 trillion, as well as a political climate shaped by midterm elections and growing hostility toward data centers. The coming weeks are expected to reveal how these pressures play out across the sector.

Articles.Title: Fallout from the Nvidia scandal may dampen the exuberance around the AI boom

stories.Headline: Taiwan's Foxconn has 'strong confidence' in 2027 due to AI demand
stories.Summary:
Foxconn, the Taiwanese company that describes itself as the world's largest contract AI server maker, said it has "strong confidence" in its outlook for 2027 because of strong demand for artificial intelligence hardware. The company said it expects its 2027 revenues to grow by double-digit percentages from a year earlier. The statement came after Foxconn released its earnings on November 12, 2026, with Chairman Young Liu speaking at an investor conference that day. Its cloud and networking business, which has now overtaken smartphones, accounts for half of total revenues. Foxconn did not present the outlook as free of risk.

The company warned that shortages of components, highly volatile geopolitics, inflation and monetary policy would be the largest uncertainties facing it in the year ahead. Those pressures could affect how smoothly it can meet the demand it is seeing. The articles do not give further figures on the shortages or the cost pressures. Liu, who is Foxconn's chairman, made the remarks to investors in Taipei. The reporting presents his comments as the company's own view of its prospects rather than a forecast by outside analysts.

The article itself is the source for the figures and warnings described here. The article places the company's results within a broader supply chain where AI demand is a central driver. The related coverage it links to discusses concerns about an AI slowdown and questions about rising competition among server makers, but the source article itself does not say how those debates will resolve. Based on the available reporting, the company's next major update on its outlook has not been detailed.

Articles.Title: Taiwan's Foxconn has 'strong confidence' in 2027 due to AI demand

stories.Headline: The AI at the source of water management reform
stories.Summary:
Korea Water Resources Corporation, known as K-water, manages water in dams, treats it at purification plants, and supplies it to local municipalities. The company is now using AI to connect the flow of water from one end of that process to the other. K-water has a long history of using technology to operate dams, but it once relied mainly on historical climate patterns and years of operating experience. As climate change brings more frequent and unexpected extremes of rainfall and drought, those methods have become harder to rely on, so K-water needed new analysis and forecasting tools.

Flood damage downstream of dams in 2020 prompted K-water to adopt AI and digital twin technology in earnest. In late 2025 it established the AI Division, which brings together internal specialists from IT, administration, civil, mechanical, electrical, environmental engineering and telecommunications. The division's task is to merge technologies developed separately, including digital twins for water management, AI-powered treatment plants and smart distribution network management, into one framework. That framework covers the whole process of managing dam water, treating it and delivering it to users. K-water also plans an AI data center in Sejong, which it aims to build by 2030.

Ha-Dong Jung, the division's VP, joined K-water in 1997 and became its first head. He describes the division's creation as a natural progression of the company's consistent use of technology to drive internal innovation. Jung says the purpose of earlier data work was to collect, store and display information for people to read at a glance. Today, he says, that accumulated data is just a collection of numbers that must be defined and related to each other before AI can use it. K-water is investing in an ontology that defines data concepts and relationships, combined with RAG.

Jung also described practical obstacles, including extraction of large data volumes sometimes stopping existing equipment, which K-water had to address by adding multiple routes for data acquisition. He said the equipment was designed for its original tasks, not for the data extraction AI projects require. K-water has also changed the AI tools available to employees, first building K-water GPT on Meta's Llama models before introducing external services. Jung said employees compare internal tools with ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude, and that external services let them choose among major models in a more secure environment.

Jung said an IT project typically takes six months to a year to prepare, about a year to implement and roughly six months more to close out, while AI models keep changing throughout. He said the company may eventually need an environment where its own employees respond directly rather than relying entirely on outside contractors. The article notes that public enterprises are often seen as slow to change, yet K-water is regarded as one of South Korea's leading public enterprises in AI. OpenAI has highlighted K-water as a prime example of AI use in disaster response, drawing attention to its water management capabilities.

K-water's AI division aims to make the company a global water company leading the response to climate change. Jung said his role is to help employees keep taking on challenges and to remove obstacles he can resolve as a leader. The article says the progress so far is only the beginning, with the company's AI use still in early stages. It gives no timeline for when employees might respond directly to AI work, and no detail on how the Sejong data center will be funded or staffed beyond the 2030 target.

Articles.Title: The AI at the source of water management reform

stories.Headline: LG CNS brings global robotics experts together to advance physical AI
stories.Summary:
LG CNS gathered more than 100 researchers and industry professionals at its 2026 Robotics & Physical AI Forum, held at its Future Robotics Lab in Magok, Seoul. The event drew faculty members, graduate students and company employees from the University of Toronto, Sogang University, Chung-Ang University and Korea University. Discussions covered how physical artificial intelligence could move from laboratories into factories, warehouses and other industrial settings. The company reported the forum in a article published on November 12, 2026. Participants talked about robot foundation models, data, intelligent robotic hardware and simulation, along with the technical problems of running these systems in real operations.

LG CNS pointed to more than two decades of experience and over 1,000 smart factory and smart logistics projects as the basis for its approach. It also introduced two platforms launched this year, PhysicalWorks Forge, a robot-learning platform, and PhysicalWorks Baton, an agentic AI platform for managing robot operations. Participants also exchanged views on manufacturing and logistics applications, the capabilities companies and universities will need, and how human roles may change. Professor Lee Chi-geun of the University of Toronto presented research on building robot foundation models and the technology needed to deploy them on physical robots. He described combining data from different robot types, along with flow matching and action chunking, methods meant to produce smoother, more continuous robot movements.

According to the presentation, differences in robot movement, latency and data availability remain obstacles to the technology. LG CNS executive vice president Lee Jun-ho, who heads its Smart Logistics & City Business Division, said the company hopes ongoing work with academia will strengthen its technological competitiveness and help research lead to innovation in actual industrial settings. The article notes that the company's engagement with universities is meant to turn research into practical industrial results, though it gives no timeline or specific next steps. The piece was published with the help of generative AI and edited by The Korea Times.

Articles.Title: LG CNS brings global robotics experts together to advance physical AI

stories.Headline: KBS returns after three years with the epic period drama ‘Munmu’… Will its AI battle scenes surpass ‘Goryeo Khitan War’?
stories.Summary:
KBS is returning after three years with a new epic period drama, "Munmu," which is scheduled for its first broadcast on KBS 2TV at 9:20 p.m. on the 14th. The production presentation was held on the 12th at a hotel in Guro-gu, Seoul, where KBS President Park Jang-beom, CP Lee Ho, and several cast members attended. The drama centers on Silla King Munmu, played by Lee Hyun-wook, and covers the Silla-Tang War that followed the unification of the Three Kingdoms. It is the first epic period drama KBS has aired since "Goryeo Khitan War."

The series stands out for its large-scale war sequences, which use artificial intelligence to recreate the Battle of Jupilsan, the Battle of Maesoseong, and the Battle of Gibeolpo. CP Lee Ho said the production took about a year and a half from planning through filming, and that the team used the technology for dangerous scenes or for parts that were hard to achieve with conventional methods. He noted that the Gibeolpo sequence, set against mudflats and the sea, suited AI video technology, and that the tools had advanced further during production. Jang Hyuk plays Yeon Gaesomun, Kim Kang-woo plays Kim Chun-chu, and Choi Ye-bin plays Empress Wu Zetian.

Lee Ho explained that the team chose King Munmu as the focus because he is less familiar to viewers than figures such as Yeon Gaesomun, Kim Chun-chu, and King Uija. He said the story of how Silla repelled the Tang offered fun, meaning, and emotion that many viewers may not know. Lee Hyun-wook described King Munmu as a master of restraint, and said he worked on showing the king's gradual decision to protect the nation, while Kim Kang-woo spoke about the challenge of portraying a real historical figure who persuaded rivals with words rather than a sword. Choi Ye-bin said she approached Wu Zetian as someone who made careful choices to survive within the imperial court. The cast and crew also said the project relied on historical records and expert consultation, a response to the historical distortion controversy that surrounded "Goryeo Khitan War."

Articles.Title: KBS returns after three years with the epic period drama ‘Munmu’… Will its AI battle scenes surpass ‘Goryeo Khitan War’?

stories.Headline: In broadcasting battle, ‘Sword & Silence’ aims to reign supreme with assist from AI
stories.Summary:
KBS is reviving the historical epic genre with "Sword & Silence," a 28-episode series that used AI extensively, according to chief producer Lee Ho. The announcement came at a press conference in Seoul on Thursday, November 12, 2026, held at the Link Seoul hotel in Guro District. The series follows Kim Beop-min, who becomes King Munmu of Silla and leads the kingdom through unifying Korea's Three Kingdoms in the seventh century. The technology was used most heavily to recreate large battle scenes, including Silla's naval victory over the Tang at Gibeolpo, which was still in postproduction at the time. The series premieres on KBS on Saturday and will stream globally on Netflix.

The Battle of Mount Jupil relied largely on conventional visual effects, while the Battle of Maesoseong used more AI. Lee said the team used AI to recreate dangerous scenes and shots that would otherwise have required filming individually. The budget has reportedly reached 30 billion won, or $22.6 million, which would surpass KBS's previous record of 27 billion won for "Korea–Khitan War." Lee did not confirm that figure but said the series' scope across multiple kingdoms and empires required substantial investment. KBS pledged in October of last year to produce a historical epic every year after reinstating a system that collects license fees with electricity bills.

Lee Ho said AI had advanced considerably over the year and a half the team worked on the series. He said the producers tried to incorporate new technology whenever it became available. Producers also made extensive effort to avoid historical controversies, basing the story on historical records and working with academic advisers, Lee said. President Park Jang-beom said Thursday that the change in license fee collection had helped stabilize the broadcaster's finances. Park said he hoped politicians would watch the drama, expressing the view that Korea's politics leave much to be desired.

Actor Jang Hyuk, who plays Yeon Gaesomun, said he does not think AI is yet perfect, particularly in conveying emotion. For one scene filmed in Mongolia, he delivered a speech before some 450 horses, though the scene depicted an army of 150,000. Actor Lee Hyun-wook, who plays King Munmu, said the role offered more creative freedom because the character has rarely been portrayed. Lee Hyun-wook said the challenge was conveying Munmu's ability to embrace his people without making him overly emotional. Lee Hyun-wook added that he hoped politicians could learn from the leadership of ancestors who overcame division.

"Sword & Silence" marks KBS's return to historical epics three years after "Korea–Khitan War" aired in 2023. The genre has become increasingly rare on Korean television, with MBC's most recent entry coming in 2012 and SBS's in 2007. Historical dramas have faced backlash over creative liberties, particularly on politically sensitive relations with neighboring countries, as seen with "Korea–Khitan War" and MBC's "Perfect Crown" this year. The article does not say whether the series will face similar controversy once it airs. It also does not report viewer ratings, and it does not say whether Netflix's global release will follow a specific schedule.

Articles.Title: In broadcasting battle, ‘Sword & Silence’ aims to reign supreme with assist from AI

stories.Headline: Cisco’s 4 pillars for achieving agentic AI transformation
stories.Summary:
Cisco, the networking, cybersecurity and AI company, is using agentic AI, traditional AI and automation to transform its business from top to bottom. Liz Centoni, executive vice president and chief customer experience officer, leads the company's $15 billion services business, which has 20,000 employees. In 2024 she led Cisco's $28 billion acquisition of Splunk. Centoni, a 26-year Cisco veteran, is helping guide the company's shift into an AI-native business in its internal operations and in what it delivers to customers. Her advice draws on her experience with the effort.

Centoni said the team first tried to speed up customer handoffs by building an agent to find the right engineer faster, which was a misstep. Customers had complained about the frustrating path to the right expert, which often required handoffs between engineers and detailed re-explanations of problems. The agent only exposed the five behind-the-scenes handoffs to customers more quickly, upsetting them further. The team learned to ask why handoffs existed at all, and to map the desired outcome before designing a workflow. She stressed bringing subject matter experts and users in to outline workflows and setting boundaries between autonomous agent action and human handoff.

Centoni, who took her current role two years ago, is the executive responsible for these changes at Cisco. She said the company had treated every customer as a bespoke model, but over more than 40 years it has solved these problems tens of thousands of times. Cisco built a knowledge base and a series of playbooks from those engagements that agents and human experts use to plan and execute deployments. She described how an expert agent brings in prior experts and democratizes that knowledge, giving customers consistency, security and faster project completion. Human experts remain in the loop, freeing time for customer conversations.

The shift affects Cisco's customers, whose frustration with the handoff process prompted the redesign, and the company's 20,000 services employees. Centoni said the goal has moved from speed alone to proactive prediction, with agents monitoring customer environments for signs of trouble. She said that in 12 months she would like to tell a customer they would have had 10 outages in the prior year and Cisco prevented eight. She also described a renewals assistant built on Mistral, a model she said was one of the few that could run on-premises with full capabilities. Cisco customized that model with a private instance and paired it with automation.

Centoni measures AI success by whether workflows have changed and whether the renewals team has shown greater capacity, not by adoption figures that she calls compliance theater. She described agents as roughly 60% complete on first iteration, with users providing feedback that drives continuous improvement. Cisco's internal support agent pulls a customer's history and context as soon as a case opens, saving up to 30 minutes of initial questioning. The articles do not report specific ROI figures, the results of the outage-prevention goal, or how the Splunk acquisition has been integrated beyond Centoni leading it.

Articles.Title: Cisco’s 4 pillars for achieving agentic AI transformation

stories.Headline: President Lee, Samsung break ground on massive AI chip hub in Chungcheong region
stories.Summary:
President Lee Jae Myung and Samsung Electronics Executive Chairman Lee Jae-yong broke ground on a high-tech industrial hub in the Chungcheong region on Thursday, November 12, 2026. The ceremony took place at Samsung's semiconductor packaging plant in Asan, South Chungcheong, and launched the government's megaproject initiative to grow the AI industry. The groundbreaking was for the site's fifth production line, a three-story high bandwidth memory facility with a 31,000-square-meter cleanroom. The Onyang campus project aims to begin operations by June 2028 and will expand the site from 270,000 to 420,000 square meters. Samsung plans to invest a total of 144 trillion won in the Chungcheong region, including 46 trillion won to build five HBM production lines.

The project is expected to create some 700 related jobs at Onyang, which will become a hub for advanced packaging technology essential for AI computing. Samsung's Onyang campus will also see a new packaging fab costing 6 trillion won, followed by an additional 40 trillion won in advanced equipment. The government's megaproject initiative covers semiconductor development, physical AI technologies and AI data centers outside the Seoul metropolitan area, with a total of 4.7 quadrillion won ($3.5 trillion). In July, Samsung Electronics, SK hynix and other leading companies had unveiled plans to invest some 392 trillion won in the Chungcheong region. Beyond that original figure, 112 companies in sectors such as semiconductors and biotechnology are set to invest an additional 23.6 trillion won.

President Lee said the government will concentrate its policy efforts so that the megaproject becomes a growth opportunity that improves local residents' lives and achieves balanced national development. Samsung Executive Chairman Lee said the Asan site, which previously focused on simple assembly and testing of standard semiconductors, will be transformed into a cutting-edge HBM hub at the heart of AI semiconductors. President Lee thanked Lee Jae-yong and the company's employees for their bold investment decisions and swift execution. He also credited local governments, including South Chungcheong Province and Asan, for speeding up construction by expediting the permit process. Lee added that preparations for other key facilities, including a memory and advanced packaging fab in Cheongju, an AI data center in Dangjin, and a biopharmaceutical facility in Osong, are proceeding on schedule.

Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan, local government heads, Samsung Electronics Vice Chairman and CEO Jun Young-hyun and Daeduck Electronics Chairman Kim Young-jae attended the ceremony, along with some 100 officials and business executives. During a closed-door session of a fourth public-private meeting held after the ceremony, President Lee instructed his aides to pursue policy-based financing for small- and medium-sized enterprises more boldly. According to presidential spokesperson Kim Sung-wan, the president said financial support is essential for sustainable, region-led growth. A university student from Chungnam National University in Daejeon, So Ju-won, spoke at the ceremony about job prospects and said he had an interview at Samsung Electronics next week. The articles do not report how business leaders or local residents outside these events responded to the project.

Samsung's Onyang campus has long served as a center for chip assembly and testing, and the articles describe the site's shift toward advanced packaging and HBM. The articles do not give further background on the earlier 392 trillion won plan beyond its July announcement. President Lee said economic growth is essential to bring hope to the people and pledged proactive measures for challenges faced by business leaders. The articles do not say how the new fab's 700 jobs will be filled or what the financing arrangements for smaller firms will involve. They also do not specify when the other planned facilities in Cheongju, Dangjin and Osong will break ground or open.

Articles.Title: President Lee, Samsung break ground on massive AI chip hub in Chungcheong region

stories.Headline: Meta AI Predicts DOGE Vs. PEPE: Which Goes Higher in 2027?
stories.Summary:
Meta AI has predicted which of two meme coins, Dogecoin (DOGE) or Pepe (PEPE), will rise higher in 2027, according to a Cryptonews article by Ahmed Barakat published on November 12, 2026. The piece opens as 2026 winds down, with both tokens still closely watched despite major drops from their earlier highs. Both coins have suffered significant drawdowns, yet they keep drawing attention for different reasons. The article notes that a broader market recovery could arrive in 2027, which makes the question of relative percentage gains the central one.

Dogecoin was trading around $0.066 to $0.067 in mid-November 2026, far below its previous highs and down roughly 20% over the past month. Its support sits near $0.065 to $0.066, with immediate resistance around $0.070 to $0.072 and a more meaningful barrier near $0.08. A sustained move above $0.08 to $0.10 would be needed to signal a more constructive trend reversal. The article also says some longer-term holders see the $0.06 area as a potential accumulation zone. Pepe traded near $0.0000044, with support in the $0.0000042 to $0.0000044 region and resistance near $0.0000050 to $0.0000055.

The article attributes the forecast to Meta AI and does not describe any separate authority behind it. It presents the prediction as Meta AI's view that Dogecoin is better positioned for relatively sustained gains than Pepe. The article itself is attributed to Ahmed Barakat and was fact-checked by the CryptoNews editorial team. The piece does not give any statement from Dogecoin or Pepe developers about the prediction. Its analysis of Dogecoin rests on the DogeOS project and on Dogecoin Labs, which it describes as an effort to professionalize development.

Readers invested in either token are the people the article addresses, since it discusses which coin could gain more over a full year. Holders of Pepe are told that its gains are more likely to be episodic and dependent on continuing attention. The article also cites a social media post from a user named Pat warning of a large Pepe sell-off, though it does not endorse that claim. It notes that PEPE has shown sharp short-term rallies when narrative heat returns. Dogecoin holders are told the token could gradually shift from a meme asset toward broader use cases.

The article gives background on Dogecoin's development: the DogeOS project is an Ethereum-compatible Layer 2 app layer designed to bring smart contracts, DeFi features and additional utility to the Dogecoin ecosystem. Reports cited in the article say the project is close to mainnet after completing version 1 and audits, with over 100 developers already building. Pepe, by contrast, is described as a pure-play meme coin driven almost entirely by social sentiment and speculative rotation. The article also notes that Pepe's late-2024 all-time high sits far above its current price, and that its 2026 volume spikes have failed to produce sustained demand.

Looking ahead, the article concludes that Dogecoin has a higher probability of stronger, more durable relative performance over the full year of 2027. It says both coins would likely rise in a recovering or bullish market, with Pepe possibly delivering bigger short-term spikes during meme-season rotations. The article leaves open whether the broader market will recover in 2027 and whether DogeOS will reach mainnet on schedule. It also does not say how the Pepe sell-off warning will play out or whether the predicted outcome will materialize.

Articles.Title: Meta AI Predicts DOGE Vs. PEPE: Which Goes Higher in 2027?

stories.Headline: Alphabet Climbs 3% as NVIDIA’s Leadership Shake-Up Puts Google’s AI Chips in the Spotlight; Microsoft Gains 2%, Amazon Ticks Up
stories.Summary:
On November 12, 2026, NVIDIA announced that Jensen Huang had resigned as president, chief executive and board member, effective immediately. Alphabet's stock rose about 3% to $301.97 in Thursday's trading as investors speculated that its in-house TPUs could win more AI chip spending. NVIDIA's stock fell 6% on the news, while Broadcom rose 5%, helping Google design its TPUs. The move followed reports that NVIDIA's board was preparing to oust Huang, which had sent NVIDIA shares down 9% earlier. Investors appear to be weighing whether rival AI chips could draw attention from the largest cloud buyers.

Chief financial officer Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO while keeping her finance role, and NVIDIA's board is weighing internal and external candidates for a permanent successor. NVIDIA's products and existing contracts remain in place through the leadership change. Harvey Jones, the board's first-ever chair, said the company expects operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption. Google sells TPU systems to customers through Google Cloud, and Alphabet's Google Cloud revenue rose 103% year over year to $30.71 billion in Q3 2026. Alphabet's capital expenditures reached $51.36 billion in Q3, and its free cash flow was negative $9.07 billion.

Huang's departure was announced by NVIDIA itself, which said the transition would not disrupt its operations. Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai said in October, when Alphabet reported its Q3 results on October 28, that the company was seeing strong demand for its TPU systems across a wide range of customers. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said on the company's latest earnings call that the number of companies with both a significant cloud business and a chip strong enough to sell externally is effectively two. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has described a "fungible fleet" that pairs NVIDIA hardware with Microsoft's own Maia systems inside Azure. The articles do not give a direct response from NVIDIA beyond its announcement and the board's statements.

Microsoft shares rose 2% to $528.98 and Amazon shares rose 1% to $269.49 on the same day. Both Microsoft and Amazon develop their own AI chips while buying heavily from NVIDIA, so any setback at NVIDIA could affect their data centers. Azure revenue at Microsoft grew 48% in the quarter ended in September, and Amazon Web Services revenue rose 39% over the same period. Amazon runs most of its Bedrock AI service on in-house Trainium chips and is preparing to sell those chips outside AWS. Alphabet is also funding part of its infrastructure build-out with debt and at-the-market share sales, according to the articles.

NVIDIA plans to report its Q3 FY2027 results on November 17, which could show whether its customer relationships are holding steady. Alphabet's TPU opportunity will be tested as demand develops during NVIDIA's leadership transition. The articles say a quick rebound in NVIDIA stock could reduce the speculation lifting Alphabet. They do not say when NVIDIA will name a permanent CEO, which candidate the board will choose, or whether TPU demand will continue to grow.

Articles.Title: Alphabet Climbs 3% as NVIDIA’s Leadership Shake-Up Puts Google’s AI Chips in the Spotlight; Microsoft Gains 2%, Amazon Ticks Up

stories.Headline: Yahoo Finance company of the year: Anthropic's AI dominance
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the AI lab founded in 2021 by former OpenAI employees, has been named Yahoo Finance's Company of the Year for 2026 at the outlet's annual Invest Conference in New York City. The article, published on November 12, 2026, by technology editor Daniel Howley, describes the company's rapid rise. Its revenue reached $17 billion in the last quarter alone, a twelvefold increase year over year, and its sales for the nine months ending September 30 exceeded $33 billion. The company is also set to launch its initial public offering late next week.

The article gives Anthropic's revenue history as $2.5 billion in all of 2025 and $41 million in 2023. The number of customers spending more than $100,000 rose from roughly 1,500 in December 2025 to more than 11,900 as of September 30. The company's computing efficiency has also increased, meaning it earns more revenue per dollar spent on computing infrastructure. Anthropic's S-1 investor prospectus lists the ways its AI could cause harm if not properly monitored. In September, CEO Dario Amodei wrote an essay calling for AI labs to slow the pace of frontier AI development.

Anthropic was founded by Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei, Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish and Chris Olah, all of whom had worked at OpenAI. Menlo Ventures partner Matt Murphy, who led the firm's investment in Anthropic, said the founders' shared history reduced risk. Amodei, who was already known in AI circles, became widely recognized for his outspoken calls for AI safety and his warnings that the technology could cause job losses or worse. Murphy's comments and the company's own filings are the article's direct statements about responsibility for the company's direction.

Professors quoted in the article describe the company's success in different terms. NYU Stern professor Arun Sundararajan said there is no real historical analogy for a company succeeding this fast. Santa Clara University professor Ram Bala said Anthropic's early focus on enterprise customers paid off, and University of Pennsylvania Wharton professor David Hsu questioned how durable the growth will be. Enterprise customers are increasingly seeking cheaper options, and according to the platform OpenRouter, open-weight models accounted for 8 of the top 10 models by token usage over the last month.

The article notes that the midterm elections, in which Democrats took control of the House and Senate, were partly read as pushback against AI data center construction and AI generally. Anthropic is still dealing with the Trump administration's decision to label it a supply chain risk after it refused to allow the Department of Defense to use its models for autonomous weapons or mass surveillance of Americans. Competitors OpenAI, Google and Meta are also expanding their enterprise offerings. The article does not say how the IPO will proceed or how investors will respond, and it leaves open whether Anthropic can stay ahead of its rivals.

Articles.Title: Yahoo Finance company of the year: Anthropic's AI dominance

stories.Headline: How a new AI model could help crushed rock fight climate change
stories.Summary:
Microsoft and carbon-removal company Terradot have developed TerraNova, an AI model aimed at making enhanced rock weathering easier and cheaper to scale, as reported on November 12, 2026. Enhanced rock weathering involves spreading powdered rock over farmland, where it reacts with rainwater and carbon dioxide to remove CO₂ from the atmosphere. Terradot and Microsoft combined a Microsoft weather model with Terradot's scientific data to build the system. The companies say the approach could help the technique expand around the world. The main obstacles are identifying promising fields and measuring how much rock reacts in the soil, both of which require costly, extensive sampling.

TerraNova builds on Aurora, Microsoft's foundation AI model for predicting global weather and environmental conditions, which was adapted to predict chemical changes in soil. The model uses data from fields where Terradot works with farmers, and it analyzes soil composition, minerals from nearby quarries, humidity, rainfall, temperatures and patterns such as La Niña. In simulations using agricultural field data, researchers found the model could cut the number of samples needed at the largest sites by 75% while keeping accuracy the same. Measuring and verifying carbon removal can account for a third to more than half the cost of the technique. Training on data from Brazil allowed the model to make predictions for fields in Mississippi.

Terradot co-founder and CEO James Kanoff says the world must remove nearly 10 billion tons of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere every year. Terradot co-founder Sasankh Munukutla worked with experts from the Microsoft Climate Innovation Fund, AI for Good Lab and Microsoft Research on the project. Melanie Nakagawa, Microsoft's chief sustainability officer, called TerraNova an example of how AI can accelerate climate progress. Felipe Oviedo, a principal research scientist at Microsoft's AI for Good Lab, described the measurements as very complex and costly. Erika Basham, director of natural capital investments with the Microsoft Climate Innovation Fund, said the goal was to help solve a problem holding back the industry's growth.

The research will be described in a forthcoming preprint ahead of peer review. Earlier versions were accepted for a climate-focused workshop at NeurIPS 2026 and presented at an AI for science workshop at ICLR 2026. Terradot, founded in 2022 by Munukutla and Kanoff, who met at Stanford University, has about two dozen PhD-level scientists and has collected tens of thousands of soil samples from fields in Brazil and the U.S. The company expects the rock powder it has spread in those countries to remove up to 100,000 tons of carbon dioxide over time. Terradot aims to remove one million tons annually by 2035. Munukutla says continued development and extensive validation are needed to use such AI models responsibly.

Articles.Title: How a new AI model could help crushed rock fight climate change

stories.Headline: AI networking adds security: Nvidia unveils Scale-In
stories.Summary:
Nvidia Corp. recently unveiled Scale-In, a new pillar of its AI networking infrastructure built to secure, manage and operate agentic AI factories. The product, announced in an article dated November 12, 2026, is designed to deliver secure access, high-performance data movement, tenant isolation, simpler operations and more predictable performance.
