stories.Headline: Red Hat joins race to be ‘air traffic controller’ for AI agents
stories.Summary:
Red Hat announced general availability of its agentic AI management tools for OpenShift 5 at the KubeCon conference in Salt Lake City this week. The release includes an MCP server and an MCP gateway, while MCP support for RHEL and Developer Hub is coming soon. Managing AI agents has become a top enterprise concern as models grow more capable, and uncontrolled agents can cause significant harm. Red Hat is now positioning itself as one of the options for a central control plane.

The MCP gateway sits between AI agents and the tools they call, filtering what each agent can see based on its credentials. It includes NeMo Guardrails, an open source toolkit from Nvidia, which can block prompt injections and protect sensitive data. The gateway can also require human approval for agent actions that change systems. The new OpenShift MCP server ties agent access to existing identity systems and Kubernetes role-based permissions, with audit trails for agent activity. An agent sandbox in technology preview can isolate untrusted agent code in virtual machines.

Red Hat is also promoting OpenShift LightSpeed from a conversational chatbot to an AI agent that can diagnose cluster problems, propose fixes, and assess the risk of updates. In technology preview, it can take on more troubleshooting tasks, with a human approving every change. OpenShift 5 adds hardened multi-tenancy for sovereign deployments and expands support for post-quantum cryptography. Red Hat is also offering a free year of OpenShift Virtualization for qualifying three-year agreements.

Red Hat's head of product for developer tools, Balaji Sivasubramanian, said Red Hat Developer Hub 2.1 gives developers and AI agents governed access to enterprise context. The Developer Hub 2.1 MCP server is expected to be generally available later this month. Red Hat also said an MCP server for RHEL is coming in the coming weeks, letting enterprises use agents to diagnose RHEL issues without unrestricted access. Analysts say the release matters for Red Hat customers, since OpenShift 4 came out in 2019. Dell'Oro analyst Mauricio Sanchez said enterprises with heavy server and software investments should shortlist Red Hat.

Analysts say Red Hat's advantage is that its platform runs across cloud and on-premises and works with AI systems from many providers, which helps avoid vendor lock-in. Leapwork's Donovan Brady said Microsoft's Azure Agent 365 is stronger, because it supports agents wherever they are deployed and Red Hat lacks that single control plane. Sanchez said Red Hat's capabilities lag some rivals and its oversight of agents on other platforms is limited. Brady said OpenShift Virtualization is technically viable as a VMware alternative, but switching requires rearchitecting the data center. ABI Research's Dimitris Mavrakis said the one-year free license is not the strongest reason to migrate.

Sanchez said the race for agent management has not been decided and is only in its early stages. IDC analyst Jim Mercer said OpenShift is increasingly competing in virtualization, AI infrastructure, agentic operations and enterprise security. Matt Kimball of Moor Insights & Strategy said Red Hat's approach gives agents governed access and keeps a human in the loop. The articles do not say whether Red Hat can take on more agentic AI management, and they do not say how the MCP server for RHEL or Developer Hub 2.1 will perform after release.

Articles.Title: Red Hat joins race to be ‘air traffic controller’ for AI agents

stories.Headline: Abu Dhabi data centre leaders unite to meet soaring AI demand
stories.Summary:
Abu Dhabi's push to become a regional artificial intelligence hub is pushing government, hyperscalers and data centre operators toward closer collaboration, as demand for computing power accelerates across the UAE. The topic is set to dominate Data Center World Middle East, which makes its regional debut in Abu Dhabi on 17 and 18 November, bringing together technology companies, infrastructure operators and policymakers. According to JLL, Abu Dhabi already has the Middle East's largest data centre market, with 374MW of IT capacity. The emirate's Department of Energy expects AI infrastructure to need about 2GW of power in its initial phase, rising to 5GW over time, supported by AED250 billion of planned energy and water investment between 2025 and 2035.

Industry leaders argue that meeting these goals requires a coordinated approach rather than isolated projects. Mehdi Paryavi, chairman and chief executive of the International Data Center Authority, said the biggest gap for Gulf data centres is the lack of coordination at scale, and that the region needs adaptable standards, a skilled workforce, long-term planning, reliable energy and greater stability. He added that developers must work with governments, utilities and industry partners to build an ecosystem that supports sustainable, large-scale AI infrastructure. Morten Tidemand, senior director of operations at Khazna Data Centers, which runs 30 data centres with 673MW of capacity, said operational readiness cannot begin at handover, since higher densities require new cooling strategies, maintenance routines and emergency procedures well in advance. He also said staff must understand how increasingly complex systems interact.

The conference will feature speakers from AWS, Google, Microsoft and Oracle, along with representatives from the UAE Ministry of Energy and Infrastructure and the Ministry of Investment. Sessions will cover topics including liquid cooling and managing mixed-density data halls. Tara Gibb, senior event director for Data Center World, said Abu Dhabi has made its commitments and that turning them into capacity that runs reliably at 50°C depends on everyone working from the same plan. The articles do not describe any outcomes from the event, which has not yet taken place at the time of reporting.

Articles.Title: Abu Dhabi data centre leaders unite to meet soaring AI demand - Khaleej Times

stories.Headline: RAVEL Plans Power-Aware Scheduling Study for Distributed AI
stories.Summary:
RAVEL announced on November 12, 2026, a research collaboration with Sandia National Laboratories called Project Quicksilver, a multi-phase study of power-aware scheduling for AI workloads spread across geographically distributed computing sites. Phase One will cover three Sandia locations and compare air-cooled and immersion-cooled systems. The study will test whether power availability, operating conditions and workload requirements can guide where and when work is scheduled, in order to address energy, capacity and cost limits. Its stated aim is to inform data-center design and operations by examining how to make power and computing capacity more productive rather than assuming more capacity automatically yields more useful infrastructure. The announcement describes planned measurements, not completed findings or demonstrated savings.

Phase One will evaluate the two cooling environments across the three locations, which are linked by a wide-area network, using Box–Behnken experimental design for the air-cooled systems and Plackett–Burman design for the immersion-cooled ones. Network bandwidth and speed will be varied alongside other factors. The energy analysis will compare identical workloads across cooling environments and account for compute, IT infrastructure and data-center operations, measuring energy use, TUE and PUE-adjusted efficiency, and possible heat-reuse benefits. A separate total-cost-of-ownership analysis will cover capital and operating costs for infrastructure, power, cooling, networking and operations. A third workstream will measure AI workload time-to-completion alongside energy and cost so researchers can study the trade-offs between them.

RAVEL describes its Orchestrate AI product as a federated orchestration layer for managing AI workloads across heterogeneous, geographically distributed resources, treating those locations as one system rather than optimizing each separately. RAVEL's chief executive and co-founder, Denise Muyco, said the project will examine how orchestration can make AI infrastructure investments more productive while supporting more responsible energy use. Dave Martinez, engineering program and project lead for Infrastructure Computing Services at Sandia, said that under a Cooperative Research and Development Agreement with RAVEL, the teams will explore whether dynamic workload placement can make better use of available power and computing resources while balancing performance and cost. Sandia is the initial research lead.

The collaborators plan to extend Project Quicksilver to additional US Department of Energy national laboratories and to explore further environmental and performance-optimization use cases. RAVEL and Sandia are scheduled to discuss the experimental approach, planned test phases and expected research outputs at the Department of Energy booth during SC26 on November 17, 2026. The central question of the project is whether treating separate data centers as one coordinated system can improve energy use and computing economics without hurting workload performance. The articles indicate that cooling, networking, capital costs and completion time will all be weighed alongside power consumption to judge whether such scheduling makes distributed computing more productive.

Articles.Title: RAVEL Plans Power-Aware Scheduling Study for Distributed AI - Unite.AI

stories.Headline: AI Governance Fragmentation Cause For Concern
stories.Summary:
Kenya is building an artificial intelligence governance framework at speed, and the article from CIO Africa, written by Bowmans lawyers Ariana Issaias and Mumbi Kiragu, was published on 12 November 2026. The authors say several instruments have appeared in a short period, including a national AI strategy, multiple draft policies, sector-specific guidance and a private member's AI Bill. The authors note the volume signals momentum but raises concerns about harmonisation. These instruments come from several institutional sources and, in some cases, propose different governance structures for overlapping areas. Policy and legislation have so far advanced in parallel, which the authors describe as a departure from the norm.

The Ministry of Information, Communications and the Digital Economy launched the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025-2030 in March 2025. The strategy sets out a roadmap for responsible AI development and aims to position Kenya as a leader in AI research, innovation and commercialisation. It emphasises infrastructure, data readiness, skills, investment, ethics, equity and inclusion rather than binding obligations. In June 2026, Cabinet established a Standing Cabinet Committee on Artificial Intelligence to steer implementation of the strategy and coordinate AI policy across Government. In July 2026, the Ministry published the draft Kenya Artificial Intelligence and Other Emerging Technologies Policy, 2026, for public participation, and that consultation closed on 11 August 2026.

The draft AI Policy proposes governance across the whole AI lifecycle, from design and deployment to monitoring and accountability, and makes "Sovereignty and Strategic Autonomy" a standalone pillar. Its proposed measures include data localisation for sensitive and strategic public-interest datasets and a sovereign cloud and computing strategy. The draft has a broad extraterritorial scope, reaching foreign AI providers whose systems are used in Kenya or have foreseeable effects there, and it sets no clear threshold tied to intentional targeting of the Kenyan market. It also proposes a shared accountability model, with future legislation to allocate liability across developers, deployers, operators, vendors and users. The draft National Data Governance Policy, 2026, whose public consultation closed on 5 June 2026, treats data as a national asset and extends beyond personal data regulated under the Data Protection Act, 2019.

It proposes a National Data Governance and Emerging Technologies Council and a National Chief Data Officer. In October 2026, the State Department for Science, Research and Innovation published the Draft National AI Policy for Science, Research and Innovation for public participation. The draft AI Bill, proposed earlier in 2026, would classify AI systems as unacceptable, high, limited or minimal risk, with the strictest obligations applying to high-risk systems. It would impose transparency duties on all providers and deployers, require labelling of certain AI-generated synthetic media, and criminalise harmful non-consensual uses of synthetic media. It would also mandate workforce impact assessments where AI is likely to affect employment, and would establish an independent Office of the Artificial Intelligence Commissioner.

That office overlaps with the National AI and Other Emerging Technologies Council proposed in the draft AI Policy. In October 2026, the Senate Standing Committee on Information, Communication and Technology recommended that the Senate not proceed with the Bill until a comprehensive national AI policy is finalised. Sectoral rules are also emerging: the Media Council's Code of Conduct for Media Practice, 2025 requires disclosure of AI-assisted editorial material, human review of AI-generated content, and consent before cloning a real person's likeness, voice or persona. In September 2026, the Central Bank of Kenya published a Draft Guidance Note on AI in the Banking Sector setting mandatory guardrails for licensed financial institutions.

The authors attribute the policy drafting to the Ministry of Information, Communications and the Digital Economy, the Cabinet committee to the Government, and the Central Bank guidance to the Central Bank of Kenya. The Kenya Bureau of Standards' Code of Practice for AI Applications (KS 3007) provides voluntary technical and governance guidance. The draft Copyright and Related Rights Bill, a proposal from the Kenya Copyright Board to repeal and replace the Copyright Act, 2001, contains a text and data-mining exception limited to non-commercial research and does not expressly address training commercial AI systems. Businesses developing or relying on AI in Kenya are the parties the authors say face the implications, and foreign AI providers are within the draft policy's reach.

The Judiciary's draft Artificial Intelligence Policy proposes a risk-based approach to AI in court processes, including disclosure and verification of AI-assisted work. In February 2026, the High Court certified as urgent a petition seeking to compel the Government to adopt a comprehensive AI policy, arguing that unregulated high-risk AI threatens constitutional rights. The Court later declined to restrain AI deployment but directed the matter to a full hearing. The article also links AI-driven disinformation to the 2027 general elections.

Next, the Kenya Intellectual Property Bill, 2026, already before the National Assembly, would replace the existing copyright framework, and the draft Copyright and Related Rights Bill would need to be considered alongside it, though the draft has not yet been formally tabled in Parliament. The Senate's position on the AI Bill is recorded, but the article says the Bill formally remains before the Senate and appears unlikely to proceed in its current form. The authors state that the immediate priority is a national AI policy framework to guide future legislation, and that the instruments must be aligned into a coherent framework. The articles do not say when the national AI policy will be finalised, how the overlapping institutional mandates will be resolved, or whether the High Court petition will reach a final decision.

Articles.Title: AI Governance Fragmentation Cause For Concern - CIO Africa

stories.Headline: ‘Do not let Sauron have the ring’: Voorhees warns against a government veto on AI
stories.Summary:
Erik Voorhees, founder of the AI service Venice, posted on November 12, 2026, warning against giving politicians control over artificial intelligence. His post, written as @ErikVoorhees, said "Do not let Sauron have the ring," targeting the concentration of political power over machine intelligence. The warning followed a clip of All-In co-host David Sacks predicting a Democratic push for a federal department to approve frontier AI models before release. That clip was published by @firesidealpha on November 7, and it came from the November 7 All-In episode. Voorhees argues that open-source transparency and decentralization offer better safety, and that licensing undermines equality.

Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Greg Casar announced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act on September 23, 2026. The introduced Senate version, S.5493, would establish a Department of Artificial Intelligence and pause advanced AI development pending a regulatory framework. It would also prohibit artificial superintelligence. Section 9(d) would bar anyone from deploying, releasing, importing or transferring an advanced AI system before receiving the department's approval. The secretary would withhold approval if dangerous characteristics, including superintelligence and precursor characteristics, were present.

Sacks, in the November 7 episode, predicted a major Democratic push for AI legislation in the next Congress, describing a federal AI department that would review the most advanced models. He alleged that Democrats want AI-powered surveillance and censorship, and he predicted a bargain in which government gains power while closed-model companies gain regulatory protection. Abdul El-Sayed's October 13 "AI Under Control" platform calls for an independent, Cabinet-level agency able to inspect laboratories, block releases, order pauses and command shutdowns. The platform also reiterates opposition to warrantless surveillance. Voorhees's objection is to anyone holding gatekeeping power over AI releases.

Those affected include developers of advanced AI systems, whose models could be held from release pending federal approval. Under S.5493, a covered developer would need a charter, and maintaining it would entail giving regulators access to systems, processes, staff and physical infrastructure. The bill would also prohibit artificial superintelligence and require pauses and shutdown measures for specified dangerous systems. El-Sayed's platform proposes freezing training and release of the most powerful systems until safety rules and enforcement exist, with independent scientists certifying safety before the pause lifts. It also calls for independent pre-release audits and breach reporting to government within 24 hours.

Sanders and Casar's bill, introduced as S.5493, would require Senate confirmation of the secretary, provide for independent scientific advice and restrict employees' financial interests. It also provides Federal Circuit review of findings underlying charter revocations. El-Sayed's platform proposes a scientific board chosen outside the agency, public disclosure of exemptions, industry-fee funding and a bar on officials later cashing in on companies they regulate. The campaign document explicitly builds on the Sanders-Casar legislation. Both are proposals, not an enacted system, and the articles do not establish that the next Congress has agreed to create such a regime.

Articles.Title: ‘Do not let Sauron have the ring’: Voorhees warns against a government veto on AI - CryptoSlate

stories.Headline: The Real AI Misalignment Problem Is Capitalism
stories.Summary:
Two resignations in September drew attention to AI safety concerns at leading developers. David Robinson, OpenAI's Safety Officer, and Jacob Coxon, a developer at Anthropic, each quit because they felt their companies were not taking seriously the risks frontier models pose to humanity. The article describes these fears as based on careful argument rather than hype. A September 6 blog post by Jakub Pachocki, OpenAI's chief scientist, is cited as an example. Three weeks later OpenAI decided to pull its GPT-6.1 Astra model, which had been slated for release, for now.

Pachocki's blog raised concern about "recursive self-improvement," in which models take autonomous control over their own refinement. The article says this could let humans lose control of AI development quickly, even when it involves concentrations of computational power that threaten human life. A second worry is that companies are losing the ability to check whether their models are aligned with the values they were designed to serve. OpenAI had relied on reviewing a model's chain-of-thought, but Pachocki wrote that this ability is progressively diminishing. Researchers at the UK's AI Safety Institute found alternative evidence of how OpenAI's latest model was going rogue.

Pachocki's blog did not call for halting AI development, only for recursive self-improvement to be "paced" for economic competitiveness. The article quotes him saying that this process is the only way to remain at the AI frontier. The author argues that the underlying problem is capitalism, meaning powerful computation built mainly to serve profit, national competition and efficiency. He says this produces a conflict between the drive to optimize profit and a tolerable life for humans. He writes that Big Tech avoids discussing this conflict openly, and that failing to confront it risks making AI predatory on humanity's future.

The article describes three present-day ways commercial AI is predatory on human life. Models are trained on almost all human-produced content, prompting ongoing legal disputes with cultural industries over copyright and compensation. Workers in the Global South were exploited to train early AI, and professionals are being paid to show AI how medical reasoning works, work that becomes redundant once training ends. AI also shapes habits of thought and imagination, and it progressively overvalues disembodied machine intelligence while undervaluing human and animal embodied intelligence, a shift the author links to René Descartes.

The author urges workers in every workplace and freelance network to assert their capacity to refuse commercially imposed AI. He notes that AI is being pushed onto society quickly and with little consultation because Big Tech needs wide adoption to recoup huge investments and make reliable profits. Evgeny Morozov is cited as arguing for communities to decide, rather than reject AI outright, the social goals for which AI might be used, on what terms, and when and where. The article says this would require radical changes in how work institutions function, and it concludes that the outlook for the AI era is bleak without bold alternatives. The articles do not say whether OpenAI will resume releasing the paused model, nor whether Anthropic's mooted $2 trillion flotation will proceed.

Articles.Title: The Real AI Misalignment Problem Is Capitalism - Jacobin

stories.Headline: Executive Perspectives: Iowa leaders share their AI outlooks
stories.Summary:
Executive leaders across Iowa shared their outlooks on artificial intelligence with the Business Record in November 2026, following the newspaper's final Power Breakfast of that year, which featured speaker Mike Stitt. The newsroom reached out to several additional leaders after that event to gather further views on how AI is shaping their businesses. Joel Veenstra, president of Baker Group, said the biggest change so far has been in the office rather than on the jobsite. Mike Harryman, general manager of McGough Construction, said AI could reduce the time needed to process information and identify risk, changing construction economics.

Veenstra said Baker Group is using AI for contract review, proposal generation, takeoffs, estimating, submittals, RFIs, document review and coordination. He said the tools save time, minimize rework and allow teams to take on more work. Harryman said AI can speed quantity analysis, document review, scope comparison, scheduling and cost forecasting. Ryan Wiederstein, broker-owner of WB Realty Co., said AI could reduce operating costs for commercial property owners while improving tenant service. Neil Schroeder, chief information officer of Des Moines Public Schools, said AI could help draft and check repetitive finance, payroll, human resources and enrollment work.

Veenstra said Baker Group is investing in a clean database, forming a cross-functional steering group and building policies for data handling and acceptable use. He said the company keeps people in the loop, avoids commitments to a single tool and is building AI literacy across the company. Harryman said McGough is focusing on the quality, consistency and accessibility of its project data and on early VDC planning and model-based coordination. Brianne Schulte, vice president of strategy, risk, information technology and financial planning at Vermeer Corp., said her company is building strong data systems and integrations rather than depending on individual software ecosystems.

Wiederstein said AI could increase demand for highly amenitized office projects that offer collaboration difficult to replicate remotely. Schroeder said that within five years he expects families, students and employees to have personal AI assistants, requiring schools to support systems that work safely with them. Schulte said AI could increase the capacity of current team members and improve margins by shortening the time needed to pull information together. Joe Murphy, president of the Iowa Business Council, said the council is considering how to provide tools and educational and literacy opportunities so current and future workers can use AI to become more productive.

Veenstra described the company's approach as one that keeps people accountable for work while still investing in talented staff as it adopts AI tools. Harryman said McGough has built its approach around its existing project practices and lessons-learned processes. Wiederstein said his firm plans to stay nimble and pivot as the technology evolves. The articles provide no further detail on the timing of these investments, the costs involved or how the Iowa Business Council's workforce programs would be funded or delivered. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Executive Perspectives: Iowa leaders share their AI outlooks - Business Record

stories.Headline: After $604M verdict, fleets face AI camera blind spots
stories.Summary:
After a $604 million jury verdict against C.H. Robinson, trucking defense attorney Doug Marcello warned fleets that AI-only dash cams create new liability exposure. Marcello made the case at the American Trucking Associations' Management Conference & Exhibition in Charlotte, North Carolina, on a panel with Sean Ritchie of Solera Fleet Solutions. The panel took place days after a Dallas County judge upheld the verdict, which stems from a 2021 crash in Jackson, Mississippi, that killed three people and the truck's driver. Marcello argued that plaintiff attorneys look for evidence of systemic failure, and that risky driving recorded on video but never flagged by the AI can supply it. The article was published on November 13, 2026.

Ritchie described how camera review has changed, saying early systems recorded events when an accelerometer sensed G-forces past a threshold, and reviewers checked each event frame by frame. Five or six years ago, he said, almost every video passed through a human reviewer before reaching the fleet. Today's computer vision cameras often send videos straight into coaching workflows without human review. The Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration's windshield rule allows safety technology mounted no more than 8.5 inches below the top of the area swept by the wipers, but it does not cover how video is reviewed. Ritchie said Solera analyzed AI-triggered videos and found up to 30% held other risk the AI did not flag, though the company has not published its sample size or method.

Marcello said fleets should treat any footage they hold as discoverable and said that the AI missing a risk would not be an excuse. He said that if video captures a driver's activity, the fleet will be responsible for it. Marcello also said that with no government standard for AI review, juries will set one. Ritchie, who opened the session by asking attendees about their false-positive and false-negative rates, said no one in the room knew their false-negative rate.

He said vendors dialed down sensitivity in response to industry feedback that false positives were too high, which created more opportunity for unlabeled risk. Ritchie also said that drowsy driving was the most common miss. Marcello described a mock trial he ran with a Philadelphia focus group, in which jurors heard about a 35-truck carrier whose driver killed two people after hitting traffic over a hill. The driver had several overspeeds and hard brakes the week before, and the company's lone safety director had not caught up on them, which made the jury unsympathetic.

In the C.H. Robinson case, the jury assigned 23% of fault to the broker and 45% to the driver, Gorgonio Gonzalez. Plaintiffs argue Gonzalez was a borrowed employee of the broker, which would combine the two shares above 50% and leave C.H. Robinson owing the full verdict. Ritchie said most safety staff are very lean and often trained to coach only the risk the provider labels. Ritchie said providers typically keep video with no identified risk for 30 days at most and video with flagged risk for six months or longer.

Marcello called the habit of avoiding data analysis to prevent discovery the discovery fallacy, saying the data would be discovered anyway. Ritchie grouped vendors into three approaches: sending video straight to fleets, using human review only to remove false positives, or reviewing for both false positives and false negatives. He said human review alone is no better than AI alone. Ritchie said he felt compelled to raise the issue because the industry moved quickly to AI-only cameras without anyone discussing false negatives.

Articles.Title: After $604M verdict, fleets face AI camera blind spots - FreightWaves

stories.Headline: Independent AI auditors have a recruitment problem - Transformer | Substack
stories.Summary:
Independent AI auditors have been drawing attention because there are not enough qualified people to staff the oversight bodies that policymakers want. The article describes a growing consensus among safety-minded lawmakers and policy researchers that frontier AI companies will need ongoing monitoring by third-party organizations not tied to industry or government. These bodies are called independent verification organizations, or IVOs. Researchers and advocates are now sounding the alarm that the talent pool is too small for the demands of strong proposals. The strongest proposal discussed is in Massachusetts, where an IVO regime would give auditors advance access to models and the power to question AI firms and make recommendations.

Under that bill, which is part of the Mass Wins Act and currently in conference in the state legislature, auditors would conduct annual compliance audits and independent catastrophic risk evaluations of models roughly every four months. Illinois passed an auditing regime in July that measures companies against their own promises, a lighter requirement than Massachusetts. The federal FRONTIER Act, introduced by House Reps. Jay Obernolte and Lori Trahan, would require independent third-party audits of the largest AI companies' risk monitoring and mitigation practices. Reps.

Sara Jacobs and Don Beyer told Transformer they are working on IVO legislation that would include a protocol for ramping up capacity. Kevin T. Frazier, a professor at the University of Texas School of Law, says the AI field is very small and few people can answer the technical and governance questions involved. Nat Purser, director of US policy at the AI Verification and Evaluation Research Institute, calls ongoing auditing a really intensive ask that will not be insurmountable but needs a concerted effort. OpenAI spokesperson Shana Mansbach said the company is concerned about capacity regarding the Massachusetts bill. Ben Snyder, Encode's director of state policy, said the Massachusetts bill is stronger than any AI safety regulation on the books today.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for a third-party auditing regime in September. Existing evaluators include METR, Redwood Research, FAR.AI, RAND and SecureBio, and in October Anthropic gave six METR staff employee-like access to assess its models. METR's president, Chris Painter, has said that staff capacity constrains the organization's work. Ajeya Cotra, a METR researcher, drew criticism because she is married to Paul Christiano, who recently joined the OpenAI Foundation board. METR says it does not receive payment for frontier company assessments and points to its disclosure policies.

Patricia Paskov, director of standards at AVERI, says three categories of workers are needed: model and system evaluators, hardware evaluators, and governance analysts. Anka Reuel says technical evaluators need both frontier model knowledge and evaluation domain knowledge, and most such people join well-paying frontier firms. Frazier says adequate training for model-level evaluation does not currently exist. Several fellowships and bootcamps, including MATS and GovAI, train people to move into AI safety.

Paskov has discussed a certificate program with the University of Wisconsin, Madison, and the AI Evaluator Forum has a stated goal of building a pipeline of qualified candidates, though Paskov says it is still working out what that will look like. Patricia Paskov argues that talent from cybersecurity, IT, policy, accounting and business can be drawn into the field. Most training programs for senior-level model evaluation are still in development. The articles leave open how quickly these programs can produce enough qualified auditors, whether the Massachusetts and federal bills will pass, and how the ramp-up protocol described by Jacobs will work.

Articles.Title: Independent AI auditors have a recruitment problem - Transformer | Substack

stories.Headline: Texas Has A Power Grid Unlike Any Other State, And AI Is Exposing Its Biggest Weakness
stories.Summary:
Texas is facing a growing strain on its electricity grid as demand from AI data centers surges. The Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) has received interconnection requests from data center developers that the grid cannot supply. The state's grid reached an all-time high demand of about 91.1 gigawatts on July 22, 2026, while current project proposals, about 90% of which are for data centers, total more than five times that July peak. Texas grid operators are largely isolated from other states, and much of its generation comes from renewable sources such as wind, which the article notes is the largest number of turbines in the country.

Senate Bill 6, which Gov. Greg Abbott signed into law on June 20, 2025, requires AI data center developers to share the cost of infrastructure upgrades needed to deliver power to their facilities, costs that had previously fallen on ratepayers through their power bills. The law also sets guidelines that could mandate shutting down data centers during emergencies like Winter Storm Uri in 2021, which caused the largest controlled outage in U.S. history. After the law took effect, Abbott ordered a comprehensive audit of ERCOT's interconnection requests. As a result, ERCOT delayed its Batch Zero screening process, and new approvals for large data centers are on hold until the audit is finished.

The article credits Texas lawmakers and Abbott with these actions, and it describes the state's response as an effort to bring interconnection requests in line with what the grid can support. It also notes that many proposed data centers are not viable because they lack funding and support. According to the article, the audit will significantly affect the timelines and feasibility of some affected developments, but it is expected to help Texas maintain a stable electricity supply. The article does not give a completion date for the audit or say when approvals might resume.

Articles.Title: Texas Has A Power Grid Unlike Any Other State, And AI Is Exposing Its Biggest Weakness - BGR

stories.Headline: AI deepfake legislation loophole could see predators escape harsher sentences
stories.Summary:
Queensland's government has introduced legislation to criminalise the creation of non-consensual sexually explicit images or audio made with artificial intelligence or other digital technology. The bill was introduced to state parliament last month and would carry a maximum penalty of three years in prison for adults and 18 months for children. Attorney-General Deb Frecklington told parliament that the state's laws must keep pace with technology, noting that the targets of deepfake images are real people, increasingly young people. She described the bogus content as overwhelmingly sexual and said certain AI tools were complicit in spreading it. The government's aim, as she framed it, is to protect victims from the humiliation of content created without their consent.

Victims' Commissioner Kate Connors welcomed the crackdown but raised concerns in a parliamentary committee submission. She noted that adults who create sexually explicit deepfakes of children are currently charged under the existing child exploitation material offence, which carries up to 20 years in prison. Her concern is that the new law could overlap with that offence, allowing an offender to plead to the lesser charge and avoid a harsher sentence and the reportable sex offender scheme. She recommended that the proposed AI deepfake laws not apply to adults who offend against minors, and she also argued the scope should be widened beyond sexual content to cover humiliating or degrading depictions.

Legal Aid Queensland raised a separate issue, arguing the bill should include an intent element as New South Wales and Victoria do. Its submission warned that a person who prompts an AI tool for a generic image could commit an offence carrying three years in prison because of a resemblance they neither intended nor knew of. The Queensland Sexual Assault Network accepted that the technology is evolving rapidly and called for stronger training for first responders and education in schools and the community. A parliamentary committee will now report back to the government before the legislation returns to parliament for debate.

Articles.Title: AI deepfake legislation loophole could see predators escape harsher sentences - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation

stories.Headline: How crypto and AI lost the midterms, and why they say they didn’t
stories.Summary:
Crypto and AI super PACs spent roughly $250 million this cycle trying to shape the next Congress, and most of that money backed candidates who lost. The most expensive loss came in the Ohio Senate special election to fill the seat vacated by JD Vance. There, the industry spent $64 million to keep Sherrod Brown from returning, yet Brown won anyway. Crypto's flagship Fairshake PAC, which had celebrated Brown's 2024 defeat, has said much less about this year's results. Industry groups have nonetheless presented the outcome as a success.

Fairshake's spokesman said its network backed winners in 86 of the 93 races it spent in, a figure the articles describe as a roughly 92% success rate. The articles say that figure is misleading because the PACs back candidates who were already likely to win. Fairshake went 74 for 74 in races where its candidate was a clear or likely favorite, but 10 for 18 in competitive races. About half of the $154.5 million it spent backed candidates who lost. In competitive primaries, industry PACs spent $48.5 million, with $30.8 million backing winners and about $12.8 million backing losing candidates.

Fairshake's leadership, which includes its spokesman, has described its results as a sign that voters were clear, and the articles say the PAC is overstating its record. Fairshake has also insisted it is bipartisan, although the articles say its spending told a different story. Tyler Winklevoss of the exchange Gemini celebrated Brown's 2024 defeat in strongly partisan terms. The AI industry's PACs, which spent about $80 million, followed a similar back-the-winners strategy.

The articles describe these PAC backers as trying to influence elections while claiming success. Crypto's losses affect its influence in Congress. Brown chaired the Senate Banking Committee until 2024, and Elizabeth Warren looks likely to take that spot. House Financial Services Committee members Bill Huizenga and Bryan Steil both lost their races, and Maxine Waters is expected to lead the committee next year.

Waters is reportedly working on a market structure bill that expands her crypto consumer protection proposal. Voters in the affected districts, along with the industry's allies in Congress, are the people most directly touched by these results. Background from the articles: crypto PACs have long relied on backing favorites, and Fairshake claimed a 91% win rate in 2024. The industry spent heavily on Democrats in 2024, including more than $10 million each for Elissa Slotkin and Ruben Gallego.

This cycle, crypto spent little to help Democrats outside primaries and created explicitly partisan PACs. The AI network Leading the Future spent $8.2 million opposing Alex Bores in New York's 12th District, and Bores lost to Micah Lasher. Greg Brockman reportedly canceled a planned second $25 million donation after pushback from OpenAI employees. More to follow.

Articles.Title: How crypto and AI lost the midterms, and why they say they didn’t - Citation Needed by Molly White

stories.Headline: SC26 Preview: AI-HPC Convergence Takes Center Stage in Chicago
stories.Summary:
Ahead of the SC26 supercomputing conference in Chicago, Data Center Frontier aired a preview episode of its podcast hosted by contributing editor Doug Black. The conversation brought together Lois Curfman McInnes of Argonne National Laboratory, Addison Snell of Intersect 360 Research, and Earl Joseph of Hyperion Research. The episode also launched the outlet's new Frontier Computing channel. The conference runs November 15 to 20, and the article was published on November 13, 2026. The panel's central theme was that artificial intelligence is changing how scientific computing itself is carried out, rather than serving only as an add-on to traditional supercomputing.

McInnes said the field is moving beyond simply building bigger and faster machines toward integrating AI into software development, simulations, and research workflows. Joseph cited new Hyperion research finding that 70 percent of respondents already use AI for code generation. The panel also discussed the Department of Energy's Genesis Mission, an effort to link supercomputers, large-scale AI infrastructure, and cloud resources for scientific discovery. The speakers raised concerns about the economics and sustainability of the AI buildout. Snell said the industry's focus on rapid construction has outpaced serious discussion of infrastructure lifecycles and upgrades.

Joseph said it is increasingly hard to finance supercomputers costing $100 million or more when new GPU generations arrive roughly every 12 months. He also argued that the industry has not done enough to explain the societal value of its infrastructure investments amid growing public opposition to data center development. The discussion also looked ahead to the SC26 exhibition floor, touching on quantum computing's longer-term prospects, photonics, advanced cooling, processor sovereignty, and whether traditional high-performance computing capabilities can be preserved as hardware becomes more optimized for AI. The article presents these topics as a preview of a conference defined as much by the trade-offs of building next-generation AI and scientific infrastructure as by raw computing performance. Listeners were directed to the full podcast episode for the complete conversation.

Articles.Title: SC26 Preview: AI-HPC Convergence Takes Center Stage in Chicago - Data Center Frontier

stories.Headline: Researchers Validate Consumer-Centric AI Governance Framework for Indonesia
stories.Summary:
A research team in Indonesia has empirically established and operationalized a consumer-centered artificial intelligence governance framework, according to a study published in Discover Artificial Intelligence. The study was conducted through a sequential mixed-method investigation across Indonesia and is credited to Nurkholis, Rusydi, Puspita, Mujahidah, Hanifan, Lubis and Putri, published on November 11, 2026. The authors say the work responds to three deficits in existing international frameworks: the principles-to-practice gap, the developing country gap and the consumer-centric gap. Reviewing academic literature, the team found that consumers made up only 2.2 percent of active stakeholders represented in AI governance scholarship. The researchers used a Value-Criteria-Indicator-Observable architecture to translate normative commitments into measurable standards adapted to Indonesia's decentralized institutional environment.

The framework draws on Regulation Theory for enforceability, Governance Theory for procedural requirements across Indonesia's thirty-four provinces and Business Ethics Theory for moral justification toward end-users. It adapts three factors identified in earlier structural equation modeling by Shrivastava, namely Sociolegal, Risk and Functional factors. In the first phase, a confirmatory factor analysis using SmartPLS involved 236 citizens aged seventeen and older who had used AI-driven platforms. The sixteen indicators across eight criteria all exceeded the 0.7 loading threshold, and the second phase, a focus group discussion, expanded the criteria into eighteen operational indicators. Legal validation against Article 4 of Law Number 8 of 1999 and Law Number 27 of 2022 confirmed eleven indicators, modified five and reclassified two observables as supplementary evidence.

The review also created new observables addressing rights under Articles 7, 8 and 10. The authors, led by Nurkholis of the research team, present the framework as a bottom-up measurement tool that treats consumers as rights bearers, platform users and data subjects. The study notes that Indonesia has relied mainly on soft law, including the non-binding Surat Edaran Menkominfo Number 9 of 2023, while draft Presidential Regulations on AI had not been signed into law by the third quarter of 2026. The researchers said the framework could be integrated into future ministerial implementing regulations. They also contrasted it with the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act, the United States' revoked Executive Order 14110 and multilateral instruments from the OECD, UNESCO and APEC, which they describe as focused on institutional producers.

The sample was 60.2 percent male, with 42.4 percent aged seventeen to twenty-five and 62.7 percent holding a bachelor's degree, and respondents were concentrated in East Java at 31.4 percent and West Java at 28.8 percent. The authors acknowledge that the cross-sectional design captured a single point in time and that the sample was modest and concentrated within Java, excluding outer-island populations. The expert panel of three specialists lacked formal representatives from consumer advocacy groups such as the National Consumer Protection Agency or the Indonesian Consumers Foundation, so the observables remain provisional. The framework also omits criteria for behavioral manipulation and algorithmic vulnerability, which the authors flag for future research. Indonesia recorded over 200 million internet users and a 78 percent public optimism rating toward AI in 2023.

Articles.Title: Researchers Validate Consumer-Centric AI Governance Framework for Indonesia - Bioengineer.org

stories.Headline: Self-learning AI separates particle jets from background noise in simulated heavy-ion collisions
stories.Summary:
A team of physicists and computer scientists led by researchers at Brookhaven National Laboratory developed a new artificial intelligence approach that separates high-energy particle jet signals from background particles in heavy-ion collisions. The work was published in Scientific Reports and reported by Phys.org on November 13, 2026. The team included researchers from Columbia University and the University of Colorado Boulder. The method learns on its own, without the paired signal-and-background examples that conventional training would require.

The model is a generative AI method trained on simulated physics collision data rather than on labels supplied by scientists. Researchers gave it simulated detector data containing collision background, along with separate simulated jet images that contained no background. From these, it learns to extract the underlying jet signal while removing the background. In simulated sPHENIX data, it reconstructed jets' positions, energies and internal structure more accurately than conventional background-subtraction methods, particularly for larger jets. The simulated data came from calorimeters at sPHENIX, a detector that operated during the final three runs of the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider.

Yeonju Go, a Brookhaven Lab physicist and Stony Brook University assistant professor working on RHIC data analysis, said that improved background subtraction could allow more precise measurements of how quarks and gluons interact. Go said that the separation problem arises because the signal sits inside a dense spray of other particles. Dmitrii Torbunov, a Brookhaven Lab computer scientist, said that traditional methods require extensive human annotation of data, while the new framework does not need to be told what corresponds to a particular category. He added that scientific data can contain very large backgrounds that make manual separation difficult or impossible.

The research addresses the study of the quark-gluon plasma, a hot, dense state of matter that existed a microsecond after the Big Bang and that Brookhaven physicists recreate in heavy-ion collisions at RHIC. Jets are collimated sprays of high-energy particles produced in these collisions, and physicists use them as one of the best probes of that plasma. As jets stream through the plasma, their particles lose energy and change internal structure, and separating those changes from background has long limited the precision of jet measurements. RHIC completed operations in early 2026, and sPHENIX collected nearly 300 petabytes of data during its runs.

Researchers plan to apply the model to sPHENIX experimental data, which Go described as the next step toward extracting physics results. They also expect it may be applicable to calorimeter-based measurements at the Electron-Ion Collider or at the Large Hadron Collider in Europe, and to other experiments that must separate signal from background. The article notes that validation on experimental data remains pending. Go said the collaboration between sPHENIX physicists and Brookhaven computer scientists is ongoing across multiple projects.

Articles.Title: Self-learning AI separates particle jets from background noise in simulated heavy-ion collisions - Phys.org

stories.Headline: Latham & Watkins devotes $1M to AI program for associates
stories.Summary:
Latham & Watkins has set aside $1 million to reward associates who lead or contribute to artificial intelligence initiatives for the firm and its clients in 2027. The program, reported on November 12, 2026, covers all associates, who will be eligible for the awards. Awards will be allocated after a nomination and review process held in the spring. The firm has said the awards will be based on the significance, impact and scalability of each contribution.

The article places the Latham move within a wider trend of law firms investing in AI. Ropes & Gray now lets its more than 1,000 associates and counsels count 100 hours of AI experimentation and training toward required billable hours. Earlier, that firm allowed first-year associates to devote up to 20% of their billable hours to AI testing. Kirkland & Ellis has reportedly committed $500 million of its revenue to a custom AI platform over the next several years.

The reporting attributes the Latham program to the firm itself, which has described the award criteria. Amanda Robert wrote the report for the American Bar Association Journal, citing Reuters for details of the awards. The article does not say who will sit on the review panel or how many awards will be made. It also does not indicate whether the program will continue beyond 2027.

Articles.Title: Latham & Watkins devotes $1M to AI program for associates - ABA Journal

stories.Headline: LEOTEK Highlights AI-Enabled Transportation and Energy Management for Resilient Cities at COP31
stories.Summary:
LEOTEK, a smart transportation and energy management company, used the COP31 conference in Antalya, Türkiye, to highlight its AI-enabled systems for traffic and energy management, according to a press release dated November 13, 2026. The company presented its work as a way to help cities manage traffic in real time, improve roadway safety and respond to changing energy needs. The release points to U.S. policy context, noting that the Department of Transportation's SMART program funds public-sector demonstrations of smart traffic signals, sensors and connected vehicles, and that the Department of Energy sees energy storage as a tool for balancing electricity supply and demand. COP31, the release says, is focusing on energy and transport, resilient cities and technology innovation, including electrification, smart mobility and artificial intelligence.

LEOTEK's Interlux AI Traffic Signal System combines camera and radar sensing, edge AI computing and digital twin technology to monitor traffic and pedestrians and to model traffic scenarios before field changes are made. The system supports adaptive signal control and priority passage for emergency vehicles. The company says Interlux is being evaluated at Curiosity Lab in Peachtree Corners, Georgia, and that it was deployed at intersections near a medical center in eastern Taiwan as part of an ambulance-priority signal trial. A companion product, LEOLink, connects roadway lighting, traffic signals and other municipal assets through IoT connectivity and cloud management, and the company reports 49 new and pilot deployments across 19 U.S. states, along with experience in more than eight countries and regions.

The company's cloud platform, RenAI, brings asset status, energy consumption, fault detection and maintenance data into one environment, and LEOTEK says its analytics and predictive maintenance can help operators reduce costs and improve reliability. An AI assistant within RenAI, called LiSA, lets operators ask natural-language questions about their equipment and receive recommendations. LEOTEK is also extending RenAI to electric vehicle charging infrastructure and battery energy storage systems so that charging demand, equipment performance and storage availability can be managed together. Bob Flaherty, Vice President of IoT at LEOTEK, described the platform as simplifying operations for users regardless of technical expertise, and Torrent Chin, President and Chief Sustainability Officer, said cities need infrastructure that can sense conditions and respond.

Articles.Title: LEOTEK Highlights AI-Enabled Transportation and Energy Management for Resilient Cities at COP31 - PR Newswire

stories.Headline: California Turns Legal AI Guidance Into Binding Rules
stories.Summary:
California has moved to put artificial intelligence rules for legal work into statute, with Senate Bill 574 signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom on Sept. 30. The law regulates generative AI use by attorneys and arbitrators, and an Oct. 26 analysis by Mayer Brown attorneys calls it the first such statute in the United States aimed specifically at these uses. The measure follows a series of fabricated case citations in legal briefs that raised concerns about lawyers relying on automated systems. Many of its provisions restate existing ethical duties, but placing them in statute gives those obligations a clearer legal footing. The statute takes effect Jan. 1.

For lawyers, the law bars delegating the practice of law to generative AI and requires reasonable steps to verify AI output, including every case and statutory citation. Attorneys must correct erroneous or hallucinated material. Documents filed with courts may contain only citations the responsible attorney has personally read and verified, and attorneys must disclose generative AI use in those documents. Confidential, personally identifying or other nonpublic information may not be entered into AI systems unless access is restricted to the attorney and authorized people bound to protect confidentiality. For arbitrators, a new section of the California Arbitration Act prohibits delegating any part of the decision-making process to generative AI.

Arbitrators also may not rely on AI-generated information from outside the record without first disclosing it to the parties and, as far as practical, letting them comment. Sen. Tom Umberg, the measure's author, said decisions entrusted to arbitrators should be made by people, not algorithms, according to a Law.com report from Oct. 1. The analysis by Mayer Brown describes the rules as reinforcing procedural fairness, since parties should be able to challenge information that influences an award. The analysis also points to a Quebec Superior Court ruling in ARIHQ v.

Santé Québec that annulled an arbitral award over improper delegation of decision-making to AI. California's action comes as the American Arbitration Association's International Centre for Dispute Resolution introduced an AI Arbitrator in November 2025, a service that generates draft awards for consenting parties in documents-only construction disputes, subject to human review. The analysis says it remains unresolved whether such safeguards satisfy rules requiring human decision-making. Other open questions include what counts as delegating legal practice and whether the court-focused filing and disclosure provisions extend to arbitral submissions.

The analysis recommends that attorneys and arbitrators review their AI practices before Jan. 1, document how AI services are used, and confirm that confidential material stays in restricted systems. It also suggests parties set AI protocols at the outset of disputes and discuss expectations with tribunals early. The analysis warns that awards showing undisclosed AI involvement or improper delegation could face challenges grounded in statute as well as procedural fairness. For legal professionals, the analysis concludes, keeping responsibility now requires demonstrable controls over how AI participates in the work.

Articles.Title: California Turns Legal AI Guidance Into Binding Rules - PYMNTS.com

stories.Headline: MCPS approves broad new AI policy; student trustees ask for more guidance
stories.Summary:
Missoula County Public Schools approved a broad new artificial intelligence policy, and student trustees have asked for more guidance. The board took up the policy at its Nov. 10 meeting, and the Missoulian reported the story on Nov. 11, 2026. The article describes the policy as broad and notes that it applies across the district. Minor language changes were made during the meeting before the policy was approved. The policy sets out how the district expects students and staff to use AI tools.

Student trustees raised questions about how students will be taught to use AI responsibly and whether teachers will be required to follow AI guidelines or protocols. The article indicates the trustees want more detailed guidance than the approved policy provides. It does not give further figures for the policy's requirements. The board approved the policy, and the district is responsible for how it is applied in its schools.

The article does not give a direct statement from the board chair or superintendent on the trustees' request. The reporter, Nicole Girten, covers education for the Missoulian and the Ravalli Republic. Her report describes the trustees' concerns without attributing further quotes to district leaders. Students and teachers in the district are the people most directly affected by the policy's rules on AI use.

The article notes that the trustees' questions concern what students will learn and what teachers must do. Parents and other residents of the county, whose children attend district schools, would also be affected. The article does not report reactions from parents, teachers or students beyond the trustees' request. The article does not supply further background on the district's earlier AI discussions or prior policies.

It refers to the district's internet network policy as the document the board considered. It also refers to the board meeting held the previous week as the forum for the vote. The surrounding page lists other unrelated local stories, which the article does not connect to the policy. More to follow.

Articles.Title: MCPS approves broad new AI policy; student trustees ask for more guidance - The Missoulian

stories.Headline: Trustpoint Xposure Launches Program to Help Startup Founders Check How AI Search Platforms Describe Their Companies
stories.Summary:
Trustpoint Xposure, a public relations agency based in New York, launched its Startup Visibility Program on November 13, 2026. The program helps startup founders review and improve how AI search platforms such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, and Google AI Overviews describe their companies. It uses methods the agency calls Answer Engine Optimization. The announcement was distributed as a press release through Newswire.com.

The program begins with an AI visibility audit that records how those platforms describe the company and its founders. Based on the audit, the work can include aligning company and founder details across online profiles, adding structured schema markup to the company's website, and identifying credible third-party sources that confirm company facts. The audit is then repeated to document what has changed. Founders can request a complimentary AI and Media Visibility Audit to see the current picture before deciding whether to proceed. The release presents accurate, consistent information as the basis for making a company easier to identify and describe correctly.

Trustpoint Xposure says that it does not guarantee that any AI platform will mention or recommend a company. It also says it does not guarantee search rankings, website traffic, investor interest, or funding, since those depend on factors outside any agency's control. The release notes that the agency's AEO Certification Framework is its own proprietary standard and is not an independent third-party certification. Jack Smith, the agency's media director, is listed as the media contact. The release also says that no AI platform publishes its exact rules for selecting sources.

The release places the program within a broader shift in how buyers, investors, and job candidates research companies. Founders increasingly find that people check outside sources before trusting a company's own claims, and those sources now include AI platforms that can draw on public information. The agency has also launched other AEO programs in recent weeks, including one for real estate professionals and another for published authors. The articles do not describe any further timeline or next steps for the Startup Visibility Program.

Articles.Title: Trustpoint Xposure Launches Program to Help Startup Founders Check How AI Search Platforms Describe Their Companies

stories.Headline: 2026 Oracle Excellence Awards AI Innovation on Oracle AI Database Excellence Award Global Winner
stories.Summary:
Tokyo-based BLUEISH Inc. said it won the Global Winner award in the AI Innovation on Oracle AI Database Excellence Award category of the 2026 Oracle Excellence Awards, run by Oracle Corporation. The company, which described itself as the only Japanese firm to take a global award in the program, was recognized for work building AI agent memory management on Oracle AI Database. The announcement was published on November 13, 2026, and the awards reception was held on October 25, 2026, at The Venetian Resort in Las Vegas, alongside Oracle AI World Las Vegas. BLUEISH CEO and CTO Akira Tameto attended the reception on the company's behalf.

The award recognizes the use of AI features built into Oracle AI Database to solve problems in new ways or extend existing solutions. BLUEISH said that in December 2025 it adopted Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and Oracle AI Database as the data foundation for its "BLUEISH Agents" platform, which it said went into production across Google Cloud, AWS and Microsoft Azure. The company described three elements of the work: high-precision search across structured and unstructured data using AI Vector Search, a development approach that reduces preprocessing through JSON Relational Duality and Select AI, and secure production operation on a multicloud foundation. It also said it was an early adopter of Oracle Agent Memory, which lets AI agents retain enterprise knowledge and business experience.

Akira Tameto said in a statement that enterprise AI agents need a foundation that can handle a company's own data safely and accurately, not just strong AI models. He credited customers, partners and Oracle staff for the recognition. The company said that going forward it plans to offer industry-specific agents for sectors including hotels, transport, finance, media, education and professional services, and to support on-premises and hybrid deployments as well as closed-network architectures for higher security requirements. The articles do not give further details on timing or pricing for these plans.
