stories.Headline: Jensen Huang's biographer says Nvidia had a culture of omertà and deference toward Huang, who was quite arrogant, that enabled him to "be his worst self" (Stephen Witt/New York Times)
stories.Summary:
Stephen Witt, who wrote a biography of Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang titled "The Thinking Machine," published an opinion essay in The New York Times on November 12, 2026, describing what he calls Huang's downfall. The piece follows Huang's sudden departure from the company, which Witt says came after revelations that he carried on at least two affairs. One relationship was reportedly with Alice Huang, an executive who ran a Singapore-based firm owning data centers in Southeast Asia, and U.S. intelligence determined she was a Chinese spy. The other was reportedly with Kimberly Powell, a health care executive who reports directly to him.

The affair with Alice Huang matters, Witt argues, because her data centers are suspected of helping Chinese A.I. developers get around U.S. restrictions on Nvidia equipment sales. He cites a recent report in The Information suggesting those facilities served as a way station for smuggling some $7 billion of equipment into China. Witt contends that, given U.S. intelligence captured evidence of the relationship, it is hard to believe Huang did not understand what was happening. The Powell relationship, according to a former Nvidia employee Witt spoke with, was common knowledge inside the company, which employs both of Huang's children in executive roles. Witt writes that this openness was a stunning display of arrogance, and that the employee described it as a kind of narcissist's high.

Witt says he heard rumors of Huang's infidelities earlier in the year but could not confirm them at the time. He attributes the lack of disclosure to a culture of omertà inside Nvidia, a code of silence that he says allowed Huang to be his worst self. He recalls sensing deference in the sycophantic laughter of subordinates when Huang was present and in the remarks they made after he left a room. In Witt's account, government intelligence and the Times reporting ultimately broke that silence, and he expects more women may come forward. He also reflects on how Huang, when they met in 2023, worked to project humility, deflecting credit and generously tipping service workers, including a $1,000 tip in hundred-dollar bills at a Denny's breakfast that Witt had to track the waitress down to learn about.

Articles.Title: Jensen Huang's biographer says Nvidia had a culture of omertà and deference toward Huang, who was quite arrogant, that enabled him to "be his worst self" (Stephen Witt/New York Times)

stories.Headline: AI Is Destroying the Trust Between Writers and Readers
stories.Summary:
Rachel Kadish, a novelist, wrote in The Atlantic on November 13, 2026, about how AI-enabled fakery is eroding trust between writers and readers. Her account began one evening in late 2025, when a middle-aged couple approached her at a book signing. The husband, who has Parkinson's disease, believed her novel The Weight of Ink had a character with Parkinson's who chooses assisted suicide, which the book does not contain. Kadish had earlier asked ChatGPT questions about the novel, and it gave her a false account of that plotline.

Kadish describes a wider problem in which artificial intelligence is turning the reader-writer connection into a distorted, untrustworthy space. She says the technology threatens the trust that bond depends on. She cites the Monty Python "Bookshop" sketch as a comic precursor to a world now overtaken by literary fakery. The article does not say how many such books exist in total.

Kadish says that in 2017, when she published The Weight of Ink, no other book in English had that title. Since the fall of 2025, at least five other novels with the same title have appeared on Amazon, three of them within three weeks. Her friend, the novelist Daphne Kalotay, found in late 2024 that a novel she had not written was listed on her Amazon author page. The Authors Guild, of which Kalotay is a member, got Amazon to remove it. Mary Rasenberger, the Guild's CEO, told Kadish that Amazon works to block such books but is always playing catch-up.

Kadish notes that Amazon allows individuals to upload up to six books a week, and that AI makes generating book-length texts nearly costless. Writers also receive AI-generated phishing emails posing as appreciative readers, which turn into offers of paid marketing services. The Authors Guild keeps a running list of such scams. In one case, a writer forwarded Kadish an email from someone impersonating her, and when she replied, the impersonator acknowledged the ruse and promised to stop using her identity.

Kadish is the author and the person most directly affected by these practices, and she describes how the misrepresentation reached real readers. The couple at the signing deserved an honest conversation about what she had actually written. She also says that the fakery harms readers and writers alike, because they can no longer reliably connect. She sets this against earlier literary deceptions, such as The Education of Little Tree and Binjamin Wilkomirski's Fragments, which at least taught readers something about human folly. She describes these newer frauds as a bleaker kind of deception.

Kadish invokes the history of reader-writer exchanges to show how readers' responses have shaped writing. Charles Dickens revised his depiction of Jews after a reader's rebuke, and Arthur Conan Doyle revived Sherlock Holmes in 1903 after readers' grief over his 1893 death. Kadish quotes Toni Morrison's 1993 Nobel lecture, in which she said narrative is radical. Kadish's concern is that AI intrusion separates people from the growth and empathy that such stories can provide. The article does not say what steps, beyond the Authors Guild's certification program, are planned to address these problems.

Articles.Title: AI Is Destroying the Trust Between Writers and Readers

stories.Headline: Marvell Stock Could Have a Bigger AI Opportunity Than Investors Realize
stories.Summary:
Marvell Technology's stock has fallen sharply while the company's operating results have improved, according to a 24/7 Wall St. analysis published November 13, 2026. The article's model sets a price target of $232.41 for Marvell (NASDAQ: MRVL), implying 37.69% upside from the $168.80 close, and rates the stock a buy with 90% confidence. Shares fell 39.04% over the past month but remain up 91.03% year to date, trading at $162.07 premarket. The last close sits 48.8% below the 52-week high of $329.73. The selloff deepened after Marvell agreed on November 2, 2026 to acquire optical components maker Lumentum (NASDAQ: LITE) in an all-stock deal.

Marvell reported Q2 fiscal 2027 revenue of $2.7393 billion, up 36.55% year over year and ahead of the $2.7068 billion consensus. Non-GAAP earnings per share came in at $0.94, beating the $0.9289 estimate and extending a four-quarter beat streak. Data Center revenue grew 46% and now makes up 79% of sales. Management raised its fiscal 2028 revenue outlook to about $18 billion, and guided Data Center growth of more than 60% for that year. Q3 revenue guidance is $3.150 billion, and the company expects its non-GAAP operating margin to reach the 38% to 40% target range in Q4.

The article is written by Vandita Jadeja, a financial publisher and Chartered Accountant who covers stock price predictions for 24/7 Wall St. The Lumentum deal was reported by Barron's to have put both stocks on track for historically bad weeks. The article's author attributes the selloff to the deal and says the operating results look much better than the stock chart. Management's CEO said fiscal 2029 custom revenue "would be a lot larger than anybody has been modeling so far," according to the article's account of the August call. The author states that the selloff has overshot the fundamentals.

Analyst ratings on the stock are 8 Strong Buy, 35 Buy and 4 Hold, with no Sell ratings. The article notes that revenue is concentrated in data centers and that hyperscalers could bring more chip design in-house. It also cites China trade restrictions and $4.963 billion of long-term debt as pressures, and says the Lumentum deal will dilute shareholders. Q1 net income fell 80.61%, largely because of a $331.8 million contingent consideration charge. Competitors named include Broadcom (NASDAQ: AVGO), whose AI semiconductor revenue reached $16.70 billion, up 221%, and NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA), which trades at about 35 times trailing earnings against Marvell's 28 times forward earnings.

The article's bull case reaches $351.61 and its bear case reaches $181.75, which it says is still above the last close. Its price target path runs from $232.41 in 2026 to $239.90 in 2027, $278.83 in 2028, $342.39 in 2029 and $377.76 in 2030. The article says the case strengthens if Q3 revenue meets guidance and the Lumentum integration goes smoothly, and weakens if dilution or hyperscaler insourcing reduces per-share earnings. Results could vary widely depending on the Lumentum integration and how fast hyperscalers spend. The articles do not say when the Lumentum deal is expected to close.

Articles.Title: Marvell Stock Could Have a Bigger AI Opportunity Than Investors Realize

stories.Headline: 3 signs AI stocks may be a great trade again
stories.Summary:
Shares of several artificial intelligence companies have recently rebounded after an early fall slump, according to a column by Brian Sozzi on Yahoo Finance published on November 13, 2026. The rebound followed the resignation of Jensen Huang as chief executive of Nvidia, which had drawn heavy attention and worried some investors. Sozzi argues that several under-the-radar moves in the sector this week may have been overlooked amid that focus. The column identifies three of them as reasons the trade could be attractive again. Cisco reported results late on Thursday that beat expectations on both sales and earnings for its most recent quarter.

Its guidance for the current quarter also came in above estimates. The company raised its forecast for sales of AI infrastructure to hyperscalers to $9 billion for the current fiscal year, which would be more than double the prior year's results. Cerebras also beat on sales and earnings and projected a core gross margin of 47% to 49% and sales of $310 million to $330 million for the current quarter. Its shares rose 13% in premarket trading on Friday.

Cisco CEO Chuck Robbins said the company was executing its strategy and seeing growing demand for infrastructure, while KeyBanc analyst Brandon Nispel described Cisco's stock as attractively valued after earnings. Barclays analyst Tom O'Malley said Cerebras faced pressure over the prior month but that new customers should more than offset industry-wide concerns about delays in certain components. CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator said the company already had a robust pipeline of customers for its capacity. He estimated that 2027 renewals at current pricing would generate nearly $4 billion of incremental annualized revenue, rising to nearly $10 billion when including 2028 renewals.

Shares of CoreWeave were up 22% for the week. The column places these developments in the context of a broader AI rally that has lifted Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom, while noting that investors had worried about AI financing and spending. Sozzi's piece does not forecast how long the rebound will last. Its main point is that the strong results and guidance from these companies may offer reasons to reconsider the sector.

Articles.Title: 3 signs AI stocks may be a great trade again

stories.Headline: AI's anti-change agents
stories.Summary:
Businesses have spent billions of dollars giving workers access to AI tools, but most companies have not yet worked out what to do once those tools are in place, according to executives who spoke to Axios. At a private dinner attended by Axios, HR executives debated whether widespread individual use of AI can translate into real gains for an organization. One participant described inheriting a $10 million AI bill without a clear account of the value created. Other executives said entire workflows may need redesigning before the opportunity can be fully captured.

Brian Elliott, an executive in residence at a workplace consulting firm, said almost every company has seen the same pattern, with individuals reporting productivity gains that do not show up at the level of the company or its parts. He said AI has made writing code faster but has not sped up the work of deciding what to do with that code. Pressure from boards is also mounting, and Jeff Christian, CEO of an executive recruiting firm, said some companies are replacing 20 to 30 percent of their executive leadership teams over their inability to drive AI-led transformation. Rob Hornby, global co-CEO of AlixPartners, said the idea that technology alone transforms an organization has never held up and will not hold up for AI either. His firm, he said, is seeing a surge of demand as companies try to work out their next steps.

Companies are also holding back on major transformations because of security concerns, Axios reports. Banks, for example, worry about hacks and about liability when a rogue AI agent uses a customer's account to make a purchase the customer did not want. Hornby said anyone who might be liable further down the chain is simply stopping the activity. This helps explain why AI has not yet clearly appeared in overall productivity figures. In its filing to go public, the frontier AI company Anthropic named the natural resistance to change within organizations as an obstacle to its growth.

Axios places the current moment in a longer history, noting that electricity took decades to transform factories and that computer productivity gains were slow enough for Nobel-winning economist Robert Solow to remark in 1987 that the computer age was visible everywhere except in the productivity statistics. Ben Dattner, an organizational development consultant, likened the situation to inventing cars before building roads. Torsten Slok, chief economist at Apollo, wrote recently that despite massive investment and hype, AI has delivered no financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech. Revenue per worker and profit margins for S&P 500 companies outside the Magnificent Seven have been flat, according to data Slok shared. The article notes that software engineering is an exception, where AI has clearly changed work and workflows.

Articles.Title: AI's anti-change agents

stories.Headline: The biggest AI bubble risk: investing in celebrity founders over fundamentals
stories.Summary:
A Yahoo Finance video published on November 13, 2026 featured Bradley Tusk, managing partner and co-founder of Tusk Venture Partners, speaking with executive editor Brian Sozzi about the risk of an AI bubble. The discussion was framed around recent turbulence at Nvidia, which the article's ticker data shows trading lower that morning. The piece itself is a short interview rather than a report on a single event, so its main subject is an argument about how investors value companies. Tusk argued that bubbles form when investors back individuals and stories rather than financial fundamentals.

He named Jensen Huang, Elon Musk, Sam Altman and Dario Amodei as examples of figures whose reputations draw money, and he said a company can be valued on what it might become rather than on profits or revenue. He pointed to SpaceX as a case where, in his view, nothing justified the valuation, while granting that the company's ambitions and its founder's talent were real. The article does not say whether any of these points amount to a specific recommendation to investors. Tusk suggested that investors and analysts should press company leaders with blunt questions about why their business is a sound investment, setting aside talking points, communications staff and legal advice.

He said leaders who can answer with facts will have no trouble, while those relying on vibes or narrative will start to obfuscate. He framed this as a test of candor rather than a formal rule, and the article gives no further detail on how such questioning would be applied. The video sits within a broader market backdrop that day in which the Nasdaq composite fell 1.34 percent and the S&P 500 dropped 0.80 percent. The article does not describe any regulatory action, company response or follow-up commitments, so beyond the continued debate over AI valuations, the source does not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: The biggest AI bubble risk: investing in celebrity founders over fundamentals

stories.Headline: Why 85% of micro-businesses still aren't using AI for benefits
stories.Summary:
Principal's Amy Friedrich, President of Benefits and Protection at Principal Financial in Des Moines, Iowa, is calling the low adoption of AI among micro-businesses for employee benefits shockingly low but fixable. The 2026 Global Financial Inclusion Index, released in October 2026, found that about 51 percent of firms with two to ten employees use AI to support benefits or financial wellbeing. Friedrich spoke to Insurance Business Benefits US, which published the interview on November 13, 2026. Her views come from more than 20 years of work with small business clients, and she sees AI as a way to give small employers benefits support they have rarely had.

Around one in five micro-businesses say they do not use AI at all, compared with only 4 to 7 percent of firms with 101 or more employees. Only 15 percent of businesses with two to ten employees use AI for financial education, against 46 percent of firms with 1,000 or more employees. For understanding employee financial needs, 19 percent of micro-businesses use AI, compared with 44 percent of large employers. The index also found that 70 percent of US businesses surveyed use AI to identify gaps in benefits uptake, and 33 percent do so as part of regular human resources operations.

Friedrich oversees a portfolio of about 180,000 small businesses with average employee counts of 35 to 40 people, and she says the brokers who understand AI earliest will define the next era of group benefits. Her point is that the value lies in effectiveness rather than efficiency, meaning benefit dollars should be spent in ways employees will actually use. She says the best brokers load client census files into basic generative AI tools before annual plan reviews, then bring prompt-based recommendations to clients. Friedrich also notes that many brokers are building their own technology so small employers do not have to wait for it to be built for them.

The index recorded that US employer support for financial inclusion fell 1.7 points to 61.1 and slipped two places to 14th globally, a fourth consecutive annual decline. Pension contribution support fell 8.0 points among large employers and 7.5 points among medium-to-large employers, though employer insurance plan scores improved across every business size segment. Friedrich said small business owners are among their employees' most trusted people, and that many small employers put employee welfare before economics when they consider benefits. She added that a client with 14 employees may have 100 within 12 months, so brokers who help early often keep those clients as they grow.

Brokers serving small businesses typically manage between 500 and 1,200 clients, and Friedrich said manually preparing tailored recommendations for every account was once too time-intensive and risky. She described how AI now lets brokers test options such as disability coverage or paid family and medical leave against a census file, and she said a workforce mostly in its 20s and 30s calls for paid leave while a workforce aged 45 to 60 calls for elder care coverage. She also said AI-driven prompts can narrow choices to two or three options, which helps with the decision paralysis that too many options create. Friedrich said chatbot-assisted enrollment is now reaching companies of 25 to 50 employees, a market previously served only by large enterprises.

The index and the interview leave several points open. The articles do not say how quickly micro-business adoption will rise, nor whether the widening gap between small and large firms will narrow. They also do not describe the cost of the AI tools brokers and employers would need, or what regulators or carriers will require around the use of employee census data. Friedrich's comments on brokers' technology investments are not tied to named firms, and the articles give no outcome data showing whether AI-tailored benefits lead to higher employee use. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Why 85% of micro-businesses still aren't using AI for benefits

stories.Headline: Disney Embraces AI It Once Fought, From Animation to Finance and Film
stories.Summary:
Disney is embracing artificial intelligence across its businesses, after years of fighting AI-generated content, according to a Bloomberg report published November 13, 2026. The world's biggest entertainment company is exploring AI in animation, finance and film under Chief Executive Josh D'Amaro. In December, Disney will bring Ozzy Fox, a children's series rendered by AI, to its Disney+ streaming platform. The series is the product of a year-long collaboration with French startup Animaj, whose tools convert hand-drawn images and text into three-dimensional animation. The effort is part of a wider push, led by D'Amaro, to bring the company into the AI era.

Disney is building Disney Financial Insights, or D-Fi, an AI-enabled platform meant to replace and automate manual budget reports. The company is also testing AI-powered suggestions with some US subscribers to Disney+, letting people describe what they want to watch. Patent filings point to further ideas, including an AI character at Disney's resorts that asks guests about their favorite memories. Another patent describes AI-enabled microphones that detect changes in ride sounds to flag maintenance needs. Disney's planned deal with OpenAI, which would have involved a $1 billion investment and licensing more than 200 characters, collapsed after OpenAI shut down its Sora platform.

D'Amaro leads the AI push, and Disney named Karandeep Anand as its first chief technology officer in September. Anand, a technology veteran, previously served as CEO of Character.AI, and he will oversee and centralize the company's AI efforts. Disney's leaders have described AI as a tool for creators rather than an end in itself. D'Amaro said at a media event at Disney's Burbank, California, headquarters that the company is being aggressive about exploring emerging technologies. Dana Walden and Alan Bergman also visited Amazon's MGM studios in Los Angeles in October to see its AI demonstrations.

Disney's approach differs from the previous strategy under former CEO Bob Iger, who had litigated against startups including Midjourney and MiniMax over alleged copyright infringement. The change also raises concerns among Hollywood workers, since fears that AI could replace artists fueled the 2023 actors' and writers' strikes. Disney's broader move comes as the company cuts costs, which has led to regular rounds of layoffs as its traditional TV channels struggle to retain viewers and advertisers. Disney is acquiring some assets of Character.AI and hiring 60 employees in a $20 million deal, after that chatbot startup filed for bankruptcy following lawsuits over negligence and wrongful deaths.

Disney is also expanding its AI use through a new multi-year agreement with Adobe, giving it early access to generative AI and editing tools across the company, from ESPN to Disney cruises. A senior executive said Disney is more focused on controlling the use of its characters than on being paid by AI companies for training their models on its content. Anand and the company's new AI efforts will shape the entertainment giant's future, but Disney has not articulated an overall AI strategy. Jamie Voris and Eddie Drake, who previously led AI and technology roles at Disney, are retiring, according to people familiar with the matter. Neither responded to requests for comment.

Articles.Title: Disney Embraces AI It Once Fought, From Animation to Finance and Film

stories.Headline: Liftoff Sees Big Wins Ahead For Mobile As AI Pushes Budgets Into Apps
stories.Summary:
Liftoff, a mobile growth marketing platform, reported its second-ever quarterly earnings on a Thursday after the market closed, and its shares rose almost 25% overnight. The company beat its revenue target and projected an optimistic profit margin outlook going forward. Liftoff's CEO, Jeremy Bondy, presented the results to investors on the earnings call. The report covered the company's third quarter of 2026, and the article gives the date of publication as November 13, 2026.

Liftoff earned $237.5 million in Q3 2026, compared with $179.5 million in the same quarter a year earlier. The company posted $86.7 million in profit for the quarter, after a $5.7 million loss in Q3 of the prior year. Its capital expenditures, which include AI and data infrastructure costs, totaled $14 million for Q3, or about 6% of revenue. Bondy said Liftoff had 396 customers who spent more than $100,000 over the past 12 months, up from 362 a year earlier. Liftoff will also stop reporting "Core Advertising" revenue as a separate line, because advertising now makes up almost the entirety of its business.

Bondy said the company benefits from two trends that he described as tailwinds: growth in the mobile economy and an influx of AI-generated apps. He said large language models are lowering the barrier to building apps, and that new apps released in the Apple App Store doubled in the first half of 2026 to roughly 560,000. He argued that AI search is answering more questions without sending people to websites, pushing businesses to invest more in their own apps. The article also reports that AppLovin said Apple's plan to stamp out web tracking on all iOS devices would shift marketing budgets from the mobile web to mobile apps. The article does not name the author of Bondy's remarks beyond the company's own statements, and it presents these claims as the company's pitch to Wall Street.

Bondy said the mobile app advertising market is drastically under-monetized, at about seven cents per hour of attention time, which is less than a sixth of what TV earns. He said most mobile marketing gains have so far gone to mobile gaming apps, a category dominated by AppLovin, which is about 40 times bigger than Liftoff by market capitalization. He said more than half of Liftoff's business is outside gaming. Liftoff rode momentum from the FIFA World Cup and is seeing a similar surge for the NFL season, as advertisers invest more in live sports. Bondy said Liftoff has converted event-based customers into steadier, higher-spending accounts.

Bondy said Liftoff's models have improved ad targeting and personalization through AI advances, and that the models now have greater longitudinal data for understanding returns over a year or more. He said campaign returns from the week after budgets are spent remain the most important data for the models' decisions. He said Liftoff's profit margin expansion over the past year came from its relatively low cost of infrastructure and AI services. Bondy contrasted this with Meta and Google, which have committed hundreds of billions of dollars to capital expenditures. He told investors that Liftoff's business is capital light, and he said the company has dropped parts of its business such as a mobile ad network and a game developer analytics toolkit.

The article's other pieces concern different companies and do not address Liftoff's results. They cover The Trade Desk, Viant, Google Ads, Schibsted, WPP Media and Shopify. The article does not say how these developments will affect Liftoff's advertisers, customers or competitors beyond the points Bondy made. It also does not describe any plans beyond Bondy's comment that there is "a tremendous amount of space" for the business to continue growing. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Liftoff Sees Big Wins Ahead For Mobile As AI Pushes Budgets Into Apps

stories.Headline: This water technology stock is set to get a big boost from AI, says Wells Fargo
stories.Summary:
Wells Fargo has upgraded Ecolab to overweight from equal weight, saying the water technology company is positioned to benefit from the artificial intelligence build-out. The bank raised its price target on the shares to $380 from $315, implying roughly 25% upside from Thursday's close. The note was published Friday, November 13, 2026, and was written by analyst Jason Haas. Shares have already climbed more than 16% so far this year.

The upgrade rests largely on Ecolab's July acquisition of CoolIT Systems, a direct-to-chip liquid cooling firm, for nearly $5 billion. Haas wrote that the deal significantly expands Ecolab's Cooling-as-a-Service opportunity in data centers, which could benefit from both new builds and conversions of existing facilities. He noted that direct-to-chip cooling was less than 20% penetrated, while opportunities in the space are growing rapidly as rack densities rise. Ecolab is also expected to gain from roughly 70 new semiconductor fabs projected to be built by 2030. Haas added that semiconductor water demand could grow more than 600% by 2050.

Haas also pointed to Ecolab's recent purchase of Ovivo's Ultra-Pure Water business, which he said lets the company serve the full fab lifecycle. In his view, this extends Ecolab's reach into ultra-pure water for chip production and creates an end-to-end circular water solution that sets it apart. Wells Fargo's call matches the broader Street view, as 21 of the 26 analysts covering Ecolab rate the stock buy or strong buy, according to LSEG data. The article does not describe any specific risks or next steps beyond these analyst views.

Articles.Title: This water technology stock is set to get a big boost from AI, says Wells Fargo

stories.Headline: How to protect your IP against the army of AI clones
stories.Summary:
Generative AI use in game development has grown sharply in recent months, and Steam Next Fest featured over 8,000 demos in October 2026, many built partly or entirely with such tools. AI is also enabling a new wave of rapidly assembled, unauthorised clones, mods, and ports of existing games. Some developers have reported cancelling public demos for fear of being cloned before their games reach market. The new environment reverses conventional logic, since early access, trailers, and prototypes shared on social media, once ways to build an audience, now carry greater risk. Lawyers at Pryor Cashman, writing in an article dated 13 November 2026, set out practical steps for protecting a game under US law.

Developers should assess the risk of sharing in-progress work, because games that rely on unique mechanics may be more exposed to cloning than heavily story-based games or those with a strong existing brand. It is best practice to require NDAs before sharing footage, demos, or code, prohibiting recording, video capture, and the input of game media into any LLM or chatbot. Watermarking, password protection, and revocable or limited-time access can support these measures. Contributions from employees, contractors, composers, voice actors, and outside studios should be made on a work-for-hire basis or assigned exclusively to the developer. Each company should also adopt an AI policy, since a contractor using AI with confidential material can open the door to infringement or lose trade-secret protection.

Pryor Cashman's Simon Pulman, Josh Weigensberg, and Joshua Greenberg, the firm's partners and counsel in its Interactive+Gaming practice group, make these recommendations. The lawyers note that studios take different approaches, with some clients described as "zero AI" and others embracing the technology. They advise that rightsholders should register copyrights in scripts, character designs, key art, music, and trailer footage with the US Copyright Office before publicity or release. A registration is generally required before a federal infringement suit, and timely registration can unlock statutory damages of up to $150,000 for wilful infringement along with attorneys' fees. The firm also recommends filing an intent-to-use trademark application for the game's name with the USPTO several months before release.

Developers and other rightsholders, along with the many studios and independent creators using generative AI, are affected by these risks, and the article presents the advice as relevant to all of them. The USPTO trademark process currently takes around 10 months from start to finish, so applicants can file early and submit a Statement of Use after release. Common-law trademark rights may arise on release, but a federal registration strengthens enforcement, especially with third-party distribution platforms. Rightsholders should also secure domain names and social media handles to prevent cybersquatting, and registered trademarks support action under ICANN's UDRP and platform takedown systems. Monitoring services can detect unauthorised use.

When copies are found, the response may include cease-and-desist letters, takedown notices, or a civil lawsuit seeking a preliminary injunction. A developer seeking such an injunction must show irreparable harm, and any delay in acting may undermine that claim. Each day that unauthorised clones remain on sale can cause consumer confusion and divert sales, which makes early registration important before any infringement begins. The article recommends a rapid-response protocol that covers platform complaints, cease-and-desist letters, and litigation. The practical goal, the lawyers say, is to have chain-of-title documentation, registrations, and enforcement procedures ready before a game's first public reveal.

Articles.Title: How to protect your IP against the army of AI clones

stories.Headline: Amazon's secret AI plan could change how Americans shop
stories.Summary:
Amazon is reportedly weighing a plan to build a global product database that would reduce shoppers' reliance on Google and other websites, according to an internal document reviewed by Reuters. The database, called World Product Graph, would gather information on products sold online, including items Amazon does not currently carry. The document describes a plan to merge data from manufacturers with information from retail websites, and it says Coke and Bayer are already sharing product information. Amazon is also considering an experiment with Procter & Gamble.

The project could benefit Amazon's shopping assistant, Alexa for Shopping, which was previously called Rufus. An internal paper cited in the report said the assistant's replies were sometimes wrong or partial and that the service was expensive. Amazon disputed that paper and said its shopping assistant is 97% accurate worldwide. The initiative also reflects competition from AI shopping bots that can compare prices and make purchases across different websites.

Amazon described the paper as preliminary and said it may not reflect the company's current goals. The company has not confirmed a launch plan, although the concept reportedly included an October 2027 start date. Retail sales and advertising revenue depend heavily on shopping traffic, which is why the plan matters to the company's business. The article notes that investors will be watching what Amazon does with the database and its AI-powered retail services.

Articles.Title: Amazon's secret AI plan could change how Americans shop

stories.Headline: IFF’s AI tool speeds up product concept creation
stories.Summary:
IFF, a New York-based company, has launched Concept Muse, an artificial intelligence tool designed to help generate food and beverage concepts. The tool identifies marketing opportunities and uses prompts to produce differentiated concepts. It draws on IFF's consumer insights, flavor expertise and market intelligence. The announcement was reported by bakingbusiness.com on November 13, 2026.

According to the company, each concept features a narrative, visual mockups and suggested technologies. IFF says research teams can move from inspiration to conceptualization in minutes rather than weeks using the tool. The company presents this as a way to speed up the early stages of product development. Concept Muse is aimed at manufacturers seeking new product ideas.

Benjamin Mattei, vice president of intelligence and digital transformation for IFF Taste, spoke about the launch. He said food and beverage innovation has long balanced art and science, and that digital transformation now adds a new dimension to that balance. Mattei described the tool as a place where AI meets human imagination. He said it is meant to accelerate innovation and help manufacturers think beyond conventional approaches.

The article places the launch within a set of related industry news, including other AI and data tools for suppliers and food companies. The article does not give pricing, availability dates or the names of customers using the tool. It also does not report any independent evaluation of how well the concepts perform. Further details about the tool's rollout are not included in the source material.

Articles.Title: IFF’s AI tool speeds up product concept creation

stories.Headline: Keeping an eye on AI costs: How tokens make consumption, costs and benefits measurable
stories.Summary:
A KPMG Germany article published on 13 November 2026 explains how companies can use the token, the smallest processing unit of a language model, to measure how much artificial intelligence they use and what it costs. The piece presents the token as comparable to a kilowatt-hour for electricity, giving firms a common unit for judging scope of use, expense and added value. It notes that many companies are expanding their AI use but often lack clarity about the actual extent of usage, the resulting costs and the value delivered. The article is built around a white paper titled "Managing AI Value in Organisations," which the firm published alongside it.

The white paper uses a manufacturing company as an example to show the financial effect of growing AI use. According to the article, token prices are expected to fall by a factor of about 1.9 by 2031, while volume is projected to rise by a factor of between 5.7 and 8.5 over the same period. Together these trends would lift the company's annual AI operating costs from roughly six million euros to between 19 and 28 million euros. The authors present this as a reason to track consumption closely rather than assume that falling unit prices will keep total spending in check.

To address this, KPMG describes an integrated AI management model with three components. The first maps how much AI is used across the organisation, in which areas and by whom, whether employees, agents or machines, and compares this with best-practice figures to reveal over-consumption and untapped potential. The second forecasts token price trends over five years across different providers to produce cost scenarios. The third identifies the AI agents that contribute the most value and derives a prioritised implementation roadmap within the available budget. Taken together, the model is meant to link consumption and cost to achievable added value.

The article says the model can show where excessive consumption can be reduced and where AI use should be expanded, and which agents promise the highest returns. It also suggests that future cost trends can be built into budget planning at an early stage. The text does not report any particular company adopting the framework, and it offers no further detail on the forecasting methods or the figures behind the scenarios beyond what is summarised above. The piece closes by noting that few industries are as central to digital transformation as the TMT sectors.

Articles.Title: Keeping an eye on AI costs: How tokens make consumption, costs and benefits measurable

stories.Headline: GreyNoise Unveils Benchmark for AI Cyber Defense Performance
stories.Summary:
GreyNoise, a threat data company, has introduced the GreyNoise AI Cyber Index, a public benchmark that tests how well artificial intelligence models perform cyber defense work. The company announced the index on a Thursday, and the article is dated November 13, 2026. The index is publicly accessible on the company's website, which the company said coincides with its threat data platform surpassing 100,000 users. The first edition tests 46 closed and open-weight models against attack traffic captured by GreyNoise's Global Observation Grid.

The index measures tasks such as triaging alerts, writing detection rules and investigating intrusions, and it reports each model's task scores, refusal rates, and time and cost per problem. In the first round, Opus 5.5 earned the top raw score, while Grok 4.5 ranked first on the leaderboard, which counts refused tasks as zero. The article says the index is meant to give security teams a practical basis for choosing a model for their operations. Faster, AI-driven attacks are prompting government and industry to rethink how they select and deploy network defense tools.

Andrew Morris, founder and chief architect of GreyNoise, said most public benchmarks focus on offensive capabilities and few check whether models can help defenders in live environments. He said the company has watched attackers for eight years and tests models against what attackers actually do against GreyNoise sensors rather than a made-up lab setting. Morris added that more evaluations are in development and the benchmarks will be updated as new ones arrive. GreyNoise CEO Ash Devata said chief information security officers want to know how fast the next critical vulnerability will be exploited, and he argued that AI defenses are only as good as the data behind them.

The index builds on GreyNoise's broader work on AI-driven threats, including an April report warning that AI models in cybersecurity may be trained too late to detect emerging threats. The company has also expanded its platform with C2 Detection, which gives security teams visibility into compromised edge devices, and has pitched it to federal agencies amid warnings about Iranian cyberthreats. On the leadership side, GreyNoise named Mike Habte director of federal sales and added four senior leaders to support U.S. and allied government agencies. The article does not say what the company plans to release next beyond the additional evaluations Morris described.

Articles.Title: GreyNoise Unveils Benchmark for AI Cyber Defense Performance

stories.Headline: HCLTech, PTC launch PLM solution for semiconductor companies
stories.Summary:
HCLTech has launched a pre-configured product lifecycle management solution aimed at semiconductor companies, according to a TechGig report published on November 12, 2026. The offering runs on PTC's Windchill platform and covers intellectual property management, new product introduction, supplier collaboration, quality, and regulatory compliance. It can connect with a company's existing business, manufacturing, and design systems. HCLTech says it uses a digital thread to link people, processes, and data across the full product lifecycle.

The launch fits into a broader push to expand India's chip design and manufacturing capacity. At SEMICON India 2026, Union Minister for Electronics and Information Technology Ashwini Vaishnaw said that 70,000 design engineers had been trained in four years, against an initial target of 85,000 over a decade. More than 105 chip design startups have gained access to electronic design automation tools. The second phase of the India Semiconductor Mission aims for at least 200 chip design companies. The government's ambitions also reach into system design and product development.

John Haller, General Manager of PLM at PTC, said the partnership gives customers a stronger foundation to modernise product development and management at scale. The article does not name HCLTech executives who spoke on the launch. The companies did not disclose any customer deployments or commercial terms for the solution. The report does not say when the solution will be available to buyers or how it will be priced.

Articles.Title: HCLTech, PTC launch PLM solution for semiconductor companies

stories.Headline: Fortinet patches nearly 100 vulnerabilities across products
stories.Summary:
Fortinet on Tuesday published 89 security advisories covering nearly 100 vulnerabilities across its product line. About 17 of the newly fixed flaws are rated critical, and several of them could let an attacker run arbitrary code, bypass authentication, or take over an account. FortiMail received the largest group of critical fixes. Other affected products include FortiAuthenticator, FortiOS, FortiManager, and FortiAnalyzer, while new FortiSASE and FortiClient updates also address critical issues.

Kevin Joensen, a principal security consultant at Baldur Security, said one FortiClient bug is exploitable when FortiPAM is enabled. He described it as a flaw named Fortinet2Shell that could let an attacker execute code if a victim visits a malicious website. The root cause is a CORS misconfiguration that allows attacker-controlled web pages to talk to a local service. Fortinet also patched nearly 80 high-severity vulnerabilities, which could lead to cross-site scripting, code execution, code injection, and denial-of-service conditions. The company does not say that any of these defects have been exploited in the wild.

Fortinet framed the release as part of a broader effort to find and fix flaws faster. Three weeks before the release, the company said it had integrated frontier AI models into its product security testing, which it says makes discovering security defects more efficient. In its statement, the company said this approach gives customers time to prioritize upgrades before further technical details become public. The articles do not say when the vulnerabilities were reported or who discovered them. They also do not describe any further advisories or deadlines beyond this release.

Articles.Title: Fortinet patches nearly 100 vulnerabilities across products

stories.Headline: Build local AI coding workflow with open-source models
stories.Summary:
Software developers can now build a private AI coding workflow by running open-source models on their own machines, according to a report from Frontend Focus published on November 12, 2026. The setup uses LM Studio to serve these models to tools such as VS Code and terminal agents. Developers who take this route keep their code on local hardware and avoid paying per token for each request. The approach also removes the risk that a vendor will limit usage, change prices, or shut the service down.

The article says local models are now good enough for everyday coding tasks, which is what makes this workflow practical. It also explains that developers should understand model families, file formats, and quantization, because these choices shape how well a model runs on a given computer. LM Studio can be configured so that the local environment is reachable from any device, not only the machine where the model runs. The report presents this as a way to keep operational costs at zero while keeping code private.

The report, published by Frontend Focus and carried by TechGig, does not name a specific author or quote any individual developer or company. It presents the workflow as guidance for software developers rather than as a product announcement. The article offers a general description of the steps and benefits but gives no detailed instructions, benchmarks, or named models. It also does not say how many developers have adopted this approach or what performance trade-offs exist compared with hosted services.

Articles.Title: Build local AI coding workflow with open-source models

stories.Headline: Siemens, Schneider Electric issue ICS Patch Tuesday advisories
stories.Summary:
Siemens and Schneider Electric have each released Industrial Control Systems Patch Tuesday advisories covering a number of vulnerabilities in their products. Siemens published nine advisories covering 10 vulnerabilities, including one called Node2Shell, for which exploitation attempts have been observed. Schneider Electric released a single advisory on a medium-severity flaw in EcoStruxure Power Build Rapsody. The advisories were reported on November 12, 2026.

The Siemens flaws include several rated high severity, affecting products such as ROS#, Simcenter Femap, Mendix Studio Pro MCP Server, Simatic SCADA and PCS 7, Meta-iot2050, and Simatic WinCC Graphics Designer. According to the articles, these issues could allow code injection, arbitrary code execution, and unauthorized data access. Siemens said patches are not yet available for several affected products, and some versions will not receive fixes at all. Customers are therefore being told to apply the mitigations Siemens recommends. The Schneider Electric flaw could let an attacker run arbitrary code by having the software process a malicious file.

Siemens said the products concerned are not yet fully protected, and the articles do not give a list of which versions will go unpatched. Germany's VDE CERT also published eight new advisories the same week, covering products from Beckhoff, MB Connect Line, Helmholz, Weidmueller, Bender, and Ads-Tec. Several of these involve third-party components, including a flaw called PHP2Shell. Phoenix Contact and Johnson Controls had issued their own advisories earlier in the month, and Hitachi Energy confirmed that at least one of its products is affected by the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities. The articles do not say whether any of these flaws have been exploited beyond the Node2Shell attempts noted by Siemens.

Articles.Title: Siemens, Schneider Electric issue ICS Patch Tuesday advisories

stories.Headline: SUSE enhances Kubernetes management with AI agents, new features
stories.Summary:
SUSE has updated its Kubernetes management tools and frameworks, including making its AI Agent Crew generally available in Rancher Prime. The AI Agent Crew features an AI assistant named Liz that routes requests to specialised agents, which can troubleshoot Kubernetes workloads and virtual machines. The updates also add a Hosted Control Plane mode for Rancher Prime Virtual Clusters, now in open beta, which lets platform teams offer Kubernetes as a Service using RKE2. SUSE Application Collection now includes over 996 Python libraries built from verified sources, with software bills of materials to help teams assess dependencies. The announcement was published on November 12, 2026.

Liz can also call Model Context Protocol servers through an OAuth2 authorisation protocol to connect with external tools, AI agents, and applications. A command line interface for programmatically testing infrastructure updates is now in beta. SUSE Observability StackPacks has also been updated to extend the SUSE Observability platform to third-party platforms and applications. The company says these additions aim to simplify complex Kubernetes operations for IT professionals. Abhinav Puri, vice president and general manager of portfolio and community at SUSE, said the AI Crew sub-agents allow troubleshooting tasks to be assigned to specifically trained AI agents.

He said AI agents make Kubernetes more accessible to IT professionals who may lack the engineering expertise previously required. Puri also said SUSE's tools are designed to shorten the time to value when deploying workloads on Kubernetes clusters. He identified a chronic skills gap as the biggest challenge IT teams face in deploying Kubernetes workloads. The new features arrive as more IT teams deploy AI models and applications on-premises to reduce costs. The article does not say what further steps SUSE plans beyond these releases.

Articles.Title: SUSE enhances Kubernetes management with AI agents, new features

stories.Headline: Kent C. Dodds builds 1.5M line product without coding
stories.Summary:
Kent C. Dodds, a developer educator and former React instructor, has said he has largely stopped engaging with code this year while building a product of close to 1.5 million lines that has paying users. TechGig reported the account on November 12, 2026. According to the report, the shift began when a coding agent resolved a significant GitHub issue in a matter of hours, which prompted Dodds to rethink what software engineering skills now involve. He has since let his agents run much of the development workflow on their own.

Dodds' agents have merged around 1,300 pull requests in the past 30 days, often without his direct supervision. After each deployment, the agents produce what Dodds calls "friction reports" describing the obstacles they ran into, and another agent works through those reports overnight. To coordinate this, Dodds built a product called Kody, which is meant to let several AI agents work together and to centralise automations and credentials. The report says Kody relies on deterministic code for critical steps such as its "ship PR" pipeline, which the article presents as more reliable and cheaper than looser interactions with large language models.

Security is also part of the design. According to the article, Kody includes a credential system that stops agents from reaching sensitive keys directly, and it limits each credential to specific domains, request components, or packages. The report frames this as a response to a serious weakness in AI-driven development environments. Dodds is scheduled to lead a workshop at the AIE Code Summit on November 10, where he will outline a three-pillar framework covering how to use agents to build correct software, catch errors before production, and limit the damage if a problem reaches deployment.

Articles.Title: Kent C. Dodds builds 1.5M line product without coding

stories.Headline: GitHub makes agentic workflows generally available with controls
stories.Summary:
GitHub has made Agentic Workflows generally available, allowing coding agents to run inside GitHub Actions. The announcement was reported on November 12, 2026. The tool is aimed at repository tasks such as issue triage and continuous integration failure analysis. It is available on GitHub Free, Team, and Enterprise plans on github.com.

Agents start with read-only permissions, and any proposed changes are applied by separate jobs that hold their own write tokens. These protections do not automatically cover direct write permissions or custom jobs that a workflow author adds, so safety depends on how the workflow is configured. Authors can add a GitHub Environment protection rule that requires a human reviewer before a write job runs. Developers describe their work in natural-language Markdown with YAML frontmatter, and the project compiles this into a standard Actions workflow. Agents run in a sandboxed container behind an Agent Workflow Firewall, and a threat-detection job scans proposed changes before they are applied.

Spending is capped by default. GitHub's documentation prices AI Credits at $0.01 each and sets a cap of 1,000 AIC, or $10, per run. The enterprise controls reference default caps of 5,000 AIC per day and 400 AIC per threat-detection run, along with a 20-minute timeout on the agent step, and organisations can override these limits. The gh aw forecast command, no longer experimental, estimates monthly AI credit spending. The default Copilot CLI engine requires a Copilot licence, though teams can also use Copilot or integrate other coding agents.

GitHub has added support for Actions Runner Controller, its Kubernetes operator for self-hosted runners, with Docker-in-Docker since the public preview in June 2026. This lets the agent start its sandbox containers inside the runner pod. The project's guide notes that ARC runs the Docker-in-Docker sidecar as a privileged container by default. GitHub's FAQ says conventional Actions remain the better choice for reproducible builds and tests, while agent workflows are intended for tasks that need interpretation or generation.

Articles.Title: GitHub makes agentic workflows generally available with controls

stories.Headline: Railway cloud hosting firm faces $740,000 AI fraud after zero-day exploit
stories.Summary:
Railway, a US-based cloud hosting company, reported a zero-day vulnerability in its build infrastructure that let attackers steal customer AI API keys and cloud credentials. The stolen keys were used to run roughly $740,000 in unauthorized AI usage, which the company believes was likely tied to large-scale model training and automation. The attack began on October 20 at about 07:28 UTC and ended on October 21 at 09:24 UTC, when Railway contained the intrusion and rotated credentials after 26 hours of effort. The company is working with AI providers to refund the fraudulent charges and has said it will cover any losses that are not reimbursed. The company's account describes the exploit as having taken advantage of a flaw in the build system, and the details released so far focus on that initial breach.

Attackers then exploited a misconfigured authentication mechanism inside Railway's internal codebase, which gave them further access beyond the first breach. From there they reached a production database holding encrypted customer environment variables along with information needed to decrypt them. Railway believes the compromised keys were sold on the black market, possibly for use in model distillation, a technique in which a smaller AI model is trained to imitate a larger one by querying the original extensively. The company said environment variables for up to 100,000 customer workspaces could have been decrypted during the incident. It stressed that this figure is an upper limit and not a count of confirmed compromised accounts.

Responsibility for the breach rests with the attackers, who exploited the zero-day flaw and the misconfigured authentication mechanism, and Railway has stated that it is responding to the incident and making customers whole for unreimbursed charges. The articles present these facts as Railway's own account of what happened, and they do not include independent verification of the attackers' identities or motives. The incident is notable because it involved stolen AI API keys being turned into costly, automated usage, which shows how cloud credentials can carry financial risk as well as data risk. The articles do not say whether any customer data was confirmed as accessed or misused beyond the decryption exposure described. They also do not give further details on the status of the refund process or any regulatory response.

Articles.Title: Railway cloud hosting firm faces $740,000 AI fraud after zero-day exploit

stories.Headline: Google releases A2UI 1.0 protocol for generative UI agents
stories.Summary:
Google has released A2UI 1.0, the first stable version of an open protocol for generative user interfaces, which lets AI agents respond with interactive screens such as forms or charts instead of text-only outputs. The announcement was published on November 12, 2026, by TechGig. Developers can use open-source renderer SDKs for the web, Android, and iOS, along with agent SDKs for Python, TypeScript, and Dart. Under this approach, an agent describes what should be shown, and each application draws the interface using its own native components. The articles say this keeps latency low and preserves native fidelity across platforms, so one agent output can work on any screen.

Developers can build a view once and have it rendered natively on phones and laptops. The protocol is described as stable, and Google is also upgrading Gemini Enterprise to A2UI 1.0. Google is the company behind the release, and the articles report that it has made the protocol and its SDKs open source. Several companies are already building with A2UI, including Atlassian, Alation, Bloomberg, and ByteDance. Atlassian is integrating it into Jira so AI agents can use interactive cards for follow-ups on work items, and Alation uses it to build feeds with metric cards and charts.

ByteDance released an A2UI renderer for Lynx, its cross-platform framework, in June 2026. The articles also note that Jetpack Compose support for A2UI 1.0 is expected soon. Google Cloud documentation gives guidance on registering and hosting A2UI agents on Cloud Run. The articles further state that A2UI works alongside MCP Apps, allowing A2UI screens to operate within an MCP App. No further dates or commitments beyond these are provided.

Articles.Title: Google releases A2UI 1.0 protocol for generative UI agents

stories.Headline: Cognizant commits 25,000 staff to Claude AI deployment
stories.Summary:
Cognizant announced on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, the formation of the Claude Frontier Capability Group, a dedicated global organization of more than 25,000 professionals committed to delivering Anthropic's Claude for clients. The Nasdaq-listed company, with its base in Teaneck, New Jersey, made the announcement through a PR Newswire release. The group is built around execution excellence, transformation and client success. It has the scale to take AI from pilot to production across the core operations of enterprises. Cognizant also introduced a managed services model for Claude, under which it runs Claude-powered systems in production on behalf of clients.

The managed services model combines dedicated talent, licensed access to Claude and Cognizant's own intellectual property, including its AI Delivery Operating System. It gives clients more predictable AI spend and runs every engagement within enterprise-grade security and governance controls. Those controls are customized to each client's connectivity, architecture and risk requirements. The new group will initially focus on four areas, starting with redesigning business domains around AI and building and modernizing the systems that support them. The other two areas are operating agents securely at scale and establishing AI-native software engineering as a core delivery capability, and for modernization Cognizant brings purpose-built Claude agents that speed analysis and refactoring of legacy and mainframe code.

Ravi Kumar S, Cognizant's chief executive, said clients want a partner who will take responsibility for delivery once AI is running inside their business. He said the company is putting more than 25,000 of its people on Claude and taking on the job of running it for clients through managed services. Kumar described this as a significant bet on Claude and on what enterprises can achieve with it in their core operations. Both initiatives draw on Cognizant's Frontier workforce model, through which it is developing Frontier Certified Engineers and Frontier Business Operators credentialed directly by frontier-model companies. Cognizant did not disclose the commercial terms of the offering, according to TechGig.

Paul Smith, Anthropic's Chief Commercial Officer, said every enterprise is racing to bring AI into its organization, but people with the skills to make it work inside a real business have become the hardest talent to find. He said Cognizant is working to address that gap by committing more than 25,000 people to help customers put Claude to work across their businesses. Cognizant cited client results from the work already underway, including a global pharmaceutical manufacturer where Claude-powered shop-floor agents cut downtime by 35%. At that manufacturer, troubleshooting time fell from 90 to 120 minutes down to 10 to 15 minutes. A media and entertainment company cut time to market from three to four weeks to about 15 minutes by automating requirement data sheet creation, and a North American insurer accelerated campaign brief generation and retirement plan support by 40% to 60%.

Cognizant has built Claude skills across its workforce, with more than 44,000 associates in business units and corporate functions already trained or certified on Claude. The company holds more than 26,000 Claude certifications and ranks first globally for Claude Certified Architect: Foundations. It is deploying Claude across its workforce, including corporate functions, engineering and delivery teams, as announced in November 2025. TechGig reports that the latest announcement builds on an expanded partnership with Anthropic in July, when Cognizant outlined plans to integrate Claude into its engineering platforms. Other Indian IT services companies are also building teams around frontier AI models, and HCLTech signed a partnership with Anthropic in October and set up a dedicated business unit and a Centre of Excellence for Claude-based enterprise solutions.

The sources do not say when the group or the managed services model will begin operating for particular clients, or how many clients have signed up. Cognizant has not disclosed the commercial terms of the managed services offering, so pricing and contract structure remain unknown. The group will start with four priority areas, and the articles do not say whether more will be added later. Rediff lists related stories about Cognizant forming an OpenAI Frontier Capability Group and a Gemini Frontier Capability Group with Google Cloud, each with 25,000 professionals, though it gives no details of them. The articles also leave open how the developing Frontier Certified Engineers and Frontier Business Operators credentials will progress and how many people will hold them.

Articles.Title: Cognizant commits 25,000 staff to Claude AI deployment

stories.Headline: Austrian Bishops Adopt First Rules for AI in the Church
stories.Summary:
The Austrian Bishops' Conference has adopted its first rules on artificial intelligence in the Church, stating that AI may never take the place of human relationships, pastoral conversations, or the rites of the Church. The bishops adopted the framework at their autumn plenary in Salzburg, which ran from Monday to Thursday, and announced it in a press statement on Thursday. The rules are titled "Framework Regulation on the Use of AI Systems in the Catholic Church in Austria and Its Institutions." They take effect once they are published in the next official gazette of the bishops' conference.

The core provision says AI may only play a supporting role in the celebration of the sacraments, preaching, liturgy, and pastoral care. Replacing human relationships, pastoral conversations, community, or rituals with AI is explicitly rejected. The bishops stressed that in preaching, liturgy, and pastoral care, the irreplaceability of personal encounter must be preserved. The framework also requires every diocese to appoint a person responsible for AI. A new working group will bring together all diocesan AI officers, along with experts in data protection, information technology, and theological ethics, and the Austrian Conference of Religious Orders will take part.

The bishops said the rules rest on the Christian image of man, the inviolable dignity of every person, and respect for human freedom. They argued that AI should serve the human person rather than replace him, and that its use therefore requires critical review, human oversight, and orientation toward truth, justice, and the common good. The bishops also acknowledged that AI opens new possibilities for the Church's mission while raising ethical, legal, and social challenges. The working group that prepared the framework was set up in November 2025 and led by Bishop Hermann Glettler of Innsbruck.

The framework follows the bishops' June plenary in Mariazell, where they explicitly endorsed Pope Leo XIV's social encyclical Magnifica Humanitas. In that statement they drew on the encyclical's call to preserve the greatness of the human person and to ensure AI builds a universal human family where digital closeness becomes a real chance for encounter and mutual care. The bishops said the perspective of the poor, weak, and disadvantaged is needed because the rich and powerful are the ones who develop and profit from AI systems. They concluded that the future will be decided by whether people take responsibility for the human person and for a culture of encounter, love, and peace.

Articles.Title: Austrian Bishops Adopt First Rules for AI in the Church

stories.Headline: Why your clients probably aren’t covered for AI
stories.Summary:
Insurance Business reported on November 13, 2026 that AI exclusions are spreading through commercial general liability, errors and omissions, and professional liability policies across the United States, and that many clients do not know their cover no longer responds to AI-related claims. Major carriers, including Chubb, Travelers, and Berkshire Hathaway, obtained or sought state approval to add AI exclusions to CGL policies, while W.R. Berkley filed an absolute AI exclusion, form PC 51380, covering D&O, E&O, and fiduciary lines. ISO also introduced several generative AI exclusion endorsements for CGL forms effective January 2026. Gallagher Re figures cited in the piece show US generative AI lawsuits rose 978% between 2021 and 2025, with filings growing 137% in 2024 and 2025.

Under CG 40 47, an insurer may deny a claim if the loss arose from generative AI, meaning the trigger is any connection to AI rather than how much of the work AI touched. The article warns this matters for law firms using AI drafting tools, lenders running automated credit checks, and hospitals using AI diagnostic aids, where a single AI link could void coverage. Cyber policies typically respond only to breaches, so they often do not apply when an AI system produces harmful output without an outside intrusion. Businesses that are not technology companies usually lack tech E&O, leaving their exposure between policies.

George Lewin-Smith, CEO and co-founder of Testudo, a Lloyd's coverholder writing standalone generative AI liability cover in the US, says brokers are reluctant to confirm coverage because insurers have not priced for AI risk and are not accounting for it. He says vendor contracts and model provider terms make the deployer of an AI tool responsible for its outputs, whatever the vendor sold. He also said brokers and carriers are pulling in different directions, with brokers resisting AI exclusions while some carriers push standalone products. The Lloyd's Market Association has already filed AI endorsements, a process he described as taking two years compared with twenty for cyber.

The article presents Testudo's Lloyd's-backed program, expanded with Atrium and QBE capacity in March 2026, as one answer, offering up to $9.25 million per insured for third-party claims from AI outputs. Its underwriting relies on proprietary litigation data instead of audits or system integrations. Lewin-Smith expects a large uninsured AI loss will eventually force the issue, though he is unsure how frequent or severe such losses must become. Brokers whose clients renew within six months are already in the window the new ISO forms took effect, and the article advises checking policy language before a claim arises.

Articles.Title: Why your clients probably aren’t covered for AI

stories.Headline: Exclusive / Gen Z hasn’t made up its mind on AI, survey finds
stories.Summary:
A new survey from Milltown Partners, shared first with Semafor and published on November 13, 2026, found that Gen Z has not settled its views on artificial intelligence. Seventy-three percent of Gen Z adults said they had not made up their minds about AI, and half said they expect the technology to harm society. Those figures are close to the views of older generations, with baby boomers at 50 percent and Gen Xers at 48 percent expecting harm. Millennials were the most optimistic group, with 39 percent expecting harm.

The survey points to a paradox in how young people relate to AI. Many say the technology makes them worse at thinking for themselves and harder to find a job, yet 46 percent said they use it every day, the second-highest rate behind millennials. Young people are also less worried than older generations about existential risk, the concern that dominates much of the AI safety debate. At the same time, they are more conflicted about their own use, with 30 percent of Gen Zers saying they sometimes feel guilty using AI, more than double the rate among respondents over 30.

The reporting does not name a single party responsible for the findings beyond the survey's publisher, Milltown Partners, and the article's author, J.D. Capelouto, a tech reporter at Semafor. The article notes that companies and politicians are eager to understand the generation's stance because young people drive many technology trends and because AI and data centers played an outsized role in the US midterm elections. The article frames Gen Z as often portrayed as souring on AI, and presents the survey as evidence that this portrayal is not accurate, since the generation is no more negative than its parents and grandparents. The articles provided do not say what further steps, if any, will follow from the survey.

Articles.Title: Exclusive / Gen Z hasn’t made up its mind on AI, survey finds

stories.Headline: China’s great AI chip loophole: How American espionage stopped China — this time
stories.Summary:
Nvidia, the American AI chipmaker, has been caught up in a suspected Chinese scheme to obtain its advanced processors despite U.S. restrictions. According to the article, China may have used ostensibly legitimate companies in Singapore and Malaysia, exploited weaknesses in American export enforcement, and cultivated personal relationships with the leadership of the chipmaker. The article suggests the episode could have come dangerously close to succeeding, and that some of the technology may already have reached Chinese customers. Congress and the CIA will have to determine how much China gained and who assisted it. The article describes the scandal as unfolding, with the public record still incomplete.

The most troubling open question concerns roughly 50,000 Nvidia processors whose locations could not be reconciled with the company's reported inventory records. Nvidia later said it had located hardware in additional warehouses, but the article notes that full public reconciliation and independent verification of final locations remained unknown. The chips at issue include the H100, H200, and newer Blackwell-family processors, which the article calls among the most strategically important technologies behind modern artificial intelligence. Such chips help train advanced models used in military intelligence, cyberwarfare, scientific research, autonomous weapons, and economic competition. The article notes that President Trump has spent years restricting Chinese access to the most advanced versions of these technologies.

At the center of the controversy is Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a Chinese businesswoman associated with Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based company that acquires Nvidia processors for cloud computing. According to reporting by The New York Times, American intelligence concluded that Huang had been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security, the civilian intelligence organization responsible for foreign espionage and technology theft. American intelligence officers reportedly identified concerns about Huang's activities and her relationship with Nvidia's founder, Jensen Huang. The individuals who uncovered the suspected operation have not been publicly identified. The article cites the public record as not yet establishing whether Alice Huang transferred Nvidia secrets to Chinese intelligence.

The apparent weakness lay in the distinction between selling advanced processors directly to China and selling them to companies operating data centers elsewhere in Asia. Singapore and Malaysia have substantial cloud-computing industries, and companies there can legitimately buy American processors and rent computing capacity to customers worldwide. The article says this arrangement offers China two possible routes: processors destined for facilities outside China could be physically diverted, or Chinese firms could rent computing capacity in overseas data centers without the chips entering China. Reuters reported on November 12 that Chinese AI companies were seeking additional overseas Nvidia computing capacity amid fears that Washington might close this gap. The article notes that the second method is not necessarily illegal under existing regulations.

Bloomberg reported a discrepancy of roughly 50,000 processors between Nvidia's initial government tally and shipments made through hardware partners. Nvidia subsequently said it found hardware during inspections of additional Megaspeed warehouses but has not publicly disclosed exact counts. A November 11 letter from Senators Elizabeth Warren and Christopher Coons stated that Megaspeed had purchased more than $4.8 billion in advanced Nvidia AI chips since June 2024. The article says Congress must resolve whether the processors can be physically identified, their serial numbers verified, and their locations traced. Bloomberg and The New York Times reported that Nvidia representatives communicated with senior Commerce Department officials while investigators examined the matter.

Articles.Title: China’s great AI chip loophole: How American espionage stopped China — this time

stories.Headline: Chrome releases Modern Web Guidance 1.0 for AI coding agents
stories.Summary:
Chrome has released Modern Web Guidance version 1.0, a set of skills that embeds web platform expertise, best practices, and browser compatibility data into AI coding agents. The release was announced as a stable version and is aimed at a known weakness in AI-generated code, which often works but falls short on performance, accessibility, and security. An expanded guide database targets hundreds of verified knowledge gaps with cross-browser solutions. The release also adds a modernization workflow that scans existing codebases to find opportunities for safe upgrades.

Each guide goes through human expert review before release, including sign-off from content area tech leads and a dedicated accessibility review. The guidance is now a cross-browser effort, with Firefox and Edge joining Chrome to support and contribute to the project. The modernization workflow analyzes HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and package.json files to guide agents through upgrades. The initial release uses static analysis focused on patterns that produce predictable results, with plans to expand to agentic audits later. The guidance also recommends HTML or CSS features over JavaScript where they offer better efficiency and accessibility.

The articles credit Chrome with the release and say Firefox and Edge are contributing to the shared effort, which builds on their earlier work with Baseline. The articles do not name a specific person responsible for the release. The guidance is described as reinforcing practices that frontier coding models often miss, including in accessibility, user experience, performance, and security. Early users reported results: Indian fintech Pensionbazaar said the guidance with Chrome DevTools for agents shortened turnaround by over 90 per cent and reduced UI bugs by over 90 per cent. Its sister platform Policybazaar reported a 92 per cent cut in manual auditing effort across 30 high-traffic landing pages.

MetaMask, a self-custodial financial platform, ran the guidance as an automated review bot on pull requests.
