In its first five weeks the bot reviewed about 480 pull requests, and engineers fixed 43 findings, mostly related to accessibility and HTML semantics, with a median fix time of 15 minutes. The articles present these figures as company-reported results and do not describe independent verification. They also do not say how the guidance will be priced or distributed beyond the release itself. Further details on expansion of the audit features are not given beyond the stated plan.

Articles.Title: Chrome releases Modern Web Guidance 1.0 for AI coding agents

stories.Headline: New AI Learning Matrix Brings Nuance to “Wild West” Moment
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Harvard's Graduate School of Education have launched an online tool called the AI Guidance by Age matrix, aimed at educators, caregivers and learners. The launch was announced in an Inside Higher Ed article published on November 12, 2026. The tool was built by the Compass Collaborative, a research group at the school, and draws on more than 5,000 studies in education, psychology and human development. Its purpose is to show how using AI may help or hinder learning depending on a student's age and other context.

Users of the matrix first choose their role from a list of nine options, which includes K–12 educator, higher education educator, workforce educator, student, researcher and policymaker. They then pick a developmental area, such as cognitive foundations, social understanding and interaction, or language and literacy, and enter the age range of the learners involved. The tool returns a summary of the best uses of AI for that situation, suggestions for designing assessments, a list of ways AI may help or harm the specific learning goals, and additional resources. The article gives one example in which the matrix advises that AI should widen a young adult's reading or reflect their writing back to them, while the composing and problem-solving stay with the student.

Jeffrey James Curley, chief of strategic initiatives for the dean of the Harvard Graduate School of Education, described the present as an unprecedented, experimental period and said colleges have been slow to recognize that students feel pressure to use AI in ways that offer short-term gains but may carry long-term costs. He said many institutions have left decisions about AI to individual faculty, so rules differ from course to course. Tessa Forshaw, a cognitive scientist and researcher at the school who also helped create the Compass Collaborative, said there is still little independent research on how AI learning tools affect outcomes. She said the team combined newer work with older, well-established studies to give educators a starting point.

The article notes that much of the research behind the matrix predates generative AI by decades, though it has identified consistent patterns in how people learn. Forshaw hopes the tool will move educators away from broad judgments about AI and toward asking what the technology is used for, who uses it, in what setting, and what it replaces. The article does not say how many people have used the matrix so far or whether any institutions have formally adopted it. It also gives no indication of planned updates beyond Forshaw's hope that more research will appear in the field.

Articles.Title: New AI Learning Matrix Brings Nuance to “Wild West” Moment

stories.Headline: The Five Nine: Can Voice AI give telecom a new voice?
stories.Summary:
Voice AI, the use of artificial intelligence within live phone calls, is being pitched by vendors as a way to revive voice services that many in telecom consider stale. Fierce Network's Diana Goovaerts hosted an episode of The Five Nine on the subject, published on November 13, 2026. Guests Brandon Larson of Mavenir, Dag Peak of Alianza and Kris Efland of Deepgram appeared in the episode. The episode examines whether AI can give the oldest service in the network a second life, and it covers both the promise and the difficult parts. Those difficult parts include latency, consent, data privacy, where the AI should run and how to price it.

Voice AI is a broad label that can describe several different things. Peak and Larson divide it into three categories: AI-handled calls, applications that engage in live conversations, and post-call intelligence. Larson offered examples such as real-time translation between two people speaking different languages, an AI receptionist for small businesses, and AI that detects deepfake voices, non-human voices or social engineering. Peak argued that human conversation is the richest form of communication and that bringing calls into the application and AI space opens many possibilities. Larson said operators' product teams see an opportunity to create value that does not depend entirely on handset makers such as Apple and Samsung.

Larson said operators could use these services to raise revenue through uplifts, step-up plans and add-on plans. Peak said operators are losing subscribers, lines and SIP trunks to vendors such as Twilio that bring intelligence to voice or messaging. He described bringing AI-powered services into operator networks as a defensive move that could help them keep customers, as well as an offensive move that could generate revenue. Larson advised operators to begin with a customer problem, estimate how many people have it, determine what they would pay to solve it, and then work backward to the technology. Efland said successful voice AI depends on low latency, accurate speech recognition and reliable turn-taking, and he noted that accuracy matters more in specialized fields such as healthcare, where recognizing drug names is important.

Efland said the highest value for enterprises comes from integrating AI with their data and systems, and he said Deepgram deploys wherever customers operate, including air-gapped devices, their own infrastructure, virtual private clouds and data centers. He added that Deepgram spends considerable time understanding customers' use cases and outcomes before working back from those outcomes. Efland used a drive-through example, describing a parent ordering while children shout, to illustrate the unpredictable conditions these systems must handle. Larson said context engineering, including knowing a subscriber's preferences and history, can matter more than choosing a more powerful model. Peak said the major problems have been identified and that the pieces are coming together.

The three guests disagreed about how much of the work remains unfinished. Larson described a design in which the other caller hears an announcement and actively accepts before the AI begins, while Peak said Alianza's trust framework covers consent, announcements and data collection along with vetting the experiences attached to calls. Peak and Larson described these as their own companies' approaches rather than a universal legal rule for every service or location. Peak said trust, privacy and consent remain central to getting people comfortable with such services. Efland said users need to understand when AI is involved in a conversation.

The guests all said the test is whether the whole system works for the person using it. The episode was written and hosted by Diana Goovaerts and edited by Goovaerts, Matt Rickman and Nikki Grcic, with Liz Coyne as executive producer. The articles do not say how the services discussed will be regulated, priced in the market or adopted by operators. They also do not say how far the consent designs described by the guests will be used across the industry. Whether operators will turn these pitches into revenue remains an open question in the coverage.

Articles.Title: The Five Nine: Can Voice AI give telecom a new voice?

stories.Headline: Why I’m Not Afraid of AI: A Matter of Faith
stories.Summary:
Mendi Glik, a software engineer and regular columnist for The Jewish Press, has published a blog post on The Times of Israel's Blogs section titled "Why I'm Not Afraid of AI: A Matter of Faith," dated November 12, 2026. In it he responds to recent warnings from employees of AI companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI, who have spoken about risks ranging from AI taking over the internet to the extinction of humanity. Glik writes that he is not worried about AI, artificial general intelligence, or artificial superintelligence, and he grounds that view in his belief in God. He argues that if God chose to end humanity, He would not need AI to do it.

Glik's central claim is that humans will always be superior to AI because they were created by God and possess a soul, while machines can only perform routine tasks or tasks humans assign them. He notes that programmers who use AI know it makes mistakes and must be monitored, and he says people are better at creativity and thought. He compares AI to earlier tools such as oxen used for plowing and computers and CNC machines used in manufacturing, calling large language models sophisticated machines built to finish tasks faster. He also argues that because human intelligence is a gift from God, AI is more likely meant to improve the world than to destroy it. He acknowledges that technology companies have a moral duty to build secure systems and strong safeguards, and he suggests engineers will be able to restrict AI and use other AI agents to keep it under control.

Glik also contrasts believers with those who fear AI, writing that people who do not believe in God, and who he says are mostly on the progressive side, tend to feel helpless in the face of threatening technology. He writes that believers trust that the world is under God's guidance and control. He says he could offer technical reasons for his confidence but that the ultimate reason is his trust in God. The article is a personal opinion column, and the post itself notes that its views are solely the author's and not those of The Times of Israel. The article does not describe any specific next steps or policy changes.

Articles.Title: Why I’m Not Afraid of AI: A Matter of Faith

stories.Headline: 6 UCLA Samueli doctoral students win Qualcomm fellowship to push AI forward
stories.Summary:
Six UCLA Samueli School of Engineering doctoral students have won Qualcomm fellowships, each team receiving $100,000 in funding after the awards were announced in June. The fellowship, offered by the communications and computing company Qualcomm, goes to 16 two-person teams each year based on project proposals. This year's UCLA recipients are working on new technology for microchip design, self-driving vehicles and artificial intelligence. The reporting was published by the Daily Bruin on November 12, 2026.

Qualcomm received 392 applications from scholars across research areas including AI, autonomous driving, and hardware and theory. Applicants submitted a one-page abstract and a three-page proposal, then gave a final PowerPoint presentation. Seth Zhao described the process as long and challenging, saying many strong doctoral students submitted good proposals. The article notes that the research produced by fellows will be accessible to the public.

Sujoy Ghosh said his team is working to reduce the size and increase the efficiency of chip components, which power nearly all electronic devices, from smartphones to data centers. He credited UCLA equipment, an advising team, industry partnerships, software, technical support and his professor for helping the project succeed. Zhao and Zewei Zhou are using their funding to research ways to improve autonomous vehicle safety, with Zhou saying current consumer driving systems are not advanced enough and that their group hopes to speed up advanced AI models for use in cars. Samyak Chakrabarty, in an emailed statement, said his team is redesigning chips to make AI more efficient on hardware in cars and robots.

The article places the fellowship in the wider funding landscape, noting that federal grants are the primary source of research funding at higher education institutions. It adds that industry funding still contributes more than $6 billion a year, about 6% of total academic research funding, according to the National Center for Science and Engineering Statistics. Chakrabarty argued that moving data between memory and processors is one of the biggest bottlenecks in AI hardware, and that current solutions throw large resources at the problem without fully solving it. The article does not describe any further steps or deadlines for the projects.

Articles.Title: 6 UCLA Samueli doctoral students win Qualcomm fellowship to push AI forward

stories.Headline: ‘Are robots scary?’ Phoenix Hill art exhibit examines humans’ AI thoughts, fears
stories.Summary:
Erin McGee Ferrell, a Louisville visual artist, opened a solo exhibition called "Robots Y'all" at Garner Narrative, a contemporary fine art gallery off East Market Street in the Phoenix Hill area, in the week before the article was published. The show features her oil paintings of robots attempting human tasks, and it runs until Dec. 13. Ferrell said her interest grew after two of her family members were scammed online in March, an experience that left them with significant financial losses. The exhibition is open Wednesday through Sunday from 1 to 6 p.m.

Ferrell began the paintings in March after a visit to Pittsburgh International Airport with fellow artist Tobey Fraley, whose installation "Fraley's Robot Repair" was commissioned by the airport in 2015. She said she was drawn to the colorful, square tin toy robots made in Japan in the 1950s, and she painted her robots in vibrant colors to make them look playful. One large work, "Birthday Robot," shows a smiling machine offering a gift, with the word "friendly" on its feet, which Ferrell said invites viewers to question whether it truly is friendly. She also built a larger-than-life robot named "Saturday" on the sidewalk outside her Smoketown studio with four volunteers, using aluminum pans, chicken wire, tomato cages and clothes dryer vents. The robot is equipped with a motion sensor that greets visitors with a hello, and it will be on display during Louisville Visual Art's Open Studio Weekend.

Ferrell described her own mixed feelings about artificial intelligence, saying it helps streamline her business, financial and marketing planning so she can focus more on making art. She said a task that once took four days can now take about two hours, which she described as career-changing. She also said she worries about AI's capacity to deceive people, and she hopes the exhibition will open a conversation about whether the technology should be loved, hated or feared. The article cites a 2025 Pew Research Center study in which 53% of surveyed U.S. adults believed AI will worsen people's creative thinking, and more than a third believed it could worsen problem-solving. It also notes that voters in 12 states rejected 47 ballot measures on election day, according to PBS News, and that many chose to restrict construction of AI data centers in their communities.

Articles.Title: ‘Are robots scary?’ Phoenix Hill art exhibit examines humans’ AI thoughts, fears

stories.Headline: Teachers are struggling over how to address AI use in the classroom, but agree that having strong policies is a good start
stories.Summary:
A column published by Inlander on November 12, 2026, examines how teachers are handling artificial intelligence in their classrooms and concludes that clear school policies are a sound first step. The piece draws on a survey of 222 high school math and English teachers conducted in May of that year by faculty working with Central Washington University's College in the High School program. The column was first published in the Washington State Standard and is reprinted under a Creative Commons license. It opens with the observation of one teacher who wondered whether teachers or students would remain relevant in the future.

The survey found sharp differences by subject. Of the English teachers, 57.0 percent said their overall attitude toward teaching had worsened since AI appeared, compared with 37.6 percent of math teachers, and 83.7 percent of English teachers voiced academic integrity concerns against 54.9 percent of math teachers. English teachers also reported more confidence in teaching students to use AI responsibly, at 45.5 percent compared with 24.4 percent for math, and were more likely to require students to experiment with AI, at 34.1 percent against 14.6 percent. The author suggests the gap may reflect the tools themselves, since large language models produce convincing prose but often make errors on simple calculations. The survey also linked clear institutional policies and useful, subject-specific professional development to greater teacher confidence, though it found no link to attitudes toward teaching or to concerns about cheating.

The authors, who are faculty members in the Central Washington University program, argue that both clear institutional guidance and discipline-specific training are needed so that teachers can decide how to use AI in ways that serve student learning. They suggest English teachers might benefit from training on designing assignments that AI cannot easily complete, while math teachers might learn to use AI to save time on tasks such as writing story problems. The column cautions against reflexively rejecting or embracing the technology, noting that about one in six survey responses mentioned moving all writing to in-class, pen-and-paper assignments and some teachers had stopped assigning homework. The authors compare this to the arrival of graphing calculators in the 1990s, warning that abandoning a skill over cheating could leave students unprepared. They conclude that teachers and students both remain essential, and that the central question is how AI can be used while preserving the human relationships that drive learning.

Articles.Title: Teachers are struggling over how to address AI use in the classroom, but agree that having strong policies is a good start

stories.Headline: AI Changes the Work, but Trust Remains Essential
stories.Summary:
Tungsten Automation's SVP and GM of AP and Payments, John Gibbon, wrote in a new PYMNTS eBook, "Payments Leaders Rethink What Works in 2026," published November 12, 2026, that automating one part of finance does not ensure that information and decisions carry through to the next. He says he once expected AI to bring fewer manual steps and more automated complex processes in accounts payable and payments, and assumed greater capability would make products more valuable. He still believes AI will reshape work but has come to doubt that capability alone produces a better product. Gibbon's view is shaped by a finding from Tungsten Automation's eInvoicing and Payments Report 2026: 77% of business leaders have modernized invoice processing, yet only 30% fully automate payment reconciliation with invoice data. Another 73% plan to automate reconciliation over the next 12 months.

Gibbon argues that payments decisions depend on context that a more capable system cannot supply on its own. Timing affects cash, controls must meet compliance requirements, and payment choices influence supplier relationships. A team may need to weigh payment terms against cash priorities or decide whether a different payment method suits a particular supplier. He says product design has to reflect these trade-offs, since a system must understand how a specific business operates before it can decide what matters most to that business.

The useful question, in his telling, is what a finance team needs a product to accomplish and what evidence would show it has done so. Automation has to fit the customer's workflow and produce an outcome the business values. Gibbon says he is asking product teams to state those requirements explicitly before choosing a solution. The questions include which part of the process needs to improve, which compliance obligations shape it, and what business result the customer should be able to measure.

He wants those answers to guide both what gets built and how it is assessed. A product hypothesis, he suggests, should tie a real customer need to a practical outcome such as reducing manual reconciliation work, improving payment traceability, or helping a team act on cash priorities. That approach gives a clearer basis for deciding whether AI is the right tool for a given problem. The article presents this as Gibbon's own position on the design of finance products rather than a policy change announced by any company.

Articles.Title: AI Changes the Work, but Trust Remains Essential

stories.Headline: AI in Hotel Operations: Productivity Gains and Frontline Challenges
stories.Summary:
A new industry study examines where artificial intelligence is improving hotel productivity and why many frontline tasks remain hard to automate. The American Hotel & Lodging Association and Actabl published the report in November 2026, drawing on a Destination AI survey of 107 hotel-company leaders. Ninety percent of respondents said AI improved the time spent on routine tasks, and 84% said it improved their own work. Only 15% identified improvements in frontline operations, and just 6% of respondents held operational roles. The findings therefore mostly reflect management perceptions rather than direct frontline experience.

The report also includes workforce data showing labor hours per occupied room fell 3.1% at participating full-service hotels and 3.5% at select-service properties in the first half of 2026. The authors do not establish AI as the cause of these declines. A separate study in the November 2026 edition of Annals of Tourism Research, by Santiago Melián-González, analyzed 202 tasks across 12 hotel occupational categories in Spain. Across those categories, an average of 90.78% of tasks faced at least one moderate-to-severe automation bottleneck. Counting only severe constraints, the average fell to 40.48%.

The study does not say how many jobs will disappear or remain, since it measures technical obstacles rather than replacement. Receptionists and their assistants faced moderate-to-severe constraints in 85.71% of tasks, compared with 93.55% for waiters and 94.59% for housekeepers. The study weighted all tasks equally regardless of frequency or duration, and it assessed technical feasibility without testing automation in operating hotels. The survey also found that only 24% of respondents believed their organization's AI investments had paid for themselves overall, while 28% said it was too early to tell. Just 42% expressed confidence in their organization's data readiness.

The research points to particular effects on the employees who use property management and point-of-sale systems. Property management systems hold reservations, guest profiles, room availability and room status, and receptionists rely on that information daily. AI-assisted functions could shorten the time spent finding available rooms or locating conflicting records, but resolving a guest's situation still requires judgment and explanation. Incorrect room statuses or incomplete reservations could produce unsuitable recommendations and add work rather than remove it. Restaurant staff face a similar split, since POS systems already handle orders, payments and room-charge postings while waiters manage service and disputed charges.

The sources describe these issues as relevant to the staff who deliver guest services, and they stress that hotels need to measure outcomes rather than assume gains. Relevant measures include reservation processing times, room-assignment accuracy, unresolved requests and manual correction rates for reception, and transaction accuracy, billing corrections and guest feedback for restaurants. Housekeeping could benefit from better scheduling data, which may support demand forecasting and help prioritize rooms for arriving guests. Physical cleaning and inspection, however, involve manual dexterity and changing conditions that the academic study identifies as difficult to automate. The articles add that faster processing offers limited value when incomplete updates create problems elsewhere in the hotel.

Shiji, a hospitality technology company, supplied the article and describes its cloud-based portfolio, which includes property management, point-of-sale, guest engagement, distribution, payments and data intelligence solutions for over 91,000 hotels worldwide. The articles do not say how hotels will adopt these tools or what the next research cycle will examine. They also do not state whether the labor-hour declines will persist beyond the first half of 2026. Nor do they say whether the Spanish task-level findings apply to hotels outside the four- and five-star sun-and-beach segment studied.

Articles.Title: AI in Hotel Operations: Productivity Gains and Frontline Challenges

stories.Headline: Jeff Bezos predicts AI could let families live on one paycheck. Amodei and Gates warn of a rougher road
stories.Summary:
Jeff Bezos has predicted that advances in artificial intelligence could let American families live on one paycheck, with productivity gains allowing workers to support a household on a three-day week. He made the remarks in an interview with Fox News' Bret Baier at Blue Origin's factory floor in Cape Canaveral, Florida, recorded for the network's 30th anniversary and reported by Fortune on November 12, 2026. Bezos said a two-earner household would no longer be required, and that one partner might choose to step back. He also expects a labor shortage rather than mass unemployment, saying employers will find it difficult to hire people who can afford to work less. He made a similar argument in June at VivaTech in Paris, where he said AI will create more jobs than it eliminates.

The stakes are large because dual full-time earning has become common. According to Pew Research Center, both parents worked full-time in 52% of U.S. different-sex couples with children under 18 in 2025, up from 31% in 1975, so a one-paycheck norm would reverse a half-century shift. Bezos has a financial stake in the outcome. He is co-founder and co-CEO of Project Prometheus, an AI startup that launched with $6.2 billion in funding to apply the technology to engineering and manufacturing in computing, aerospace and automobiles. He told Baier the company aims to make tools so easy that anyone can be an engineer.

Other leaders have offered sharply different views. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei told Axios in May 2025 that AI could eliminate roughly half of all entry-level white-collar jobs within five years and push unemployment to between 10% and 20%. Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates has floated a two-day workweek, but in an August essay on Gates Notes he warned that the shift to AI will be among the most turbulent periods in human history and that world leaders are unprepared for its risks. MIT Sloan research, cited by Fortune, finds AI is already changing how tasks are performed, who gets hired and which skills employers value.

Skeptics note that the forecast depends on who captures the gains. Productivity improvements translate into shorter hours or a single-income lifestyle only if savings reach employees, while companies that keep the gains as profit or cut headcount could leave families without a second income and without the promised free time. Amazon, which ranks No. 1 on the 2026 Fortune 500 with more than $700 billion in revenue, has cut about 30,000 corporate roles since late 2025 while planning more than $200 billion in capital spending this year, mostly on data centers. The article does not say how the debate will be resolved, and it leaves open whether the technology's benefits will show up in paychecks or in profits.

Articles.Title: Jeff Bezos predicts AI could let families live on one paycheck. Amodei and Gates warn of a rougher road

stories.Headline: AI partnerships go beyond Nvidia: Merck KGaA CEO
stories.Summary:
Merck KGaA, the German pharmaceutical and chemicals group, has been discussed on CNBC's Squawk Box Europe in the context of its artificial intelligence investments and its partnership with Nvidia. The interview with Kai Beckmann, the company's chief executive, was published on November 12, 2026, following the release of Merck KGaA's latest results. The segment runs about two minutes and forty seconds and is listed as having aired two hours before the article was posted. The articles available describe the discussion only at this level, so the specific details of the deals, amounts and timelines are not known from this source.

Beckmann reflected on the company's spending on artificial intelligence and on what the partnership with Nvidia means for its business. According to the segment summary, his remarks also made clear that the company's AI work is not limited to that one relationship. The headline frames this as the central point, namely that the company's AI collaborations extend beyond Nvidia. Nvidia, the chipmaker whose ticker appears alongside the coverage, is the only other company named. No figures, dates for new projects, or changes to operations are given in the available material.

Beckmann is responsible for the comments reported, and the summary attributes to him reflections on AI investment and the Nvidia partnership. The CNBC piece is a short video segment with a written summary, so the full wording of his answers is not reproduced here. The segment connects his comments to the company's most recent results, which suggests the AI topic came up as part of a broader review of the company's performance. The articles do not describe any regulatory response, market reaction or company statement beyond the interview itself. More to follow.

Articles.Title: AI partnerships go beyond Nvidia: Merck KGaA CEO

stories.Headline: Micron vs. Sandisk: The AI Memory Supercycle Is Big Enough for Both, but Here's the Better Buy.
stories.Summary:
Micron and Sandisk, two memory chipmakers, have seen their shares rise sharply in 2026 as memory has become a major bottleneck in the artificial intelligence build-out. Sandisk shares are up over 200% this year, while Micron shares have soared around 150%. Memory prices have surged, raising the cost of AI data centers as well as smartphones, PCs and other electronic devices. The article, published by The Motley Fool on November 11, 2026, compares the two companies as investments. Both stocks have benefited from the same market conditions over the course of the year.

The memory market is split into volatile memory, which loses its data without power, and nonvolatile memory, which keeps data when power is off. The main volatile type is dynamic random access memory, known as DRAM, which is fast and serves as short-term workspace for processors. The main nonvolatile type is NAND flash memory, which is slower and less expensive and is used in solid-state drives, hard disk drives and memory cards. Micron is the smallest of the big three DRAM makers, which together control about 90% of the DRAM market. Micron holds over 20% of the DRAM market and around 15% of the NAND market, with about 73% of its last-quarter revenue from DRAM and 26% from NAND.

Sandisk is a pure-play NAND maker that makes up just over 10% of the flash market. The article says the overall memory market is currently driven by high bandwidth memory, or HBM, a special form of DRAM packaged with graphics processing units and other AI accelerators. HBM is made with the same extreme ultraviolet lithography machines used for advanced logic chips, and ASML is the only company in the world with this technology. HBM requires upward of three times the wafer capacity of conventional DRAM, and building new cleanroom facilities takes years. These constraints have led the big three DRAM makers, which also include Samsung and SK Hynix, to focus on HBM at the expense of conventional DRAM and NAND.

The article's author, Geoffrey Seiler, states that the memory market is historically cyclical with boom and bust periods, but that this time is different because AI is a powerful secular tailwind. Both companies have been signing longer-term deals, and both stocks trade at forward price-to-earnings ratios of 4 times or less. Seiler concludes that Micron is the clearer stock to buy if an investor could only buy one, because the market has far fewer DRAM players than NAND players. He expects the current memory supercycle to last longer for DRAM. Seiler says he has no position in any of the stocks mentioned.

Conventional DRAM and NAND prices have risen more quickly than HBM prices, which has fueled the strong growth at Micron and Sandisk. The NAND market is also seeing strong demand because AI labs need to store their training data in massive flash-based solid-state drives. The article notes that the rise in memory prices has affected the cost of AI data centers and consumer electronics alike. It does not report any other responses from companies, analysts or consumers beyond the author's view. The article also includes a Motley Fool promotion for its Stock Advisor service.

Sandisk shares are up 613% this year according to a related headline, while Micron is described in that headline as not far behind. The article's background includes the note that Micron and Sandisk have been among the market's biggest winners of 2026. Earlier memory cycles have been boom and bust, which the author contrasts with the current situation. The related headlines on the page were published by The Motley Fool in the weeks before this article. The article gives no other history of either company.

The article does not say how long the memory supercycle will last, and it gives no date by which new EUV or cleanroom capacity will come online. It does not state whether the forward price-to-earnings ratios will change or what the companies' future earnings will be. The article presents Micron as the better pick but offers no price target or timeline for that view. It also does not say whether the big three DRAM makers will change their allocation between HBM and conventional memory.

Articles.Title: Micron vs. Sandisk: The AI Memory Supercycle Is Big Enough for Both, but Here's the Better Buy.

stories.Headline: Kudu has given Leidos a cyber boost and an AI surprise
stories.Summary:
Leidos, the defense contractor, has been reporting gains from its 2025 purchase of Kudu Dynamics, a cyber company it bought for $300 million. In October, Leidos won two contracts from U.S. Cyber Command: a $160 million operations support contract and a $99 million other transaction authority contract to keep developing a cyber mission planning platform that Kudu brought over from the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency. Together these amount to nearly $260 million in new business over the next several years. Leidos Intelligence president Jason O'Connor said the customers are ones the company had not really worked with before.

The acquisition was announced in May 2025, when CEO Tom Bell said it moved Leidos into offensive cyber by 18 months compared with building those capabilities internally. Kudu brought roughly 170 employees, and much of its earlier work was in research. O'Connor said the company's artificial intelligence work has also benefited, pointing to Parcata, an AI-driven tool that finds and ranks software vulnerabilities so teams can fix the most serious ones first. Leidos introduced Parcata in August, and it grew out of Kudu's work on DARPA's AI Cyber Challenge. O'Connor said Leidos is testing it on its own software before a commercial release, and Bell discussed it on a November 5 earnings call as part of a cyber product business the company hopes to launch later this year.

O'Connor credited Kudu with a broader effect he called a "halo," in which its offensive background lets Leidos view the systems it builds the way an attacker would, which he said has improved the company's chances on engineering, software development and analytics bids as well. He said Leidos has worked to protect Kudu's culture, which had a 47,000-employee parent to worry about, and that Kudu engineers are now being placed on traditional Leidos contracts to coach and mentor staff. O'Connor linked the shift to fixed-price, outcome-based contracts and to rapidly changing technology, saying customers now expect solutions that are ready to go. He described the Leidos Intelligence cyber business, which sits in one of five sectors the company formed on January 1, and said the company is "just getting started," with possible wins in weapon system and communications cyber.

Articles.Title: Kudu has given Leidos a cyber boost and an AI surprise

stories.Headline: How companies can support emerging AI data center policies
stories.Summary:
AI data center measures played a prominent role in the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, and the electoral results pointed toward tighter restrictions and regulation of these facilities. Trellis, a sustainability news outlet, published an analysis on November 13, 2026, arguing that companies need to prepare for an evolving policy landscape. The piece was framed around how businesses can respond to these shifts rather than reporting a single discrete event. The articles provided describe the broader political trend, not a specific enacted measure with a named date or vote. The guidance centers on two main actions for companies.

First, they can make sure their trade associations advocate for responsible data center buildouts. Second, they can align their own policy agendas with legislation that responds to public concerns. The articles also suggest that companies and policymakers follow guidelines that serve the public interest, including roadmaps for data centers powered by cleaner energy. No specific dollar figures, deadlines, or bill numbers appear in the material provided. The author of the commentary is Deborah McNamara, executive director of ClimateVoice, who has spent more than 20 years in sustainability activism and advocacy with social change, environmental, and climate justice-focused nonprofits.

Her position, as described, is that companies should support policies that respond to public concern. The articles do not include direct statements from elected officials or industry groups on the midterm outcomes. The broader context is that data centers serving artificial intelligence are drawing growing scrutiny from voters and regulators. The articles indicate that sustainability executives and business leaders should prepare for further regulatory and policy changes. Beyond that general expectation, the material does not specify which rules will follow or on what timeline.

Articles.Title: How companies can support emerging AI data center policies

stories.Headline: How On-Page AI Assistants Are Transforming Digital Reading and Deep Research
stories.Summary:
This is not a news event but a sponsored opinion and overview piece published on vocal.media on November 12, 2026, by Qeemah Cloud, the creator of the Vezz me on-page AI reading assistant. The article argues that people who research dense digital text lose focus when they copy passages into separate AI chatbots in other tabs. It describes a shift toward small floating assistants that appear inside the browser page, triggered by a keyboard shortcut or a text selection, so the source text stays visible. The piece also presents this approach as a more ergonomic alternative to persistent sidebars that compress page layouts.

The article says these in-page tools are built around several features, including customizable hotkeys, adjustable panel size and opacity, and follow-up questions that do not create new browser history entries. It sets out security expectations as well, saying that responsible tools should send only the text a user selects, keep queries apart from browsing histories, and use secure backend proxies to protect API keys. It also states that such extensions should act only on user-initiated triggers rather than continuously reading background page content. The article gives no specific figures, dates for product releases, or measured results from studies.

Responsibility for the content rests with Qeemah Cloud, which the article describes as an accounting, ERP and POS platform with ZATCA Phase 2 compliance, and which also created Vezz me. The article notes that it was drafted with the help of an AI tool and reviewed against usability research, cognitive ergonomics and browser extension security standards, and it describes itself as an objective informational overview rather than formal commercial advice. The piece itself names no independent researchers or studies beyond general references to human-computer interaction findings. The article does not describe any next steps or planned changes beyond its general conclusion that in-page intelligence is a step toward more sustainable information use on the web.

Articles.Title: How On-Page AI Assistants Are Transforming Digital Reading and Deep Research

stories.Headline: The sketch Qwen refused to write: How abliteration restores local AI control
stories.Summary:
Oleg Mikheev, a senior technology leader and software architect, published an InfoWorld article on November 12, 2026, describing how to remove refusal behavior from the open-weight Qwen 3.8 27B model using a technique called abliteration. He said that while testing the model, it wrote a satirical sketch mocking American politics but refused an identical sketch criticizing the Chinese government. The article presents the method as a way to restore local control over AI models running on consumer hardware. It describes the model's refusals as a barrier that developers may want to remove.

The article explains that abliteration uses representation engineering to delete a refusal vector from the model's activation space, instead of requiring fine-tuning or full retraining. Mikheev describes a custom five-stage pipeline he built, which he says runs in a Docker container on an NVIDIA GB10 with 128 GB of unified memory. The process extracts the text model from a roughly 56 GB checkpoint spread across 18 safetensors shards, and it captures activations across 64 layers. The refusal direction was found at layer 60 of 64, and the modified weights were applied to residual-writing modules across layers 1 to 63. The full run takes about an hour, with the weight surgery taking only a few minutes.

Mikheev is responsible for the article and the custom harness he published on GitHub. He wrote that the technique builds on work by a developer known as FailSpy and the open-source abliterator library. He said the harness was built with Qwen's own help, which he described as an irony given the model's refusals about China. He also said that using pre-abliterated models from HuggingFace is bad practice because their producers are unknown. He stated that a globally abliterated model stripped of all safety rails could produce genuinely harmful answers.

The article notes that the technique affects users and organizations deploying open-weight models locally, along with developers who want to control model behavior. Mikheev argues that open-weight models carry risks, including the need to trust the producer that no backdoors are embedded and the bias introduced by Chinese government regulation. He describes the problem as a double standard in which the model critiques other countries while censoring China. The article does not present reactions from Alibaba, the Chinese government, or any other outside party.

The article states that refusals are typically created through alignment techniques such as Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback, and that these mechanisms can be used for state-level censorship. It distinguishes hard refusals, where the model halts and declines, from soft refusals, where it answers in a deflected or biased way. Mikheev writes that abliteration can remove hard refusals but that soft refusals require fine-tuning, and he says the final result remains heavily biased on most political questions. He also cites an earlier article on building a zero-cloud photo deduplicator with OpenCLIP.

Mikheev's article leaves open whether the modified Qwen 3.8 27B model's soft refusals can be addressed in practice, and it says only that techniques for them exist. The article does not say how many prompts were ultimately used, beyond stating that a combination of two prompts worked. It also does not describe any response from Alibaba, and it does not say whether the uploaded HuggingFace repository has been reviewed by others. More to follow.

Articles.Title: The sketch Qwen refused to write: How abliteration restores local AI control

stories.Headline: Data Center Backlash Is Bipartisan, and That Changes the Math for AI Investors
stories.Summary:
According to data tracked by Ballotpedia as of Nov. 4, voters decided 47 local ballot initiatives on whether to support or limit AI data centers in the midterm elections. Of those 47 measures, 46, or 98%, resulted in outcomes against developing AI data centers. A CNBC poll found that 56% of voters ranked data centers as a crucial or major factor in how they voted on Election Day. The Motley Fool article, written by Ben Gran and dated Nov. 12, 2026, frames this result as a public relations problem for the AI industry. In Ohio and Texas, newly elected Democratic governors have proposed moratoriums on new AI data center construction.

Many voters worry that AI data centers will raise utility costs, and they do not want local land and resources used without visible economic benefits to their communities. The articles state that voters support candidates who are skeptical of AI data centers. The Nasdaq-100 fell 5.5% between Nov. 3 and Nov. 5, while the iShares Semiconductor ETF dropped about 15% over the same period. Caterpillar lost about 11.3% during those two days after the election. The articles say Dan Ives, partner at Yorkville Ives & Co., wrote on Nov. 4 that his firm now sees Big Tech capex growth peaking in 2027, rather than in 2028 or 2029 as previously expected.

Ives wrote that the midterm elections will likely slow the planned 800 to 1,000 data centers across the US, a view the article quotes as a clear yes. Dominique Toublan, Barclays Investment Bank head of U.S. credit strategy, wrote in a Nov. 4 note that AI pushback is bipartisan but local, making the buildout pricier rather than stalling it. Toublan also wrote that scarce power favors the biggest balance sheets. The article reports that CoreWeave has drawn investor concern about its high debt and rising interest expenses. Its shares were up 24.71% on the day the article was published, and Alphabet shares were up 2.00% for GOOG and 2.11% for GOOGL.

The Fool article is written for investors, and it says the backlash could make AI data centers more expensive and slower to build, creating short-term winners and losers. Semiconductor stocks and pick-and-shovel stocks whose earnings have been boosted by hundreds of billions of dollars in corporate data center investment could be hurt if the capex boom ends in 2027. The article also notes that Stock Advisor's total average return is 835%, compared with 208% for the S&P 500, as of Nov. 12, 2026. The article does not say whether any of the newly proposed moratoriums in Ohio or Texas have taken effect. It does not say how long the slowdown in AI data center construction might last.

Articles.Title: Data Center Backlash Is Bipartisan, and That Changes the Math for AI Investors

stories.Headline: Doctors want liability shield from AI mistakes
stories.Summary:
The American Medical Association, the nation's largest physicians group, has called for federal and state legislation that would shield doctors from liability when AI products injure patients, even when physicians use those tools as intended. The announcement came this week, according to Axios, which reported it on November 13, 2026. The push reflects growing concern that AI systems are taking on more consequential medical tasks, such as deciding whether to order a diagnostic test or prescribe an expensive drug, with less direct oversight. The question of who is responsible when something goes wrong has become more pressing as a result.

The AMA policy also asks lawmakers to require AI companies to carry adequate liability insurance and to disclose product limitations and performance data. It states that hospitals, health systems, insurers and health tech vendors should bear responsibility if the required use of a specific AI product leads to harmful errors. The group points to particular risks, including triage errors in which an AI system misjudges how severe a case is without the attending doctor knowing. It also warns that a physician may be unable to verify inputs such as incomplete laboratory results or outdated diagnoses. In such cases, the AMA argues, liability should fall on manufacturers and vendors, and possibly on health systems that require the tools, rather than on physicians through malpractice claims.

The AMA's position is shaped by earlier lawsuits over algorithm-driven medical decisions. Axios cited a wrongful death case in Alabama involving a screening tool for heart abnormalities, where the software developer was not held liable because its licensing agreement left final medical decisions to doctors. Martin Hilbert, a professor at the University of California, Davis who studies digital information and algorithms, told Axios that courts around the country are concluding that companies designing, training and deploying AI systems bear responsibility for what those systems do. He said different parties are responsible for different cases and that the end user cannot simply be held responsible for everything. Hospitals have generally supported placing monitoring duties on developers and vendors, citing the "black box" nature of many systems.

The Food and Drug Administration is weighing whether a new framework is needed for regulating AI-enabled medical devices, though its authority covers only software that meets the definition of a medical device, not all AI used in health care. AdvaMed, the trade group for device makers, has urged the FDA to keep its current approaches for evaluating generative AI-enabled devices and to avoid post-market monitoring burdens unrelated to a product's actual risk. Axios reported that the AMA's proposals are aimed at situations where use of an AI system is mandatory. The article did not report whether any legislation has been introduced or what action lawmakers have taken so far.

Articles.Title: Doctors want liability shield from AI mistakes

stories.Headline: Orange walks AI tightrope to capture 'hundreds of mil' in value
stories.Summary:
Orange Business Services, the enterprise unit of French operator Orange, is using AI to pursue value in the hundreds of millions of euros, according to an article by Iain Morris published on November 12, 2026, on Light Reading. The piece profiles Miguel Alvarez, Orange Business Services' chief data and AI officer, who was interviewed on the sidelines of the Techritory event held in Latvia the previous month. The article frames Alvarez's position against warnings from critic Cory Doctorow about AI's effects on workers. Alvarez describes his approach as treating AI as another tool rather than letting the machine direct people.

The article describes how Orange is meeting its AI value targets. Orange's group-level value creation target is in the hundreds of millions of euros, and Orange Business Services had a 2025 target of €50 million (US$55.5 million), which was achieved. This year that target has reportedly been raised to €70 million ($77.7 million). Orange is exploring several hundred AI-based use cases, with thirty already in production at Orange Business Services and twenty being industrialized in a subsequent AI expansion. Orange has also reduced its global workforce by roughly 10,000 employees since the end of 2022, to around 126,000 in September.

Alvarez says the value is measured across cost savings, cost avoidance, revenue protection and additional revenue generated. He attributes much of the gain to shorter development times and faster activity rather than headcount reduction. He gave a product example in which a working version was reached in a couple of months, a process he estimates would otherwise have taken four to five times longer. Software development has also changed, with some teams now automating most steps of the development lifecycle through requirement-driven development. Alvarez also expects agentic systems, not humans, to write most future code, while people will still learn core coding concepts.

Alvarez stresses that Orange must maintain control over AI, particularly because the technology is non-deterministic. He says he must balance guardrails against giving agents enough freedom to find better solutions, which could also lead to more errors. Orange uses a mix of commercially available frontier models and open-weight alternatives, deployed on its own infrastructure including on-premises, so it does not depend on public cloud from the start. Agents are built on an open-source framework from LangChain, a San Francisco-based nonprofit, so they can be moved between environments. Alvarez notes that open-weight models are about six months behind the frontier models, though they have improved enough to handle more sophisticated use cases.

Doctorow, a former guest on the Telecoms.com podcast, has warned of AI's "reverse centaur" dynamic, in which humans are steered by AI, and fears companies will use AI to cut jobs. The article notes that little evidence links AI to mass layoffs in any sector. It cites the US unemployment rate of 4.2% in October, down from 4.5% in November last year, and a Bank of England Monetary Policy Report for November finding AI's contribution to UK productivity growth at just 0.1 to 0.2 percentage points annually since 2024. Alvarez's own children, he says, are not learning rudimentary math by hand because they will not need to in the future. Adoption within Orange has grown well beyond expectations, with more than 100,000 active users, against an original hope of 10,000 to 20,000 within a couple of years of ChatGPT's launch.

The article does not state how the €70 million target for this year is progressing or whether it will be met. It also does not detail how many of the several hundred use cases will reach production, or how Orange will address the tension between agent freedom and the risk of errors. Alvarez's remarks on the future balance between human and machine roles in coding remain expectations rather than established outcomes. The article also leaves open how Orange's reliance on open-weight models will develop as frontier models continue to advance.

Articles.Title: Orange walks AI tightrope to capture 'hundreds of mil' in value

stories.Headline: AI reshaping infrastructure, energy and connecting networks
stories.Summary:
A survey of 2,000 adults across 11 markets, conducted in September 2026 by RETN, an independent global network service provider, found that AI is reshaping digital infrastructure, energy use and the networks that connect them. The findings were published by Computer Weekly on 12 November 2026. The survey polled 600 people in the US, 800 in the UK, Germany, the Netherlands and Spain, and 600 in China, Hong Kong, Taiwan, Singapore, Malaysia and the Philippines. RETN supplemented the results with views from its senior network experts.

The survey found that 53% of respondents named AI tools as the biggest driver of new datacentre construction, and that half of respondents did not want such facilities built near them. Growing power and cooling demands are pushing datacentres toward remote sites where land and energy are available but fibre may be scarce, so RETN warned that developers now need to involve network carriers two to five years before a site goes live, up from one to two years previously. The research also found that AI traffic makes up only a small share of open internet growth, with 80 to 90% of RETN's AI-related requests being for private point-to-point links, dark fibre and dedicated interconnects. Real-time AI processing, fed by connected devices, is expected to reverse the download-heavy pattern of the current internet and push computing toward the network edge.

RETN chief executive Tony O'Sullivan said the industry is only at the start of the changes AI will bring to networks. He argued that the networks best placed for the future will be those able to adapt when geopolitics shifts and to keep running when individual parts fail, rather than simply those that build the most capacity. The article also says that 84% of those surveyed use AI and that 54% said losing access would disrupt their lives within days. Three-quarters had experienced problems with their preferred AI service in the past year, and 18% had begun regularly using an alternative provider. The article's accompanying links describe carriers introducing AI-based network management tools and expanding capacity, but the survey itself does not set out any binding requirement or regulatory change.

Articles.Title: AI reshaping infrastructure, energy and connecting networks

stories.Headline: PARTNER CONTENT: Your AI agent is only as good as your endpoint data
stories.Summary:
PHP2Shell, a pair of critical flaws in PHP, was disclosed in 2026 after details leaked ahead of the planned disclosure, and PHP shipped fixes the following day. The article reports that frontier AI helped researchers find the flaws, and that the flaw reportedly went undetected for more than a decade. Several security firms saw exploitation attempts before the fixes were released, and Cloudflare reported early attacks hours ahead of the patch. The article frames these events as a sign of how quickly the threat landscape is now shifting for IT and security teams. The piece argues that autonomous IT operations need a governed loop in which software finds risks, ranks them, proposes fixes and carries them out within limits people define.

Routine, low-risk actions can run automatically, higher-impact ones wait for human approval, and some actions are never delegated at all. Every step leaves a reviewable and reversible record. The article says that three problems make this difficult: incomplete visibility into every copy of PHP, the need to hop between separate asset, scanning and attack-surface tools, and the shrinking gap between disclosure and exploitation. It adds that putting an AI agent on top of stale, fragmented data scales these problems rather than solving them. The article is written as partner content, and it presents Tanium's real-time endpoint data as the foundation for trustworthy automation.

It names four qualities such data should have: accuracy, speed, control, and shared truth across IT, security and the system of record. Matt Psencik, a threat research engineer at Tanium, is quoted saying that the installations he worries about most are those a security team does not know it owns. The article also says World Wide Technology, a Tanium partner, hosts a Tanium lab where customers can test approaches before production, and it promotes Tanium Atlas as the product intended to reduce tool-hopping. The article gives practical first steps: find every copy of software, including bundled copies, by comparing the CMDB with what is actually on the network; rank systems by internet exposure and decide in advance which actions are automatic, which need approval and which are never delegated; and pilot one contained, low-risk workflow with approvals and a reviewed audit trail before widening scope.

Articles.Title: PARTNER CONTENT: Your AI agent is only as good as your endpoint data

stories.Headline: Corporate AI Training in Australia: Paloren Trains Whole Departments on Approved AI Tools and Real Tasks
stories.Summary:
Paloren, an AI strategy, implementation, automation and training company, is offering Australian organizations corporate AI training that covers whole departments, according to a press release dated November 12, 2026, republished on FinancialContent. The offer is aimed at organizations planning training for 2027, and it is built around the AI tools each company has already approved and the tasks its teams repeat every week. Paloren delivers half-day and full-day workshops, four-to-six-week department programs and executive coaching. The company is co-founded by Aaron Agius and Alex Agius.

Before any session, Paloren records which tools each team is approved to use, such as Microsoft Copilot, ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini, and which functions are switched on. Cohorts contain six to 16 people, with multiple cohorts for larger groups, and role-specific practice lets finance, operations and customer service teams each work on their own material. Each format includes a baseline exercise, safe practice materials, reusable task instructions, a later independent attempt and a workplace trial with a named reviewer. The article says managers receive work they can inspect rather than just an attendance list. Remote sessions run in Australian working hours, and onsite delivery is available by arrangement.

The training is delivered by founders and senior practitioners at Paloren. The company says organizations can start a discussion by sharing team sizes, approved tools and two or three priority tasks. The article describes Paloren as a business that builds AI into the systems companies already run and trains their people to own it. It notes that course selection for Microsoft 365 users can start from the Word, Teams and Outlook work staff already do.

Paloren's Australian AI Training Price Index, checked on November 10, 2026, found a median published starting price of A$4,900 per group for private team sessions. The index covered 13 offers from eight providers, and session lengths ranged from about one hour to a full day. Because of that spread, the index advises comparing duration and group size before comparing price. The article also notes that it is third-party content and that the publisher makes no guarantees about its accuracy or completeness.

Articles.Title: Corporate AI Training in Australia: Paloren Trains Whole Departments on Approved AI Tools and Real Tasks

stories.Headline: ‘Ahead of his time’: AI helps unlock discoveries hidden in notebooks of man who transformed maths
stories.Summary:
Kurt Gödel left 1,009 pages of densely written notebooks, and an AI model has now helped reveal that they contain hundreds of proved theorems. Jan von Plato, a Finnish logician, has led a project at Helsinki University since 2017 to understand 16 notebooks Gödel wrote in the early 1940s. Much of the text is written in Gabelsberger, a German shorthand that was already obsolete when Gödel used it. Progress was painfully slow, at about a page a week, until September, when von Plato enlisted the AI model Claude. Within a couple of days, Claude had produced a digest of the entire material.

Claude found that the notebooks contain 663 theorems for which Gödel had a proof, a sketch of a proof, or an idea for one. When checked in the proof assistant Coq, about 400 were verified as stated and about 200 were repaired. About 50 were found to be false. Von Plato also said the workbooks contain dozens of anticipations of results not known until the 1970s and 1980s. He received a €2.5m (£2.1m) grant from the European Research Council for the project.

Von Plato leads the work and described himself as flabbergasted by the findings. He said Gödel was far ahead of his time, and that the notebooks contain 14 themes in logic that have not been pursued. Von Plato said he met computer scientists in August, at a conference in France on AI and theorem proving, who suggested using Claude. Joel David Hamkins, a logic professor at the University of Notre Dame in Indiana, said the findings would be remarkable and historically interesting if they stood up.

Gödel's incompleteness theorems, published in 1931, showed that in any mathematical system there are true statements that cannot be proved or disproved. Gödel fled Austria under the Nazis in 1940 and settled in Princeton, New Jersey, where he became a close friend of Albert Einstein. Gödel died of starvation in 1978, after refusing to eat food not cooked by his wife. In 1966, the American mathematician Paul Cohen won the Fields medal for showing the independence of the continuum hypothesis and the axiom of choice.

Claude's reconstruction indicates that Gödel was one step away from a proof of the independence of the axiom of choice, which von Plato said would have confirmed Gödel's 1966 claim that he had proved it in the 1940s. Von Plato believes that had Gödel published that work, he would have won the 1940 Fields medal. The notebooks also contain marginal remarks such as "falsch" and "schlecht," which Gödel added when rereading his notes. Von Plato plans to explore Gödel's physics and cosmology notebooks once his present logic projects are finished. More to follow.

Articles.Title: ‘Ahead of his time’: AI helps unlock discoveries hidden in notebooks of man who transformed maths

stories.Headline: Siemens Q4 profit jumps 32% on AI infrastructure demand; raises growth targets
stories.Summary:
Siemens AG shares climbed to an 11-week high on Thursday, 12 November 2026, after the German industrial group reported quarterly results that beat expectations and raised its medium-term growth targets. Strong demand for AI-related data centre equipment and rail contracts pushed orders to a record for the quarter. The stock rose 4.44% to €289.30 after touching an intraday high of €291.45, its highest level since August 28. It also outperformed Germany's DAX, which gained around 0.9% during the session.

For the quarter ended September 30, net income rose to €2.43 billion from €1.84 billion a year earlier. Revenue increased 11% to €23.68 billion, while profit at the Industrial Business climbed 22% to a record €3.90 billion. The industrial profit margin improved to 16.8% from 15.3%. Orders surged 58% to a quarterly record €34.77 billion, lifting the book-to-bill ratio to 1.47 and the order backlog to €143 billion.

Growth was led by Smart Infrastructure and Mobility, with Smart Infrastructure's revenue rising 16% to €7.24 billion and its order intake jumping 40% on large data centre contract wins in the U.S. and Europe. Digital Industries revenue rose 11% and profit increased 50%, driven mainly by operational improvements in automation. Mobility's orders more than quadrupled, supported by major German rail contracts including a €2.4 billion high-speed train order. Siemens attributed these gains to continued investment in electrification, digital infrastructure and rail transportation.

Looking ahead, Siemens expects comparable revenue growth of 9% to 11% in fiscal 2027 and earnings per share before purchase price allocation accounting of €10.20 to €10.80. The company pointed to investment in AI and digital infrastructure, public investment programmes and a recovery in industrial activity as key growth drivers. For the full fiscal year, net income fell 9% to €9.47 billion, reflecting a €2.1 billion gain from the sale of Innomotics in the prior year. Revenue rose 6% to €83.37 billion, Industrial Business profit increased 13% to a record €13.29 billion, and the proposed dividend rises to €5.50 per share from €5.35.

Articles.Title: Siemens Q4 profit jumps 32% on AI infrastructure demand; raises growth targets

stories.Headline: Fewer hours and higher wages – or more burnout and surveillance: employers told to prepare for AI
stories.Summary:
The Australian government has issued a best practice guide on how employers should adopt artificial intelligence at work, and it warns that the technology could either improve or worsen conditions for ordinary workers. Workplace relations minister Amanda Rishworth launched the guide on Thursday 12 November 2026, as large firms cut staff in restructures linked partly to AI. Qantas announced 850 job cuts targeting finance, human resources and marketing roles, National Australian Bank announced 2,500 job losses, and Canva announced 1,200 layoffs. The guide says entry-level work may be the first to be automated.

The guide paints an optimistic picture, suggesting wider AI use could raise productivity, boost wages, offer shorter and more flexible hours, or provide more meaningful work. It also concedes "potential hazards," including intrusive worker surveillance, poor rostering, unrealistic performance standards and possible discrimination. It warns that if basic tasks are automated, the remaining work may become more intense and complex. It also flags that some employers could use expanded monitoring for performance management.

Rishworth said employers must give workers a clear plan about how automation could affect their jobs and the chance to move into new roles. In a speech in Sydney, she said adding AI without consulting workers could increase workloads, because people must navigate an extra step. The guide cautions that younger, older and First Nations workers, along with women and people with a disability, face disproportionate impacts. Labor MP Ed Husic, the former industry minister, asked at a parliamentary hearing on the big four banks who would receive the benefits of higher productivity.

Greens leader David Shoebridge accused the government of watching from the sidelines and said the guidance was too weak. He argued that a worker who loses a job to an algorithm would have no legal recourse under the current approach, and he called for the protections to be written into law. The Reserve Bank this week reported "little evidence to date" of AI disrupting the labour market, while saying future effects were highly uncertain. It noted "tentative signs" of impact on roles such as clerks, computer programmers and call centre workers.

Articles.Title: Fewer hours and higher wages – or more burnout and surveillance: employers told to prepare for AI

stories.Headline: Hybrid Swarm AI Framework Detects Synthetic Interior Renders With 97.5 Percent Accuracy
stories.Summary:
The articles report that researcher Zhengfang Wu published a study in Discover Artificial Intelligence describing a computational framework that distinguishes real interior photographs from synthetic computer-generated renderings with 97.5 percent accuracy. The system, called the Glowworm Swarm-Optimized Attention-enriched Variational Autoencoder, or GSO-Att-VAE, was described in a bioengineer.org report dated November 12, 2026. The framework is designed to run on edge devices rather than relying on centralized cloud servers, which the study says introduce latency and bandwidth problems. The study was motivated by generative tools that can produce realistic interior spaces while often containing subtle structural and lighting inconsistencies.

The framework combines image and numerical data through a unified pipeline that includes statistical filtering, sparse spatial encoding, convolutional feature extraction, attention-based probabilistic modeling, and swarm optimization. Training and testing used the publicly accessible Edge AI Interior Spatial Design Dataset hosted on Kaggle, which contains 4,000 synthetic interior scene records and 69 tabular columns. The dataset includes 68 predictor variables and one binary target labeled Image_Authenticity, which classifies each record as Real_Interior or AI_Generated. Images were smoothed with two-dimensional Gaussian filtering, and 58 pre-computed spatial metadata attributes were standardized using Z-score normalization. The attention mechanism uses eight heads, and the encoder compresses features into a 128-dimensional latent space, with glowworm swarm optimization running 60 candidate solutions over 100 iterations at a step size of 0.03.

Wu is identified as the sole researcher behind the framework, which the articles present as a response to fragmented workflows in which image generation, aesthetic scoring, layout planning, and authenticity detection operate as separate silos. The articles state that Wu formulated the framework to couple visual features with structured spatial attributes in a single edge-compatible architecture. The study's authors describe the approach as establishing a reliable mathematical foundation for authenticating interior scenes without requiring centralized server infrastructure. The articles attribute these claims to the study and to Wu directly, without offering additional quotations from the researcher.

The articles report the test results in detail: on 800 test instances, the model correctly identified 392 of 400 AI-generated images and 388 of 400 real photographs. The overall accuracy was 97.5 percent, with 97.3 percent precision, 97.4 percent recall, a 96.9 percent F1-score, and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 97.2 percent. The articles say the model was benchmarked against classical classifiers and established deep learning backbones retrained on identical data, but the comparison results are cut off in the available text. The articles say nothing about the reactions of architects, designers, or other researchers, nor about which users or industries would be affected by the framework.

The articles describe the problem background as an escalating challenge in architectural visualization, where generative systems such as StyleGAN variants, diffusion frameworks, and vision-language systems have accelerated interior concept creation. They note that classical classifiers often rely only on two-dimensional pixels and ignore physical parameters such as room dimensions and lighting vectors. The articles also state that centralized cloud architectures introduce communication latency and bandwidth demands that limit real-time responsiveness for interactive smart interior installations. The study was published in Discover Artificial Intelligence, and the articles provide no further history of prior detection efforts. The articles do not say whether the framework has been tested outside the Kaggle dataset or deployed in any commercial or professional setting.

Articles.Title: Hybrid Swarm AI Framework Detects Synthetic Interior Renders With 97.5 Percent Accuracy

stories.Headline: Silk Road in orbit: China to build 20-satellite ‘space AI’ system for Oman
stories.Summary:
Hangzhou-based Star Vision has agreed to build Oman a network of 20 satellites that use artificial intelligence to process images in orbit and spot ships and floods in real time. The deal, which the start-up called China's most valuable commercial space contract ever, was signed in Beijing last week with Omani firm Oman Lens. It was concluded during a landmark state visit by Oman's ruler, Sultan Haitham bin Tariq. The contract is reportedly worth over US$200 million, according to Star Vision. The package goes well beyond the satellites themselves.

It includes a satellite assembly and testing centre inside Oman, scholarships for 30 Omanis to pursue master's and doctoral degrees in China, and training for 1,000 local specialists. The two sides also plan to set up a joint laboratory focused on space artificial intelligence. Together, these elements are meant to build local capacity alongside the orbital system. Liao Zhenhua, who heads Star Vision's Oman project, said smaller nations want satellites of their own so they are not left behind as major powers fill up space.

In an interview, he said that a country may not have as many satellites as the United States but could still observe whatever area it chooses with even one or two. The article presents his remarks as the company's rationale for the deal. The article places the agreement within a broader push by smaller states to acquire their own space capabilities, though it gives no further detail on other contracts. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Silk Road in orbit: China to build 20-satellite ‘space AI’ system for Oman

stories.Headline: Forget ‘sponsored’ tags in AI answers. Agent loyalty is what matters.
stories.Summary:
Paragraph one: No one loves ads, but people will tolerate them if they get something free or cheaper. What people won't forgive is being lied to. A study of native ads on news sites found that fewer than 10% of consumers could identify them as advertising. In a Contently survey, two-thirds of readers said they felt deceived after learning an article or video was sponsored by a brand. That is why regulations and standards around advertising disclosures exist to protect consumers.

Paragraph two: It is unclear to what extent those disclosures should carry over into AI answers as AI becomes a central part of the media ecosystem. According to an impact.com survey, 47% of U.S. shoppers who use AI started their last product search with AI. Meta says shopping is the most common use of its new personal AI agent, Muse. Given this, it seems intuitive that users should see plainly the commercial interests of the sites that informed an answer. A reliable label raises complications, because it might suggest the AI platform itself was paid rather than the original publisher.

Paragraph three: OpenAI's answer to the disclosure question so far is the citation link, which ChatGPT has included in answers since it launched ChatGPT search. ChatGPT's own ads are separate from the answer and labeled as sponsored. OpenAI has promised that ads do not influence the answers ChatGPT gives, and that ads appear only in its free and Go tiers. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said on Meta's October earnings call that the company will build commerce tools so it gets paid a fee based on transactions it helps facilitate. Perplexity made similar promises when advertising was part of its business model, but walked away from ads earlier this year.

Paragraph four: Some people turn to AI to avoid billboards, with 24% of shoppers in the impact.com survey saying they use AI to avoid sponsored results and ads. Affiliate content is central to AI answers, as one study found about a quarter of pages cited by ChatGPT, Google's AI Overviews, and Perplexity carried a commercial disclosure. Those disclosures rarely survive into AI answers, even though FTC guidelines require affiliate sites to disclose their links. Researchers at the University of Michigan found people rarely noticed when a chatbot wove ads into responses, and about half missed labeled ads. Early Frankfurt School research found shoppers who clicked ChatGPT ads bought at 0.37%, versus 2.21% for those arriving through regular answers.

Paragraph five: When Pew tracked Google use, people clicked a link inside an AI summary on just 1% of visits. In the impact.com survey, 11% of Gen Z never click through to sources, while 21% always do. Consumer Reports' work on AI agents has prompted calls for "loyalty by design" in agentic systems. Sen. Mark Warner has floated draft legislation that would write a duty of loyalty into law for some AI agents. The columnist argues that the better question is whether an agent is loyal and how users can check, since labels protect readers from sketchy sources but nothing yet protects users from sketchy agents.

Articles.Title: Forget ‘sponsored’ tags in AI answers. Agent loyalty is what matters.

stories.Headline: New AI 'copilot' lets engineers guide structural designs as algorithms create them
stories.Summary:
Researchers at MIT have developed a system that acts like an AI copilot, letting engineers give feedback while algorithms are generating structural designs. The work is described in an open-access paper in Communications Engineering, and the lead author is Dat Ha, who was a doctoral student in civil and environmental engineering at MIT.
