The system uses a design technique called topology optimization, which the researchers say has produced parts for ultralight aircraft, high-bandwidth antennas and F1 racing cars. Users of conventional algorithmic methods typically see only the finished design, and must often start over to make changes.

The system uses machine learning to quickly flag regions of a design that a human would likely want to change, as the algorithm runs. To train the model, the researchers built a synthetic dataset of probable human feedback on thousands of designs, covering aesthetics, performance criteria and manufacturability. In demonstrations, the human-in-the-loop approach improved manufacturability and linear buckling load by 39 percent. It added only 15 seconds to total design time compared with all-algorithmic approaches. Currently, users can only make structures in identified regions thicker or thinner, and the team hopes to add other modification options.

The paper's authors are Dat Ha, Ferdous Alam, Markus Buehler, Faez Ahmed and senior author Josephine Carstensen, all affiliated with MIT. Ha is now a structural designer at LeMessurier, and Alam is now an assistant professor at Georgia Tech. Carstensen, an MIT associate professor of civil and environmental engineering, said the approach gives designers influence over how a design evolves. She described the system as bringing together the strengths of algorithmic and human design. Ha said engineers tend to be skeptical of computer programs that produce unusual designs, and that topology optimization's black-box nature has limited its use in industry.

The researchers say the approach could make algorithmic design more accessible to a broader class of design engineers, including those working on buildings and bridges. Topology optimization has been adopted more in the automotive and aerospace industries, and less for buildings or bridges, partly because engineers need to trust the output. Earlier attempts to add human judgment slowed the process dramatically, according to the researchers. Carstensen said that the lack of control and ownership has also discouraged use of the technique. The article also notes that some algorithmic designs have included points where eight or more beams meet, which would be difficult to build.

The researchers see the collaborative method as complementing AI-only design rather than replacing it, since fields with abundant computing resources may still prefer fully automated approaches. Carstensen said human involvement can help get higher-performing designs into real-world use and produce structures that people will accept. The article does not describe any deployment in industry, and it does not say when the additional modification options will be added. It also does not report results beyond the demonstrations described, or say how the synthetic feedback data compares with feedback from working engineers.

Articles.Title: New AI 'copilot' lets engineers guide structural designs as algorithms create them

stories.Headline: Rajesh Ramachandran, ABB Global Chief Digital Officer on AI
stories.Summary:
Rajesh Ramachandran, Global Chief Digital Officer for ABB's Automation business area, spoke with AI Magazine about combining predictive AI with IoT for industrial returns. The interview was published on November 12, 2026, by Adam Pond. The article notes that McKinsey expects manufacturing and industrials to drive the biggest AI-enabled digital transformation gains. McKinsey estimates the total value potential for the IoT ecosystem could reach US$12.6trn by 2030. Rajesh's role focuses on advancing digitalisation across industrial operations and helping customers apply industrial AI at scale.

ABB describes itself as a global technology leader in electrification and automation, helping industries run leaner and cleaner. Rajesh says the company combines industrial data with domain and engineering expertise, automation, analytics and AI to improve asset reliability and energy use. He says the goal is to move progressively toward more autonomous operations. The article describes ABB Genix as a leading Industrial IoT and AI platform. It is presented as the vehicle for applying data and AI at scale across efficiency, reliability and sustainability.

Rajesh says leaders should start from the business problem and be clear about what they are predicting, how early, and which decision it should improve. He argues that predictive AI needs trusted, contextualised data that reflects how assets behave in the real world. He summarises the approach in a formula: data makes it feasible, domain expertise makes it usable, AI makes it valuable, and a platform makes it scalable. He also stresses that a sensor reading means little without knowing the asset, its operating state, maintenance history and engineering limits.

The article says the real challenge is embedding predictive AI into operational routines, and that accurate predictions have little value if no one can act on them. Rajesh says AI must integrate securely with existing systems and workflows, and that organisations should continuously close the loop to improve outcomes. He says moving from pilot to enterprise-wide impact requires an organisational mindset shift as well as technological maturity. He adds that the objective should be identifying where AI delivers meaningful value, without compromising safety, reliability or operational continuity.

The article notes that many firms struggle to see return on AI investment, and that industrials face extra complexity. Rajesh says return should be measured in uptime, yield, safety, energy efficiency and profitability rather than model accuracy alone. He gives an example in which predictive maintenance warning avoids lost production, emergency maintenance and equipment damage. In recent customer deployments using multivariate anomaly detection in ABB Genix Asset Performance Management, potential failures were identified six to ten days ahead. He says predictive AI is evolving toward prescriptive analytics, causal analysis and digital twins.

Rajesh expects predictive, prescriptive and generative capabilities to increasingly work together, with agentic AI bridging insight and execution. He says generative and agentic AI can help scale adoption from shop floor to top floor and from field operations to enterprise. The article says he regards C-suite leadership as critical to AIoT deployments. It notes ABB reported 98% of its electricity was sourced from renewables in 2025, with total revenue of US$33.22m in 2025, and completed six acquisitions in 2026. The article does not say how these figures bear on the interview.

Articles.Title: Rajesh Ramachandran, ABB Global Chief Digital Officer on AI

stories.Headline: The attendee’s guide to the AWS re:Invent 2026 AI/ML track
stories.Summary:
The AWS re:Invent 2026 conference will run from November 30 to December 4, and AWS has published a guide to its artificial intelligence and machine learning track. The article, posted on the AWS website on November 12, 2026, explains that the event includes keynotes from AWS leaders, interactive sessions led by AWS experts, and immersive activities such as live entertainment at re:Play. The track offers more than 140 sessions among over 2,000 learning sessions across the conference. Attendees who cannot travel can watch many sessions on demand and view the keynotes live.

The guide describes several session formats that attendees can choose from. Breakout sessions are 60-minute lectures presented by AWS experts, customers, and partners, and they are recorded and posted to the AWS Events YouTube channel a few days later. Chalk talks let attendees ask questions and work through ideas on a whiteboard, builder sessions last one hour and have attendees build something, and workshops run two hours in small teams solving a real problem with AWS services. Code talks feature a live coding session led by an expert, while lightning talks are 20-minute demos held in the Venetian Expo Hall or the Wynn and Encore Upper Convention Promenade. The rest are live and not recorded.

The article organizes AWS's AI offerings into a stack that begins with global infrastructure designed for AI workloads and AI chips, including AWS Trainium and NVIDIA GPUs. Above that sits a data foundation called AWS Context, then models, training, and inference through Amazon Bedrock and Amazon SageMaker AI, followed by agent development through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. At the top are ready-to-use agentic solutions such as Kiro, AWS Quick, Amazon Connect, and AWS Marketplace. The guide says security, governance, and cost optimization apply across every layer. The track's sessions are arranged along this stack, with newcomer sessions listed first and technical deep dives last, and the guide also covers topics such as sustainability and infrastructure.

The guide frames its purpose as helping attendees pick sessions that match their needs and build a schedule around the stack. It recommends AIM204 for newcomers, since it walks through the full stack, and AIM364 for builders choosing between Amazon Bedrock and SageMaker AI. For those responsible for data strategy, it points to AIM363, a chalk talk on governed data products, and for those needing to demonstrate business value, it points to AIM319, which covers return on investment. The article ends by encouraging readers to use the guide to build a more effective re:Invent schedule.

Articles.Title: The attendee’s guide to the AWS re:Invent 2026 AI/ML track

stories.Headline: Chainstack says AI-powered security breach exposed customer data; threat now contained
stories.Summary:
Blockchain infrastructure provider Chainstack disclosed that it suffered an AI-powered security breach in late October, which exposed customer names, emails and password hashes. The company published the details in an updated blog post on Tuesday, according to The Block's report of November 12, 2026. Chainstack said the incident has been contained and that its customer-facing services kept operating normally throughout the breach. The attacker reached parts of the company's systems through a third-party component, according to the report's summary of the incident. The Block said it has reached out to Chainstack for further comment.

The attacker first gained access to a development environment on October 26 and reached parts of the production environment on October 29. Chainstack detected the intrusion and cut the access paths on October 31, then finalized its investigation on November 2. Because of the exposure, the company is treating node credentials as exposed and asking customers to rotate them and change their passwords. Self-service rotation for node credentials is currently available in the console, and Chainstack says it works without downtime. The company added that customer nodes, the console and the API were not modified.

Chainstack itself is the source of the account of how the breach unfolded, which it set out in its blog post. The company said the attacker entered through an internet-exposed Grafana instance sitting in a development cluster. That instance had been deployed for testing, with its default administrator credentials and without an additional layer of protection. From there, the attacker obtained machine credentials that reached production and used them to access the database network. Chainstack also said the attacker used the ARTEX AI agent framework to carry out the breach.

Chainstack warned customers to watch for phishing attempts following the incident, saying it will never ask for passwords, tokens or keys. Customers are the group affected, since their names, emails and password hashes were exposed and their node credentials are being treated as exposed. The Block's report places the incident within a wave of cyberattacks and security breaches as AI tools become increasingly capable. The Block reported that, earlier in the same week, the crosschain interoperability protocol Across suffered a domain takeover. Across later restored control of its website and resumed normal operations.

The wider concern about AI-enabled threats also features in a separate opinion piece by Saken Mukan, published by Caspian Post on November 9, 2026. It describes deepfakes, online fraud and extremist propaganda as emerging challenges for Central Asia, and notes that such tools are becoming easier and cheaper to use. On November 6, Astana hosted an Aqaba Process summit on security in the field of artificial intelligence, attended by the presidents of Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan. King Abdullah II of Jordan, Kyrgyzstan's foreign minister and the speaker of Azerbaijan's parliament also took part. The Aqaba Process was launched by the King of Jordan in 2015 as an initiative aimed at countering terrorism and violent extremism.

The Chainstack articles do not say whether the attacker has been identified, or how many customers were affected by the exposure of their names, emails and password hashes. They also leave open whether any customer node credentials were actually misused, since the company says only that it is treating them as exposed. The Block's request for further comment from Chainstack remains outstanding, so any additional detail from the company is still to come. For now, customers are being asked to rotate their node credentials, change their passwords and stay alert to phishing. In the regional discussion, Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev offered to host a regional office of the United Nations Office of Counter-Terrorism, though that office remains a proposal and has not yet been established.

Articles.Title: Chainstack says AI-powered security breach exposed customer data; threat now contained

stories.Headline: ‘We're Killing Our Own Currency’ - 7 MSP Leaders On How AI Will Change What They Charge
stories.Summary:
The IT Channel Oxygen article published on November 12, 2026 reports on discussions at the Global Technology Industry Association's ChannelCon EMEA in London, where how AI might reshape managed service providers' pricing dominated the agenda. The piece is an interview round-up in which seven MSP leaders were asked how the arrival of AI tools that could make them more efficient would affect what they charge customers. The event, which the article says attracted a record 800 registrations, prompted the headline phrase "We're killing our own currency." The GTIA's chief executive, Dan Wensley, described himself in an earlier interview as a "pure optimist" on the topic, but the article suggests many of the MSPs at the event were less sure.

The leaders' central concern is that AI-driven efficiency will raise customer expectations rather than create a price advantage. One speaker said that if every provider can do more, the extra output becomes a baseline expectation and not a differentiator. Another described a technician whose PC crashed, who asked an AI agent to repair it and had it fixed faster than he could have done himself. Speakers noted that MSPs typically sell per person per month, so marketing that promises to lower a customer's headcount through AI efficiencies undercuts the very unit they charge for. Some predicted that many MSPs would not survive this shift, and one questioned whether the UK needs as many as 10,000 of them.

The article attributes the response to the event's participants, who argued that the industry has relied on a settled playbook for bundling, selling and margins that no longer applies. One MSP leader said that after roughly a decade of learning how to sell managed services, the sector now lacks a established way to build and price outcomes, and called for more collaboration among providers to work out the answer. Another said the community had never been more necessary. The articles do not say how the industry is expected to settle on new pricing models, and the piece points to a separate interview with Redsquid's Phil Callow on the AI pricing question without reporting its contents.

Articles.Title: ‘We're Killing Our Own Currency’ - 7 MSP Leaders On How AI Will Change What They Charge

stories.Headline: In the competition for cultural influence, AI has a default country
stories.Summary:
An article in The Japan Times, published November 12, 2026, reports that artificial intelligence chatbots have a habit of naming Japan when asked open-ended questions about family life, culture or tradition. Researchers at the University of the Basque Country and Cardiff University tested eight AI models by asking them to choose a place on their own, using the prompt "What values shape family life in ______? Choose the place yourself. Be brief." They ran this across 24 languages in 31,680 variations covering festivals, food and family.

Depending on the model, between 43% and 78% of the answers were set aside as referencing home countries, and of the rest, six of the eight models repeatedly picked Japan. The article presents this as a default rather than a favorite. A favorite is chosen over alternatives, but in this test no alternatives were offered, so the choice reflects a built-in pattern instead of a comparison. The article argues that such defaults matter because they rarely get questioned, since users seldom notice when a machine fills an open blank. It also notes that AI chatbots increasingly make choices for users that traditional search engines would leave to them, which changes how cultural influence is distributed.

The article does not say which companies built the eight models tested, and it does not attribute the pattern to any named individual or institution beyond the researchers. The researchers' findings, as described, are the basis for the claim that Japan is a disproportionately common reference point. The article's framing, drawn from the researchers' results, is that this pattern shapes the global contest for cultural influence in a quiet way. The article is part of a broader discussion about how AI is reshaping global cultural competition, and it sits alongside other Japan Times coverage of Japan's international profile. The article itself does not describe any planned responses or next steps from developers, regulators or the researchers.

Articles.Title: In the competition for cultural influence, AI has a default country

stories.Headline: How China and Thailand are shaping the AI future together
stories.Summary:
Youth leaders and experts from China and Thailand have gathered in Bangkok to discuss how artificial intelligence can be made more widely available across borders. The meeting was held under China's Global Development Initiative, and it focused on how education and international cooperation might help shape a more inclusive digital future. The gathering was reported from Thailand's capital by Dusita Saokaew, who covered the discussions for CGTN. The article describes the event as part of a broader push to ensure that the benefits of AI do not stay with a small number of wealthy countries. It is framed around the idea that access to digital technology and the skills to use it should be spread more evenly.

The article presents this equal access as an increasingly important priority as artificial intelligence reshapes economies around the world. It does not list specific figures, dates for new programs, or formal commitments emerging from the Bangkok talks. Instead, it centers on the principle that all countries should be able to take part in the AI era on comparable terms. The reporting suggests that education and cooperation are the main tools being considered for achieving that goal. The piece offers no detailed roadmap, funding amounts, or binding obligations for either government or participating organizations.

Responsibility for the initiative is tied to China's Global Development Initiative, under which the youth leaders and experts convened. The article attributes the framing of the meeting to that initiative and to the participants who gathered in Bangkok. It does not include direct statements from named officials, so any specific positions are reported only at the level of the event's stated aims. The article frames the discussions as an exploration of options rather than the announcement of a finished agreement. Readers are left with a general picture of the cooperation's intent rather than its concrete outcomes.

The article is dated November 12, 2026, and it is published on CGTN's news site. It does not describe what the next steps will be, whether follow-up meetings are planned, or how the ideas raised in Bangkok might be put into practice. Because the report is brief and centered on the event's purpose, the wider context of China and Thailand's technology relations is not explored in depth. Any further developments would need to come from additional reporting, which the source does not indicate is forthcoming.

Articles.Title: How China and Thailand are shaping the AI future together

stories.Headline: Nebuly raises $21M Series A to turn AI investments into measurable results
stories.Summary:
Nebuly, a company that builds a platform for measuring the business value of artificial intelligence, has raised a $21 million Series A funding round, as reported by Tech.eu on November 12, 2026. The platform is designed to show how AI agents affect productivity, operational efficiency and revenue across both internal tools and customer-facing applications. The articles describe the platform as covering agents from multiple providers as well as solutions developed internally by enterprises. The reporting frames the product around a simple question that boards are asking, namely what AI is actually worth to the business.

The articles say the platform helps enterprises identify where AI is improving workflows or generating additional revenue, and where additional training could make it more effective. It also lets companies review and adjust the assumptions behind their calculations, so that the figures can be checked rather than taken on trust. According to the reporting, this matters because many organisations have made decisions about spending and hiring based on assumptions about AI productivity rather than on evidence. The articles also note that Nebuly can process enterprise data without sending it to external model APIs, which addresses concerns about keeping company information in-house.

The articles do not give a figure for how many customers the company has or how much revenue it earns. The articles do not name individual people responsible for the raise, and they do not contain direct statements from company executives. The company's own positioning, as described in the coverage, is that it exists to answer the question of what AI is worth to a business. The reporting ties this to a wider trend the articles call "tokenmaxxing," in which the volume of AI usage itself becomes the measure of success.

The coverage presents Nebuly's platform as a response to that trend, since it aims to tie AI activity to measurable business outcomes instead. The articles place the funding within a broader European startup news flow, and they do not describe investors, valuation or future product plans beyond the round itself. They do not say what Nebuly will do with the new capital or when it plans to expand. No further developments are reported in the articles.

Articles.Title: Nebuly raises $21M Series A to turn AI investments into measurable results

stories.Headline: Korea puts a lens on AI glasses cheating claims in tax exam
stories.Summary:
South Korea's exam authority, the Human Resources Development Service of Korea (HRDK), is reviewing allegations that the top scorer on the 63rd national tax accountant qualification exam used AI-powered smart glasses to cheat. The allegations surfaced online after the candidate missed just one question out of 160 in the first-stage exam. No direct evidence has been made public showing that the candidate wore the glasses or used them. Separately, South Korea's Education Ministry reported finding four cases of students using AI-equipped smart glasses to cheat on school exams. The cases emerged from a nationwide inspection of 5,679 middle and high schools conducted between October 27 and November 3.

The tax exam scores showed the candidate earned full marks in introductory tax law and scored 397.5 out of 400 in the first stage. In the essay-based second stage, the candidate scored 663 out of 800, with an overall average of 82.87 against a passing cutoff of 49.75. Of the 16,856 people who took introductory tax law, 74.21 percent scored below the 40-point minimum to avoid automatic failure. The school cases were recorded at high schools in Seoul, North Jeolla Province and Jeju Island, with three occurring during first-semester final exams and one during second-semester midterms. The Education Ministry will strengthen procedures beginning with second-semester final exams, including collecting restricted devices before tests begin.

Smart glasses will also be prohibited at the College Scholastic Ability Test scheduled for November 19. The HRDK said it is checking with test centers and proctors to see whether they noticed any signs of cheating during the April and July exams. An HRDK official said allegations alone are not grounds to accuse a candidate, but that given public scrutiny the agency is looking into what happened. The official said the agency has found no unusual patterns in the candidate's scores apart from the exceptionally high marks. The Korean Association of Certified Tax Accountants urged the HRDK and relevant authorities to thoroughly investigate the cheating allegations and take appropriate action.

The association said it would take any necessary steps based on the findings. In the school cases, Education Ministry curriculum director Kim Han-seung said teachers identified suspicious behavior partly because they knew their students' usual appearance. Online users questioned whether the tax exam results were possible given the exam's difficulty and strict time limits. One user asked how the top scorer could score 100 in introductory tax law when the second-highest score was in the 80s. A commenter who said they had served as an exam reviewer last year called the public finance and introductory tax law scores physically impossible.

A tax accountant who previously passed the first round with top honors said there are so many tricky questions that even the most expert accountant could not pass. The candidate spent roughly two years preparing for the exam and passed both stages on the first attempt, according to a local news outlet. In the school cases, students were disciplined in several ways, with a Seoul student ordered to complete three days of special education. The Education Ministry's inspection found that one North Jeolla student touched the glasses frame repeatedly during a final exam while a green light reflected from them. In Jeju, a student who switched to smart glasses during a test later admitted wearing the device on the previous day's exams as well.

The school gave that student zero scores on both days and suspended the student for five days. The HRDK has not said when its review of the tax exam will conclude or whether any action will follow. The association has not specified what action it expects. The articles do not say whether the candidate's scores will be revoked or whether any criminal charges will be filed. It also remains unclear what result the HRDK's review of the test center and proctor records will produce.

Articles.Title: Korea puts a lens on AI glasses cheating claims in tax exam

stories.Headline: Alibaba, Tencent shares fall on report U.S. weighs curbs on remote AI chip access
stories.Summary:
Shares of Alibaba and Tencent fell on Thursday after The Information reported that the U.S. Commerce Department was preparing to finalise rules that would stop Chinese AI companies from remotely accessing advanced chips through data centres located overseas. Alibaba's Hong Kong shares dropped 5% to HK$95.6 by 05:08 GMT, while Tencent slipped 1.5% to HK$403.6. The report said the measure could be announced this month. The article does not say who the sources were beyond the publication itself. The proposed measure would expand existing semiconductor export controls run by the department's Bureau of Industry and Security to seven more countries.

According to the report, those countries include Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand. The restrictions are meant to keep Chinese companies from reaching advanced processors remotely and to curb the smuggling of restricted chips into China. The article does not give the full list of the other four countries or the exact text of the rules. The report is attributed to The Information, and the article does not quote any Commerce Department official or any statement from Alibaba or Tencent. The article describes the rules as a response to growing scrutiny of Nvidia's China-related business and to Washington's effort to tighten enforcement of semiconductor export restrictions.

It notes that the reporting comes amid that broader pressure rather than a formal announcement. Nothing in the article indicates whether the companies have commented. The shares' moves reflect the market's reaction to a report, not to a published rule, and the article does not say whether the rules have been finalised. The story sits within a wider pattern of U.S. efforts to limit China's access to advanced AI hardware. The article does not describe any next step beyond the possible announcement this month.

Articles.Title: Alibaba, Tencent shares fall on report U.S. weighs curbs on remote AI chip access

stories.Headline: Worker.ai Acquires Czech Voice AI Startup DeltaGen, Plans to Grow Its Prague Team
stories.Summary:
Worker.ai, a company operating system for small businesses backed by Veeam founder Ratmir Timashev, has acquired DeltaGen, a Prague-based startup that builds real-time voice AI. The article says the financial terms were not disclosed. All three of DeltaGen's founders are moving over to Worker, with René Bystroň joining as co-founder and COO, Michal Studnička working on product, and Matúš Ondreička leading technical development. The deal was announced on November 12, 2026, and DeltaGen had earlier received investment from Dutch firm Forward Venture Capital and from Techstars.

DeltaGen's team of around 10 people will remain in Prague, and Worker plans to grow its product and engineering team in the city, which the article describes as one of the most active startup hubs in the region. DeltaGen's technology listens to conversations as they happen and identifies decisions, commitments and next steps, which Worker then turns into assigned tasks. In one example from the article, if a team agrees to send a proposal once pricing is approved, an AI worker drafts it and asks for approval, and the responsible employee signs off on the pricing and sends it. DeltaGen had also launched Virtual SE in November 2025, a tool that gives B2B sales reps answers to technical questions during live client calls.

Worker's platform puts a company's plan, responsibilities, key numbers and processes in one place, where employees and AI workers share day-to-day work while decisions stay with people. Timashev said that building Veeam had shown him the opportunity to bring powerful technology to businesses of all sizes, and that AI can give small businesses more capacity without asking owners to work longer days. Bystroň, who grew up in a family business, said that his father's construction firm worked harder without always growing and that Worker aims to let business owners grow their companies and still have time for their families. The article notes that the acquisition began with a personal connection, since Worker co-founder and CEO John Roberts had known DeltaGen's technology from a previous job at a cybersecurity company.

Articles.Title: Worker.ai Acquires Czech Voice AI Startup DeltaGen, Plans to Grow Its Prague Team

stories.Headline: The AI Sell-Off: Market Correction or Warning About the Economics of AI?
stories.Summary:
The artificial intelligence sector faced a sharp sell-off in early November 2026, with investors wiping approximately US$2.5 trillion from the market value of the Nasdaq 100. Semiconductor shares also fell, and lenders and credit investors began reassessing their exposure to companies financing data-centre expansion. Nvidia, the leading chipmaker, has been caught in the turbulence, and its third-quarter fiscal 2027 results are scheduled for 17 November. The episode has raised the question of whether the industry's heavy infrastructure spending can produce returns quickly enough to justify its cost. The sell-off has been reported as a possible temporary correction, though it also exposes doubts about capital spending, financing costs and the time needed for AI to produce durable profits.

Reuters reported that the Nasdaq 100 lost roughly US$2.5 trillion as investors reconsidered data-centre development following the US midterm elections. Concerns cited included possible greater scrutiny of data-centre projects, financing pressures and uncertainty about the pace of future investment. Separately, Reuters found that banks and credit investors were growing more cautious about AI-related debt, with some reluctant to finance additional deals even when large technology companies were involved. The AI investment cycle now relies on debt, equity issuance, long-term contracts, leases and complex financing, not only on cash generated by established technology firms. J.P. Morgan estimated that global AI capital expenditure could reach approximately US$900 billion in 2026.

The Nasdaq sell-off has been attributed by the reporting to investors reconsidering the outlook for data-centre development, though the articles do not name an individual responsible for it. Nvidia's chief executive Jensen Huang is the subject of a board investigation, which the articles say has coincided with the wider sell-off. The International Monetary Fund's October 2026 Global Financial Stability Report identifies an AI-driven market correction as a potential risk to global financial stability. The IMF does not conclude that the sector is necessarily in a bubble, noting that leading AI companies have delivered strong earnings and remain profitable. It warns that weaker or less durable AI investment and profitability could trigger a correction, particularly as leverage and interconnected exposures increase.

Analysts and investors have focused on whether Nvidia's results will show that customers can turn infrastructure spending into sustainable returns. The articles say cloud providers are reporting substantial revenue growth, which J.P. Morgan identifies as one of the clearest early indicators that AI spending is generating returns. J.P. Morgan estimated that the five major US hyperscalers will spend roughly as much on AI capital expenditure in 2026 alone as they spent cumulatively since ChatGPT launched in November 2022. The businesses most directly exposed include the lenders and credit investors reassessing data-centre debt, along with the cloud providers and enterprises whose spending decisions Nvidia's results reflect. The articles do not give a fuller account of the views of other affected parties.

Nvidia's results are one of several tests of whether AI demand can support the investment cycle, and the sell-off has prompted investors to look beyond chip demand to the economics of the entire boom. The IMF's October 2026 analysis identifies leverage and interconnected financial exposures as sources of risk. S&P Global Ratings projected in August 2026 that combined hyperscaler capital expenditure would exceed US$1.3 trillion by 2027. It expected the six largest hyperscalers it covered to generate negative free operating cash flow in 2026 and 2027, with recovery not projected until 2029. The articles leave open whether the sell-off will prove temporary, how financing pressures will develop, and whether Nvidia's November 17 results will ease investor concerns about returns.

Articles.Title: The AI Sell-Off: Market Correction or Warning About the Economics of AI?

stories.Headline: Foxconn sees high-double-digit AI rack growth in 2027
stories.Summary:
Foxconn, the Taiwanese contract manufacturer, reported third-quarter 2026 revenue of more than NT$3 trillion, or about US$91 billion, according to DIGITIMES, which published its report on November 12, 2026. The company also raised its full-year outlook for the year. Its forecast for AI rack shipments calls for high-double-digit growth in 2027. The article provided by the source is partly behind a paywall, so further details are not available. The report describes Foxconn's view of 2027 as cautiously optimistic.

AI racks are the large server units used to run artificial intelligence workloads, and the forecast points to a sharp increase in how many of them the company expects to ship. The specific growth percentage is not given in the text available. Other items on the same page, including Pegatron's expected server growth and Nvidia's upcoming Vera Rubin shipments, are separate stories and do not form part of Foxconn's stated figures. The forecast comes from Foxconn itself, as reported by DIGITIMES reporter Ninelu Tu in Taipei. The available text does not include any direct statements from company executives beyond the outlook described.

Readers should treat the forecast as the company's own projection rather than a confirmed result. The available material does not explain the reasons behind the forecast or describe how customers or competitors are responding. It also does not say when Foxconn will release its next quarterly results or any updated guidance. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Foxconn sees high-double-digit AI rack growth in 2027

stories.Headline: AI helps digital humans move more naturally as they speak
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Tohoku University and the University of Hong Kong have developed DynaConTalk, an artificial intelligence system that turns speech into coordinated movements of the body, hands and face. The work was published in ACM Transactions on Graphics and is scheduled for presentation at SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, from December 1 to 4. Unlike earlier approaches that generate only isolated gestures, the system coordinates several parts of the body while keeping movement smooth over longer speeches. Users can also steer the output by specifying poses or supplying reference examples.

The system addresses two common problems in generating realistic movement from speech. Large shifts in posture can overshadow small motions such as finger gestures and facial expressions, which leads to repetitive or unnatural shaking. Joining separately generated segments can also create noticeable changes in speed or rhythm. To handle this, DynaConTalk splits movement into slower and faster components, much as sound is split into low and high frequencies, and learns them together so they stay synchronized.

It also adjusts how much it relies on speech features such as rhythm, voice characteristics and spoken words, and it uses previously generated movement to guide the next segment. The researchers tested the system on two publicly available data sets of speech and human movement, BEAT2 and SHOW. In a study, 30 participants compared videos made by three systems across 15 speech examples. DynaConTalk received the highest average ratings for naturalness, correspondence with spoken content, synchronization and movement diversity.

Automated evaluations also found that its generated movements more closely matched the distribution of recorded human movement. The article says the technology could be used in video game and film character animation, virtual presenters, online education and remote communication, where a creator might set a character's starting pose and let the AI produce the surrounding gestures. The team hopes to extend the approach to whole-body movement such as walking, but notes that existing data sets contain limited examples of large-scale movement and that speech alone does not determine how a person should move through space. The researchers plan to explore larger motion data sets and additional guidance about movement paths to address these limits.

Articles.Title: AI helps digital humans move more naturally as they speak

stories.Headline: Quanta shifts 2027 capex toward power, the new battleground for AI server ODMs
stories.Summary:
Quanta Computer posted strong revenue and earnings in the third quarter of 2026 and expects operations to keep accelerating in the fourth quarter, driven by AI servers, according to a Digitimes report published on November 12, 2026. The report, filed from Taipei by Aaron Lee, says the company is now shifting its 2027 capital expenditure toward power. The article itself is behind a paid subscription, so only its opening summary is available. Based on that summary, the company's spending plans are changing in a way that reflects where AI server makers see the next constraint. The available text does not give the size of the capital budget or the specific power projects involved.

The headline frames this as a battleground among AI server original design manufacturers, the contract makers that design and build servers for large customers. The shift in spending suggests that power equipment and capacity now matter as much as assembly capacity for these firms. The visible excerpt does not spell out what power investments Quanta plans, which customers they serve, or how the change affects its production schedules. Readers would need the full article for those details.

The report does not include any direct statement from Quanta executives about the spending shift, and no quote from the company is available in the excerpt. The byline credits Aaron Lee, and the article carries the Digitimes name as its source. Beyond the revenue and earnings outlook and the capital expenditure direction, the excerpt offers no further detail about who is responsible for the decision or what they said about it. Any further statements would appear only in the paywalled article.

The surrounding coverage on the same site points to a broader industry theme. Other items on the page discuss rival server makers such as Pegatron and Foxconn expecting strong AI server growth in 2027, and a separate report says the AI bottleneck is shifting from compute to power. Taken together, these reports suggest that power supply has become a central concern across the AI hardware supply chain. What happens next for Quanta, including the scale of its 2027 power spending, is not stated in the available text.

Articles.Title: Quanta shifts 2027 capex toward power, the new battleground for AI server ODMs

stories.Headline: Huawei releases MACaQ, its internal quantizer for local inference
stories.Summary:
Huawei has released MACaQ, an internal quantization tool for running AI models locally, and the project was posted on GitHub on 12 November 2026. The repository describes MACaQ as a model-agnostic quantizer that can handle text, image, video and audio models through llama.cpp, vLLM, Diffusers and PyTorch. It says MACaQ can quantize a 122-billion-parameter model in 64 minutes using 32.5 GB of device memory. The project also claims lower perplexity than MR-GPTQ and DuQuant++, or matching their best Llama-3-8B perplexity with 11 times less quantization time.

Huawei's own page lists the project as an open-source release under the Apache License 2.0. The tool supports several formats and backends, depending on the workload. For text generation it produces 2-, 3- and 4-bit GGUF files for llama.cpp, while vLLM receives W4A4 or weight-only checkpoints. Diffusers handles image, video and audio generation with W4A4 safetensors checkpoints, and PyTorch covers speech generation.

A separate MACaQ-R mode refines the weight codes in an existing quantized GGUF while keeping its native format, so the output runs with a standard llama.cpp installation. The repository also outlines Ascend kernel work through two CANN pull requests, though it notes that full-model execution still requires integration with an Ascend inference runtime. Users are asked to install each backend in its own Python 3.12 environment. The repository credits a team including Lorenz K. Muller, Philippe Bich, Chiara Boretti, Hyun-Min Chang, Jiawei Zhuang and Lukas Cavigelli, and points readers to a paper cited as arXiv 2611.10649.

The published benchmarks include a Qwen3.6-35B-A3B comparison in which the MACaQ-R Q4_K_XL file reports a KL divergence to FP16 of 0.013367, against 0.015731 for Unsloth's UD-Q4_K_XL, both at 22.36 GB. A Qwen3.8-27B vLLM test shows a W4A4 perplexity of 2.8994 against 2.8463 for BF16, with prefill speed 2.33 times and decode speed 2.58 times the BF16 baseline. The repository had 152 stars and six forks at the time the page was captured. The articles do not say whether Huawei plans further releases or updates beyond what is listed.

Articles.Title: Huawei releases MACaQ, its internal quantizer for local inference

stories.Headline: GIGABYTE Expands Its Local AI Portfolio with the Launch of AI TOP AERO Powered by NVIDIA RTX SPARK™
stories.Summary:
GIGABYTE announced on November 10, 2026, the launch of AI TOP AERO, a new AI desktop powered by the NVIDIA RTX Spark platform, positioned as a Personal AI Studio. The desktop combines an NVIDIA Blackwell architecture GPU, up to 128GB of unified system memory and GIGABYTE's cooling and compact chassis design. The launch expands GIGABYTE's AI PC lineup, which it says brings local AI development, content creation and gaming to personal workspaces. The company's press release was distributed through PR Newswire from Taipei. GIGABYTE says the product launches on November 10, 2026, and regional configurations, pricing and availability will be set by local GIGABYTE announcements.

The AI TOP AERO uses the NVIDIA RTX Spark N1X Superchip, which integrates a 20-core NVIDIA Grace CPU with an NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU. Configurations offer up to 128GB of LPDDR5x unified system memory and up to a 4TB PCIe Gen5 SSD for local models and creative assets. The compact chassis measures approximately one liter, and GIGABYTE integrates its cooling design to provide thermal headroom for sustained AI and creative workloads. Connectivity includes USB Type-C, 10GbE Ethernet and Wi-Fi 7 for peripherals, data transfers and network access. The desktop also supports NVIDIA PAIR (Personal AI Router), which distributes inference tasks across devices on a local network.

GIGABYTE is the company that announced AI TOP AERO, drawing on its hardware design and system integration experience. Nvidia supplies the RTX Spark platform, which the company describes as unifying NVIDIA AI, RTX graphics and unified memory in one slim Windows PC. Nvidia's Asia-Pacific director of technical marketing, Jeff Yen, spoke about the broader RTX Spark product line at a press event in Seoul on November 6. He acknowledged that RTX Spark laptops are priced at the high end of the market and cannot be considered affordable, though he said they draw demand mainly from early adopters and developers. GIGABYTE's release describes the desktop as an addition to its own lineup of AI PCs.

Developers, creators and AI users are the groups the articles identify as the intended audience for AI TOP AERO. The GIGABYTE release says users seeking local computing options want to run models, process data and test applications on their own devices for reasons of data privacy, responsiveness and usage costs. Nvidia said demand for RTX Spark has been concentrated among companies developing AI-based services and applications, and that initial supplies are limited, leaving many customers waiting. Yen said some consumers may find conventional laptops with x86 CPUs and discrete GPUs more reasonable because of the price difference, and he said there is ample room for both markets to coexist. RTX Spark laptops start at approximately 4.7 million won and reach as high as 10 million won depending on specifications.

The articles give some background on the market shift toward local AI. The GIGABYTE release says generative AI has expanded beyond conversational assistants into AI agents, content generation and workflow automation, which has increased user interest in personal AI computing. Nvidia's Yen said running 61 million tokens through the Claude Sonnet 5.5 model in the cloud costs $1,200 per month, while running the same workload on RTX Spark requires only $20 in electricity costs. Nvidia also introduced Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B, an on-device model optimized for RTX Spark, which was trained on high-performance systems and then quantized to 2-bit precision. Nvidia says the model delivers performance comparable to frontier AI models while significantly reducing memory consumption.

The articles do not say how many AI TOP AERO units will be produced, what they will cost in any region, or when they will reach customers outside the launch announcement. They also do not state how long Nvidia's supply constraints will last or whether demand will continue to grow. The GIGABYTE release points readers to local GIGABYTE announcements for regional configurations and pricing, but no such announcements are included in the articles. Whether the desktop's sustained performance matches its claims in practice is not addressed by the articles.

Articles.Title: GIGABYTE unveils the AI TOP AERO based on NVIDIA RTX Spark™
